scoring out the well-towered city named Dardania,
marking the Idaean dust with a ploughman's track;
and drinking the stream of Heptaporus and the floods of Rhesus
he left the heritage to his brother to hold, and the sceptre of the Cabeiri.
Dardanus, brother of Emathion, whom the bed of Zeus
begot, whom Justice the nurse cherished, when, taking
the sceptre of Zeus and the robes of Time and the wand of Olympus,
the Hours ran to the house of royal Electra,
prophets of the unbreakable sovereignty of the Ausonians;
and they reared the infant, and by the unswerving voice of Zeus
the boy, springing up like the flower of ever-renewing youth,
left the house of Electra, when the flood of the third rain
towered with waves overwhelmed the seats of the universe.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
For Ogyges first made trial of the sounding flood,
cleaving the air through the towering water,
when all the earth was hidden, flooded over, and the tip of the Thessalian
rock was covered, and on high the Pythian peak,
the cloud-near rock, surged with the snowy flood.
The second rain was when over the rim of the circling earth
the snow-laden water hid it with a raging stream,
when Deucalion alone, fellow-voyager with his agemate Pyrrha,
amid the perishing mortals, in a hollow ark cutting
the back-whirling flood of the unmeasured downpour
of the watery air, was ferried, a whirling sailor.
And the third rain of Zeus was when it washed the seat of the earth
and hid the cliffs, and even the unwetted back
of the Sithonian hill of Athos itself was covered,
when, cleaving the flood of the high-faring downpour,
Dardanus set foot on the ancient neighbouring Ida.
His brother then, lord of the snowy Sithonian land,
Emathion, leaving the heavy-sounding assembly,
marvelled at the man's form, since his inborn youth
mingled manliness and beauty in a matched shape,
he marvelled at so great a form; for of distinguished lords
the looks are themselves voiceless heralds, speaking unbidden.
And taking him in he gave him hospitality, and with weary Electra
he adorned the varied dinners of the rich table,
welcoming the stranger with friendly and blameless words,
setting much before him. But he, bowing his bent neck to the floor,
apart from the attendants, drew his eyes uncharmed,
and scarcely feasted; and as the hospitable bride
sat facing him, with a stealing glance from his face
he stretched in shame his chaste hand to the table.
And as they feasted, in close succession one after another
the breathing reed of Corybantian Ida crashed out;
and from the much-pierced passage, with the leaping of hands,
the dancing fingers, pressing the song,
beat out the concordant tune of the bellowing pipe;
and the booming cymbals, clashing with rolling shakes,
sounded a concordant echo with their double bronze
joined to the reeds; and beneath the plectrum the very
upright string of the seven-toned lyre quivered.
But when after the feast he had had his fill of the Bistonian pipe,
drawing near to the inquiring queen, who loves to ask,
Cadmus, setting aside the frenzy of his sea-wandering care,
told of his bright lineage, and a stream of ever-flowing words
he poured from his opening throat like a fountain:
"Dear lady, why do you ask me so much of the blood of my race?
I liken the race of swift-fated mortals to leaves;
the leaves that the frenzied breezes pour down on the earth
when the autumn season comes, and others in the springtime
season the wooded trees foster, in fresh bloom;
so the short-lived race of men: one is subdued
by destruction, having run its course of life, while another still flourishes,
that it may yield to another in turn; for, creeping back again,
the age of man flows from grey to new, taking shape afresh.
But I will tell of my far-famed, fair-childed race.
There is a city, glorious Argos, the equestrian seat of Hera,
the navel of the island of Tantalus; there a man
sowed a fair maiden with female-bearing seed,
Inachus, the famed citizen of the Inachian land,
a temple-keeper, who plotted the dreadful rites
of the city-guarding goddess with prophetic, mystic art,
an elder; and Zeus, the chief of the gods, the leader of the stars,
he refused to have as a son-in-law, keeping reverence for Hera, . . .
when, bull-formed, the heifer Io, her face changed,
was driven into the field-herd, a fellow-grazer,
and Hera set over the heifer a sleepless herdsman,
many-eyed Argus, adorned with unwandering eyes,
the watcher of Zeus' cow-horned wedding,
of unseen Zeus, and the girl went into the pasture
trembling at the eyes of the many-pupilled herdsman;
and Io, her body scored by the limb-devouring gadfly,
scored the swell of the Ionian sea with roving hoof;
she came even to Egypt, of my stream—which the citizens
called the Nile by a fitting name, because to the land
year after year, borne along, the watery bedfellow
with muddy flood throws around it new silt—
she came to Egypt, where after her cow shape,
changing the image of her divine horn,
she became the fruit-bearing goddess; and as the fruit is kindled
of Egyptian Demeter, of my horn-drawn Io,
the vapour rises, fellow-traveller with the fragrant breezes.
There she bore Epaphus to Zeus, since of her unsullied bosom,
of the Inachian heifer, the divine bedfellow had touch
with love-maddened hands; and from a god-begotten father,
from Epaphus, came Libya; and journeying to Libya's bridal chamber
even to Memphis came Poseidon as a wanderer,
tracking the maiden daughter of Epaphus, and then the girl,
receiving the dweller of the deep as a landward traveller,
bore Libyan Zeus, Belus, the ploughman of my race.
And the new oracle of Asbystian Zeus, an answering voice,
the thirsty prophetic sands proclaim to the Chaonian dove;
and as a father, equal in number to five,
Belus sowed a succession of children,
Phineus and Phoenix who left his city, with whom flourishing together
the citizen of cities exchanged in turn, the roaming Agenor
of unsettled life, my father, held his course
to Thebes after Memphis, to Assyria after Thebes;
and wise Aegyptus, the dweller of the Egyptian land,
of grievous birth, many-childed, who with male-born offspring
sowed the short-lived flocks of so many children,
and Danaus who left his fatherland, who armed against the male race
the female kind, stretching the wedding sword, when the bridal chambers
were reddened with the blood of slaughtered weddings,
and with hidden swords upon the iron-bearing beds
female Enyo lulled to sleep naked male Ares;
yet to Hypermnestra the evil-bridal slaughter was not pleasing,
but thrusting aside the grim-kindred ordinances of her father
she entrusted her father's word to the airy gust,
and kept her hand pure and bloodless of the iron;
and the marriage of both was holy. And my newly-blooming
sister the bold roving bull carried off,
if truly it was a bull; for I do not know how to believe
that bulls long for women's weddings.
And Agenor sent me, fellow-traveller with my brothers,
to track our sister and the wild ravisher of the bride,
the bull, the false sailor of the waveless sea,
for whose sake I come here, an unsteady wanderer."

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Such things within the well-piped hall
Cadmus told, pouring forth speech from his eloquent throat,
telling of the child-saving frenzy of his father's threat
and the false-sailing bull-traveller of the Tyrian surge,
the unattainable, unknown ravisher of the Sidonian bride.
And Electra, hearing, cried out a comforting voice:
"Stranger, your sister and your fatherland and your father
give over to the whirl of Lethe and to forgetful silence;
for thus the life of mortals is borne, holding toil
on toil, since all, as many as a mortal womb has borne,
are enslaved to the compulsion of the Fates' spinning thread;
I am a witness, queen though I am, if ever of those
Pleiades I too was born one, whose mother once
brought to birth the female pangs within her bosom,
calling seven times upon Eileithyia at her childbed
to lighten the sting of repeated birth—
I am a witness; for far from my parents I dwell,
having neither Sterope nor Maia my fellow,
nor my sister Celaeno near as a hearth-mate; nor in my bosom
of my sister Taygeta have I held Lacedaemon with a double leap,
embracing the joyful boy with child-nursing arm;
nor near do I see the house of Alcyone, nor of Merope herself,
do I hear her speaking the mind-delighting word.
And besides, this I lament still more: for newly-blooming
my son who left his fatherland, when he had the down of first beard,
Dardanus, migrated to the bosom of the Idaean land,
and to Phrygian Simoeis gave the first-fruits of his hair,
drinking the alien water of the Thymbraean river;
and at the boundary of Libya my father still labours
with pressed shoulders, old Atlas bent over,
heaving up the seven-zoned hollow of the air.
Yet, having suffered so much, I feed a comforting hope
on the promises of Zeus, that with my other sisters
from the earth I shall come to the Atlantean pole of stars,
having heaven as my house, and shall be the seventh star.
And you too, soften your cares; for unforeseen,
rolling upon you the whirl of life-wandering fortune,
the dreadful thread of unmoving Fate has sealed it;
endure to bear, as one who left his fatherland, the unbending bond of compulsion,
feeding a higher hope as the herald of things to come,
if first-sown Io rooted your race,
if you have got from Libya the Poseidonian blood of your line;
remain among strangers, like Dardanus, dwelling in a house,
inhabiting a foreign city, as your father Agenor,
as Danaus your father's brother; for he too,
another man bearing his house, having the god-inspired race of Io,
a heavenly Zeus-fallen shoot, by name Byzas,
drinking the seven-mouthed water of the self-born Nile,
allotted a neighbouring land, where beside the Bosporus shore
the water crossed by the Inachian heifer is drawn,
giving light to all the dwellers around, when of that
unbending, maddened bull he bent the neck aslant."
She spoke, lulling to rest the cares of the son of Agenor.
And father Zeus sent the long-winged son of Maia
to the house of Electra, a swift messenger, that to Cadmus
he might give Harmonia for the harmony of wedlock,
a maiden migrant from heaven, whom for Aphrodite
in secret love the marriage-thieving Ares begot;
and the mother, ashamed of the babe, the self-announcer of her hidden bed,
did not rear her, but from her heavenly bosom
the nursling girl, reclining on her arm at the breast,
she brought to the house of Electra, fit for nursing, whose own child
the childbed Hours had brought to wet birth, whose dense breasts
still welled with swelling white moisture;
and receiving the bastard daughter by an equal law
the contemporary of Emathion she joined to one breast,
the newly-born girl, and with kindred-loving purpose
she lightened the double offspring with a nursing arm.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
As some wild, twin-bearing lioness within the thicket,
shaggy, with milky dews
fitted her twin breasts to both cubs
and gave the divided teat to the twin young,
and licking their flesh and their still-hairless neck
reared the agemate brood with equal care:
so then with child-nursing loving teat she gave suck,
tending the yoked pair of newly-born children;
often she embraced the infant son, fellow with the agemate girl,
turning him here and there to the moisture of her rich breast,
with the loving hollow of her outstretched hand;
and on her knees she set the male child beside the female girl,
spreading her gaping thigh beside the neighbouring thigh,
widening the bosom of her deepening tunic;
and crying a sleep-charming melody to her children
she lulled both to sleep with nursing art,
spreading her arm to support the neck of the children,
and made her knee their bed, and over the two
she turned the edge of her robe, fanning their faces,
cooling the children, and quenched the rush of the heat
by pouring an answering blast, a made breeze.
While Cadmus sat near the prudent queen,
meanwhile, escaping the gatekeeper with his thieving foot,
unforeseen and unattainable, Hermes went into the house,
like a youth; and about his rosy face
the trailing track of his uncovered hair hung loose,
spreading wide, and crowning the edges of his new-haired cheek
the slender circle of his growing first-beard reddened,
freshly grown, running round on either side; and like a herald
he lifted his accustomed wand; and with face unseen,
adorned with clouds from head to the tips of his feet,
he came upon the finished dinners of the rich table;
nor did Emathion see him near, nor did
Harmonia herself, nor Cadmus the hearth-mate, nor the chorus of servant
men; but to god-fearing Electra alone appeared
Hermes of varied speech; and taking her into the recess of the house,
unforeseen he conversed and spoke with human voice:
"Mother's sister, bedfellow of Zeus, hail, of women
all the most blessed hereafter, since the son of Cronos
keeps the sovereignty of the universe for your children,
and all the cities of the earth your offspring will govern,
the bride-gifts of your love, and with my mother Maia
you may flash among the seven-pathed stars upon Olympus,
fellow-runner with the Sun, rising together with the Moon.
I am of your race, child-loving one, kindred Hermes,
the long-winged messenger of the immortals, and from heaven
your hospitable, high-ruling consort sent me
concerning your god-fearing guest; but you yourself
obey your son of Cronos, and your daughter Harmonia
send to go dowerless, fellow-voyager with her agemate Cadmus,
and do a favour to Zeus and the blessed; for the worn-out
immortals this stranger saved them all by singing;
this man came to the aid of your labouring consort,
this man spread a free day over Olympus.
Let not your daughter charm you with mother-loving lament;
but give her in marriage to the evil-averting Cadmus,
obeying the son of Cronos and Ares and Cytherea."
4. Tracking your fourth course over the sea, you shall behold
Harmonia sailing as companion to Cadmus, her equal in years.
So speaking, Hermes of the fair wand departed for Olympus,
fluttering his light wings, and as his sandals stretched out
his ankle was rowed onward in company with the breezes of the air.
Nor did the Thracian woman, steerswoman of the Cabeiri, . . .
but reverence for Zeus held her, and to the unwedded girl, daughter of Ares,
spinning her wise fingers upright with a thoughtful gesture,
she called Harmonia by the cunning mark of speech;
and the girl, straining toward the gleam that met her eyes,
gazed on the unsmiling round of Electra's face,
and the deep, new-welling weight of an unspoken grief
her silent cheeks proclaimed as by an oracle.
The maiden sprang up and went with the woman who had reared her
into the high-built house; and her mother, drawing open
the much-prized bolt of the seven-chambered bridal room,
crossed the stone threshold; and with affectionate intent
the trembling bride's knees were shaken unsteadily,
and she lifted up the rose-arm hand of her own child,
gripping it with her snow-white palm; and you might almost say
you saw white-armed Hera holding the hand of Hebe.
But when, treading the floor with her purple sandals,
she passed within the last glittering circuits of the hall,
the Atlantid nymph seated the grieving maiden
upon a well-wrought throne; and she in turn herself,
sitting in order on a silver-gleaming chair,
told to the unwilling girl the message of the son of Cronos,
and taught her all that, in the likeness of a mortal form,
the Olympian herald, the youth of changed appearance, had declared.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
But the maiden, hearing of a much-wandering marriage,
and of a husband without footing, a houseless wanderer beneath a borrowed roof,
refused to take a stranger, and all that, from Zeus her father,
Hermes the host of Cadmus, the driver of oxen, had told;
and she wished rather for a husband of her own city, that she might escape
a wedding that bears no bride-gifts, a yoke without dowry;
and gripping with her hand the dejected hand of her nurse,
drenched with tears she broke into a voice of much reproach:
“Mother of mine, what has come over you to deny your own child?
Is it thus you join your daughter to a newly-arrived man?
What gift will the seafarer ever place in my hand?
Will he grant me, as bride-gifts, the stern-cables of his ship?
I did not know, you who love your child, that you were keeping your daughter,
a maiden bereft of fatherland, for a wandering marriage.
Other suitors I have, better men, citizens of my own;
what need was there to take some naked husband without gifts,
a foreigner roaming about, a fugitive from his own father?
But you will say, he came to the aid of your bedmate the son of Cronos;
how then did he not receive a privilege of Zeus upon Olympus, if indeed,
as you tell me, he fought at the front of Olympus, and Hera, Zeus's consort,
did not join the maiden Hebe to the helper of Zeus?
Your husband, Zeus who rules on high, has no need of Cadmus;
may the son of Cronos be gracious—the marvellous Hermes lied
about Zeus the father; but I do not know how to believe
that Zeus left furious Ares, the steersman of the battle-din,
and called a mortal man to be his fellow-contestant in the struggle,
he who rules the cosmos and the upper air. Ah, great wonder,
he shut up so many Titans in the pit,
and yet had need of Cadmus, to destroy one single foe.
You know the twin and kindred marriage-beds of my forefathers:
Zeus my ancestor held the bed of his sister Hera,
keeping the law of a kindred wedding-chamber; and both,
Ares and Cytherea, mounting one single bed,
the parents of Harmonia, are born of one same father,
sharing a kindred couch—alas for necessity—
sisters keep their brothers, while I keep a fatherless husband.”
As she spoke thus her mother wiped away the shower
from her mourning eyes, in distress; and torn in her resolve
she pitied Harmonia, yet shrank from the threat of Zeus.
But, girding her body with the heart-charming girdle,
the cunning life-zone, crafty Aphrodite,
and clothing her flesh in the loving robes of Persuasion,
entered the sweet-scented maiden-bower of Harmonia;
and changing the cast of her heavenly countenance,
she likened her form to Peisinoe, the neighbour-girl,
as though she too longed for Cadmus, and as if with some secret sickness
sending a faint gleam over her pale-green face
she sped away the handmaids; and sitting beside her alone,
as if from modesty, she heaved up a deceitful voice:
“Blessed are you, what a handsome wanderer you have in your house,
what a suitor you have, most happy one—what a husband
you shall behold, full of charm, such as no other maiden has won;
truly he brings the blood of his Assyrian fatherland,
where flows the stream of lovely Adonis; for full of charm
is this youth from Lebanon, where Cytherea dances.
I was wrong—surely no earthly womb bore Cadmus,
but he holds the lineage of Zeus, and belied his true stock.
I know whence this youth is, an Olympian; if ever upon Maia
the Titan Atlas begot her sister Electra,
then to Harmonia has come a husband, her wingless cousin Hermes,
and not in vain is Cadmilus sung; for only his heavenly
shape did he change, and still he is heard called Cadmus.
But if he is some other god holding a mortal-seeming form,
perhaps Emathion welcomed Phoebus in his hall.
Maiden, the care of all, you are more blessed than your mother
in your longing, in your Olympian marriage—ah, great wonder,
in secret crafty Zeus wedded Electra,
while openly Apollo himself courts Harmonia;
blessed she, whom the far-shooter desired; would that of Peisinoe
herself too Apollo would hasten to make a marriage.
For I would never refuse Phoebus, as Daphne did,
nor will I imitate the mind of Harmonia; but leaving
my portion and my house and the parents whom I love,
I would go with Apollo as fellow-traveller to the wedding.
I remember once such a form; for once,
following my father into our oracular house,
I saw the Pythian image, and as I saw your wanderer,
I fancied I beheld again the statue of Phoebus here.
But you will say that Phoebus wears a gold-gleaming headband;
Cadmus is golden in all his body; and if you should wish,
take all my slaves beyond number, and in his place
I will hand over to you all my gold and my silver,
and I will give you royal robes of the Tyrian sea,
and a house, if you wish, an ancestral one; if it is right to say it,
take my father too and my mother, take all
my handmaids, and only grant me this man for a husband.
Maiden, why do you tremble? You in spring shall sail the sea,
voyaging the narrow water, while with lovely Cadmus
I will cross the boundless ocean through the storm.
Do not fear the deep-roaring swell of the brine, for Aphrodite,
daughter of the sea, will save in the sea her cargo of Love.
Maiden, you have Cadmus—do not seek a seat on Olympus.
I have no longing for the glittering Erythraean stone of the Indians,
nor for the all-golden tree of the Hesperides, nor does the amber
of the Heliads delight me, so much as one mist of the night
in which this wanderer shall embrace Peisinoe.
And if you trace your lineage from Ares, from Aphrodite,
your mother, the dispenser of marriages, has found you a marriage worthy of marriage.
Never have I beheld so great a flower; for of her own accord
Nature gave to Cadmus a springtime gift;
I saw the rose-fingered hand, I saw the face
dripping sweet honey; and of his love-begetting countenance
his cheeks blush like roses, and bright at their tips,
two-coloured, the prints of his snow-white feet gleam,
crimson in the middle, and his palms are like the lily.
I will leave aside his tresses, lest I provoke Phoebus
by reproaching with their hue the hyacinth of Therapnae.
If ever, wheeling the mind-delighting circle of his eyes,
he flashed his glances, all Selene shone
with sparkling radiance, and if ever, shaking his curls,
he laid bare his neck, the Morning Star appeared.
Of his lips I would keep silence; but his mouth, the channel of the Loves,
where Persuasion dwells, pours forth a honey-sweet voice,
and the Graces tend his whole body; the tips of his hands
I am ashamed to judge, lest I put white milk to shame.
Take me, wretched, to share your hearth; and touching
the right hand of the young man and caressing his tunic,
may I find soothing remedies for a hidden sickness;
may I see his bare neck, and as he sits press
his finger as if against my will, and through my own bosom
may I die, only when, relaxing his unsparing hand,
he should press the free circle of both my breasts,
fixing his shut lips upon my own shut lips,
delighting me with the lightest of kisses; and the young man
still embracing I would pass even to Acheron
of my own accord, and sweetly beside much-weeping Lethe
I will tell even to the dead my fate, that I may rouse
both pity and envy in heart-charming Persephone;
and I will teach those Grace-breathing kisses
to the ill-loving women, all whom the lovely fire has slain,
and I will make the dead jealous, if even beside Lethe,
toward the Paphian after death, women still feel envy.
I will follow, if you wish, as your companion, and I do not tremble
at untaught wandering. Pitiless one, become the wedded
wife of Cadmus; let me be the chamber-tender,
a servant to you both, to Harmonia and her husband.
But again I tremble for you, even if you mean to hide it,
lest through your marriage-bed I rouse anger and jealousy,
since Hera, though a goddess and ruler of the upper air,
grudges Zeus his mortal bastard wives;
she was angry at Europa and harassed restless Io;
nor did she leave the goddesses alone—when their mother was angered
Ares drove away Leto in her labour, heavy with child.
If jealousy does not hold you, that I may find a remedy for my desires,
grant me this man for a single dawn,
yes, I beg you, for one course of a single night; but if you grudge it,
slay me with your own hand, that I may know respite
from a fire so unappeasable, that for ever night and day
I tend deep within, feeding about my heart.”

title: Dionysiaca
text:
She spoke, and with her girdle drove the bed-fleeing Harmonia
into the voyage, goading with desire the now-yielding girl.
And she, turning her mind to a twofold counsel,
longed to take the stranger and yet wished to dwell in her fatherland,
and spoke some word, her mind lashed by the goad:
“Alas, who has changed my mind? Farewell, fatherland,
rejoice, Emathion and all the house; caves of the Cabeiri,
farewell, and Corybantian peaks; no longer do I behold
the nightly revel-torch of my mother's Hecate.
Farewell, maidenhood—I am wedded to sweet Cadmus;
Artemis, do not be wroth, I shall cross the swell of the bright-green sea.
But you will say the sea is pitiless—I do not heed
the raging surge; let my mother's water receive,
perishing together, Harmonia and my Cadmus.
I follow the young man, proclaiming my marriage to the goddesses;
if eastward my husband bears me sailing,
I will tell of the longing of Orion for the Dawn,
and I remember the chamber of Cephalus; but if ever I come
to the misty west, then over Endymion
the Latmian Selene, having suffered the like, will comfort me.”
Such things the girl cried out in her mind-distracting cares,
helpless, her mind torn by the lovely goad;
and with the wailing drop that wetted her face
she kissed Electra's hand and her eyes and the tips of her feet
and her head and her breast, and the face of Emathion
with modest lips, though he was her brother,
and she embraced all the handmaids; and lamenting
she greeted the wrought and much-carven rounds of the doors,
breathless things, and the couch and the fences of her maiden-bower;
and taking the dust of her fathers the girl embraced it.
And then, holding her hand, under the witnessing escort of the gods,
Electra brought Harmonia, dowerless, owed to Cadmus,
having wiped the streaming shower from her face.
And the morning wayfarer, taking the Cyprian daughter,
left the house with an aged handmaid, the queen's gift,
keeping the servant as his guide through the city as far as the sea.
And seeing the maiden, high on the shore beside the deep,
following the stranger, seething with fiery compulsion,
Mene, fond of mockery, cried out blaming the Cyprian:
“Cypris, do you arm yourself even against your own children, and did the sting
of the Loves not even spare your own offspring?
Her whom you bore, did you not pity, pitiless one? And what other maiden
do you pity, when you drag your own kin into desire?
Wander you too, dear friend; child of the Paphian, say to your mother:
Phaethon mocks you, and Selene shames me.
Harmonia, fatherland-forsaking, ill-loving, leave to Mene
her bridegroom Endymion, and tend the wanderer Cadmus,
have the heart to bear an equal toil, and in your love-begetting care
remember that you too have suffered, worn out by love-stricken Selene.”
As she spoke thus, Cadmus, hastening his comrades over the shore,
loosing again the moorings of the straight-running ship,
filled the sail to the bellying with a stormless spring wind;
and fastening the two ropes to a peg
he steered through the swell the timber-jointed chariot of the sea,
balancing on either side the ship's sheets, and like a Phoenician,
knowing the ancestral familiar craft of seafaring,
he stayed by the rudder; and on the stern he set
Harmonia herself, the untouched fellow-voyaging girl,
seeing on the ship the stranger passengers whom then the sailors
were taking on as hired men. And quietly the fellow-voyaging man,
looking on both, mingled with wonder his voice:
“Love himself is this seafarer; for it is no marvel
that sea-born Aphrodite should bear a sailor for a son;
but he holds an arrow and a bow and lifts a torch,
little Love, adorned with wings; and I behold
a Sidonian ship. Crafty, thieving Ares perhaps
sits in the stern, bringing within Lebanon
the western Aphrodite as she sails from Thrace.
Be gracious, mother of Love, and in unwaved calm
send me a favouring breeze for my stormless mother the sea.”

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Such a secret word the fellow-voyager spoke,
turning sidelong toward Harmonia his answering eye.
And Cadmus accomplished the voyage to Hellas, with the goad
of the Phoebean oracle in his heart, and ever urging him on
the inspired word of Zeus ran upon his unwandering ears.
There, holding out to all the Greeks newer gifts,
he hid away the life-bringing craft of Danaus the source of evil,
of water-bearing Danaus; for what greater thing did he find for the Achaeans,
if ever with bronze ground-digging mattocks
hollowing out the streaming hollow of an earthly chasm
he stopped the thirst of Argos, and to its dust-covered citizens
gave a watery footing for their feet, a guest-gift of water,
a little stream from the deep flanks of the earth? But the other,
bringing to all Hellas vocal and intelligent gifts,
fashioned harmonious instruments of speech, and of a kindred
harmony, mingling in order the unyoked with the yoked,
he rounded a written image of unsounding silence,
having learned the ancestral mysteries of a divine art,
a migrant of Egyptian wisdom, when Agenor,
dweller of Memphis, founded hundred-gated Thebes;
and, drawing the unspeakable milk of the sacred books,
tracing with a backward-moving hand the slanting marks,
he wrote curved circles; and showing the ivy-rites
of Egyptian Dionysus, of Osiris the wanderer,
he was taught the mystic nightly rites of the secret art,
and a magic hymn he chanted with frenzied voice,
holding a thin shrill cry; and the carved
intricate work, engraved upon the deepening wall
of the stone-image temple, he learned in his boyhood; and with much-pondering mind,
having measured the fiery rim of the countless stars
and learned the course of the Sun and the measure of the field,
bending the twined fingers of his well-turning hand,
he understood the restless circles of the returning Moon,
how with threefold spirals she shifts her changing shape,
new-shining, half-full, glittering with her whole face,
and how, drawn together and flowing away by the male fire
of her father the Sun, she is born from his motherless radiance,
stealing from her father his self-born, renewing fire.
Such was he; and swiftly going to the cities of Achaea
he laid aside his seafaring; and bringing with Harmonia
the swarm of his sea-wandering comrades as a wayfarer on land,
with horse-drawn chariots and burden-bearing wagons
he came to the prophetic shrine; and arriving there
he questioned the oracle of Pytho's never-silent
navel-stone at Delphi, and the wise Pythian stone
of itself, self-shouting, prophesied with a hollow voice all around:
“Cadmus, in vain, wanderer, you wind a much-roving track;
you seek some bull whom no cow's womb bore,
you seek some bull whom no mortal knows how to overtake;
renounce Assyria, and as the leader of your journey
tend an earthly cow, do not seek the bull of Olympus;
the bridegroom of Europa no herdsman knows how to drive;
he goes to no pasture, no meadow, obeys no goad,
is commanded by no whip; he knows how to lift
the soft trappings of Cypris and not the yoke-band of the plough,
and stretches his neck to Love alone and not to Demeter.
But, leaving aside the longing for your Tyrian father,
stay among foreigners, and of your Egyptian Thebes
found the city of your fatherland, namesake of it, where, falling,
a divine cow shall rest her heavy-kneed foot.”
So speaking, he laid to rest the frenzied voice of the tripods,
and the crags of Parnassus were shaken as they heard
the neighbouring Phoebean echo, and with its oracular stream
the inspired water of wise Castalia bubbled up.
The god spoke; and Cadmus withdrew, and beside the temple
he saw a cow, and went along with her as she journeyed; and following,
the men, with the slow-obeying hoof of the unstraying cow,
made their sparing, measured journey,
those nimble servants; whence then Cadmus, as he travelled,
beheld a sacred land set out before him, where, perceiving it,
the Pythian had laid to rest the death-bringing venom
of the Cirrhaean viper, the nine-coiled drag of the mountain serpent.
Leaving the heights of Parnassus, the migrant man
trod the bordering soil of Daulis, whence I hear
of the speaking robe of silent, ill-spindled Philomela,
whom Tereus defiled, when conjugal Hera fled
the danceless wedlock of mountain-dwelling marriages,
and the girl groaned upon the unspread ground-bed
of the wayside chamber; and as the tongueless girl
lamented the Thracian, compulsory Aphrodite,
with mimic tears voiceless Echo groaned,
mourning the bed-fleeing maiden Philomela,
when mingled with a crimson stream of blood
the blood of her freshly-cut maidenhood gushed up with her freshly-cut tongue.
And he saw the city of Tityos, where the bold son of Earth,
passing through the fair-leaved groves of Panopeus,
pulled aside the sacred robes of Leto as he forced her;
and he set the print of his foot in the Tanagraean hollow,
and from Coroneia crossing the Haliartian soil
and the city of the Thespians and the deep-shinned Plataeae
he came near Aonia, travelling the Boeotian plain,
where once Orion, the ill-loving son of Earth,
the scorpion, helper of the loveless arrow-pourer,
laid low so great a one, when he had lifted the very
lowest hem of the unwed goddess's tunic,
that slow-creeping earthly monster; and striking the heels
of his enemy with its hailing sting he scored them.
And he set foot on the Chaeronian land, where the hoof
of the cow whitened as it cut the silvery dust,
and pursuing the much-bending circles of the rugged journey
she shook from her dusty feet the white defilements.
And the oracular hoof of the cow, sinking to her ground-bed, gave way,
the herald of a city to be. But when for Cadmus
the Pythian decree of the earthly echo was fulfilled,
setting the sacred cow beside the incense-smoking altar,
he sought a flow of spring waters, that he might cleanse
his prophet hands, and pour over the offerings
pure water; for not yet in the wine-planted vineyards
did the delicate fruit of the ripening vintage appear.
And he set his feet beside serpent-fed Dirce;
and he stood astounded, where, slanting, appeared in his serpent-coil
the spangle-backed snake of Ares, who had girdled the spring,
and terrified the host, all the great throng that followed Cadmus;
this one, biting beneath the breast with his glaring jaws,
that one, striking, he scored with his blood-red tooth,
and tearing the life-sustaining liver of another as he fought
he made him a corpse; and the dry hair flowed from his neck
of its own accord, slipping loose from his sodden head;
another he terrified, leaping over the rim of his temple,
a human one, and through the throat of another he ran
unrestrained, and striking the eye with venomous spray
he darkened the marble gleam of the shut eye;
another's foot he seized, and scoring it with his jaw
he held it in his bite, and belched the green foam of his teeth
into the body of the young man, and, like the livid iron,
his flesh was chilled to death by the green venom;
of another, gasping beneath the blows of the jaws,
the unsteady membranes of the head heaved like waves
with the poison-bite, and as the brain poured forth,
through the sodden nostril streamed the down-rushing gore.
And swiftly the writhing serpent, creeping up the shins,
girdled Cadmus with a threatening bond,
and raising his body with a limb-mounting throb
he sprang to the rounded navel of the ox-hide shield;
and the man, his feet swathed in the crooked coils,
grew weary, heavy-bound by the dragging snaky cord,
bearing a dreadful burden, and the burdened bearer,
standing upright, the serpent dragged down to the ground, hauling him;
and he loosed his bitter mouth, and as the deadly thing gaped
the bloody gateway of his raw-devouring throat widened,
and he held his head aslant, and as his head was shaken
the high-stretched neck writhed, curving in the middle.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
But when Cadmus grew weary, then near at hand came Athena,
brandishing the aegis, the herald of victory to come,
maned with the snaky head of the Gorgon,
and to him in his terror the host-rousing goddess cried out:
“Cadmus, fellow-contestant of Zeus in the Giant-slaying battle-din,
do you tremble at the sight of one single snake? In the battle-din
Cronion, trusting in you, laid low Typhon,
maned with so many serpent heads.
Cease to tremble at the hiss of beastly teeth;
Pallas urges you on, and beside murderous Dirce
no bronze Ares shall rescue the crawler, his guardian.
But, taking the dreadful teeth of the slain
beast, sowing the earth with the snaky harvest,
reap the serpentine crop of the Giant battle,
and join the phalanxes of the earthborn in one common ruin,
leaving five alive; for in the Thebes that is to come
the bright-fruited race of the Sown Men shall spring up like grain.”
So speaking, Athena heartened the astonished Cadmus,
and inscribed the deep air with her windy foot,
entering the house of Zeus. And he, beside the firm clod,
the marble boulder, the well-rounded boundary-stone of the broad cornland,
stood lifting the rugged missile, and with a straight-flying
stone he crushed the top of the serpent's head;
and drawing the sharpened blade from his thigh
he cut the beast's neck; and the head, severed,
remained outside the body, and rolling in the dust
the restless tail wound its familiar, re-loosing circle,
and the serpent lay stretched on the ground, a corpse. And about the dead
furious, heavy-wrathed Ares cried aloud; and as he raged
Cadmus, his limbs changing into a coiling shape,
was destined to take another form, beside the foothills of the Illyrian land,
to wear a strange likeness of a serpent's face.
But these things were fated to come after a time. Meanwhile he,
in the middle of his bronze helmet, gathered the harvest of ruin,
the grim crop of the beast's jaws; and the native
plough of Pallas, hooked, dragging from the meadow into the soil,
and ploughing the war-breeding furrow of the bright-green earth,
he sowed the many-ranked swathe of the venomous teeth.
And the self-born crop of Giants grew up,
of whom one, high-headed, ran up stretching the tips
of his well-armoured chest, while another, with thrusting head,
reared his dreadful shoulder above the opening cornland;
another peered up to the navel, and one upon the earth
half-finished rose, lifting the earth-nourished weapon;
another, stretching out the jutting crest that peered above,
did not yet show his chest, and still creeping from his mother's
flanks, little by little, fought fearlessly against Cadmus,
helmeted in his self-grown armour—ah, great wonder,
Eileithyia armed him whom no mother delivered;
and one hurled a kindred spear, fumbling for it,
half-visible, while another, light, drawing his whole body into the light,
left the unfinished tips of his feet fixed fast in the cornland.
But Cadmus did not forget the command of Athena,
but reaped the stubble of the re-born Giants;
this one he struck above the breast with his windy lance,
that one he smote upon the collarbone beside the broad neck
and split open the bones of his shaggy throat;
another he scored with a hurling stone,
visible only to the belly; and as the blood of the dread Giants
poured river-like, Ares slipped in the gore,
reddening his own limbs, and as Nike stood by in the battle-din
the tunic of Nike was reddened with the crimson drops.
Another, as he fought, he struck with his sword beside the hip,
and cut through his close-grown back together with the ox-hide loins.
And the slaughter was unspeakable; and as the Giants were cut down
the deadly pipe of bloody dew spurted up
from those smitten by the sword. And he, by the wise counsel of Pallas,
lifted up a stone against the heads of the earthborn;
but they, drunk with the blood-red longing of Enyo,
raged in Bacchic frenzy for Ares, and with their kindred iron
the slayers of one another were entombed in the dust.
One strove against another; and with the reddening gore
the dappled, drenched backs of the ox-hide grew black
of the slain earthborn; and by the earthly sword's
kin-slaying point the harvest of the cornland was cut to pieces.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
5. Watch your fifth course still, and you shall behold Actaeon,
whom no doe brought to birth, a wandering fawn torn by dogs.
But when, reaping the snaky harvest of war,
Cadmus had mown the stubble of the teeth-sown Giants,
pouring out the gore as a thank-offering of battle to Ares,
and cleansing his limbs beside serpent-fed Dirce,
he sacrificed the Delphian cow upon god-built altars,
a fair offering to Pallas. As he began the sacrifice
the twin horns were sprinkled here and there
with barley-grains; and taking the naked sword
that hung beside his thigh from its Assyrian baldric
he cut the topmost hair from the long-snouted head
with the hilted blade; and Theoclymenus, gripping
the horn of the calf, drew back its straining neck,
and Thyestes crushed the sinews of its throat
with the double-edged ox-axe, and with the bloody flow of the cow
the stone altar of Onca-Athena was reddened,
and as the horned brow of the ox was smitten
the calf fell forward; and as it was cut up by the iron
they split its flanks and carved it with the knife,
and stripped off the rough ox-hide covering,
stretching it out; and rolling the bright fleece on the ground
the king himself laboured, and the raw flesh of the well-shaped thighs
cutting it up, he wrapped in a double fold of fat,
carving little by little, and stretching upon the coals
the entrails pierced long upon iron skewers
he drew them out, roasting them with a gentle fire; and the half-cooked pieces,
threaded in order, pierced by the point of the bronze,
the carver set down upon the flower-decked, low-standing table,
lifting in succession the spits all steaming.
And the wandering vapour of Assyrian incense
curled fragrant through the air. And when the sacrifice was finished
the meal was ready, and Cadmus, taking it, distributed to each,
holding out to all an equal-weighted portion of the chosen food.
And the ranks of the feasters at the well-rounded table
laid aside their longing for the banquet with a sated heart.
Nor for serpent-slaying Cadmus was there an end of toils,
but after the crawler, after the wild tribes of Giants,
he fought against the champions of the Ectenes and the Aonian host,
mowing the barbarian crop of Ares, and assailed
the neighbouring Temmices; and when he summoned his warriors
a motley swarm of neighbouring allies came.
And Strife joined the two armies with Enyo,
labouring to bring forth battle; and as they met in the din
the bow was bent, the spear was brandished, the helmet shaken,
and the missile whistled, and on the bossed circle
of the shield, struck by a millstone-rock, the ox-hide rang.
And the blood of the slain flowed; and many a man, half-dead,
rolled head-foremost in the dust upon the nourishing ground.
And the host of the foe bent as suppliants to Cadmus;
the struggle was loosed. And after the bloody whirl of the battle-din
Cadmus laid the foundations of unwalled Thebes.
And many furrows were cut here and there as the hollows were divided,
and the seats of the many-branching streets
were scored by the jagged-toothed iron of oxen;
and many an avenue, allotted in the four-yoked order
of the facing winds, was measured out among the meadows.
And the Aonian city was wrought with Tyrian craft
in beauty of stone; and one laboured after another,
cutting with the earth-cleaving point the many-coloured rock,
the workman, beneath the Boeotian crag, which beside the thicket
of oak-clad Teumessus the hills brought to birth,
which Helicon put forth and which Cithaeron travailed.
And he completed temples of the gods and houses of men,
rounding them by the rule; and on the unbreakable foundations,
scoring the encircling city with a seven-gated wall,
he imitated by his own craft the seven-zoned heaven,
leaving for the inhabitants to come the wall of Amphion,
guarded by the tower-building lyre. And to the heavenly
wanderers he dedicated seven gates, equal in number,
of like type; first, fixing toward the western clime,
he assigned the Oncaean gate to grey-eyed Mene,
named from the lowing of the ox, since she herself,
bull-shaped, horned Selene, the driver of oxen,
holding a triple form, is Tritonian Athena;
second, to Hermes, the radiant neighbour of Mene,
he gave a gate as a privilege; and marking out the fourth
named from Phaethon as Electra's, since when he appears
the morning gleam of like-coloured Electra glitters,
he dedicated to the fiery Sun the gate facing the Dawn
in the middle, since he is midmost of the planets;
and the fifth he gave to Ares, the third he granted to Aphrodite,
that on either side of both Phaethon might be in the middle,
parting his neighbour furious Ares from Aphrodite;
the sixth, the glory of Zeus, he wrought with brighter adornment,
high-shining; and the last the seventh star of Cronos received.
Such a seat he made; and founding the sacred city
he named it of like name with the city of Egyptian Thebes,
having fashioned a varied earthly likeness, equal to Olympus.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And the daughters of the Aonians struck up in their dances
the wedding-song of Harmonia; and over the fair bridal hall
the Thracian dancers chanted the name of the bride.
And the Paphian, the lovely mother, adorned the newly-built
bridal-chamber for Cadmus, singing the god-summoned marriage
of her own child; and the father, in delight at his daughter,
naked, without his shields, gentle Ares danced,
leaning his ironless right hand toward Aphrodite,
and with the marriage-trumpet he made music for the heart of the Loves,
matched against the pipe, and from his iron-bearing head
he shook off the wonted crests of his warlike mane,
binding his locks with bloodless garlands,
weaving a revel for Love; and dancing with the immortals
Ismenian Apollo came to the marriage of Harmonia,
beating out on his seven-toned lyre a song of love;
and the nine Muses struck up a life-giving strain,
and Polymnia, the nurse of the dance, shook her hands,
and traced the mimic image of voiceless speech,
uttering with her palms a wise shape in thoughtful silence,
rolling her eyes; and on twirling sandal,
to please Zeus, Nike stood as bridal attendant,
hailing Cadmus, the champion of Zeus, and around the bridal bed
with virgin lips she wove a marriage-song,
and wheeled the print of her foot, and in the well-rounded dance
modestly she shook her wings beside the wings of the Loves.
And from the many-scattered torches of like-shining radiance
the light of an evening, lying Dawn arose.
And with clear-voiced lips beside the dance-loving bridal bed
all night long there was a revel of unsleeping dance
of singers; for hastening to the wakeful wedding . . .
he left his wonted wand, since he is the steward of sleep.
And Thebe was an Olympian dance-floor; and one might behold
Cadmus and Zeus together touching one same table.
And bringing to the marriage-chamber the bride-escorting hour,
the Dragon of the northern Wain rose, its fellow-traveller,
a herald of things to come, that consorting with his age-mate bride,
from mortal shape the bridegroom of Harmonia
was destined to take a serpent form. And one immortal after another
gave a gift to Cadmus as he hastened to the chamber;
Zeus made all things perfect; and honouring his sister
Hera, the care of all, since she was mother to Ares,
the dark-haired Earthshaker, lord of horses, gave gifts of the sea;
Hermes gave a sceptre, Ares a spear, Apollo a bow,
and a crown adorned with stones in many-coloured array
Hephaestus hung upon the head of Harmonia,
suspending a golden fillet over her temples;
and golden-throned Hera gave a well-jewelled throne;
and to honour Ares, much-counselling Aphrodite
joined to the girl's white, reddening neck
a golden necklace holding the intricate gleam of stones,
the cunning work of Hephaestus, which he wrought for the Cyprus-born,
that it might be a birth-gift for the archer Love;
for the heavy-kneed husband always hoped Cytherea
would bear a limping son, the image of his father's feet;
but he hoped in vain, and seeing a son sound of foot,
shining with wings like the son of Maia,
he made the intricate necklace, which on its star-bright back
had a coiling body like a serpent; for as
the two-mouthed amphisbaena winds in the middle of its drag,
spitting venom through both its heads,
writhing about with the cross-yoked throb of its limbs,
and creeping joins head to head,
leaping about its curved back in a slanting course;
so that intricate necklace, stretching its broken back,
was bent, holding a doubled, arching neck,
ample with scales, reaching as far as the navel,
a plaited, two-headed serpent; and under the whirl of the craft
the golden circle of the dragging spine writhed,
and its head, wreathing with much-whirling throb,
belched a false hiss from its throat.
And on either side of the mouths, where end and beginning meet,
there was a golden eagle, as if cleaving the broad air,
upright between the two snaky heads,
high-shining with the four-yoked muzzle of its four wings;
on the one side yellow jasper ran, on the other it held
the all-white stone of Selene, which, when the fair-horned goddess
wanes, diminishes and grows, when Mene,
new-shining, glittering the moist gleam from her horn,
draws the self-born fire from her father the Sun;
another held the light-bringing pearl, by whose grace of radiance
the grey swell of the Erythraean sea glitters
as it shines; of another, in its midmost, with fiery adornment,
the Indian agate spat forth a slender, moist gleam.
And as the heads on either side joined to one another,
the two gaping jaws of the dragon's heads widened,
enclosing the eagle with both their jaws,
intertwined here and there; and through its bright face
carbuncles shot from the eyes an innate radiance,
sending a sharp gleam, like a blazing lamp
when kindled; and adorned with the many-formed shape of stones
there was a sea, and a stone green with grey emerald
receiving crystal yoked with it, like to foam,
held the whitening image of darkening brine;
in it were all the intricate things wrought, in it all
the gold-gleaming sea-fed flocks of the deep glittered,
as if leaping about; and many a moist wayfarer,
a dolphin half-visible, danced grazing the brine—
and it lashed its false self-darting tail—
and a chorus of birds of varied hue, of which you might almost say
you heard the windy beat of their flying wings,
since Cytherea gave the necklace as a gift to the girl,
golden, well-jewelled, hanging at the bride's neck.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And yoked by the desire-guiding girdle of marriage,
Harmonia brought to birth in her womb a many-childed offspring,
born little by little; and with successive child-bearing
she loosed the pregnant burden of daughter-bearing labour,
having filled out four times nine circles of the Moon.
First Autonoe leaped from her mother's fruitful womb,
unfolding her nine-month labour
with first-born throes; and of the same kindred stock
fair Ino grew up, the bride-fellow of Athamas,
a mother of two; and third Agave arose,
who once, wedded in a Giant marriage,
bore a son like to her teeth-sown husband;
and the image of the Graces, a face shot with longing,
Semele blossomed fourth of the daughters, kept for Zeus,
and to her alone, though she was the youngest,
Nature gave the privilege of an unconquered beauty.
And a male, late-completed, yoked with the female stock,
Harmonia bore as a new son to rejoicing Cadmus,
Polydorus, the morning star of his Aonian fatherland,
younger than rose-fair Semele, whom in Thebes
the lawless king Penthe deprived, taking up the sceptre.
And these things old time was destined to accomplish late.
And to chosen husbands Cadmus betrothed his daughters
in the four-yoked bridal of successive marriage,
and joined bed after bed; for first the gift-bringer
Aristaeus, the Herdsman, surnamed the Hunter too,
the blood of wise Phoebus and of skilful Cyrene,
wedded Autonoe by the law of yoked ploughings;
nor did the son of Agenor refuse to have as son-in-law
the knower of much-feeding craft, the life-giving son of Phoebus,
but to him who, with the life-sustaining breezes of the Zeus-sent winds,
had laid to rest the deadly star of fiery Maera,
he betrothed his daughter to that exceedingly wise husband.
And the marriage was rich in blessings, since as a gift to the unwed girl
he gave oxen, granted goats, bestowed a mountain-reared flock;
and many a swathe, burdened with the load of toil,
lifted the cargo of an oil-bearing jar,
the bride-gifts; and much intricate travail of the wise bee
he brought, the cunning offering of the much-pierced birth-pang.
That man first, mountain-ranging with the spring of his feet,
found the crag-loving toil of the deer-driving hunt,
how with intelligent nostril, by the flanks of the feeding wood,
the hound divines the scent of the trackless beast,
straining upright its ears toward the winding course,
and learned the much-twined nets of cunning craft
and the upright form of the stakes, and over the sand the print of beasts
freshly scored at dawn upon the untrodden field . . .
and having taught the hunter-man to wear buskins on his feet,
darting unrestrained into the dog-driven course of the hunt,
to carry his robes as far as his gleaming knee,
lest ever, as the hunter's foot presses onward, its rush
be checked back by the trailing tunic.
That man understood the rows of the much-pierced hives,
and stayed the works of the wandering, lonely bee,
which within the meadow shifts from flower to flower
to a bright-fruited plant, and flying upon the clusters
with its topmost lips draws off the tip of the dew;
and binding his limbs with the linen meshes of his much-woven tunic
from nails to hair, he guarded himself
against the dreadful stings of the arming bee,
and with a cunning, choking, craftsman smoke of fire
he soothed the angry swarm, and shaking against the wind
the threatening torch of the hive-loving bee
he lifted the double bronze, and at the housed brood,
as the never-silent din clattered with its buzzing tumult,
beating with his much-rattling hand a twin clash,
and cutting away the many-pointed cover of the wax
he pressed out the gleaming gifts of the honey-dripping birth.
He first found the dew of well-dropping oil,
when, cutting the fruit with a heavy millstone,
he pressed out the rich, moisture-bearing offspring of the olive.
And to the shady, much-treed crag of the well-fed wood,
to the marsh, to the meadow he brought and taught the herdsmen
to pasture from the showing of the Sun until evening.
And of the straying flocks, untraceable, unyielding to the roving hoof,
he joined in one path the slow-going, backward-treading row
of the sheep that followed, to a flowery pasture,
taking a goat as forerunner of their like-eager journey.
And he understood the pastoral mountain song of Pan.
And the fire-blazing star of Maera he laid to rest,
and kindling the fragrant altar of Zeus the Moistener
he poured over it a sweet libation with the blood of a bull,
the varied altar-gifts of the wandering bee,
filling the delicate cups with a honey-mixed draught;
and father Zeus heard, and honouring his son's son
he sent the counter-blowing breeze of the evil-averting winds,
holding back Sirius from its smouldering fever.
Even now the Etesian breezes from Zeus, the heralds
of Aristaeus' sacrifice, cool the earth,
when the dappled-clustered grape of the vine grows ripe.
Him Love escorted to the Aonian wedding,
the Cean son of Phoebus; and at the ox-marked sacrifice
all the city was garlanded, and the straight-cut streets
were busy with dancing, and beside the porch of the bridal hall
the citizens performed the winding wedding-dance,
and the women struck up a sweet-voiced song,
and the Aonian flutes sounded with the marriage-pipe.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Thence from the bed of Aristaeus and Autonoe
Actaeon arose; and with crag-loving heart,
bearing the blood of the Hunter, he wiped clean his ancestral hunting,
a mountain-ranging servant of Artemis—and no wonder
that ill-fated Actaeon learned the cares of the chase,
being the grandson of lion-slaying Cyrene—
never did the mountain bear escape him, nor did
the deadly eye of the lioness in childbed terrify him;
often, watching the leopard leaping high in the air,
he laid it low; and ever high in the thicket
goat-herding Pan beheld him with astonished eyes
outrunning the journey of the swift deer.
But the running of his feet did not help him, nor did his quiver
avail, nor the straight aim of his arrows, nor the cunning of the chase;
but Fate destroyed him, a wandering fawn torn by dogs,
still breathing of the battle-din after the Indian war,
when, sitting high upon a long-stemmed oak,
he beheld the whole body of the arrow-pourer bathing,
an insatiable gazer at the unseen goddess,
measuring the holy body of the unwed maiden
close at hand; and him, as he watched with secret eye,
with sidelong eye, the unrobed form of the queen,
an unveiled Naiad Nymph saw from afar,
and in terror cried out, and announced to her queen
the wild boldness of the love-maddened man; and half-visible
Artemis, snatching with her garment the round headband,
covered her chaste breasts with the maiden girdle,
and sinking with her moist limbs into the streams,
modestly the girl hid her whole body little by little.
Actaeon, heavy of doom, your human form
at once left you, and the hoof of your four feet was cloven,
and your cheeks lengthened into long jaws,
your shins grew slender, and curved upon your brow
grew the two long clusters of the long-shooting antler,
and with dappled limbs a bastard form was wrought,
and you had a shaggy body; but in the wind-swift fawn
your mind alone was still steadfast; and with swift-going
leap of the hoof you ran through the inhospitable mountain,
a hunter fearing the hunters. And of changed appearance
the dogs no longer knew their former master; for at the unmoved
nods of the grieving, heavy-minded arrow-pourer,
maddened with the raving breath of frenzy,
they scored the yoked swathe of their fawn-slaying teeth,
and led astray by the false aspect of a deer
they devoured the dappled bastard body in mindless frenzy.
And the goddess devised another thing, that the dogs with slow jaws
should rend Actaeon little by little, still breathing, gifted with a thinking mind,
that they might tear his heart the more
with sharper pangs; and in his mortal mind
groaning for his own fate he bellowed with a mournful voice:
“Blessed Teiresias, for you beheld, beyond destruction,
the naked form of pitying, unwilling Athena;
you did not die, you did not take a deer's body, nor on your brow
did the antlers hang jutting forth;
you live, having lost the light of your eyes; but the gleam
of your eyes Athena removed into your mind;
the arrow-pourer is angered with worse anger than the Tritonian.
Would that she had granted me a like grief, would that she too
had assailed my eyes as Athena did,
would that she had changed my mind as she changed my body; for an alien
beast's form holds me, and I keep a man's character.
When do beasts ever groan over their own destruction?
Senseless they live and know not their end.
I alone keep a thinking mind; and as I perish
beneath beastly brows I shed understanding tears.
Be wilder now, my dogs; never so much
did you rush down with raving leap upon lions.
Cry the dirge for Actaeon, dear hills,
yes, I beg you, and you beasts too the like; tell, Cithaeron,
to Autonoe what you saw, and to Aristaeus my father
with your stony tears proclaim my end
and my maddened, unsparing dogs. Alas for necessity,
I myself with my own hands reared my own slayers.
Would that a mountain-ranging lion had subdued me, would that,
dragging me, the spangle-backed leopard had torn me, would that
with bitter, unsparing claws raving bears
had carved me, fawn-seeming, with their glaring jaws,
and not the dogs of my own house had subdued me; no longer
do they know my form, no longer my alien echo.
Half-dead he spoke these things, and to the beast-hound
that mad and heard not his prayers he pleaded with mournful voice;
he sent forth thoughtful words, but instead of a human voice
there sounded the noise of an unmeaning echo.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And now self-fulfilled mountain Rumour flew,
crying out to Autonoe the dog-torn doom of her child,
not how he took the shaggy form of a deer,
but only that he had perished. And with affectionate heart,
barefoot, unveiled, the mother was lashed with grief;
and she tore her locks, and rent her whole tunic,
and with mourning nails scored her cheeks,
reddening them with blood, and over her bare breast
she reddened the life-giving circle of her child-nursing breasts,
remembering his birth; and the bride bathed her robes
with the ever-flowing tears of her mourning face.
And the dogs of Actaeon, coming from the crag,
confirmed the ill-tidings; for with their silent tears
they divined the end of the young man.
And seeing them mourning, the mother groaned far more;
and Cadmus, the old man, cut off his grey lock,
and Harmonia cried aloud; and of the weeping women
the heavy-sounding echo, gathered together, filled the whole house.
And Autonoe, going with Aristaeus her husband,
went searching the much-scattered remains of the corpse;
she saw and did not know her own offspring, she beheld the form
of an intricate deer and did not see the face of a man,
and often passed by the bones of the unknown fawn
lying on the ground, and did not know; for as her son
perished she expected to see a mortal-seeming form.
Ill-fated Autonoe I do not blame; for an alien
remnant of her child she beheld, and of an unrecognizable face
she perceived the jaws and did not see the round of an eye,
and touched the horns and did not know her son's hair;
she found slender feet and did not mark them for feet,
she saw slender feet and did not see the round of sandals.
Ill-fated Autonoe I do not blame; for of the perished one
she did not behold human eyes, did not see the likeness
of a human form, and did not perceive the throat
scored with the purple flower of the first down.
And with roving feet, passing through the ridge of the wood,
she trod the rugged, hard-to-climb backs of the hill,
ungirt, unsandalled; and from her mountain-wandering toils
she came home again to the house; and over her unprofited intent
grieving, scarcely she slept beside her grief-bearing husband.
And both consorted with shadowy dreams,
snatching with their eyes the wing of nightingale Sleep.
And the soul of the young man stood beside his downcast father,
having the dappled, shadowy body of a deer, and from its eyelids
it shed thoughtful tears, and spoke in a human voice:
“O father, you sleep, and you do not know my doom;
awake and know my bastard, unrecognized face,
awake and embrace the antler of your dear deer,
and kiss the thinking beast whom Autonoe's womb bore.
You gaze on me myself, whom you reared; for both
you behold Actaeon and you hear Actaeon.
If you long to touch the palm and fingers of your child,
look at my forefeet, and you will find a hand;
if you long for my head, you will perceive a deer's head;
if for my human temples, look at the long antlers;
if for the feet of Actaeon, see my hinder hoof;
if you saw the hairs of my limbs, they are my tunics.
Know your son, father, whom Apollo did not save;
groan, father, for your son, whom Cithaeron did not guard.
Hide your alien child in the downcast dust;
let not the bastard, untrustworthy face lead you astray;
do not leave your perished fawn unburied.
Would, father, that you had guarded me, unused to hunting;
then I would not have had longing for the lonely arrow-pourer,
then I would not have seen an Olympian form. Would that of a mortal
maiden I had had love; but mortal-born women
leaving to others, and swift-fated weddings,
I longed for an immortal one; and at the angered goddess
I became the meal of my own whelps, father; the hills
are my witnesses; if you do not believe the crags, ask the Naiad
Nymphs; my oaks know it; and of like form
ask my beasts, and those whom I called my herdsmen.
But, father, grant me a last favour, and in your senseless
child-loving grief do not slay my slayers,
pity the blameless child-killers; for by my
beastly aspect, unwilling, they were led astray.
What dog ever spares the deer? Or what man
is angered at fawn-killing whelps? Ah, how the poor things,
running round here and there about the circling hills,
track the corpse, whom I slew; and from their eyelids
they pour thoughtful tears, and with their forefeet
they embrace the nets with some affectionate bond,
like grieving men, and over my
ground-bed they weep with mournful howls.
Yes, I beg you, do not slay the mourners; for my
shaggy hide and face they gazed on,
and were not persuaded by prayers, and did not check their teeth,
hearing the alien bellowing of my voice,
and with mournful mouths they questioned my crag:
‘Today someone snatched away Actaeon; tell, rocks,
where he plies the deer-driving course; tell, Nymphs.’
Such things the dogs uttered; and the hill answered:
‘What mountain-roaming doe holds the deer-driving hunt?
I have not learned of a deer that shoots the deer; but of alien form
Actaeon was changed and became a thinking fawn,
who once slew beasts; and by a man-slaying goddess himself,
bearing the blood of the Hunter, he is hunted by the arrow-pourer.’
Such things the crags cried out for the grieving whelps.
And often Artemis said to my seeking slayer:
‘Cease, much-toiling hound, winding your much-roving track;
you seek Actaeon, whom you carry within your belly,
you seek Actaeon, whom you slew; if you wish,
you shall see only the bones, the still-left remnants of your food.’
But, father, in order I will cry to you my fate.
There was a long-leaved bush, one of wild-olive, one of olive;
wretched I; for leaving the shoot named from the wild-olive
I ran up to the holy olive-stock beside the path,
watching the bare flesh of unseen Artemis.
I sinned; for fostering a twofold reckless outrage
I came to the tree of Pallas, to see the body of the arrow-pourer
with daring eyes, whence a heavy-wrathed threat
assailed Actaeon both from Artemis and from Athena.
For just then, sweating with the fire-bright vapour of the heat,
Artemis, after the well-toiled course of her wonted hunt,
was bathing in pure waters, and as she bathed
the facing gleam flashed upon my eyes,
shooting snow-white rays into the streams;
you would say that, beside the back-flowing current of Ocean,
the western, plenteous Mene shone through the water.
And the kindred Naiads cried out; Loxo cried aloud,
holding Oupis in like cry, and in the calm stream
checked her swimming sister Hecaerge.
And an air-roaming darkness covered my eyes;
and head-foremost from the tree I slipped into the dust,
and suddenly took a dappled body, and instead of human
form an unrecognizable down covered my body,
and the hunting dogs together scored their teeth.
I will keep silence on all this; why should I tell a second grief?
Lest, sleeping, I bring you again to groans.
Often you passed that tree, where lies
the remnant of Actaeon, and the bones of the intricate
fawn, loosed upon the ground,
often you passed by, pitiful, of much-devoured limbs, scattered on the earth,
apart from one another. But I will cry to you another
sure sign of my death; for of the source of evil
you shall see the quiver and my arrow near the tree,
unless the winged arrows too were transformed,
unless angry Artemis again into a tree of the wood
changed my bow, and altered my quiver.
Blessed was Otos, since he was no wandering fawn;
no dogs . . . Orion the deer-driver . . . would that
a scorpion too had slain Actaeon with its sharp sting.
Wretched I; for an empty rumour deceived my mind;
for hearing that Phoebus, the brother of the arrow-pourer,
lay beside Cyrene, and sowed my father,
I fancied I was drawing Artemis into a kindred marriage.
And again hearing that bright Dawn snatched away
Orion as her bridegroom, and Selene Endymion,
and that Deo embraced mortal Iasion as her husband,
I fancied that such was the mind of the arrow-pourer.
But, father, give burial to my bastard, antler-bearing form,
and do not leave it to become the sport of other dogs.
And if you hide my remains in the hollow earth,
grant me this gift too: fix bow and arrows
beside my tomb, which is the privilege of the dead.
But leave aside the arrow and the bow, father, since in shafts
the arrow-pourer delights, and bends her curved bow.
And beseech the cunning, many-turning sculptor, that he may carve
my dappled bastard form from neck to feet;
let him fashion only the likeness of my human face,
that all may know my false form.
But do not, father, inscribe my fate; for the wayfarer cannot
weep at once for my form and for my doom.”
So spoke the dream-borne thinking deer, and unforeseen
it departed, taking wing; and the husband of Autonoe
sprang up, casting off the wing of oracular Sleep.
And rousing from her bed his much-frightened wife,
he told the beastly, antler-bearing face of his child,
and recounted all the words the thinking fawn had spoken.
And the lamentation grew the more; and the bride of Aristaeus
went searching a second time, and grieving
often she passed through the inmost places of the long-stemmed thicket;
and treading the rugged, hard-to-climb circles of the paths
scarcely she found that murderous tree, and found too
the quiver and the bow beside the lonely tree.
And the bones scattered here and there upon the strewn earth,
fallen remains, scarcely the mother gathered,
and with loving hand embraced the sweet antler,
and kissed the shaggy lips of the ill-fated fawn.
And keenly wailing the mother entombed the corpse,
and inscribed for him beside the tomb all that
the nightly dream-voice of Actaeon had spoken to his father.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
While grief roared through the hall of Aristaeus,
meanwhile fair-breasted Agave bore to Echion
a bold, god-fighting son of the earthborn; and as the fresh
grief stood newly-slain, he was named Pentheus, from grief.
And after the bed of Nephele, after her former wedding,
the maiden Ino came reveling into the chambers of Athamas;
and she bore ill-fated Learchus and Melicertes,
destined to be a wanderer of the sea, as a fostering nurse,
the life-giving child-nurse of Bromios; for to both
she joined one breast, to Palaemon and to Dionysus.
And Semele was kept for a brighter wedding;
for already Zeus who rules on high longed to rear a new Dionysus,
a bull-shaped likeness of the elder Dionysus,
having desire for ill-fated Zagreus,
whom Persephone bore in the serpent bed of Zeus,
the bride of the dark-cloaked king of the underworld,
when Zeus the much-coiling, holding a false form,
gentle, a serpent rolling in a desire-stirring drag,
plundered the maidenhood of unwed Persephone
as she was hidden, when all who dwell on Olympus
were charmed by a single girl, and over the bride-to-be maiden
the gift-bringers held a Cyprian strife for her unplundered marriage;
not yet come to the couch of Persuasion,
Hermes held out his wand, the bridal privilege,
and Apollo offered as bride-gifts his well-hymning lyre,
and Ares gave a spear and a marriage breastplate,
bringing a shield as a bridal gift, and from the fair-sounding
forge the Lemnian, newly-finished, still breathing of the furnace,
the god of both crafts stretched out an intricate, many-coloured necklace;
for already, unwilling, he had refused his former bride,
watching Aphrodite revel with Ares;
and he showed even to the blessed ones the marriage-thief, the ravisher of his bed,
at the message of Phaethon, with a spider-like bond
binding naked Ares to naked Aphrodite.
But Zeus the father was charmed far more by Persephone;
and as Zeus gazed on the fair-maiden bloom of her body,
his foremost eye became the escort of the Loves,
insatiable of Persephone; and beneath his heart ever
the storms of unsleeping care whistled;
and little by little he was kindled with a greater flame for the Paphian
from a small spark; and over the fair-bosomed goddess
the eyes of love-maddened Zeus were enslaved.
And once the girl, holding bright bronze, delighted
in the judge of her reflected beauty, and to the self-acting,
silent herald she entrusted the shape of her form,
judging her false body in the shadowy mirror,
and laughed at the mimic image; and Persephone,
gazing on the self-carved likeness of her face,
beheld the bastard form of a lying Persephone;
and once, fleeing the noontide track of the parching Hour
in the fire-bright vapour of the thirsty heat,
the girl rested from the loom-toiling labour of the shuttle,
and wiping the moist sweat from her face,
loosed the chaste girdle bound about her breast,
and bathing her flesh in toil-loosing waters
was carried to the spring's cooling stream,
leaving the threads pierced upon the loom of Pallas.
Nor did she escape the all-seeing eye of Zeus; and the whole
form of the unsheltered, bathing Persephone he beheld;
not so longing did he rave for the Cyprus-born,
whom desiring he sowed the unreachable seed upon the field,
shooting the warm self-darting foam of the Loves,
whence within child-bearing, horned Cyprus
the two-coloured stock of the fair-horned Centaurs blossomed.
And he, ruler of the cosmos and charioteer of heaven,
the so-great one, bent his neck to desire; nor did thunderbolts,
nor lightning help when Aphrodite arrayed herself for war;
and he left the house of Hera, refused the bed of Dione,
cast away the love of Deo, fled Themis, abandoned Leto,
and was charmed only toward the wedding of Persephone alone.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
6. Seek out the marvellous sixth book, where honouring Zagreus
rainy Zeus flooded all the seats of the earth.
Nor was the father then alone in his desire; but they themselves,
all who dwell on Olympus, holding one same arrow,
sought the wedding of the goddess Deo as a bride-gift.
There Deo, changing the gleam of her rosy face,
was lashed in her mind, surging with griefs;
and she unbound the fruitful veil of her head,
loosing the curls that hung down her neck's hair,
shuddering for her child; and as the goddess was burdened
her cheeks were wetted with self-poured tears,
because so many suitors, goaded by one fiery shaft
into strife of rival weddings,
shared Love drove to frenzy, contestants of the Loves;
all of them she feared, but the plenteous mother feared most
to have Hephaestus the lame as her child's husband.
And she went to the house of Astraeus with well-footed step,
the oracular deity; and from her backward-flowing tresses
the unbound curl was shaken by the unsteady breezes.
Eosphoros, seeing her, announced her; and hearing,
old Astraeus arose; he, scoring with lines,
sprinkled dark dust about the back of the table,
and tracing in spirals with the hook-toothed iron
he inscribed a four-sided base in the glowing ash,
and made another figure with an equal-pointed triangle.
But these things he laid aside and came near the doors
to meet Demeter; and as they hastened through the hall
Hesperos led the way, and seated Deo on a throne
beside the seat of her father; and with affectionate intent
the Winds, mixing from the nectar-bowl,
greeted the goddess with toil-loosing cups,
the sons of Astraeus; but Deo refused to drink,
drunk with care for Persephone; for parents who bear but one child
always tremble for their cherished children;
but scarcely Astraeus, sweet of speech, persuaded her
as she still refused, holding heart-charming Persuasion.
There the old man prepared a great feast, that he might scatter
the heart-biting cares of Demeter at the table.
And girding belts about their flanks, the four
Winds, the servants of their father, bound themselves;
and holding out cups beside the nectar-bowl,
the East Wind poured the wine, and the South Wind held
in a pitcher the water for the meal, and the North Wind, bringing,
set upon the table the ambrosia, and the West Wind, pressing out the sound of the pipe,
the female Wind made music with springtime reeds;
and Eosphoros wove garlands, binding flowers
that bloomed at dawn with dewy clusters;
and lifting the wonted torch of the nightly lamp
Hesperos whirled with the dancing sole of his feet,
shaking his curving step, since he was the escort of the Loves,
and busied himself with the leaping of dance-woven weddings.
But when, after the feast, the goddess was sated with dancing,
having shaken off the heavy sting of mind-bereaving care,
she asked for prophecy, and of the affectionate old man
with her left palm she touched his knees, and entreating
with her right she stroked his deep-braided beard;
and she told of the many suitors of her own daughter,
seeking comforting oracles; for prophecies
steal away grief with hopes of things to come.
Nor did old Astraeus refuse; and perceiving the newly-born
birth-measures of his only-bearing daughter,
and the time that does not falter, and the course of the unwandering Hour
of the first-born, bending the shifting fingers of his hands
about the migrant circle of the returning number
he measured from palm to palm with twofold throb;
and at his bidding a servant lifted up a well-rounded
revolving sphere, the image of the upper air, the likeness of the cosmos,
Asterion, and set it down, taking it, upon the lid of a chest.
There the old man laboured, and turning the tip of the axis
about the zodiac circle he stretched out his gaze,
looking here and there at both the fixed stars and the wanderers;
and he whirled the pole; and with much-whirling rush
into an unsteady course it was bent at an endless turning-post,
the bastard upper air, wheeling with artificial stars,
pierced by a central axis; and the deity discovered,
gazing at the sphere wreathed round, that with full face
the Moon ran along the curving back of the bond,
and Phaethon shared an equal lot with the facing Mene,
borne at a point beneath the earth, and a dim
cone, soaring aloft from the earth, creeping up sharp,
covered the whole Moon, set against Phaethon;
and hearing of the contestants for the wedded love
he sought rather Ares, and over the western hall
he perceived the thief of marriage with the western star
of the Cyprus-born; and he found the portion named from the parents
of the maiden, under the starry ear of corn; and around it
ran the Light-bringing star of the rain-bearing son of Cronos.
But when he had perceived all things, having numbered the rim of the stars,
he hid away the ever-whirling sphere in the hollow chest,
the dappled-backed sphere; and to the goddess as she questioned
he belched up the threefold decree of the oracular echo:
“Child-loving Demeter, beneath the shadowy cone,
when the unlit Moon's ray is stolen away,
guard against the bridegroom, the ravisher of Persephone,
the secret plunderer of your unplundered daughter,
if the threads of the Fates obey. For unforeseen
you shall behold before the wedding a bastard, secret husband,
beast-mingled, crafty-minded, since beside the western point
I see Ares, the marriage-thief, walking with the Paphian,
and I watch the Dragon rising beside them both.
Most blessed I call you; for in the four-yoked cosmos
you shall be bright with fruit, since you shall give fruit to the earth
the barren; for over the daughter's lot of her parents
the maiden Astraean stretches out her corn-bearing hand.”
So speaking, he laid to rest the oracular voice beneath his mouth.
But when Demeter the sickle-bearer heard the hope
of fruits to come, and of a self-bidden husband,
the unbetrothed ravisher of her cherished, unwed daughter,
she groaned, smiling; and through the lofty path
hastening to her own house she descended with downcast step,
and beside the snaky stall the well-whirling yoke
balancing about the twin crest of beasts
she harnessed the unyoked crawlers with the breast-band;
and binding their jaws with the hook-toothed bridle,
golden-formed Deo led through the grim chariot
her child, hidden in the dark-fronted band of a cloud,
and the counter-going noise of the bellowing wagon
she whirled with the beast-driving whip of the North Wind,
