seeing his son as though a horned beast; and with a straight-aimed
bow, unreachable, he sprang upon Learchus,
thinking him a high-antlered stag in the false shape,
like in body to a wild beast; but the boy in flight,
terrified, was borne along, plying his knees more swiftly.
And drawing the wind-borne arrow with frenzied hands
the father bound his young son fast with the child-slaying shaft;
and he crushed the unknown head with his knife,
made into a fawn by the phantom; and of the unrecognized face,
he laughed, fingering the tip of the bloodied chin,
handling him as though a beast, and he ran with a leap of frenzy,
while still the boy Learchus, unburied, gasped,
seeking the mother, and rolled his eyes in restless turning.
And none of the handmaids came near; but ranging madly
he passed through the seven-chambered house with swift foot,
calling his own son, the one he had slain. And in the hall,
beholding the infant Melicertes, just brought in,
and setting a fire-breathing cauldron upon the hearth,
he placed his son in the midst; and as the flame was kindled,
the murderous cauldron seethed with watery steam.
And his own child cried out, crying "Papa," and none
of the handmaids helped him; but the mother, swift as a storm,
snatching from the cauldron the child half-burnt by fire,
with frenzied bounds Ino ran, wind-footed;
and cleaving the dust of the White Plain
she was named Leucothea, that bore the fitting name; and out of the hall
the maddened Athamas, plying his windy knees,
pursued in vain swifter Ino, runner of the mountains.
But when her much-distraught husband came near her
with unsteady track on stumbling foot, then the wretched woman
stayed her wetted foot at the sea close by,
and to her plaintive child she uttered a mournful, wailing voice,
blaming Cronion and the son of Maia, the messenger:
"Fine indeed, white-lightning god, the nursing-fee you gave me for Bacchus!
Behold your child Lyaeus's coeval, half-burnt!

title: Dionysiaca
text:
If you wish, strike down with your unsparing bolt
the mother and the young son, whom I reared in one bosom,
foster-brother of your god-born Dionysus.
Child, Necessity is a great goddess; to whom do you flee?
What mountain receives you in flight, here beside the sea?
What Cithaeron will hide you in a dark hollow?
What mortal pities you, whom your own father does not pity?
Either the sword or the sea will receive you; if it must be,
better to be overcome in the deep than by the knife.
I know whence this woe was rolled upon you, your mother;
I know whence: for a cloud sends the Furies against me,
that I may die in the sea, where the maiden Helle fell.
I have heard that Phrixus, borne through the air to the land of the Colchians,
the high-riding charioteer of the snatching ram,
yet lives, an exile; would that he too,
my own son, fatherless, fleeing, might travel the airy path
of the golden-fleeced ram, Melicertes;
and would that, after Phoebus, taking pity on you, Ino,
Poseidon, host of Glaucus, might save you.
I fear lest, after the death of unburied Learchus,
I behold you too dead, a corpse unburied and unwept,
gasping under your father's bloody knife.
Hasten to flee mad Athamas, and do not perceive
your child-slaying father, the destroyer of your mother who bore you.
Receive me too, O sea, after the land; receive me, Nereus,
with a hospitable hand, after Perseus and Melicertes;
receive Ino too, sailing with the ark of Danae.
I too have suffered what is deserved of impiety, since Cronion
made even my own offspring barren of seed,
as I made the life-bearing furrow of earth barren;
for, being a stepmother, I planned to reap
the bastard brood of Athamas, and Hera rages against me,
having become the stepmother of newly reared Dionysus."
So speaking, on trembling feet she leapt into the sea,
plunging swiftly with her son; and Leucothea
the dark-haired god received with open hands,
a sharer of hearth with the gods who walk the waters; and from there she aids
sailors who wander astray, and Ino became a sea-goddess,
a Nereid, the steerer of the calm sea without surge.
Her lord Cronides showed to the mother of Lyaeus,
that the goddess was for Bromius's sake; and she, rejoicing,
uttered a mocking voice to her sea-faring sister:
"Ino, you have the sea; Semele has won the circle of Olympus.
Yield to me; for I have Cronides, the ploughman of my brood,
an immortal husband, who brought the travail of my child-bearing
to birth in my stead, while you were wedded
to an earthly bedfellow, Athamas, the destroyer of your offspring.
Your child has won the sea; my offspring will come to dwell in the upper air,
will come to the higher house of Zeus; for I do not liken
heavenly Dionysus to Melicertes beneath the waves."
Such things did airy Semele, the bride, bellow,
mocking the life of her sister Ino, dweller of the sea.
Meanwhile Dionysus too, beneath the Lydian region of the land,
whirling the Bacchic instruments of Cybeleian Rhea,
flowered, having such stature as he wished; and fleeing
the noonday scourge of the high-coursing Sun
he gently brightened his body in a bubbling bath
of the Maeonian river, and to gratify Lyaeus
Pactolus murmured, pouring gold-bearing water
over its purple sands, and from the deep-rich lodes
the gilded fish rolled in the wealthy depth;
and the Satyrs playing, casting their feet into the air,
poured themselves into the river with somersaulting head,
of whom one swam self-borne, rowing with his hands,
and another, pressing his foot, face-down, in the surge and the swell,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
with feet stretched backward clove the wealth-flowing water;
and one dived to the bottom of the underwater channels
seeking down below the many-coloured catch of fishes,
stretching a blind hand over the swimming fish,
and again he left the deep, and held out fishes to Bacchus
reddened with the silt of the wealth-holding river;
and joining his fitted feet entwined together,
hunchbacked, vying with a Satyr, wandering Silenus,
headlong, self-tumbling, sprang into the stream
from on high into the deep gulf, and his hair touched the silt,
and he set his two feet in the gleaming swim,
mining the well-pebbled wealth of the river;
and one, showing his back to the air in the streams,
left his shoulder dry through the water, dipping his loins,
deep beside the bank, unshaken; and another, stretching his bare ears,
wetted his shaggy thighs in the glittering flood,
and his own coiling, natural tail lashed the stream.
And the god, raising his head and spreading his chest,
oaring with his hands, furrowed the golden calm;
and the waveless banks spat forth a self-made rose,
and the lily blossomed, and the Hours crowned the shores
while Bacchus bathed, and in the lightning-bright stream
the unbound locks of his dark hair reddened.
And once, hunting beneath a shady covert of the woods,
he was enchanted by the rosy-faced shape of a coeval youth.
For already beneath the ridge of Phrygia the boy at play,
Ampelos, had grown, a newly reared shoot of the Loves;
nor had the soft down of his reddening chin
scratched the snowy circles of his downless cheek,
the golden flower of youth; and from his back-flowing hair
the curling clusters ran upon his silvery shoulders
unbraided, and quivering together with the shrill breeze
were lifted lightly by the breath; and as the locks were drawn aside
the middle neck rose into view, growing bare,
and shot forth a gleam undimmed by shade, such as shines
the Moon half-revealed, splitting a moist cloud in the midst;
and from his rosy mouth a honey-breathing voice flowed forth;
and from his limbs the whole spring appeared; and as he walked
from his silvery foot the meadow reddened with roses;
and if he turned his eyes in the bright-shining circle
of his ox-eyed glances, the whole Moon shone.
Having him as companion, Dionysus, playing tenderly,
questioned, pouring forth a wondering voice upon his beauty
as a mortal, while the deceiver hid his immortal form:
"What father begot you? What heavenly womb bore you?
Which of the Graces gave you birth? What fair Apollo sowed you?
Tell me, friend, do not hide your race; if you come
as another wingless Eros, without arrows, apart from the quiver,
which of the blessed begot you, lying beside Aphrodite?
For I too tremble to name your mother Cypris,
lest I call Hephaestus or Ares your father.
But if you are the one they call Hermes, come from the heaven,
show me the light wings and the living wings of your sandals.
How do you keep your uncut hair hanging on your neck?
Surely you have not yourself come to me without lyre, without bow,
Phoebus of the unshorn locks, shaking your loosened curls?
If Cronides begot me, while you from an earthly stock
bear the short-lived blood of ox-horned Satyrs,
reign equal with me, a mortal with a god; for your
heavenly form will not disgrace the Olympian blood of Lyaeus.
But why do I call you of short-lived stock?
I know your blood, even if you wish to hide it;
the Moon, lying beside the Sun, bore you,
wholly like to graceful Narcissus; for you have an airy
likeness in form, the image of the horned Moon."

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Such words he spoke; and the young one gloried in the speech,
exulting, because his beauty surpassed his coeval youth
with a brighter form. And within the mountain thicket,
if the boy wove a song, Bacchus was delighted to hear;
if the youth stayed outside, he kept his cheeks unsmiling;
if a Satyr at the feast of the sport-loving table
beat the drums with his hands, striking a resounding noise,
and the youth was outside, pursuing the deer-killing hunt,
with the boy not present, he rejected the noisy echo;
if ever beside the flowery stream of Pactolus
he lingered and tarried, that he might bring as a banquet-gift
himself sweeter water to his king,
with the boy staying away, Bacchus was lashed with grief.
If the youth raised the bold pipe, the instrument of Libyan Echo,
sending a thin breath against his swollen cheek,
Bacchus thought he heard the Mygdonian piper,
whom divine Hyagnis bore, who to his own hurt contended with Phoebus,
pressing the pierced, double-sounding pipe of Athena;
but if the youth touched the same table together with him,
while the boy spoke, he had most delightful hearing,
but when the young one ceased, he had downcast cheeks;
and if, borne by the goad of deep-leaping desire,
Ampelos was set whirling in the dancer's beating of feet,
and entwined his hand in the dance with a sporting Satyr,
changing slantwise foot for foot in turn,
Bacchus, gazing, was stirred with jealous care.
If ever he kept company with the Sileni, if with any youth,
a coeval hunter, he ran together into the course of the chase,
jealous Dionysus restrained him, lest some servant of the Loves,
stricken with a like dart that beguiles the heart,
should turn aside the purpose of the light-minded boy,
and remove the lovely youth from Lyaeus,
as a youth in his prime delighting a coeval of his years.
But when he raised the thyrsus against a raging she-bear,
or hurled the fennel-rod at a mighty lioness,
he stretched his eye toward the west, looking sidelong at the air,
lest the death-bearing breath of Zephyrus should blow again,
as before the bitter wind slew the youth,
turning back the cast discus against Hyacinthus;
he feared lest Cronides, the love-winged bird of the Loves,
unforeseen, unreachable, should appear above Tmolus,
bearing the boy with sparing talons into the air,
like the Trojan boy, the servant of his cups;
he trembled too at the love-sick steerer of the sea,
lest, after the son of Tantalus, the mounter of golden chariots,
leading the winged car into the airy course,
the love-maddened Earth-shaker should snatch away Ampelos.
And he had a sweet dream on his dream-bearing bed,
and conversed in friendly words with the false image of the youth,
beholding the shadowy phantoms of a mimic form.
And if anything ill-shaped marred his lovely face,
this too was lovely to love-stricken Dionysus,
dearer than the whole skin of the youth; and if at the end
a tail hung upright, joined slantwise through his loins,
it was sweeter to Bacchus than sweet honey;
and the unkempt locks of his careless head
themselves the more delighted the eye of the love-maddened one.
By day he rejoiced in his companion; but he grieved ever
when night came on, when, no longer hearing the boy
with enchanted ears, he received the accustomed voice,
sleeping in the caves of Rhea, mother of a mighty son.
And one of the Satyrs, seeing him, was charmed by his divine form,
and stealing forth a secret, lovely voice, he said:
"O Persuasion, steward of the human heart, friend of love,
may this one youth alone, lovely, be gracious to me;

title: Dionysiaca
text:
and having him, like Bacchus, as my companion, I do not long
to dwell in the upper air as an exile, I did not wish
to be a god, not Phaethon who gives light to mortals, I draw no longing
for nectar, and I lack not ambrosia; I do not care
whether Ampelos loves me and Cronion hates me."
So he, tending the love-arrow beneath his heart of the Loves,
cried out a hidden word with a jealous voice,
holding his love-charm mingled with wonder. But Euios himself too,
stricken by the sweet sting of the youth,
cried out smiling to Cronides, his love-sick father:
"Grant me one favour, who love, O Phrygian Zeus;
while I was an infant, my nurse Rhea told me even now,
how you gave to Zagreus, the earlier Dionysus,
while he still cried 'Papa,' your fiery point of lightning,
and the crash of thunder and the airy shower of rain,
and he became, while still a babe, a second rain-bringing Zeus;
but I refuse your thunderbolt's heavenly fire,
I want no cloud, no crash of thunder; if you will,
give to fiery Hephaestus the spark of the bolt,
let Ares have the breastplate-covering of your clouds,
give to Hermaon the grace of the Zeus-sent shower of rain,
and let Apollo too lift the lightning of his father;
a lesser will is mine, dear one, for sport-loving Dionysus;
it is good for me to lift Semele's modest lightning,
the mother-slaying sparks of the thunderbolt are joyless.
I dwell in Maeonia; what has the upper air to do with Dionysus?
The beauty of my Satyr is dearer to me than Olympus.
Tell me, father, do not hide it; let your young one be a witness:
when the eagle lifted the boy beneath the heights of Teucrian Ida
with sparing, snatching foot to heaven,
how great a beauty the herdsman won, whom you joined to the table
of heaven, still breathing of the cattle-stalls?
Father Zeus, be gracious, wide-winged one; do not name to me
the Trojan wine-pourer, the servant of your cups,
because, bearing the gleam of a more radiant face,
lovely Ampelos puts the form of Ganymede to shame;
the Tmolian is fairer than the Idaean. And there are many
lovely rows of other youths, all of whom together,
if you wish, embrace, but leave one boy to Lyaeus."
Such words he spoke, stirred by the goad of desire;
not so, within the shaggy Magnesian wood,
did Apollo, herdsman of Admetus, tend his oxen,
stricken by the sweet sting of the love-bearing boy,
as much as Bacchus delighted his heart, playing with the youth.
And both sported, gone together within the thicket,
now casting into the air the wandering thyrsus,
now beside a shady flat rock, at other times among the crags
they went hunting the mountain-bred cubs of lions;
and once, alone, upon a desolate height of the bank,
playing in the sands of the fair-pebbled river,
they held a contest of sport-loving wrestling;
for them there was no tripod as prize, nor was a flowery cauldron
set out for victory, nor pasture-fed horses,
but the clear-sounding double-noted pipe of the Loves.
For both the strife was lovely; and in the midst
stood wanton Eros, winged Hermes of the contest,
weaving a garland of desire, narcissus plaited with hyacinth.
And both came into the midst, contestants of the Loves,
and wreathing their hands like a crown about each other's back,
binding the clasp of their forearms upon each other's waist,
they girt their sides with the yoked draught of the arm,
and lifted each other's body above the ground
with alternating hands; and Bacchus touched Olympus
in the honey-sweet wrestling, and had a double
lovely delight, lifted and lifting . . .

title: Dionysiaca
text:
and twining his hand about the wrist of Bromius's hand,
with hands joined, pressing the unequal grip,
he locked the fitted fingers in a double bond,
clasping the willing right hand of Dionysus.
There, coiling his hands about the waist of the youth,
Bacchus, pressing the body with love-maddened hands,
lifted Ampelos; but he, getting a grip on Bromius,
struck the hollow of his knee; and Euios, laughing sweetly,
struck on the soft sole by the coeval youth,
self-tumbling on his back, slipped down into the dust;
and the boy sat upon Bacchus, who lay willing upon the earth,
with bare belly; but he, rejoicing,
stretched out, sprawled this way and that, reclined upon the ground,
bearing on his belly the sweet weight; and straight up
setting the tip of his foot, ground into the earth, upon the sand,
he raised his back, turning it over, and showed a manhood
that spared its strength, and with a contending convulsion
he shook off, from his refusing hand, the burden of the Loves;
and slanting his side, bringing his elbow to the dust,
the cunning youth leapt upon the back of his adversary
obliquely upon his sides, and clasping above the loins
the tips of his foot to the hollow of the knee, fixing his track beside the ankle,
he girt the middle belly with a double bond,
squeezing the sides, coiling his sole beneath the knee
stretched out upright; and as both rolled in the dust
the sweat, herald of toil, ran down.
And late, when he was vanquished, though unvanquished,
bearing the likeness of his father Zeus the wrestler,
Dionysus was conquered willingly, because Zeus himself too,
great Zeus, self-tumbling, wrestling at the Alpheus,
knelt down, bending willing knees to Heracles.
Such was the sport-loving contest accomplished; and the delighted hand
of the youth lightly took up the double-noted pipe as prize.
And the young one, sweating, brightened his limbs in the stream
and washed off the wet dust; and as he bathed,
from his sweating skin a lovely radiance flowed.
Nor, having accomplished the limb-strong victory of wrestling,
did Bacchus, companion of the youth, cease his play,
but he set up a wind-swift contest of speed of foot.
And bringing the dappled suitors of the contest into the love,
for the first he set as gifts the Cybeleian instruments of Rhea,
cymbals with bronze backs and dappled fawnskins;
and the prizes of victory, the second, were Pan's companion,
the sweet-voiced syrinx and the resounding ox-hide,
heavy with bronze; and for the third Dionysus at play set
the reddening sand of the ready river.
And Bromius, marking out the ground divided for the course,
measured out the two ends of the stretched track,
setting up a ten-span sign of the running on the earth,
setting as the goal of the race a tall stake; and at the opposite end
he fixed the mark of the starting-line, raising the thyrsus on the shore;
and he roused the Satyrs to contend for victory.
And as sport-loving Lyaeus keenly called them,
Leneus first rushed forth, wind-footed, and beside him
high-footed Cissos and lovely Ampelos stood;
and trusting in the swift sole of the straight-running foot
they stood chosen, in a row; and from the ground
raising on high the track of his scoring tip,
Cissos was lifted by the stormy beat of his feet;
and warming the back of the one who hastened with his breath,
Leneus ran on, running together with the airy winds,
near in sight to the one running before, and of the hind foot
he struck the tracks that touched the poured dust;
and so much of the dividing line was left between the two,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
as the rod of a weaver's beam at the breast of a girl
gains, half-revealed, a space near the unbending breast.
And third was Ampelos, behind; and seeing him
jealous Dionysus melted, looking askance,
at the two contestants running before in the games,
lest perhaps they should win and Ampelos come last;
but the god helped, and breathing strength into him
made the boy swifter than the well-running storm;
and first of the two prize-bearers in the contest,
as they sped, plying his knees on the wet shore,
Cissos slipped, falling in the sandy mud,
and the unsteady rush of Leneus's knee was dragged
back, reining in the course of his feet; and the prize-bearers,
both, were left behind, and Ampelos snatched the victory.
And the aged Sileni shouted the Bacchic echo "Euion,"
amazed at the victory of the youth; and the soft-haired
young one received the first prizes, Leneus received the second,
holding envy, and recognized the jealous trick of Lyaeus
and his desire; and with shame-faced look he saw his coevals,
while Cissos bore the last prizes with a downcast hand.
11. The eleventh, watch, and you will mark lovely
Ampelos borne off by the man-slaying, snatching bull.
The contest was dissolved; and the lovely youth, glorying
in the sport-loving victory, leapt up, companion of his coeval Bacchus,
shifting his wandering sole around the rolling-footed circle,
leaning his all-white right hand on Dionysus;
and seeing him exulting, prancing on his feet with the double victory,
Iobacchus soothed him with a friendly word:
"Hasten again, dear boy, after the victory of swift feet
and after the contest on foot, to have yet a third other contest,
and swim, unreachable, with your coeval Bacchus as he swims.
Ampelos, having beaten me wrestling on the sands,
be lighter than Dionysus also in the streams,
and leaving the Satyrs still at play with their leapings,
hasten again, alone, to a third other contest;
may you win on land and in the waters, and after victory
I will crown your lovely locks with double clusters,
Lyaeus twice defeated, yet unvanquished.
This lovely stream suited you, it suited your beauty
alone, the beauty of your limbs, that Ampelos might be double,
cleaving the gold-gleaming waters with golden palm;
and as you stretch with naked limbs for victory,
the whole Pactolian water will adorn your beauty.
Grant the river an Olympian honour equal to your own, since Phaethon too
casts his rosy rays upon Ocean;
give Pactolus too your radiance, that Ampelos
may appear rising like the Morning Star; for this stream
flashes in both ways, with the reddening metal,
as you do with your limbs; and let the deep-rich stream
receive a youth of like colour and like form,
mingling beauty with beauty, that I may cry to the Satyrs:
how did rose come to rose? whence is one radiance mingled
both in the reddening skin and the flashing stream?
Would that here too, boy, there were the stream of Eridanus,
where the tears of the Heliades flow rich, that I might wash
your limbs in both, in gold and in amber.
But since I dwell very far from the Hesperian river,
I will come to Alybe, the neighbouring city, where nearby
the Geudis whitens with the draught of its wealth-bearing waters,
that you, washed from the river Pactolus,
Ampelos, I may brighten in the silvery streams too.
Let fair-flowing Hermus be a care to other Satyrs;
for it does not bear a stream of gold; but you alone
were a golden boy, may you have golden water too."
So speaking, he was borne through the water; and from the ground

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Ampelos was lifted up and went along with Lyaeus;
and sweet was the course to them both, end from end,
as they swam in circles in the rich river.
And the god, holding a watery contest of swiftness,
ran unsteady in the water, casting his bare
breast on the streams, and shaking his feet and rowing his hands
he scored the unshaken back of the wealthy calm,
now keeping his course in company with the coeval boy,
now darting past, but guarded, only so far as he would leave
Ampelos running near the path, his companion, beside neighbouring Bacchus;
at other times wheeling his palms, as though tiring in the wave,
the swift-kneed god willingly gave the victory to the water-traveller.
And after the river's flood Ampelos went to the midst of the thicket,
holding his neck proud with the river victory.
And he girt his locks with a serpent cluster,
bearing a fearful mimicry of serpent-haired Lyaeus;
and often, seeing the spangled tunic of Bromius,
he fastened on his limbs a counterfeit, embroidered raiment,
and bound his light foot with a purple buskin,
wearing a dappled robe on his skin; and in a mountain-stalled car
watching Iobacchus driving leopards
he proudly displayed the sports of the crag-loving beasts;
now mounting the mane of a mountain bear
he reined back the grim mane of the hurrying beast,
now he lashed the shaggy neck of a lion,
at other times, mounted high upon spangled backs,
unshaken, he delighted to drive an unbridled tiger.
And seeing him, Dionysus, with a gentle threat,
spoke, consoling him with a friendly, prophetic word,
pouring a pitying voice from reproachful lips:
"Where are you borne, dear boy? Why does the wood please you so much?
Stay with me, hunting with hunting Dionysus;
when I touch the feast, feast together with Lyaeus,
reveling, when I rouse the revel for the Satyrs.
The leopard does not trouble me, nor the jaw of the wild bear;
do not tremble at the greedy mouth of the mountain-ranging lioness;
only fear the horns of the implacable bull."
He spoke, pitying bold Ampelos; and the youth
heard the word with his ears, but his mind played within him.
There appeared a great sign to loving Dionysus
announcing Ampelos short-lived; for from a crag
bearing a freshly grown fawn upon its back
a horned serpent rose, broad with scales,
and bearing it above the altar, on top of the foundations,
it dashed it down, thrashed by its fearful horn,
headlong, self-tumbling; and as the mountain-ranging fawn
bleated its shrill cry, its wandering life-breath flew away;
and as a libation was to be, self-heralding, with a draught of blood
the stone altar reddened with bloody dews,
bearing the likeness of wine poured out. And beholding
Euios the serpent, the horned snatcher of the fawn,
learning the horned destroyer of the witless youth,
he mingled laughter with grief, and held an unsteady purpose,
double, and was divided in his heart, lamenting the youth
near to his doom, laughing for the grace of sweet wine.
Yet he went, companion of the lovely boy,
to the mountain, to the flat rock, and to the course of the accustomed hunt.
And seeing him, Bacchus still rejoiced; for the eyes
never bring satiety of loves to those who gaze.
Often too, when Bromius sat beside the table,
the youth piped, rendering an unwonted Muse,
and poured forth the whole song of the reeds; and at the boy's
fair singing, even if he broke the strain of the song,
Bacchus, springing above the floor with a wind-like leap,
clapped with his hands, loud-sounding, and while the youth

title: Dionysiaca
text:
was still singing, setting his lip about his mouth
he embraced, on the pretext of harmony, with a loving clasp;
and he swore by Cronides, that so great a rhythm singing Pan
never sang, nor clear-voiced Apollo.
And death-bearing Ate, seeing the bold youth
led astray from Lyaeus hunting in the mountains,
like to the graceful youth, his coeval boy,
soothed Ampelos the deluder with such a word,
doing a favour to the stepmother of Phrygian Dionysus:
"Your friend, fearless boy, is called Dionysus in vain;
what reward of companionship have you won? You do not drive Lyaeus's
wondrous chariot, you do not rein a leopard.
Maron has won the car of your Bromius, stretching his hand
with the beast-driving whip and the well-stoned bridle;
what gift is this you have from straight-thyrsus Lyaeus?
The Pans have the lyre and the din of sweet-sounding pipes,
and to the Satyrs your steward Dionysus gave the loud-roaring
circle of ox-hide, and the mountain-ranging
Bassarids themselves sit upon the backs of lions.
What gifts worthy of your friendship do you bring,
loved in vain by Bacchus, the driver of leopards?
Often, seated high upon the Phoebean car,
Atymnius, conspicuous on high, drove, cleaving the air;
you have heard of Abaris himself, whom into the air-walking course
Phoebus escorted on a flying, wandering arrow;
Ganymede too steered the eagle in the air,
the false winged Zeus, the father of your Lyaeus;
but Bacchus never lifted up Ampelos, the bird of the Loves,
raising your body with unscratching talons.
The Trojan wine-pourer was better, who has the court of Zeus,
the house. But you, boy, still bearing a longing for the car,
refuse to drive a colt into the unsteady course,
because, shaken by the swift-whirling draught of its feet,
the stormy horse shakes off its driver;
the raging horses dashed Glaucus down to the earth,
and Pegasus, swift-flying, sharing the Poseidonian blood
of the common stock, the airy offspring of the Earth-shaker,
shook off Bellerophon headlong.
Come with me to the herd, where clear-voiced herdsmen are,
and lovely oxen; and seated upon a bull
I will make you a conspicuous, ox-driving charioteer;
for your king, watching, will praise you far more,
bull-formed Dionysus, seated on the waist of a bull.
This is a course without fear, since even Europa, being a woman,
a maiden, mounted on bovine backs,
gripping the horn with her hands and not needing a bridle."
So speaking she persuaded him, and the goddess sank into the air.
And from a crag a wandering bull ran down,
unforeseen, and his tongue, the witness of his thirst,
he held forth from his throat with opening lips,
and drank; and about the boy, as though a herdsman present,
he stood, wholly like one who knew him; nor did he hold his horn
slantwise from his brow; and as the resistless bull
drank thickly, belching up the draught from his capacious gullet,
the dripping moisture of the dew wetted the youth,
as though a prophet of things to come, that with an earthly draught the oxen,
toiling about one endless circling turning-post,
water the vine-clad fruit with their waters.
And the bold boy stood above the bovine brow,
handling the curved horn with a fearless hand;
and goaded by the sweet sting of the woodland-grazing ox,
he wished to drive the unyoked, mountain-running bull.
And plucking leaves beside the deep-rushed grass
he wove a counterfeit scourge of green withies
with sharper shoots, and with a much-twisted cluster
bending the crooked rings he made the shape of a bridle;
and with dewy leaves he adorned the body of the bull,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
and bound reddening roses round about its back,
and hung lilies and narcissus on its brow,
draping a purpling anemone on its neck;
and on either side he gilded both horns,
drawing up with his deep-digging hands yellow clay
from the neighbouring river. And spreading on high upon its back
a spangled hide, he mounted the spine of the bull;
and stretching a counterfeit whip along the bovine sides,
as though a fine-maned colt, he lashed his own bearer.
And the bold one cried out a word to bull-faced Mene:
"Yield to me, horned Selene, driver of oxen;
for I too am become horned in both ways, and I drive a bull."
Such a boastful word he cried to the rolling Moon.
And jealous Selene watched through the air with her eye
Ampelos borne by the man-slaying, snatching bull,
and sent him an ox-driving gadfly; and he, scored
in his body by the bitter, restless, roaming sting,
ran about the rough ridge, like a horse.
And the boy, seeing the unyoked bull with maddening sting
striking his track upon the high-crested hills,
terrified, before his doom, prayed with a wailing voice:
"Stand still today, bull, and tomorrow you will go swiftly;
do not kill me on a desolate height of rock,
that Bacchus may not hear of my doom unannounced.
Do not be angry, bull, because I gilded your horn;
do not be jealous, because Bacchus guards my friendship.
But if you kill me and care nothing for Dionysus,
and no pity holds you for a wailing charioteer,
because I am young, because I am also a friend of Lyaeus,
carry me to the Satyrs, and there, bull, you will overpower me,
that I may obtain, after death, my dust much-bewailed;
yes, I beseech you, dear bull; and I will think it a consolation,
that Dionysus, tearless, laments my doom.
If you deceive your horned charioteer
who has a likeness in form to your bull-faced shape,
become voiced and tell my death to Lyaeus:
bull, hostile to your Demeter and to Dionysus,
while Bromius grieves, bountiful Deo grieves with him."
Such a word the rosy youth spoke, neighbour of Hades,
ill-fated; and darting with the twin hoof of his feet
over the mountain's high peaks, hard to climb, the raging ox
shook off the youth headlong from his back;
and he fell self-tumbling; and as he fell upon his neck-joint
his slanting neck was split, faintly creaking;
and rolling him back over the ground in a whirl
with the sharp point of its horn it cast him down.
And the corpse was headless; and of the unburied corpse
the white body reddened with the reddening gore.
And one of the Satyrs, seeing lovely Ampelos
lying in the dust upon the ground, came as ill messenger to Bacchus.
And the god, hearing, ran swiftly like the breezes;
not so great a course did Heracles accomplish, when the Nymphs
hid soft Hylas in their jealous streams,
a bridegroom kept by the wet, snatching girl,
as then Bacchus rushed, mountain-running; and in the dust
he wept over the boy lying there, watching him as though alive.
And he wrapped a cloak about him, the breathless one, fastening from his shoulder
the fawnskin upon the cold breast,
and, though he was a corpse, bound buskins on his feet;
and roses and lilies he scattered on his skin, and about his hair,
as for a short-lived one fallen by a sharp sting,
he hung up the flower of the swift-perishing anemone;
and he gave a thyrsus to his hand, and covered him with his own robe
of purple; and as a gift from his uncut head
he cut one lock and laid it on the witnessing corpse
as a last offering; and taking ambrosia from his mother Rhea
he poured it on the wounds, whence the youth, changing his form,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
transferred the fragrant ambrosia into his own fruit.
And as the graceful corpse was stretched upon the ground,
no pallor was poured about the rosy body; and of the swift-fated one
the graceful locks of the love-bearing head
quivered upon his face in the sparing breezes;
and there was a lovely one, dust-covered. And about the corpse
the Sileni groaned, and the Bacchae wailed.
Nor did beauty leave him, even though he died; and he lay
a corpse like a Satyr, wholly like one laughing, as though ever
pouring from voiceless lips a honey-sweet voice.
And gazing on the corpse, grief-soothing Dionysus
raised a wailing voice, holding a mirthless look:
"Let the jealous thread of the Fates fall; do bulls themselves too
prove jealous over youths, like the winds?
What Zephyrus, after Phoebus, assailed Dionysus too?
Blessed was Phoebus's Atymnius; for from a youth
he won this name; and of a Therapnaean youth himself
Apollo lifts a flower named for the medicine of the youth,
inscribing the dirge upon the petals of the hyacinth;
what garland have I too for my locks, or what flowers
do I wield that are voiced, consolations of my boy's grief?
But avenging your death, dragging him to slaughter,
I will lead the wandering bull to your tomb, untimely one.
I would not kill your slayer with an ox-axe,
that he might win a doom equal, his brow battered,
to bulls being slaughtered; but I would tear open the whole
bitter belly of the bull with the point of my own horn,
because it cast you down with its long-horned spike.
Blessed is the Earth-shaker, since he loved a neighbour of the homeland
of my boy, a Phrygian youth, and bearing him
led him up to the golden house of Zeus, a citizen of Olympus,
and to him, when he hastened to the horsemanship of Aphrodite,
he gave the dry car, the bridal chariot of Hippodameia.
I alone have a young one untimely; for lovely
Ampelos saw no life-giving marriage, nor did this youth
yoke my bridal car upon the marriage-bed,
but dying he left grief to the once-griefless Dionysus.
Not yet, dear boy, has Persuasion left your mouth,
but even though you are dead it dwells on your breathless lips;
and though you are a corpse your cheeks still glisten,
your eyes still laugh, and the snowy palms
of your two hands are still there,
and the shrill breezes still stir your lovely locks;
the death-bearing season has not quenched the roses of your limbs,
but all these things are still kept for you. Alas for the Loves,
what need was there that you should drive an implacable bull?
If the longing for storm-footed horses dismayed you,
why did you not tell me, that from neighbouring Ida
I might bring a chariot here, and from the ancient stock
might bring to you the Trojan race of heavenly horses,
plundering the homeland of Ganymede, whom Ida reared
with a body equal to yours, whom from the man-slaying bulls
high-flying Zeus lifted with sparing talons;
if you truly longed to slay beasts in the mountains,
why did you not tell me that there was need of a car?
And then you would have driven the harmless circle of my chariot,
and, receiving the untouched reins of my Rhea,
unshaken, would have lashed the car of gentle serpents.
No longer do you sing the wine-song with the Satyrs,
no longer do you command the castanet-loving Bassarids,
no longer do you hunt together with Dionysus hunting.
Alas, that Hades is not gentle, nor over a corpse
does he receive the splendid gifts of the deep-rich metal,
that I might make Ampelos, who died, alive again;
alas, that Hades is never persuaded; but if he should wish it,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
I would freely give him all the gleaming wealth of Eridanus,
plundering the river trees, and I would bring
the flashing, gleaming Erythraean stone of the Indians
and all the silver of wealthy Alybe, and in exchange for the corpse
of my boy I would give the whole golden Pactolus."
So speaking he lamented the sweet corpse; and seeing him
lying in the dust he cried again with a mournful voice:
"Father Zeus, if you love me, and if you know the toil of loves,
set Ampelos speaking again for one hour,
a last hour and only, that he may utter one word:
'Why do you grieve, Dionysus, the one you do not raise with groanings?
I have ears, and I do not hear you crying out,
I have eyes, and I do not see you grieving;
grief-soothing Dionysus, do not shed tears for me,
but leave off your grief, since beside the murderous spring
the Naiads groan and Narcissus does not hear,
Phaethon does not know the mournful grief of the Heliades.'
Alas, that my father did not beget me a mortal, that I might be
a companion of the youth even in Hades, nor in Lethe
leave lovely Ampelos, fallen, alone.
In longing for a youth, Apollo is more blessed,
holding the beloved name of his boy; would that I too
were Ampeloeis, as Apollo is Hyacinthius.
How long do you sleep, and no longer, boy, do you dance?
Why today do you no longer go to the streams of the river
holding a fine-watered pitcher? In the mountain-stalled thicket
your season has come again for the accustomed dance.
If you are angry, dear boy, with love-stricken Dionysus,
speak to the Sileni, that I may hear your word.
If a lion overpowered you, I will destroy them all,
all that the crag of Tmolus bears, nor will I ever spare
the lions of our own Rhea, but I will overpower them,
if your slayers were born with grim jaws;
if a leopard cast down your body, flower of the Loves,
no longer will I drive the spangled body of leopards;
there are other beasts, and Artemis, mistress of the whole hunt,
drives a horn-drawn car of deer;
wearing a fawnskin robe I will ride on a car of fawns;
if shameless boars slew you, seizing them in one
I will kill them all, and I will not leave one boar alone
still living, left to the Archer-goddess;
but if a wanton bull slew you, with a sharp thyrsus
I would utterly destroy the bovine race, root and branch."
So he lamented. But Love stood near him
bearing the form of a shaggy, horn-drawn Silenus,
holding a thyrsus, and fastening a dappled skin on his body
he propped his frame on an old man's fennel-staff;
and to wailing Bromius he cried a consoling voice:
"With another love loose the sparks of your loves,
changing your goad to a new youth, a fresh one,
forgetting the dead; for of an older love
the medicine is always a new love; for time
does not know how to destroy love, even if it learns to hide all things.
But if you wish the pain-killing remedy of your grief,
embrace a better boy; desire knows how to wither desire.
The Laconian youth troubled Zephyrus; but when he died,
lovely Aetes, seeing Cyparissus the youth,
found a consolation for Amyclaean Hyacinthus.
If you wish, ask the gardener; for when he sees
a dust-covered flower lying on the ground, the ploughman
plants another, newer, as a medicine for the perished one.
Listen, that I may tell you a tale of men of old:
there was once a soft boy, surpassing his coeval youth,
beside the flood of Maeander, the many-branched river,
tall in his delicate form, swift of foot, with hair
straight, downless; and on both his cheeks
a natural Grace was leaping upon his face

title: Dionysiaca
text:
with modest eyes, and from his eyelids ever
a far-shooting radiance flowed as his beauty cast its darts;
and he had a body wholly like milk, and about the white
a rose flushed, half-seen, with a two-coloured glow.
Him his dear father called Calamus, who through the earth
billowing below, drawing his crooked stream into the light,
creeping unseen, a slanting traveller beneath the ground,
leaping up sharply lifts his neck above the earth,
inner-recessed Maeander, leading his bosom-hidden water.
Such was lovely Calamus the swift. And the youth,
rosy-armed, delighted in his lovely coeval Carpus,
who won so great a beauty as no mortal man has won;
for if this youth had been among the men of former times,
he would have become the bridegroom of fair-haired Dawn,
holding a fairer form, with rosy skin alone surpassing
the splendour of Cephalus and the look of Orion;
nor would Deo have embraced with fruitful palm
Iasion as bridegroom, nor Selene Endymion;
but that youth, perhaps, on account of his nobler form,
as one husband of both, would have wedded the beds of both goddesses,
sharing the much-furrowed bed of fair-haired Deo,
and holding jealous Mene as a common bedfellow.
Such was the lovely one, dear to Calamus, flower of the Loves,
holding beauty; and both coevals upon the bank
of the neighbouring much-winding river sported together.
For them there was a winding course of the double track, and for both
there was strife; Calamus ran on like the breezes,
and bearing the elm as starting-line and the olive as turning-post
he ran along the river's banks from end to end . . .
and swift-kneed Calamus willingly fell to the ground,
and left a willing victory to graceful Carpus.
And as the boy bathed, the playful youth bathed with him,
and again they held another like contest in the waters,
and slow he swam in the streams, leaving Carpus
to go ahead, that swimming behind, cleaving the swell with his hands,
he might come second beside the ankles of swimming Carpus,
watching the free back of the youth running before.
And there was a course from the watery starting-line; both contended,
which would beat which, that he might come back returning
to the bank, crossing both ends of the twin turning-post,
to the land on the other side, with their palms rowing;
and the flood was his path; but ever coming near him
the boy, sparing the rush of his hurrying hand,
watched the rosy-skinned fingers of their swimming hands;
and Calamus, leading the way, reined back his rush,
and yielded to the youth; and he ran on rowing his hands,
the storm-like boy, stretching his neck above the swell;
and now Carpus would have mounted from the surge onto the land,
and after the victory on land would have gained the river victory,
but Aetes, blowing against him, dashed him down,
and the implacable one slew the sweet boy; for as the youth's
throat opened, numberless water rushed in.
And Calamus, fleeing the storms of the jealous wind,
sank, away from the youth, onto the neighbouring shores;
and perceiving his friend not present and not hearing,
groaning lovingly he bellowed with a mournful voice:
"Naiads, speak, what Aetes snatched away Carpus?
Yes, I beseech you, grant me a last favour, come to another
spring, and flee the death-bearing water of my father,
nor drink the stream that slew Carpus.
Surely my begetter did not slay the youth; but in envy
Aetes, after Phoebus, destroyed Carpus for Calamus too,
and perhaps, longing for him, struck him with a jealous storm,
bringing a contrary breeze upon the youth after the discus.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Not yet has my star risen, bathed in the streams,
not yet has my Morning Star shone; but with Carpus
sinking in the streams, why should I still look on the light?
Naiads, speak, who quenched the light of the Loves?
Do you still linger, boy? Why does the water please you so much?
Surely you have not found a better friend in the waters, with whom staying
you have cast the longings of wretched Calamus to the winds?
If one love-stricken Naiad-Nymph snatched you,
tell me, and I will arm against them all; but if the wedding hymn
of marriage with our sister of the Loves delights you,
tell me, and even in the streams I will light your bridal chamber.
Carpus, do you float past me, forgetting the accustomed bank?
I grew weary calling you, and you do not hear me crying out.
If Notus or bold Eurus blew, let him wander himself,
pitiless, danceless, wanton, an enemy of the Loves;
if Boreas overpowered you, I will go to Oreithyia.
But if a wave covered you and did not reverence your form,
and my father took you with the unsparing draught of the wave,
let him receive his own son too in the man-slaying waters,
and let him hide Calamus near perished Carpus.
But falling headlong, where wandering Carpus died,
I will quench my hot love, drinking the Acherousian water."
He spoke, gushing forth the stream of his eyes; and about the corpse
he cut his dark lock with mournful iron,
which he had grown, which he had tended, and held out the mourning hair
to his father Maeander, and spoke his last word:
"Receive, after my locks, my body too; for I cannot
look upon the light for one dawn apart from Carpus;
Carpus and Calamus have one life, and both have won
a like goad of Love upon the earth; and let one watery
death be for us both, even in the streams.
Make, Naiads, on the high river-bank
a common cenotaph for us both, and about the tomb
let a word be inscribed in mournful letters:
'I am the grave of Carpus and Calamus, whom of old, both
longing for each other, the implacable water slew.'
And for love-stricken Calamus, though he is a brother,
dying, tear off one small cluster of his hair,
but for perished Carpus shear all his locks."
He spoke, and self-tumbling slipped into the stream,
drinking the child-slaying water of his refusing father.
And Calamus gave to reeds the shape named for him,
of like growth, and Carpus grew the fruit of the field.
Such things consoling, with a friendly word
did impetuous Eros soothe, lightening the sweet sting for Dionysus.
And his heart was lashed all the more with mournful grief
through the untimely doom of the youth.—And the unsteady
daughters of Lycabas, the storm-footed father,
the rosy-faced Hours, went to the house of the Sun;
of whom one, sending around her snow-shaded face
a thin gleam of dark-clouded radiance,
joined her cold feet to a hailstorm sandal,
and binding her locks upon her wet head
fastened a rain-bearing veil upon her brow,
and held a green wreath on her head, and with a snowy
white girdle covered her frosted breast;
and another spat out the mortal-delighting breeze
of the swallow-winds, breathing, and of her Zephyr-loving head
she girt the springtime hair with a dewy bond,
laughing flowery, and quivering through her robe
the long-shadowed fragrance of the morning, opening rose,
she wove a double revel for Adonis and Cytherea;
another Hour, together with her sisters, came as the harvest-Hour,
and the ear of grain, bristling round about with topmost clusters,
she lifted in her right hand, and the blade of the sharp-cutting sickle,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
the messenger of the harvest, and the girl's body was girt
with white linen, and as she whirled in the dance
through her thin raiment the mysteries of her thighs appeared,
and as her face was loosed, the moist sweats
were dampened on her cheeks by the hotter Phaethon;
and another, the leader of the well-ploughed dance,
bound an olive shoot on her hairless temple
drenched with the waters of the seven-channeled river Nile,
and tending the thin, withering hair of her temple
she had a parched body, since, being autumnal,
she had shorn her tree-like hair to the leaf-shedding winds;
for not yet, with the plaited clusters of golden tendrils,
did vine-clusters flow upon the neck of the nymph,
nor, made drunk beside the wine-loving wine-press,
did the moisture of the dew of purple Maronian wine intoxicate her,
nor did the wandering ivy run up in a whirl;
but then the appointed time came, for the sake of which the Hours themselves
ran together in company to the house of the Sun.
12. In the twelfth delight your heart, where as a new flower of the Loves
Ampelos sent up his form into the vine-clad fruit.
So they, beside the brows of western Ocean,
were sailing to the halls of the generative Sun.
And as they journeyed the star Hesperus met them,
leaping from the hall; and hastening forth herself,
newly appeared, rose Selene, driver of oxen.
And before the eyes of the life-bearing Charioteer
they bent their fruitful track. He, having just finished his course,
returned from the air; and the radiant Morning Star
set down, near the four-horse car of the fiery-eyed driver,
the hot harness and the starry whip,
cleansing beside the streams of neighbouring Ocean
the bodies of the fire-fed horses, dripping with sweat;
and the colts, shaking the wet manes of their necks,
stamped with gleaming hooves in the glowing manger.
And the daughters of Chronos, around the fiery throne,
flying in a circle about the unwearied Charioteer,
the twelve circling Hours greeted the four,
handmaids of the Sun, companions of the glowing car,
ministers of Lycabas in turn; for to the primeval
ruler of the whole universe they bent a slavish neck.
And the grape-tending Hour cried out a word to him,
holding the autumnal sickle as witness of her supplication:
"Sun, grain-giver, planter, lord of fruits,
when will the vineyards grow the wine-bearing cluster?
And to which of the blessed does Aion betroth this honour?
Yes, I beseech you, do not hide it, for I alone
of all my sisters am without honour; for I grow no fruit,
no ear of grain, no meadow, and not the rain of Zeus."
She spoke; and the Sun encouraged the nurse
of the fruit to be, and beside the opposite wall
raising his finger he showed the circling girl
the unequal tablets of Harmony, on which there lie
in one all the oracles, all that were ordained for the world
that the prophetic hand of first-born Phanes inscribed,
and embroidered with his pen the fitting house for each.
And Hyperion, the steward of fire, spoke a word:
"On the third tablet, whence the wine-fruit shall come,
you will learn, where the Lion and the Virgin are; and on the fourth,
who is the sceptred lord of the cluster, where, drawing sweet nectar,
with painted hand Ganymede lifts the cup."
As the god spoke thus, the vine-loving girl ran,
turning her eyes about, and beside the wall of the oracle
she beheld the first tablet, coeval with the endless world,
bearing in one all things, all that the sceptred Ophion
accomplished, all that aged Cronos achieved, when, cutting

title: Dionysiaca
text:
his father's male plough-share, he ploughed the bridal water,
sowing the unsown back of the daughter-bearing sea,
who once received his stone son in his gaping throat,
feasting on the counterfeit body of the lying Zeus;
and the stone delivered the brood of the children hidden within,
casting forth the burden of the pregnant throat.
But when the storm-footed Hour, the handmaid of Phaethon,
beheld the fire-bright victory of Zeus as he fought
and the hailing war-strife of the Cronian snow,
she looked in turn at the neighbouring tablet; and that one held
how the pine bore mortal offspring in travail, or whence suddenly,
unfolding its tree-like, generative childbearing,
the pine cast up an unsown, self-made son,
and whence rain-bringing Zeus flooded all the cities,
bringing the heaped-up water in towering seas,
how Notus from Boreas, and Eurus from Libs scourging,
lifted the wandering ark of Deucalion, neighbour of the Moon,
into an air-walking voyage, without a harbour.
And when the minister of Lycabas ran over the third tablet
with well-footed sole, the coiling girl halted,
gazing at the fated, many-turning oracles of the world,
reddening letters, inscribed with wise vermilion,
all that the various-storied, primeval mind had written,
such things prophesying, and she read on the tablets:
Argus, herdsman of Hera, will change into the shape of a bird,
keeping the bright form of his grim eyelids; but also
Harpalyce herself, after the bed of sinful unions,
having butchered her son for her daughter-wedding father,
will row her airy, winged journey
as a storm-like bird; and the web-toiling Philomela
will be a swallow with a spangled neck, twittering,
crying out the testimony of her tongueless silence,
having written speaking devices on a wise tunic;
and Niobe, beside the foot of Sipylus, a stone with sense,
lamenting with stony tears the rank of her children,
will stand as a piteous statue. And there will be a neighbour,
Pyrrhus, a Phrygian stone, love-maddened, still holding for Rhea
a lawless goad of unwedded unions,
and Thisbe a moist water, and Pyramus, both coevals,
longing for each other; and of the fair-crowned girl
Smilax, Crocus, longing, will be a flower of the Loves;
and after the bridal turning-post of the storm-footed weddings
and after the apples of the Paphian, into the shape of a lion
Artemis will goad transformed Atalanta.
And the restless Hour passed over all these things in one,
until she came to the place where fiery Hyperion
declared the symbols of prophecy to the storm-like girl,
where the Lion was wrought, radiant, where also
the starry Virgin herself was embroidered in a counterfeit shape
holding the wine-dark cluster, the summer-born flower of the fruit;
there the daughter of Chronos rested her feet, and read this:
Cissos, the high-flying, lovely youth, creeping into a plant,
will be the coiling ivy even among shoots; and of the youth
Calamus the upright reed, bent by the breezes,
will appear a thin shoot of the growth-giving field,
a prop of the vines; and changing his form into a plant,
Ampelos gives his name to the vine-clad fruit.
But when the harvest-girl beheld these oracles,
she sought that place, where beside the neighbouring wall
the image of Ganymede was inscribed with a fashioned form,
dripping the nectar-moisture from a golden cup,
where was the four-fold voice of the inscribed words;
there the grape-loving goddess reveled, and the nymph found
these oracles kept for ivy-bearing Lyaeus:
Zeus granted to Phoebus to have the prophetic laurel,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
and reddening roses to rosy-skinned Cyprogeneia,
the grey-green olive-shoot to grey-eyed Athena,
and ears of grain to Demeter, and the vines to Dionysus.
Such things did the Bacchus-loving girl behold in the writings;
and rejoicing she darted off, and taking her sisters
she passed into the stream of eastern Ocean,
running together with the horsemanship of Phaethon.—But for Lyaeus
there was no remedy, with his comrade fallen, nor was there
memory of the dance; but with his mind shaken by the goad of love
he sang bitter dirges, and in careless silence
he left the bronze back of the unsounding ox-hide;
nor did the lyre delight him. And as, with mirthless face,
loving Dionysus piteously wailed,
the stream of the Lydian, reedy Hermus was stayed,
though it rolled swiftly with the windy beat of its current,
and longed not to flow; and with its deep-rich stream
saffron Pactolus reined back its mournful water,
bearing the likeness of a downcast man; and about the corpse
Sangarius checked the back-rushing draught of its spring channels,
pouring its Phrygian stream; and the breathless image
of the Tantalid, ill-bearing mother, drenched by the groanings,
shed double tears, as Dionysus lamented;
and the pine, wailing, companion of its coeval fir,
whispered faintly; and the laurel herself,
being the tree of unshorn Phoebus, shook off her hair
in the mournful winds; and the sleek, unpruned olive
poured its leaves to the ground, even though it was Athena's plant.
So, as tearless Dionysus groaned with longing,
the dread, unbound threads of the Fate were turned again;
and consoling the wail of grieving Dionysus
steadfast-worded Atropos cast up an inspired voice:
"Your youth lives, Dionysus, and he will not cross
the bitter water of Acheron; for your wail has found a way to undo
the unbending, recoverable threads of unswerving Fate;
Ampelos has not died, even though he died; for into a lovely
drink, into sweet nectar, I will change your boy;
him, with the dancing beat of the well-rolling hand,
the double-noted pipe, beating out the harmony of the feast,
will hymn, holding a Phrygian rhythm or a Dorian song;
or in the theatres a rhythmic man will sing of him,
pouring the Ismenian echo of the Aonian reed,
or to the dwellers of Marathon; and the Mysians will cry "Euoi"
for lovely Ampelos along with vine-clad Lyaeus.
And leaving the crooked, serpent girdle of your locks
you will wreathe clusters of grapes about your hair,
bringing envy to Phoebus, because he wields with his hand the mournful
tree-borne dirges of the weeping hyacinths,
while you have a drink, the rest of the mortal race,
the earthly likeness of heavenly nectar, and your flowery youth
will put to shame the boast of the Amyclaean boy;
and if that one's city raises warlike bronze,
your youth's land too will grow, light-bringing,
the moist rain of the reddening river-dew,
luxuriant wholly with gold, and rejoicing not in iron;
if it glories about the stream of a sounding river,
the Pactolian water is better than the Eurotas.
Ampelos, you gave grief to griefless Dionysus,
that, when your honey-dropping wine is grown,
you might give delight to the whole four-fold world
and a libation to the blessed and gladness to Dionysus;
lord Bacchus wept, that he might loose the tears of mortals."
So speaking the goddess went, companion of her sisters.
And a great wonder appeared to mournful Bacchus, the witness;
for the lovely corpse, springing up like a creeping serpent,
Ampelos, self-made, changed his own shape,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
and became a sweet flower; and as the corpse was transformed
his belly was a tall bush, and the tips of his hands
put forth branches, and his feet were rooted,
his curls were grape-clusters, and the very fawnskin
was shaped into a many-figured flower of the growing fruit,
and the vine-cluster was his long-shadowed neck,
and like to his elbow the crooked tendril stretched,
swelling with grapes, and as his head was transformed
the bent, curved clusters mimicked the shape of his horn.
There were endless rows of plants; and self-made
the vine-clad row, coiling its green tendrils,
girt the neighbouring trees with the new wine-dark fruit.
And there was a new wonder, since the boy at play then,
coiling his slanting foot about a high-leaved plant,
high-flying Cissos made his form into a tree,
and became a curved shoot named for him, and girt
the newly grown row of vines with a crooked bond.
And with friendly leaves he shaded the overshadowed temple,
and intoxicated his locks from the wine-loving leaves,
Dionysus exulting; and of the growing boy
he plucked the fruit of the harvest just now ripening.
And the god, self-taught, without foot, outside the wine-press,
pressing the cluster with the heavy fruit of his palm,
squeezing the travail of drunkenness with entwining hands,
revealed the new-flowing mass of the purple fruit,
and found the sweet drink; the white fingers of wine-pouring
Dionysus reddened as they were drenched.
And he held a curved cup, the horn of an ox; and of the sweet-drinking
dew Bacchus tasted with the tips of his lips,
tasted also of the fruit, and delighting his heart with both
he cast up a word from his proud throat:
"Ambrosia and the nectar of my Zeus, Ampelos, you bring forth;
bearing two beloved shoots, the fruit, Apollo
ate not of the laurel, and drank not from the hyacinth;
no ear of grain travails a sweet drink; be gracious, Deo;
I will give to mortals food, and not only drink.
Ampelos, your doom too is lovely; truly the threads
of Fate herself were softened for you and for your beauty,
for you even Hades was pitying, for you even Persephone
herself changed her harsh purpose,
and brought you, a corpse, to life for your brother Dionysus.
You did not die as Atymnius died; not the water of Styx,
not the flame of Tisiphone, you did not see the eye of Megaera;
you still live, boy, even though you died; nor did the water
of Lethe hide you, no common tomb holds you; but the earth
herself was ashamed to cover your form;
but my father made you a plant, honouring you as a son,
lord Cronion changed your body into sweet nectar.
Nature did not, as on the inscribed Therapnaean clusters,
carve a dirge upon your unweeping leaves;
you keep your own colour, boy, even among shoots;
your end has proclaimed the radiance of your limbs;
your reddening form has not yet abandoned you.
But avenging your death I will never cease
pouring your wine as a libation upon your slayer
as he is sacrificed, the man-slaying one. And you bring reproach to the Hamadryads
with your lovely leaves; and from your fragrant clusters
the moistures of your Loves breathe about me.
When shall I mingle the fruit of the apple in the bowl?
When shall I drop the fig into the nectar-cup?
The fig and the apple alike have grace as far as the teeth.
No other plant can contend with your grape-clusters;
not the rose, not the fair-coloured narcissus, not the anemone,
not the lily, not the hyacinth equals the shoot of Bacchus,
because with the new drops of much-pressed fruit
your drink will receive all the flowers; one drink will be

title: Dionysiaca
text:
mingled with all, and will come to one fragrance,
blended with flowers of every kind; for your flower
will adorn the whole springtime meadow-grass.
Yield to me, famed-archer, because you girt your griefless locks
with a mournful bond of many-wailing leaves;
dirges are inscribed upon your petals; but if in a garden
the famed-archer bears a garland, I draw sweet wine,
and put about myself a lovely garland, and the sweet-drinking
Ampelos himself I lift wholly within my heart.
Yield to the grape-rich one, glittering-helmed; for bloody Ares
pours gore as a libation, while the vine-clad one pours to Dionysus
the reddening dew of the wine-drenched cluster.
Deo, you are plundered after Pallas; for the olives
bring forth no gladness, and no ear of grain charms a man,
the pear has honey-sweet fruit, the myrtle grows
fragrant flowers, but they do not, with a mind-charming fruit,
cast human cares to the winds;
I have become far better than you both; for when our
wine is not present, joyless are the meals of the table,
when wine is not present, uncharmed are the dances.
If you can, grey-eyed one, drink the fruit of your olive;
my splendid-gifted harvest has conquered your plant,
because with your sleek oil athlete-men, joyless,
anoint their bodies; but the sorely-suffering man,
having cast wife or daughter into a common doom,
or having grief for perished children or mother or father,
when he tastes sweet wine,
will shake off the gloomy, swelling mass of his grief.
Ampelos, even after death you gladden the heart of Bacchus;
with all my limbs I will mingle your drink."
And all about, the trees with downward-nodding head,
like a suppliant, bend the curving neck,
and the aged palm bowed down its high-stretched leaves;
about the apple-tree you stretch your feet, about the fig-tree
spreading your hands you lean upon them, and your
harvest the handmaids lighten, as a mistress,
when, with the coiling beat of your stretching leaves,
you rise above the shoulder of the attendants; and of the neighbouring plants
the soft, many-coloured leaves of the wide-scattered clusters,
as though you slept, quiver upon your face,
cooling breezes with sparing breaths,
as an attendant shakes a thin, accustomed fan,
bearing an artificial breeze, cool, for her king.
But if you bring the noonday threat of Phaethon,
the Etesian breeze, leading the way for your cluster, comes,
lulling to rest the thirsty star of fiery Maira,
when the course of the summer-born Hour heats you,
warming with Sirian vapour the dew as it ripens.
He spoke, exulting, and cast away his former cares,
holding the fragrant harvest, the medicine for the youth.
And these things are sung about the vine-clad cluster,
how it became named for the youth. But of the singers
there is another, older story, how once upon the earth
from heaven the fruit-bearing Olympian ichor flowed
and brought forth the drink of the Bacchic cluster, and on the crags
self-grown, untended, the fruit of the harvest grew;
and not yet was the vine named for the gardener, but in the thickets
the wild vine, flourishing among the much-curved parsley-plants,
put forth a vine-rich wood of wine-bearing plants,
gushing up the moist, crammed mass of its dew;
and there was a great row, where, creeping up in order,
cluster upon cluster, reddening, shook as it wandered;
of which one, half-finished, swelling its travail,
flushing in changing hues, appeared with two-coloured fruit;
another, whitening, ripened, of a colour like foam,
and a great one, golden-formed, pushed its yoked

title: Dionysiaca
text:
neighbour, neighbour against neighbour, and another in form was like pitch,
darkening its whole flower, and from its wine-bearing leaves
it intoxicated the whole splendid-fruited olive growing near it;
and over another, just-carved, with unripe fruit,
the self-rushing black air ran upon the silvery cluster,
bearing, in its cluster-laden mass, the swelling harvest;
and the coiling tendril of the harvest crowned the opposite pine,
shading the enveloping shoot with combined thickets,
and delighted the heart of Pan; and bringing its branches,
shaken by Boreas, near the vine-clad cluster,
the blood-dipped pine waved its fragrant hair.
And about it a serpent, coiled with crooked spines,
milked the dainty nectar of the well-dropping fruit,
and milking the Bacchic drink with grim jaws,
dropping into its throat the draught of the wine-drenched cluster,
the serpent reddened its chin with a purple drop.
And the mountain-roaming god marvelled, watching the snake
with its throat stained with the wine-coloured drop;
and coiling its dappled, turning track of scales,
it entered the neighbouring deep-bosomed crevice in the rock,
the spangled snake, having beheld the Bacchic juice. And gazing,
Bacchus marked the cluster pregnant with the reddening dew,
and recalled the older oracles of oracular Rhea.
And he dug into the crags, and with the sharp point
of his earth-digging iron he hollowed a recess in the rock;
and smoothing the brows of the deepening hollows
he made the trench into the shape of a fine-grape wine-press,
reaping the fresh-budding clusters with a sharp thyrsus,
making the likeness of the later-born curved-clawed sickle.
And there was a band of Satyrs, his companions; of whom one
leaned, gathering the vintage, another received the clusters
cut, in a hollow vessel, another, cutting the tangled leaves,
shook off the green refuse of the wine-loving fruit;
another, without thyrsus and without well-sharpened iron,
stretching his ironless right hand to the branches,
broke off the tips of the coiling cluster,
crouching, bent over, stretching his eye toward the vine;
and in a deep hollow he spread the heaped harvest,
heaping the centre-naveled back of the ravine with grapes . . .
he laid the coiling clusters one upon another in the hollow,
stretched out this way and that, and as he heaped up vintage-piles
filling the whole hollow he gathered them in the cavernous rock,
and trod the cluster with the dancing beat of his feet.
And the Satyrs, shaking their wild hair into the air,
learning the like mimicry of Dionysus,
binding dappled fawnskins about their shoulders,
shouted the song of the Bacchic, fellow-tongued echo,
with much-leaping feet pressing the harvest,
singing "Euoi"; and from the grape-rich hollow
as the wine gushed up the ravines grew purple;
and the harvest, pressed by alternating feet,
cast up the white foam of the reddening dew.
And they drew with bovine horns instead of cups,
not yet appearing, whence afterward, ever from that time,
this wondrous name belonged to the wine being mingled.
And one, gushing up the moisture of mind-charming Bacchus,
bent his crooked track of feet with a coiling beat,
shifting his right sole, changing from the left,
and wetted his shaggy beard with the moisture of Bacchus;
another leapt up, shaken by the goad of drunkenness,
hearing the fearful bellow of the struck ox-hide;
and one, drinking the irresistible stream of pain-healing wine,
reddened his dark chin with the rosy draught;
another, stretching his unsteady gaze up toward a tree,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
watched the half-revealed, unfilleted neighbour Nymph,
and now into the high-leaved plant of the mountain wood
he would have crept with the curved-clawed sole of his slipping foot,
had Dionysus not restrained him; and about the springs
another, with a wandering beat of mind-rousing drunkenness,
pursued the watery, unrobed Naiad girl,
and now he would have embraced her as she swam with his shaggy arm,
had she not, anticipating him, hidden in the deep stream.
But to the wine-drinker Dionysus alone Rhea gave
the amethyst, the warder-off of raving compulsion.
And many of the fair-horned Satyrs, with sport-loving sole,
goaded into the dance, reveled; of whom one,
holding a hot, new goad beneath his heart, the escort of the Loves,
clasped a Bacchante about the middle with his hairy arm;
another, shaken by the goad of mind-wandering drunkenness,
touched the girdle of an unmarried, chaste maiden,
dragging back to Cypris the garments of the unyielding nymph,
and with a back-cast hand touched her rosy thighs;
and one reined back an unwilling initiate girl
lighting the night-dancing torch kindled for Dionysus;
another, casting his sparing fingers about her breast,
squeezed the swelling circle of her unbending bosom.
And after the revel of his sweet harvest, Dionysus,
exulting, entered the caves of the Cybelean goddess,
stretching the cluster-laden branches with flower-loving hand,
and taught his own Maeonia his sleepless festival.
13. In the thirteenth book I will tell of the numberless army
and the champion heroes gathering to Dionysus.
Now Zeus the father sent down to the marvellous halls of Rhea
Iris to bear his message to Dionysus, rouser of battle,
that with his avenging thyrsus he should drive from Asia
the arrogant race of the Indians, untaught in justice,
mowing down the horned, sea-fighting son of the river,
King Deriades, and teach all the nations
the rites that dance by night and the wine-dark fruit of autumn.
She, with a windy beating of her plied wings,
sank into the echoing recess of the lion-nursing cave
and set down a soundless tread; and in voiceless silence,
binding her servant lips close to the mountain queen,
she stood there stooping, and with bowed head
with suppliant lips she clasped the feet of Rhea.
But the Corybantes, at a stern nod from holy Rhea,
made her welcome beside the mixing-bowl of the table;
and astonished, drinking the pour of new-made wine,
she rejoiced in her revelry. And the goddess, her head heavy,
bellowed out the will of Zeus to the present son of Zeus:
"Mighty Dionysus, your father commands you
to make an end of the Indian race, untaught in piety;
but lifting the warring thyrsus in your hands
do deeds worthy of heaven, for the immortal court of Zeus
will not receive you without toils, nor will the Seasons
fling open the gates of Olympus to you while you have not yet striven.
Hermes came to heaven only with hardship, when with his wand
he slew the herdsman Argos, flashing with eyes from feet to hair,
and loosed Ares from his bonds;
Apollo too tamed Delphyne, and then dwelt in the sky;
nor did your own father, lord of the blessed, high-ruling Zeus,
climb to heaven, that leader of the stars, without his labours,
unless he first bound the threateners of Olympus,
hiding the Titans away in the Tartarean pit.
And you, after Apollo and after Hermes, by your toil
shall win as wage of your labours your father's heaven to dwell in."
So speaking, the goddess went toward Olympus; and at once Rhea,
mother of all, sent forth her army-gathering messenger,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Pyrrhichus, dancer of the loud-clashing oxhide,
to proclaim the war of Lyaeus arming for battle.
And gathering for Dionysus a host of many shapes,
Pyrrhichus ranged over the dwellings of the everlasting world;
the offspring of Europe and the nations of the land of Asia
he led, all of them, and came home to the country of the luxurious Lydians.
But the heroic stock of the far-scattered champions,
and of the shaggy Satyrs, blood of the Centaur breed,
and the phalanx of Sileni of the rough-shanked elder,
and the line of Bassarids—tell me, Corybantian Muses;
for I could not sing so many tribes with ten tongues,
nor with ten mouths pouring out a brazen-throated sound,
all that spear-shaking Bacchus mustered; but clear-voiced
I will call the leaders, and Homer to help me,
the whole haven of fine speech, since wandering sailors
call on the dark-haired one as helper of their wandering.
First, when fair-thyrsus Dionysus called him,
swift Actaeon came, honouring his kindred blood,
leaving the seven-mouthed soil of his fatherland Aonia.
And the phalanxes of the Boeotians flowed in, those who dwelt
in the land of well-towered Thebes, and Onchestus,
the seat of the Earthshaker, Peteon and Ocalea and Erythrae,
and clustering Arne, glorying in Dionysus,
and those who dwelt in Mideia, and the famous little towns
Eilesion and Scolus and Thisbe of the sea-foundations,
the dove-haunted harbour of Aphrodite of the sea,
and the ground of Schoenus and well-foliaged Eleon
and Copae, splendid soil, where I hear is still renowned
the lake that bears its name, nurse of the eels,
and shaggy Medeon, and those who hold Hyle good for grazing,
long-shanked nurse of Tychius the leather-cutter,
and the plain of Euryalus, guarded by an oracle of the earth,
named for the late-born chariot of Amphiaraus,
and the city of the Thespians and deep-shanked Plataeae
and watery Haliartus, parted in two by the middle streams
of the mountain-poured river of Helicon,
and those who held outermost Anthedon, neighbour of the sea,
the little fishing-town of ever-living
Glaucus of the watery life, and those storm-vexed who held Ascra,
the laurel fatherland of the unsilent shepherd,
and the holy city of Graea and broad-spaced Mycalessus,
named for the likeness of the throat of Euryale,
and the Nisaean land and the city named for Coronus.
For these as they went to the eastern region of the earth
Actaeon was the leader; and over the young man's victory
his great-grandsire, the laurelled prophet Apollo, sneezed good omen.
But another company of the Boeotians was led on
by fair-haired Hymenaeus, with cheeks still unmarked by down,
freshly blossoming, beloved of Bromius; and as he went,
following the youth came a grey-haired leader, his guardian,
Phoenix by name, the very likeness of Laocoon, who long ago
boarding Argo, the ship of Jason, and coming to the land of the Colchians
sailed as comrade beside Meleager arming for war.
Such while he was still a boy, with the bloom of boyhood,
soft-haired Hymenaeus put on the battle of the Indians,
twirling on either cheek the hair of his own age;
and there followed him fellow shield-bearers of his own years,
those of the city of Aspledon, and the one Charis never leaves,
Orchomenus of Minyas, dance-trodden grove of the Loves,
and those who dwelt in Hyria, the god-receiving soil of the field,
bearing the name of Hyrieus the host-receiver,
where the boundless Giant, from a bed that knew no marriage,
Orion of the three fathers, sprang up from his mother Earth,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
when, made to grow by the seed of three races of gods,
a flow of urine was shaped into a self-made birth,
wedding the furrow of the birth-bringing oxhide,
and the hare's-bed of the soil delivered an unsown son of Earth;
and those who held the hospitable ground where the Achaeans gathered,
rocky Aulis, the seat of the Arrow-pourer,
where the heavy-wrathed goddess at the mountain-dwelling altar
received the sacrifice of the false Iphigeneia,
and a mountain-roaming hind was burnt with no faulty torch
when the true Iphigeneia's bastard shape was snatched away,
she whom wily Odysseus brought, as if to be the bride
of Achilles before the battle—from which Aulis is called
the bridal-decker of the unwedded Iphigeneia;
and over the ships of the Argives a guiding wind whistled,
lashing soundlessly the surface of the holding calm,
bringing to the fawn-slaying king a breeze come back again;
but the girl, late arriving in the land of the Tauri,
was taught the dread customs of the cauldrons that wrong their guests,
carving up a man, and at the man-slaying altar
she gave new life to her sea-terrified brother Orestes.
So great a host of the countless Boeotian men came,
following Hymenaeus to the Indian war.
With these served as fellow-soldiers, beside the wise Delphic rock,
the close-neighbouring Phocians, gathered together, who held
the seat of Cyparissus and the land of Hyampolis, which I hear
is named for the soil of the Aonian sow, that for beauty
lifted up her proud neck and vied with Tritogeneia;
and those who had Pytho for their lot and the cliff-girt orchard,
famous Crisa and Daulis and Panopeus,
having Bacchus for neighbour, since laurelled Apollo
shared his own portion with his brother Dionysus,
two-peaked Parnassus; and for the gathering peoples
the oracular, prophet-voiced Pythian rock rang out
and the self-sounding tripod, and of the unsilent spring
of Castalia the babbling swell foamed with wise current.
The phalanxes of the Euboeans were marshalled by shield-bearers,
the child-nursing Corybantes of the growing Dionysus,
who, holding the Phrygian gulf beside Rhea who haunts the mountains,
ringed about with oxhides Bacchus while still an infant,
him whom once, wrapped in a purple wine-dark robe,
they found among the crags, a horned babe, where Ino
handed him to Mystis, the child-nurse, the mother of Corymbus.
These all came then from the famous island,
Prymneus and roll-foot Mimas and hill-running Acmon,
Damneus and shield-wielding Ocythous, with whom marching
came helmet-flashing Melisseus, running beside Idaean.
These once, armed with the senseless goad of impiety,
Socus, father of the sea-girt land, banished from their fatherland
after their mother Combe of the seven children; and fleeing
they came to the soil of Cnossus, and back again were wanderers
into Phrygia from Crete, from Phrygia to Athens,
foreign dwellers at one hearth, until Cecrops
destroyed Socus with the avenging bronze of Justice,
and leaving the land of sea-washed Marathon
they bent their homing track to the holy soil of the Abantes,
the earthly race of the earlier Curetes, who knew the song of pipes,
whose life was the loud-ringing clash of swords, who to a certain rhythm
set the wheeling of their feet and the shield-bearing dance.
With these served as fellow-soldiers the warring sons of the Abantes,
