who had for their lot brow-frowning Eretria, and who had both
Styra and Cerinthus, and the seats of famous Carystus
and the harsh ground of Dion, and those who held the headland,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
the wave-beaten headland of unsilent Geraestus,
and Styx and the seat of Cotylaeum and the dwelling of Siris
and the ridge of Marmarium and the Ogygian plain of Aegae;
and with these came a people of one expedition, whose fatherland
was Chalcis, mother-city of the long-back-haired Ellopians.
Seven leaders armed the host, but all had a single
spirit for war; and on the blazing altar they propitiated the stars,
the dwellers of the Zodiac road,
entrusting the war to wanderers of equal number.
The sons of Cecrops were armed by Erechtheus, insatiate of battles—
bearing the golden blood of Erechtheus of the glorious children,
him whom once in the recess of the torch-bearing maiden-chamber
a maiden self-delivered reared at a male breast,
the child-nursing grey-eyed unploughed one; and in shame
she cradled the boy in her virginal, unaccustomed arm,
the son of Hephaestus, when the lame, ill-married god
with a strange love sowed his seed in the field,
shooting forth the hot, self-rushing foam of the Loves;
such came Erechtheus, leader of the Athenian army,
having Siphnus as fellow-toiler, a leader of the same city—
those who had for their lot the fertile plain of Oenoe, and those of the peaks
of neighbouring Hymettus, the bee-haunted dwellings,
and the deep-wooded precinct of olive-clad Marathon,
and those of the city of Celeus, and those who had the harbour of Athens,
sea-side Brauron, the empty tomb of Iphigeneia,
and the ground of Thoricus and well-bearing Aphidnae,
and those who held the Eleusinian land of Deo of the glorious child,
the celebrants of the basket and the fruitful goddess,
born of the blood of Triptolemus, who once, guiding
through the air Deo's serpent chariot,
lashed the dappled backs of the corn-bearing serpents;
and there a man came in age, brandishing iron armour
here and there, an Acharnian, holding it out to his arming sons;
and the lines of Attica came as comers, and with spear,
with swords of the hasting townsmen rousing the war,
into battle the well-helmeted Athenians ran in revel,
and as they rushed to war the harbour of Phalerum echoed;
and many a man, proclaiming his earlier earth-born stock,
bound up his locks in fine braids with a golden cicada.
His fatherland too Aeacus left, whom a bastard bird begot,
mingling with the snatched Asopid nymph,
an eagle, the winged, high-flying husband of Aegina, Zeus;
and from that marriage Aeacus was named; and beyond all others
he was eager to help his brother Dionysus;
and with skilled craft he marshalled the phalanxes of the Myrmidons,
who once were ants creeping over the field,
busy on their many-scattered feet, until from their
worthless bodies their earth-born shape was changed,
and high-ruling Zeus moulded them into another, better form,
and an armed host sprang up; for suddenly
an alien-shaped, voiceless, unsown swarm of the field,
the ant, was shaped into a speaking mortal body.
Their leader Aeacus held command, and on his well-made oxhide
he had drawn Zeus as the cunning bastard bird, a token of his birth,
lifting up a woman in sparing talons,
and a river of fire was near, and beside it a girl
in piteous dejection; and though it was a breathless image,
she strained a sidelong eye, as if lamenting her father
heavy-kneed Asopus, and seemed to cry out this:
"You won me a fair bride-gift by overcoming my own begetter."
Of Crete the leader was, of the many-tongued dwellers,
Asterius, with a bright-faced body, and both—
as much as he was lovely, so much was he strong—whom once a nymph

title: Dionysiaca
text:
untying for Minos the knot of her chaste maidenhood,
Phaestian Androgeneia, bore in a Cydonian bed;
he then, leading a hundred-citied people to wine-dark Bacchus,
came, honouring the kindred blood of his stock,
of his own father; for Minos was cousin of Semele,
shared offspring of Cadmus; and far-scattered warriors
all flowed together to one eager leader,
some warriors from Cnossus, some from Lyctus,
joined to the armies of Miletus; with whom many
citizens of high-crested Gortyn were armed,
and dwellers of Rhytion and well-bearing Lycastus . . .
and the land of Nodaean Zeus and the seats of Boebe
and the plain of Cisamus, and the fair cities of Cytaeum.
Such a leader came from Crete; and as he went,
pouring a prophetic radiance with warmer rays,
there shone for Asterius the star of like name to Ares,
first herald of the victory to come; but in the battle,
though he conquered, he came to know the bastard frenzy of an unfamiliar field,
merciless one; for he was not destined, after the Indian war,
to see his ancestral helmet-flashing cave of the Idaean crag,
but chose a life that abandoned his city, and instead of Dicte
he was a settler-citizen of Cnossus in Scythia,
and leaving grey Minos and Androgeneia behind,
the wise man came to the barbarous nations of the guest-slaying Colchians,
and named them Asterians and gave the Colchians a Cretan name,
to whom nature gave foreign customs; and leaving
his ancestral Cretan stream of nursing Amnisus
with shamefaced lips he drank the bastard water of Phasis.
Aristaeus alone came slow, last of all,
of all who dwelt in the land bordering on the land of Greece,
he who from the many-holed hives of sweet honey
lifted his proud neck, and with wine-pouring Dionysus
vied in a vain hope of honey-sweet victory;
and for both gave judgment all the dwellers of Olympus;
but the son of Phoebus, offering the newly-flowing streams of the hives
to the immortals, missed the honey-sweet victory,
because the gods, receiving the thick stream of the sprig-loving bee,
held a sharp surfeit of the joyless dew;
and the surfeit of the blessed ones was at the third cup, and they did not
taste a fourth mixed cup of the returning goblet,
though they thirsted greatly; but when Bacchus drew
and delighted their minds with a fine-dropping shower of dew,
for a whole day they drank the untiring pour of wine;
and drunk with the sweet wine each marvelled, one after another,
longing from one for another cup with glad heart,
holding an insatiate joy of mind-charming wine;
and Zeus marvelled at the works of the honey-dropping bee,
the cunning birth-pang of the honeycomb-loving travail,
the gift of Aristaeus, and to wine-pouring Dionysus
he granted to bear the first-fruits of toil-loosing victory.
From there Aristaeus came slow into the Indian war,
late, having first laid to rest the anger of his ravished prime,
leaving the Cyllenian seat, the dwelling of Hermes;
for not yet had he settled on the earlier island of the Meropes,
not yet had he stayed the fiery breath of the thirsting season,
bringing the life-giving breeze of Zeus the averter of ills,
nor, iron-clad, watching for the radiance of the star
Sirius, holding back the smouldering fever,
had he soothed it by night—the fire still thirsting,
shooting its hot heat through the air with a blazing throat,
cooled by the winds with their slender breaths;
but still he dwelt in the Parrhasian plain. And as he went
a people was armed, the acorn-eating Arcadian wanderer,
those who held Lasion and the fair groves of Lycaeus

title: Dionysiaca
text:
and rocky Stymphalus, and the famous little town
Rhipe and Stratie and Mantinea and Enispe
and well-wooded Parrhasia, where is the goddess's plain,
untrodden, still the childbed of primeval Rhea,
and the ground of Pheneus and the father of the dance,
Orchomenus rich in sheep, the seat of the Apidanes,
and those who held Arcadia, city of Arcas, whom his mother
Callisto once bore to Zeus, and his father, fixing him
in the vault of the stars, called him hailstorm-bringing Bootes;
so great a host did Aristaeus arm with Arcadian spear,
drawing into battle, with men fighting, his nomad hounds—
Aristaeus, whom once Cyrene, another Artemis hunting deer,
a lion-slaying nymph, bore in love to Phoebus,
when over sandy Libya fair Apollo
led her, a settler, on the ravishing bridal car.
And as he hastened, leaving his prophetic laurel,
his father Apollo himself armed him with his own hands;
he gave the boy a bow, and fitted to his hand an oxhide
cunningly wrought, and the deep quiver let down across his back
he fastened with a shoulder-strap.
To him from Sicily came far-darting Achates,
and there followed him fellow shield-bearers of his own years,
a great host of Cillyrians and Elymians, and those who held
the seat of the Palici, and those who dwelt by the lake of Catane,
the city near the Sirens, whom to Achelous
rosy Terpsichore bore from the ox-horned bed,
joined to her storm-swift consort;
and those who held Camarina, where with echoing stream
Hipparis, unstable, belches up its crooked water,
and the holy city of Hybla, and those who dwelt near Etna,
where the craters of fire, kindled from the rock,
spout up the hot blaze of Typhon's bed,
and those who shared their homes by frowning Pelorus,
and the island plain of sea-roaring Pachynus,
and Sicilian Arethusa, where a settler creeps,
Alpheus the wanderer, with hair crowned by a Pisan garland,
ferrying his passable swell, and through the topmost sea
drawing the higher, undrenched water, slave of Love,
holding a hot fire that touches through the cold water.
After these came Faunus, leaving the fire-sealed
Pelorian foot of the three-crested Sicilian crag,
him whom Circe bore, joined to Cronion of the deep,
sister of Aeetes, the many-throned, who beside the thicket
dwelt in the deep-shaded circle of a rocky hall.
And the Libyans served in arms by the western region of the earth,
dwelling in the cloud-near cities of wandering Cadmus;
for there, carried by the breezes of opposing winds,
Cadmus dwelt for a time, having the Sithonian nymph
as his fellow-voyager, Harmonia still a maiden, for whose beauty's sake
war-breeding rumour armed the hostile neighbours,
she whom the Libyan host renamed Charis—for more delicate
than the Bistonian grace there had blossomed another earthly grace,
from whom is the hill of the Graces in Libya—for whose beauty
the dread barbarian Ares, stirred to a ravishing battle by senseless goad,
armed himself in love-madness,
the desert-roaming Maurusian host; but brandishing
in his woman-mad hands the spear of Libyan Athena,
her bridegroom-consort fought, shielding Harmonia,
and routed the whole race of the western Ethiopians
together with armed Zeus, with Ares and Cytherea;
there too, as they tell, beside the Tritonian lake
the wanderer Cadmus lay beside rosy Harmonia,
and the Hesperid nymphs wove a song, from whose garden
Cypris together with the Loves adorned the well-married bed,
hanging the golden fruit above the chamber,
a bride-gift worthy of her love, from whose leaves
Harmonia and Cadmus beside the wealth-keeping bridal couch

title: Dionysiaca
text:
bound up their hair with rich clusters
instead of the bridal rose; and the bride was more delicate
bearing golden gifts, the prize of golden Aphrodite;
and rousing a revelling song of the starry lyre
her grandsire, ball-like with his dancing feet,
Libyan Atlas, bent low, whirled the heaven about,
and made the song of harmony with neighbouring voice;
and as memorials of the wedded love of his bride
Cadmus gave footings of feet to the Libyan field,
building a hundred cities, and to each he gave
walls hard to climb, raised on stony towers.
Keeping that man in mind the warriors went to war,
shield-bearers of fighting Bromius, champions of Enyo,
dwelling in the seats neighbouring the new-born Moon
and the southerly dwellings of Asbystian Zeus,
the prophet horned one, where often Ammon,
bearing the thrice-coiled likeness of a ram's horn,
with oracular lips prophesied as Hesperian Zeus;
and those who held the stream of Chremetes and those who by the water of Cinyps
dwelt on the sandy edge of parched field,
Auschisae and Bacales joined together, whom more than others,
delighting in Ares, the Zephyrian bend nurtured.
So great a host it was, of a hundred cities; and as the throng
came on, Crataegonus led them, whom once the girl
Anchiroe, daughter of Chremetes, beside the flats of her father,
bore to light-minded Psyllus in a short-lived bed,
a god-fighting bridegroom in her arms, whose crops
once the hot wind Notus burnt with thirsting breath;
but he, arming the helmet-flashing Ares of the ships,
gathered a sea-fighting swarm, that by an avenging ordinance
he might raise Enyo against the airy winds,
eager to kill fiery Notus; and near the island
of Aeolia came his shield-wielding host, but at the man's
madness the spear-throwers in a storm-swift uproar,
lashing his ship, the winds armed themselves,
stirring a confederate helper, a fellow-breathing breeze,
and entombed both the army and Psyllus in the sea.
Of Thracian Samos the shield-bearers flowed together,
whom their lord sent forth, he of the deep-flowing beard,
Emathion the heavy-kneed, with snowy hair,
like the limbs of the Titans, and those who held both
sea-side Myrmex and flowery Saoce,
and the land of Teumerus and the groves of well-meadowed Phesias
shaded by the wooded thicket,
and holy Zerynthus, foundation of the sleepless Corybantes,
the building, as men say, of the Perseid maiden, where
the crags hold revel-bands of mystic torches,
and those who beneath the many-pointed base of the field
dwelt about Brontion, and those whom by the neighbouring sea
I hear named the Paths of Poseidon of the deep.
So many lines came as comers; and of primeval
Electra they confirmed their kindred birth;
for there Ares, Zeus, Cytherea gave Harmonia,
born of the sky, blood of the sea, to Cadmus the gods' helper,
as a wedded wife without bride-gift.
For these as they armed with fair-thyrsus Dionysus
Electra's seventh star rose through the sky,
a right-hand sign of battle, and over the victory
the answering echo of the Pleiades' shout cried out,
granting favour to Dionysus who bore his sister's blood,
and gave the army a like courage; and as they came
Oeagrus led them on to war, a second Ares,
Oeagrus the high-headed, with the likeness of the Giants;
his whole body was unbending, and from his head
and the sinew of his neck, over his back-haired shoulders,
locks like the spine-bearing hedgehogs
flowed down as far as his loins; and he had a neck
long, of vast measure, like the neck of a rock,
keeping his ancestral barbarous nature; and none

title: Dionysiaca
text:
came braver than he to the eastern war of the Indians
except Dionysus; and he swore an oath by Victory
to lay waste the whole Indian land with his spear alone.
And the bold son of Ares, leaving his own Pimpleia,
Oeagrus of Bistonia, revelled as a townsman of the field,
leaving Orpheus on the knees of Calliope,
an infant, still cared for at the newly-streaming breast.
The phalanxes of Cyprus were marshalled by lordly Litros
and fair-haired Lapethus; and many were armed,
those who had for their lot Sphecia, the sea-beaten rim of the island,
Cyprus, the god-receiving island of well-winged Loves,
named for self-born Cypris, whose Cyprus's
headland Nereus once outlined, tracing with the deep prong of his trident
a shape like a dolphin—
for when, fertile and streaming with male gore,
Urania shaped the childbed foam, the dew,
and brought Paphia to birth, into the land of horned Cyprus
a dolphin ran over the swell with thinking heart,
lifting Aphrodite seated on its mane—
and those who held the plain of Hylates and the seats of Sestus
and Tamasos and Tembros and the little town of Erythrae
and the deep-wooded precinct of mountain-dwelling Panacrus;
and from Soli a great host was armed, and from Lapethus,
which afterwards they called by the name of its leader,
who then gathered the people, and in the fair-thyrsus uproar
died and was buried and left his name to the citizens.
And those of the city Cinyreia, still named for the rock
of primeval Cinyras, and the plain of the seat of Urania,
named for the airy hollow, because it reared its citizens
flashing like the likeness of the heavenly stars,
and those who held Crapasia, the sea-crowned soil of the field,
and Paphos, the garland-bearing harbour of soft-haired Loves,
the landing-step of Aphrodite rising from the waters,
where is the bridal water of sea-born Paphia,
lovely Setrachus, where often, taking a garment,
Cypris cloaked anew the bathed son of Myrrha,
and the city of primeval Perseus, where once Teucer,
leaving Salamis when Telamon was angered,
built a younger, famous Salamis.
And the delicate throng of the Lydians flowed in, those who held both
pebbly Cimpsus and brow-frowning Itone,
and those of broad Torebium, and those of the nurses of wealth,
Sardis of the fair childbed, of an age with the dawn,
and the Bacchic land that nurses the cluster, where to his mother
vine-clad Dionysus, holding a cup full of wine,
first mixed it for Rhea, and named the city Cerassae,
and the peaks of Oanus, and those who had for their lot the stream of Hermus
and watery Metallon, where the Pactolian mud,
spitting it out, glitters as the golden wealth of the dew;
and from Stataloi a great host was armed, where Typhoeus,
spouting hot the fire-nursed breath of the thunderbolt,
burnt the neighbouring ground, and in a storm-swift smoke
of blazing Typhon the crags were turned to ash,
his heads withering with the limb-devouring spark;
but leaving the fragrant temple of Lydian Zeus
an iron-less priest fought with goading speech,
with speech for his javelin, and not with cutting iron,
restraining with his tongue the obedient son of the field,
his weapon a fierce mouth, his word a sword, his shield his voice,
pouring out this speech with god-summoning throat:
"Stand, wretch"; and the fiery Giant by the mystic craft
of unbreakable speech was held fast in a wise bond,
dreading a man armed with thoughtful spear,
a foot-fetter without iron in his avenging speech;
nor did the vast-armed dread Giant tremble so
at the archer of the thunderbolt as at the man-breaking initiate

title: Dionysiaca
text:
shooting with his tongue a babbling shaft; and he gave way, worn out,
pierced with speaking wounds by the sharp word;
and having a wound of fire, pierced by a hot weapon,
Typhoeus suffered from another hotter, mental fire,
and by necessity rooted firm, unshaken, immovable,
his serpent-foot fixed fast to his mother Earth,
wounded with an unmarked, bloodless point in his bloodless body.
But all this an age long past brought among earlier men.
Those who beat the earth clear-ringing with rhythmic foot
both Stabius and Stamnus armed for the Indian fray;
and seeing the dancer host leaping all around
you would speak such a word, that the leader is leading
into a dance, not into war, bringing an armed man;
for as they came, striking up a dance,
the Mygdonian, battle-rousing lyre roared toward the fray,
sending out, instead of a dance, the host-rousing din of war;
and the war-trumpets were the pipes of the Loves,
and the twin Berecyntian flutes, yoke-fellows, sounded,
and a double-beating clatter from loud-crashing hands,
with brazen clashings the oxhides bellowed.
And the Phrygians served in arms beside the war-rousing line of the Lydians,
those who had for their lot Budeia, and the famous little town
tree-clad Temeneia, the well-shaded grove of the field,
and those who dwelt in Dresie and Obrimus, which by the streams
of crooked Maeander sets its own water,
and the plain named for Doias, and those who dwelt in Celaenae
of the golden roofs, and the images of the Gorgon;
with these served also those who had for their lot to dwell in the cities
neighbouring Sangarius, and the seats of the land of Hellespont.
Their leader led them on, leaving snaky Dirce,
Priasus, a settler-townsman of the Aonian field;
for when rainy Zeus flooded the plain of Phrygia,
pouring down with rain-seas the high-running water,
and the oaks were hidden, and in the thorn-bearing glens
the thirsty hills surged like rivers,
then leaving his sodden house, covered by the rain,
and the air-roaming stream, the javelin-thrower of halls,
Priasus migrated to the bosom of the Aonian field,
shunning the death-bearing rain-water of Zeus;
and ever among foreign men shedding tears
he remembered Sangarius and sought his accustomed spring,
drinking the alien water of the Aonian river;
but late Zeus the highest soothed the snow-swollen swell
and the watery constraint, and from the heads of Sipylus
he drove back again the water of flooded Phrygia;
and the Earthshaker with his trident moved the whole stream
into the deep hollows of the trackless sea,
and the crags were stripped bare of the roaring snow-flood;
and then leaving the soil of Boeotia, returning,
Priasus, late in counsel, slipped into his own fatherland,
and his heavy-kneed begetter with a harmless pull of his arm
he embraced returning, whom for the sake of pious works
great Zeus saved from the rainy destruction,
him whom they call Brombius; and from the Phrygian gulf
the proud warriors ringed about Priasus.
When Asterius had departed apart from his own begetter,
freshly-blossoming Miletus came as fellow-traveller to Bacchus,
having Caunus as fellow-toiler, his brother, who then
leading a people of the Carians, still a boy, put on the Indian war;
for not yet did he weave the love-sick, wile-plotting song,
holding the frenzy of his unknowing sister, nor of herself
did he sing—of an answering love on rival beds—
Hera his sister joined to Zeus,
about the Latmian cattle-yard of the sleepless herdsman,
blessing under love the bridegroom Endymion, beloved of the neighbouring rock,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
darling of love-stricken Selene;
but still Byblis was maiden-loving, and still the hunt
Caunus, ignorant of kindred loves, was learning;
not yet, when her soft-haired brother had fled,
rained upon with tears, did the girl shape her body anew,
and well up the watery stream of a mourning spring.
With him together the bold warriors hastened on,
those who dwelt in Mycale, and those who had for their lot the crooked water
into the land of the sinking, back-returning river,
crooked Maeander, creeping through the dwellings.
So many lines came; and with one-eager journey
of the gathering peoples the Cybelean halls resounded,
and the streets of the Mygdonian city were ringed about.
14. For the fourteenth, keep your mind here: there Rhea arms
all the divine ranks for the Indian war.
Rhea swift-sandalled, beside the mountain-dwelling manger,
binding fast the shaggy necks of her lions,
raised her feet, fellow-running with the breezy gusts,
rowing through the airy hollows with her sandal;
and gathering the divine phalanxes for Lyaeus
like a wing or a thought she ranged over the seats of the world,
to the South, to the North, to the West, to the bed of Dawn;
and to the oaks and rivers she joined one voice,
calling the Naiads and the lines of the wood's Hamadryads.
And the divine offspring, hearing the Cybelean call,
gathered from every side. And from on high to the land of the Lydians
leading her unerring track, Rhea came down through the air;
and on her return she lifted up again the mystic nightly pine,
warming the air for the Mygdonian a second time with her torch.
But after the mortal heroic stock of the champions
teach me also the divine army, breezes of Phoebus.
First from Lemnos, from the fire-pointed crag,
the storm-swift rumour beside the mystic pine of Samos
armed the two sons of Hephaestus, the Cabeiri,
bearing their mother's kindred name, whom long ago
Thracian Cabeiro bore to the heavenly smith,
Alcon and Eurymedon, masters of the hearth.
And grim warriors gathered from Crete,
the Idaean Dactyls, dwellers of the rocky crag,
the Earth-born Corybantes together, whose race once
sprang up self-made from the earth for Rhea;
they ringed about with shield-bearing dances, beside the birth-aiding rock,
the newly-delivered babe Zeus,
striking up a mountain-clashing, deceiving revel,
making the air dance; and as the bronze was beaten,
a cloud-near echo roared at the ears of Cronus,
stealing away the infancy of Cronion with the oxhides;
and the leader led on the dance-weaving Corybantes,
Pyrrhichus and Idaean the shield-wielder, with whom marching
the Cnossian Cyrbas of like name armed the shifting tribes.
And the envious Telchines came as comers to the Indian war,
gathering from the deep hollow of the sea;
and shaking with long hand a vast spear-point
came Lycus, and Scelmis followed Damnameneus,
steering the ancestral Poseidonian chariot of the sea,
after Tlepolemus' land sea-wandering settlers,
water-dwelling frenzied spirits, whom long ago
against their will from their ancestral field
Thrinax with Macareus and shining Auges drove out,
sons of Helios; and pursued, from their nurse
drawing the water of Styx with envy-heavy hands
they made the orchard of fruitful Rhodes unsown,
sprinkling the fields with Tartarean waters.
After these the gentle double-natured race of the Centaurs;
to Pholus, having a horse's shape, Cheiron joined himself,
of alien form, untamed, with unbridled beard.
And the phalanxes of the Cyclopes flowed in; for in battle
they hurled with unarmoured hands the hills

title: Dionysiaca
text:
as rocky spears, and the crags were their shields,
and a crested watchtower of the ravine was their helmet,
and Sicilian sparks were their fiery arrows;
and brandishing the flame of their accustomed hearth
with fire-bearing hands the warriors armed themselves,
Brontes and Steropes and Euryalus and Elatreus
and Arges and Trachius and proud Halimedes.
But so great and such a one was left behind, alone, from the war,
cloud-near Polyphemus, offspring of the Earthshaker,
because the watery-pathed one held him back to stay there,
another Love, dearer than war; for gazing
at half-seen Galatea he sang to the neighbouring sea,
pouring a maiden-loving echo through his bridal pipe.
And dwellers of the crags from their self-roofed halls,
bearing the name of Pan, their desert-roaming sire,
the Pans were armed together, on whose form
was mingled with a man's the look of a shaggy goat;
and having the bastard shape of a well-horned head
there were twelve Pans, horn-drawn, and of one primeval
Pan, the mountain-dwelling father, they are sprung.
One they named Celaeneus by his witnessing form,
another, by his nature, Argennus of like name; and to Aegicorus
they fitted a name, since beside the pastoral flock
he was sated, squeezing the milk of goats' udders;
another was heard as the divine Pan Eugeneios,
holding a broad meadow of beard among his locks;
and with the pasturing Omestes was armed Daphoeneus;
and Phobos joined the rough-shanked Philamnus;
to Xanthus came Glaucus as fellow-traveller; for in answering
likeness Glaucus in his limbs was of the same hue as the sea,
grey-gleaming, and Xanthus, having yellow-coloured hair,
received such a name, the horned townsman of the crag;
and bold Argos came, bearing snowy hair.
To these there were two Pans together, whom Hermes begot
mingling in chosen love with twin nymphs;
one, seeking the bed of the mountain nymph Sose,
he begot full of prophetic, god-speaking utterance,
Agreus, fenced about with the beast-slaying care of the hunt;
the other dear to the pasturing of sheep, Nomios, when
he crossed the bed of the field-dwelling nymph Penelope,
caring for the shepherd's pipe. With these Phorbas,
the insatiate flesh-eater, kept a fellow journey.
And resting his hand on a fennel-stalk, old Silenus,
double-natured, the horned son of the field, was armed,
leading three sons of the revel-band; for to battle
Astraeus was armed, Maron went, Leneus followed,
lightening the hands of their mountain-wandering father
with age-tending clubs; for these strengthless old men
their sluggish bodies were eased by a vine-staff,
whose span of years was very many, from whom the hot
double-natured race of the much-marrying Satyrs sprang.
And the horned Satyrs were marshalled by their leaders,
Poimenios and Thiasos and Hypsiceros and Orestes,
and to horned Napaeus joined Phlegraeus;
Gemon came, bold Lycon was armed; and to the deep-drinking,
rock-perched, laughing Pheres the wine-loving one followed,
and Lamis the mountain-roamer kept a fellow journey
with Lenobios, and Scirtus revelled, running beside Oistros,
and with Pherespondus went Lycus, the loud-voiced herald,
and Pronomos skilled in mind, whom Hermes begot
yoking a strong woman under secret marriage,
whom Dorus once bore, an offshoot of the line of Zeus,
root of the race of Hellen, and from primeval Dorus
from Doris sprang the Achaean blood of the race;
to these Eiraphiotes entrusted the prize and the sceptre
of the heavenly herald, their mind-strengthening sire.
Always drunk with cups loving the unmixed wine

title: Dionysiaca
text:
was all the bold-hearted race of the Satyrs, and in battle
threateners only, ever fleeing Enyo,
lions away from war, but hares in wars,
skilled dancers, knowing more than others
how to draw the sweet wine from the wine-holding bowl;
few of them are warlike, whom bold Ares
taught every kind of care for the fight,
and to marshal a phalanx; and as Lyaeus armed
some hid their bodies in untanned oxhides,
others strengthened themselves with the shaggy skins of lions,
others put on the grim coverings of leopards,
others were armed with long-sprigged clusters,
others girt about their breasts a dappled tunic
of long-horned deer, matching the stars;
over their temples, twin on either brow,
sharp-pointed prongs of horn lengthened out,
and thin hair grew on their jagged heads,
barely showing over their slanting eyes, and both ears,
as they moved, the winged winds fanned up
straight, sounding against their shaggy jaws,
stretched out; and a horse's tail, drawn down the back,
upright, coiling, flowed from the loins.
Another race of alien form, the Centaur stock, came,
the shaggy breed of fair-horned Pheres, to whom Hera gave
another man-grown horned body; for of the water-born
Naiads they were once the children, in mortal-seeming shape,
whom men call Hyades, the river-stock of Lamus,
and they nursed the well-born offspring of Zeus,
Bacchus still breathing of his much-stitched birth,
child-nursing guardians of unseen Dionysus,
having no strange form; and in the dark hall
often they cradled the boy in their bent arms,
him babbling of the sky, his father Zeus's seat,
still in his infancy, the wise babe. And like a new-born
kid he was in all things, hidden within the fold,
and thickened his body with long hair,
of alien show, and pouring forth a deceitful bleating of teeth
he mimicked a false hoof with goatish tracks;
and at times wearing a woman's false shape
he appeared in clothes, a mimic, saffron-robed maiden,
freshly blossoming, and leading astray the mind of envious Hera
with answering lips he uttered a womanly voice,
and on his locks he bound a fragrant veil,
wearing woman's robes, much-embroidered; and at his mid
breast he set a band and an upright rim of breast . . .
with a maiden's girdle, and as if a knot of maidenhood
he fitted a purple round band to his loins.
But the trick was useless, since Hera learned of it from on high,
turning everywhere the all-seeing eye of her face,
watching the ever-changing shape of Lyaeus;
and she was angry with the guardians of Bromius; and receiving
the Thessalian deceitful flowers of the grass from Achlys
she poured sleep over the heads of the bewitched guardians,
dripping potent charms from their hair;
and smearing a soft magic salve over their faces
she changed the older form of their human look;
on them appeared an eared shape of nature,
and a horse's tail rose upright through the loins
lashing the haunches of the shaggy-breasted bearer,
and an ox-horn grew from the temple,
and the eyes widened on the long-horned brow,
and crooked locks grew on the heads,
and white-toothed jaws lengthened on the chins,
and a strange, self-made, thick hair, from loins to the tips of the feet,
flowed down the shaggy neck.
Twelve leaders marshalled them all in all,
Spargeus and Gleneus the dance-treader, and of alien form
running beside Eurybius came cluster-bearing Ceteus,
and to Riphonus joined Petraeus, and the deep-drinking
Aesacus and Orthaon went together, whom into one journey
both Amphithemis and Faunus made,
and with well-horned Phanes came Nomeion as companion.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Another double-natured race of Centaurs was armed,
the Cyprian, when Cypris ran like the breezes,
shunning the track of her desiring father,
lest she should look upon her lawless begetter as a husband;
and Zeus the father gave way, leaving untouched
the swifter, uncaught, refusing Aphrodite;
and instead of Cyprian beds he sowed in the field,
pouring out the loving shower of child-begetting ploughs;
and the earth, receiving the bridal dew of Cronion,
shot up an alien horned race.
With these armed there ran together as one the Bacchae,
some from the cleft of Maeonia, some from the hill
of lofty Sipylus they darted above the peaks.
And the trailing-robed Oread nymphs with manly spirit,
raving, rushed on with the fair-thyrsus warriors,
those who lived a long span of time
at the much-whirling turning-post of the returning years, some
neighbours of the crags, sheep-keepers of the lonely pastures, some leaving
the wooded groves and the ridge of the wild forest,
the Meliae grown with the oak of their own age; who then all
hurried together to battle, some taking up
the bronze-backed timbrels, instruments of Cybelean Rhea,
some covering their locks with curling ivy,
others were wreathed with snaky clusters;
and in their hands they raised the sharpened thyrsus, with whom then the Lydian
maenads went, fearless, to the Indian war;
of whom then the Bassarids of the revel-band, in skilled craft
surpassing, hurried on, the nurses of Dionysus,
Aigle and Callichore and Eupetale and Ione
and laughing Calyce and Bryousa, companion of the Seasons,
and Seilene and Rhode and Ocynoe and Ereutho
and Acrete and Methe, and there followed, companion of Harpe,
rosy Oenanthe and silver-footed Lycaste,
Stesichore and Prothoe; and the smile-loving old
wine-heavy Trygie was armed last, even she.
Each led his own chosen host for Bacchus,
but over all led the fire-roaring Eiraphiotes,
flashing, conspicuous; and dancing to battle
he lifted no shield, no fierce spear, no sword on his shoulder,
he set no helmet on his unshorn hair,
the bronze, unbreakable shelter of the head, but his hair,
unbound, he bound with a snaky knot,
ringing his head with a grim crown; and instead of well-made,
cunning greaves up to the top of the knee
he set white feet in purple buskins,
fastening a shaggy fawnskin on his breast,
wearing a dappled corslet, a figure marked with stars;
and a golden round band he fitted to his loins.
In his left hand he held a horn filled with sweet wine,
golden, well-made, and from the wine-pouring horn
upright dropped a stream of wine-drinker's dew;
and in his right hand he lifted the goading thyrsus,
wreathed with wine-dark ivy, and on its topmost cluster
the bronze-heavy point was shaded by the leaves.
But when Dionysus, within the Corybantian court,
put on the golden, well-made gear of battle,
leaving the fair-weather dwellings of dance-delighting Rhea
he passed by Maeonia; and with the mountain-dwelling Bacchae
the warriors rushed on with the cluster-bearing god;
some, steersmen of the well-wheeled wagon,
carried the saplings of the new planting of Bacchus;
and many lines of mules went, and on their backs
they lifted the jars of vine-born nectar;
and on the patient backs of slow asses they set
crimson rugs and dappled skins of fawns;
and other wine-drinkers, with golden cups,
brought silver mixing-bowls, the weapons of the table;
and the Corybantes busied themselves near the bright-eyed manger,
binding the necks of leopards with a yoking strap,
and they fastened lions with ivy-bound traces,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
binding their lips with a threatening bridle.
And a Centaur, with his shaggy bristling beard,
stretching of his own accord his willing neck into the yoke . . .
and having far more than the Satyrs a longing for sweet wine,
the half-formed man mingled with a horse neighed,
eager to lift Dionysus on his shoulders.
And the god of the fair vine, seated on the rim of his car
beside the stream of Sangarius, about the Phrygian gulf of the field,
passed by the mourning stone of stony Niobe;
and the stone, seeing the Indian throng striving against Lyaeus,
with tearful eyes again cried out in mortal voice:
"Do not array a god-fighting war, foolish Indians,
against the son of Zeus, lest Bacchus turn into stone
you too, who threaten Enyo, as Apollo did,
mourning, a likeness equal to my rocky form,
lest beside the stream of the river named for him, Indian Orontes,
you behold the son-in-law of Deriades fallen.
Rhea in her wrath can do more than the Arrow-pourer;
flee Bacchus, the brother of Phoebus; for I am ashamed,
at the Indians' slaying, to shed tears that are not mine."
So the stone cried out, and silence sealed it again.
And the god of the vine, after the foot of the Phrygian crag,
set foot on Ascania. And the citizens, gathered all together,
all to whom Iobacchus held out his fruit,
received both the rites and welcomed the dances,
bowing their necks to unconquered Dionysus,
wishing for the calm of bloodless peace;
such was the horned army of the Bacchae, with whom the Bacchae
were armed for battle. And for the wake-loving Lyaeus
all night, weaving a starry, fire-wheeling track,
the heaven thundered, since then with a witnessing flash
Rhea prophesied the end of the Indian-slaying victory.
To battle at dawn the god went, driving out the violence
of the dark men, that he might unyoke the slavish neck of the Lydians
and the dweller of Phrygia and the citizen of Ascania
from the dread traces of cruel lordship.
Then Bacchus sent to them two heralds of battle
to speak his message, either to flee or to fight;
and as they went there marched with them goat-grazing Pan,
bearing a long beard that shadowed his whole breast.
But Hera swift-sandalled, in the likeness of an Indian's body,
bade curly-haired Melaneus not to lift the wine-dark thyrsus,
Astraeis, the spear-shaking leader of men,
nor to honour the shout of the unmixed-wine-loving Satyrs,
but to raise a truceless battle against Dionysus;
and she spoke a word, persuading the Indian leader:
"Sweet is the man who fears a soft line of women.
Astraeis, fight; arm yourself too, Celaeneus,
holding cutting bronze against cluster-bearing Dionysus;
the thyrsus is no match for the spear. But, Celaeneus,
beware mad Deriades, lest he overcome you
for fleeing a worthless, iron-less woman."
So speaking she persuaded, and the goddess sank into the air,
the stepmother angry at war-staunch Dionysus.
And the heralds of Bromius departed; and close at hand
Astraeis overweening, with loveless threat,
raged, pursuing the ox-horned Satyrs and Pan,
dishonouring the heralds of gentle Dionysus.
And they, with the timid sole of a backward-returning foot,
bent a fleeing track to Dionysus, rouser of battle.
And Bacchus armed his host against the opposing lines of the Indians.
Nor did the womanish Enyo escape gloomy Celaeneus,
but darting unapproachable he armed the whole host of the Indians;
and bold Astraeis, swelling the war-staunch frenzy,
stood about the echoing stream of the Astacid lake,
awaiting the onset of cluster-bearing Dionysus.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
But when the leaders of the double army, with unequal yoke of host,
marshalled all the lines of both,
with a shout the gloomy Indians went to battle,
like Thracian cranes, when, fleeing
the wintry lash and the airy pour of rain,
in flocks they swoop upon the heads of the Pygmies
about the streams of Tethys, and with sharp beak
they destroy the strengthless blood of the worthless race,
flying cloud-like over the horn of Ocean;
and on the other side the warriors raved into battle,
unbending servants of battle-rousing Dionysus;
and the phalanxes of the Bassarids flowed in; and as they gathered
one girt her head with a snaky bond,
another bound her hair with fragrant ivy,
another armed her hand with the bronze-bearing thyrsus,
frenzy-mad, and another, down her neck, free of bonds,
let fall the loose curls of her long hair,
a Maenalid unveiled, and over both her shoulders
the wind fanned up her unbound locks;
another shook the rattles yoked with double bronze,
tossing her curling tresses upon her head;
another in her hands, gripped by a leap of frenzy,
struck up an upright, answering echo of battle,
beating with her hands the deep-roaring backs of the oxhide;
and the thyrsi were spears, and hidden by the leaves
of the vine-shaft was a bronze-forged point;
another, longing for the bloody fray,
bound on her neck the bonds of raw-devouring serpents;
another a dappled-backed covering of leopards on her breast,
another, like a tunic on her flesh,
put on the dappled skins of crag-loving fawns,
binding close the covering of a cunning deer;
another, holding a cub of a shaggy-breasted lioness,
gave it suck at her human, milky, bastard breast;
and one bound a thrice-coiled snake on her harmless bosom,
a hidden girdle, gaping near her thigh,
hissing gently, and of the unmixed-wine-loving girl,
the sleeper, a wakeful watcher of her maidenhood;
another, bearing her feet bare of sandals over the mountains,
treading with her feet on brambles and sharp-haired thorns,
set a firm step on the sharpened wild-pear;
and one, darting upon a long-shanked camel,
cut through with her reaping thyrsus its curved neck,
and stumbling along the path with blind feet
was carried half-seen, and on its many-bent course
the headless body of the wandering camel was driven on,
and striking with its stumbling hoof the deepening earth
it rolled over of itself, backward, slipping in the dust;
another, leading her track to the cattle-rearing ridge of the wood,
irresistibly raging, seized the hide of a bull,
and from its neck, scored by her grim nails,
stripped away the unpierced bull-hide covering;
another drained out all the entrails; and one could see
a maiden, unveiled, unsandalled, high on a rock,
leaping about the rough headland of the crag;
she did not shudder at the hard-to-climb peak, nor did
the sharp-fixed nail of the hill scratch the girl's bare foot.
Many here and there beside the mouth of the Astacid lake
the Indian race was cut down by Curete iron.
And the warriors ringed about the phalanxes of the foe
with answering arms, and they mimicked the rhythm
of the shield-bearing dance with the coiling beat of their feet;
and with shaggy hand lifting a crested peak,
cutting off the topmost heads of a mountain, Leneus armed himself,
sending a jagged point against the foe;
and the Bacchant shrieked all about, and the vine-clad point
the Bassarid hurled, and of the black-skinned race
many male heads were cut down by the female thyrsus.
And cutting through a bold man with a deadly cluster

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Eupetale was armed, and with cluster-loving leaf
she sent the goading ivy as crusher of iron;
and Stesichore rich in clusters leapt into the fray,
and routed the race of the foe with man-breaking whirl,
whirling the deep-roaring cymbals of double bronze.
And great was the battle on both sides; the pipe roared,
the battle-rousing pipe, and the flute of Enyo sounded,
and the Bassarids raised the cry; and as the battle rose
with thunderous crashes the black air, bellowing,
prophesied to Bromius from Zeus the victory to come.
And a great swarm fell; and the whole thirsty field
reddened with wet gore, and the mouth of the Astacid lake
gurgled, blood-stained, mingled with the slaughter of the Indians.
And the god pitied his foes with playful heart
and poured upon the stream the gift of drunkenness, and from the flow
the snow-white water changed to yellow nature,
and the river gurgled, drawing along honey-flowing streams,
and made its outflow drunk; and as the streams changed
fragrant breezes of newly-poured drunkenness breathed;
the banks reddened; and an Indian chieftain, drinking,
broke from his lips this much-wondering speech:
"Strange and incredible was the drink I saw, not goats' milk
white was this, nor black like water,
nor like that which I have seen in the many-holed hives
the humming bee brings forth in sweet wax;
but it has a fine-breathing smell that delights the mind.
A thirsty man, in the much-warming vapour of the heat,
drawing a little flowing water in his hands,
at once shakes off the storm of his parched thirst;
and honey rather brings a quick surfeit; ah, great wonder,
drinking this I wish to drink again; for both
this stream is sweet and breeds no surfeit in men.
Hebe, lift the pitcher and come here, take
the Trojan cup-bearer, the servant of holy goblets,
that, drawing from the honey-dropping river,
Ganymede may fill up all the bowls of Zeus.
Come, friends, taste the honey-flowing river.
Here I behold the likeness of the sky; for self-poured
is that which they call the drink of Zeus, the nectar of Olympus,
which the Naiads spout up in earthly streams."
15. In the fifteenth I sing of mighty Nicaea,
the rosy-armed beast-slayer who threatened the Loves.
So he spoke, and cloud-like the swarthy Indians flowed in
about the honey-breathing stream of the river; of whom one,
stepping close, planting his double step firm on the mud,
stood half-seen, wetting his navel in the water,
bent, stretching his stooped back into the river,
with hands hollowed deep he drew up the honey-dropping water;
and another by the outflow, gripped by burning thirst,
dipping his jutting beard in the purple wave,
spreading his breast from above on the river bank,
with open mouth drew up the moisture of Bacchus;
and another lay face down, bringing his mouth to the neighbouring spring,
and resting his wet hands on the sandy floor
with thirsty lips received the thirst-quenching water;
others drew the drunkenness with an earthen cup,
lifting the base of a broken jar;
and a great swarm drank from the reddening stream,
pouring with a wooden bowl the mass of the river's dew,
holding the rustic cup of sheep-tending men. And as the foes
belched up the wine from their capacious throats,
to their seeing eyes the crags were doubled,
and to their eyelids the water seemed twin-yoked.
And the outflow of the unmixed-wine-loving river gurgled,
spouting up the yellow stream of drunkenness; and of the sweet-drinking
wine the fragrant banks belched the streams.
And the strong-wine flood made the foes drunk. There a man,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
an Indian, shaken by the frenzy of mind-stealing drink,
darted into the herd, and by the well-leaved thicket
led off a threatening bull, dragging it bound,
gripping the scored tip of its twin horns
with daring hands, as though by the twin horn
dragging bull-shaped Dionysus under a slavish yoke;
another, holding the dread jaw of an iron sickle,
cut through the throat of a mountain-grazing goat,
mangled by the whetted reaping-hook, as though cutting
the neck of well-horned Pan with hook-clawed bronze;
another destroyed the horn-drawn race of oxen,
as though mowing down the bull-faced shape of the Satyrs,
and one chased the race of long-horned deer,
gazing at the dappled, much-embroidered look of their hide,
as though destroying the line of the Bassarids; for by the cunning
fawnskins of like pattern his eyes were led astray;
and staining his whole corslet with murderous drops
the black Indian spearman reddened with gore.
And one, shouting, armed himself against a neighbouring tree,
lashing it on either side, and seeing in the spring
the coiling foliage of plants shaken by the winds
he destroyed the soft-haired shoots of the clusters,
splitting the leaves of the shaggy oak, as though with a sword
cutting through the lock of unshorn Dionysus,
fighting with leaves and not striving with Satyrs,
holding a useless delight in a shadowy victory.
And another band of the foes raved; and instead of a spear
one, taking up the deep-sounding timbrel by its shoulder-strap,
lifted it high, and with the double-beaten oxhide
struck up a bronze-clashing, twin-yoked echo of song;
and one, shaken by the cry of the many-holed flute,
danced unsteady with the coiling beat of his feet;
and one, setting the lotus-pipe to untried lips,
made the two-voiced harmony of the Mygdonian flute;
and one, leaping by the neighbouring root of an aged plant,
drew up the grey shoot of the well-dropping olive,
soaked with dewy rain, as though squeezing
with a wine-coloured drop the tip of his Maronian beard.
Others with swords, with spears, with helmets,
irresistibly raving, their minds undone by mind-stealing wine,
mimicked the rites of the shield-bearing Corybantes,
whirling their steps in an armed dance;
and with answering sweeps of their hands, coiling,
the shields were beaten with tumbling iron;
another, watching the rites of the revel-loving Muse,
leapt with the Satyrs in a mimic dance;
and one, hearing the din of the beaten oxhide,
took on a gentle temper, and with din-loving purpose
threw to the winds his dread quiver,
holding frenzy; and another, a woman-mad Indian chief,
seizing a high-necked Bacchant by her unbound lock,
dragging the untamed maiden recklessly to wedlock,
bound her over the ground, and stretching her in the dust
with love-mad hands unsealed her girdle,
borne on by a vain hope; for suddenly
an upright serpent crept hidden in her bosom, near her loins,
and darted at the foe's neck, and about his throat
with its tail-coils wove a round girdle;
and the dark-skinned man, fleeing with frightened feet,
shook off the hot goad of unwedded Loves,
wearing about his neck the snaky chain of the thorn.
While the wine-flushed Indians ran upon the mountains,
so long sweet Sleep, coiling his close wing,
fell upon the unbending, faltering eyes of the Indians,
and lulled them, their minds stung by measureless wine,
doing a favour to Dionysus, father of Pasithea;
of whom one slept face up with head bent back,
drawing wine-tottering breath through his sleepy nostril,
and one laid his heavy head on a stone,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
sluggish, lying on the pebbled river bank,
and conversed with mind-wandering daytime dreams,
setting his stiff fingers upright about his temples;
and another lay stretched face down, and had both
hands let down, drawn equal along his twin thighs;
and one rested his head on the wrist of his own hand,
belching up wine; and another, bending his curved limbs
like a coiling snake, lay sleeping aslant.
And the band of foes, carried to the ridge of the wood,
one slept under an oak, another under an elm bush,
another, falling on his side, leaned against a holm-oak,
throwing his left hand on his frowning brow;
and a great swarm slept, a babbling corpse, sending to the air
the unbridled, meaningless din of a different echo,
wine-heavy; and another, with nodding head,
leaned his broad back on the trunk of an aged laurel;
and as he slumbered heavy on a deep-spread bed
of high-crested palm or well-flowering olive
a coiling shoot, fanned by the winds, whistled over him;
and one was stretched over the ground in the loose dust,
drenching his feet's ends in the river's outflow;
another raved with the beat of untried drunkenness,
and rested his heavy head on a neighbouring pine;
and the brow-sinews of another, snorting, were shaken.
And seeing the foes asleep, with laughing face
lord Bacchus spoke, pouring out a commanding voice:
"Indian-slaying servants of unconquered Dionysus,
binding the assembled sons of the Indians without battle
take them all alive in bloodless warfare;
and bending a slavish knee to mighty Dionysus
let the Indian serve my revel-loving Rhea,
shaking the wine-dark thyrsus, and casting to the storms
the silver greave let him bind his feet in buskins,
and crown his head with my ivy bond,
stripping the locks of his crest-lifting helmet,
and leaving the war-cry and the spear's echo
let him sing the euion to cluster-bearing Dionysus."
So he spoke, and the servants busied themselves; of whom one
coiling a snaky bond about the foes' necks
dragged a man fettered with a serpent-rope,
another, taking the slackened pull of a shaggy beard,
dragged a man up by his deep-flowing throat;
and one, stretching out his hands to the crook-haired temple,
dragged a spear-won man unbound by the hair;
another, fastening his folded hands behind the back,
wreathed the foe with a coiling bond of withies
about the neck; and with trembling beat Maron tottered,
lifting an Indian weighed down on his aged shoulder;
another, taking a spearman overcome by sleep,
dragging his neck wound about with a cluster-bond,
set him over the rim of the dappled leopard cars;
and over another lying down the euion-loving wandering swarm
bound his back-strained hands with an unbreakable bond,
and mounted the necks of the stiff-footed elephants;
and one, taking the strap of a well-rounded oxhide,
held an Indian fettered with a shoulder-thong.
And one, a Bassarid, lifting up a shepherd's crook,
foaming with the mind-soothing wave of frenzy,
an Indian explorer of the deep-rich sea
with daring hand dragged by his much-bending hair
to a slavish yoke. And as Lyaeus pressed on,
iron Erechtheus held a well-armoured foe
on his unbending shoulders; and the wine-tottering bearer's
black-skinned beast a mountain Bacchant drove,
lashing the haunches of the spear-won elephants;
and Hymenaeus lifted up a golden oxhide,
despoiling a man of his golden shield, and gladly
Bacchus looked on the youth with love-mad eyes,
shining bright in the armour of the sleeping bearer;
and the young man hurled a rich radiance in the gear,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
as taking the arms of Lycian Glaucus Diomedes
flashed before the warriors, glittering with the rich shield.
And the army of the Bacchae plundered the other foes,
holding sweet sleep, companion of pleasant wine.
There a maiden, curved-bow archer, companion of the lonely wood,
reared with the Astacid Nymphs, bloomed in beauty,
fair-grown Nicaea, another hare-shooting Artemis,
a stranger to love, untried in Cytherea,
shooting beasts and tracking them over the hills;
nor was she hidden in the fragrant recess of a maiden's chamber.
And on the crags, beside the desert-roaming foot of the hills,
her bow was her distaff, and ever within the thicket
her long spinning-threads were winged arrows,
and the upright wood of her hunting-stakes the loom of mountain Athena;
and she kept company with the pure Arrow-pourer as fellow-toiler,
and on the crags she wove the net of her accustomed hunting,
dearer than the wrought thread; never with her bow
did she touch a feeble fawn of dappled form,
nor did she chase gazelles, nor lay hand on a hare,
but harnessing with a bloody bridle
she lashed the grey backs of shaggy-breasted lions,
and often she raised a spear against a raging she-bear;
and she blamed the far-shooting Arrow-pourer, that, leaving
the race of dappled leopards and the tribes of lions,
she yoked her car to worthless deer.
Nor did she care for perfume, but before honey-mixed cups
she preferred the watery drink of a ravine-spring,
pouring out cold water; and in the self-roofed hollow
was the maiden's hard-to-enter home, the desert crags;
and often, after the course of the easy, accustomed hunt,
she sat near the leopards, and under a single hollow rock
she stayed at noon, beside a lioness newly delivered;
and the gentle beast, under its calm brows,
licked the maiden's body with unrending jaws,
and like a whimpering dog with timid throat
it whined gently from the eager mouth of the raw-bearing lioness,
with sparing lip, and deeming her to be Artemis
the lion, lowering its suppliant head to the ground,
leaned against the maiden with its shaggy neck.
And in the woods a mountain-reared herdsman bloomed,
upright, of great stature, taller than youths of his own age;
his name was Hymnus, who in the midst of the wild wood
pastured his lovely cattle beside the neighbouring girl;
and shaking the herdsman's crook in his lovely hands
he came into deep love and no longer delighted in his flock,
like rosy Anchises, whom once Cypris
pastured his white line of mountain-grazing bulls,
lightening the cattle-driving girdle; and about the thicket
the herdsman, seeing the snowy girl hunting,
cared nothing for his herd of cattle; and wandering
of her own accord the lonely heifer grazed into the marsh,
strayed far from her old love-sick herdsman,
and the calf was carried about, leaping over the hills,
seeking the shepherd; and the young herdsman wandered
gazing at the rosy circle of the maiden's face.
And cunning Eros stirred the longing herdsman,
shaken by a more violent goad; for on the crags
as the maiden sped on the unapproachable course of the hunt
a light breeze swelled her whole robe into the air;
and the beauty of her flesh bloomed; her thighs gleamed white
and her ankles reddened, and like a lily, like an anemone
the rosy meadow of her snowy limbs shone forth;
and the young man, walking in longing with insatiate gaze,
watched the free rim of her uncovered thighs
[ . . . ] of [ . . .
The cluster of her back-streaming hair the breeze tossed,
lightening it on either side, and as her locks lifted

title: Dionysiaca
text:
her bare middle neck flashed white-shining.
And the young mountain-roamer often went beside the girl,
now touching the hunting-stakes or handling the bow,
now, as the love-stricken arrow was drawn,
he watched the lovely girl's rosy-skinned fingers;
if ever, as she shot, she rounded the horn against the string,
and her hand was bared, the young man, unnoticed, with sidelong eye
watched the white archer-arm of the girl,
turning back his eye, the conduit of the Loves,
whether so great, like Nicaea, was white-armed Hera;
and to the western verge he stretched his gaze,
whether more silvery was the maiden, or Selene.
And the young man, tending the wound of the Loves beneath his heart,
near her and far from her thought of the girl,
how she drew her shaft to the mark against a mountain bear,
how she fastened her hand to a lion's neck,
curving her twin arm in a witnessing bond,
how again, sweating, she bathed in a spring's stream,
half-seen, and ever more he remembered her robe,
when, shaking it and lifting it as far as her navel,
baring the bloom of her flesh, the breeze hurled it up;
keeping that in mind he prayed to the sweet gusts
to lift again her deep-folded tunic.
And the unsteady young man, beside the well-horned flock,
seeing the neighbouring high-necked girl hunting
let fly such a word with envious voice:
"Would that I were an arrow, or a net, or a quiver,
would that I were a beast-slaying shaft, that with bare
hands she might lift me; and of her back-strained bow
I would far rather be the ox-sinew, that to her snowy
breast she might bring me, outside her chaste girdle—
yes, heifer, yes, calf, outside her chaste girdle.
Maiden, you lift a blessed shaft; and your
arrows are happier than shepherd Hymnus,
because they touch your love-bearing hands.
I envy your sweet, voiceless hunting-stakes;
nor does the longing for the stakes alone carry me; but I have
envy of the very bow and the breathless quiver.
Would that, resting at noon by a love-stricken spring,
she might cool her limbs, that I might see the high-necked girl—
yes, heifer, yes, calf, free of the envious tunic.
Have you not yet, Cytherea, pitied so great a constraint?
I know not Thrinacia nor the horn-drawn flock,
I pasture no cattle of Helios on these mountains,
my father told of no secret bed of Ares.
Maiden, do not chase me, even if I lead cattle to pasture;
herdsmen too have mounted heavenly beds:
rosy Tithonus was a bridegroom, whom for his beauty
light-bringing Dawn, halting her car, snatched away;
and the cup-bearer of Zeus was a herdsman, whom for his beauty
high-flying Zeus lifted up in sparing talons.
Come, pasture cattle, and I will call you a younger Selene,
with another cowherd, with Endymion;
throw your shaft and touch your crook, that one may say:
'Cytherea pastures the cattle of shepherd Hymnus.'"
So he spoke and entreated, and grasped her dear knees
with woman-mad hands, and followed her, and to tell her
he trembled at the goad of Eros, and blamed himself in his silence.
And once, taking courage, the underworker of bridal Loves,
he lifted up the hunting-gear of Nicaea lying there,
and raised the fierce spear, and under a greater goad of desire,
while the girl was angry, lifted her sweet quiver,
and kissed the silent nets and the breathless arrows,
setting the murderous shaft to his delighting lips,
and pressed it to his breast, squeezing with unsparing hand;
and he spoke a word in some soundless voice:
"By Paphia, speak again, oaks, as in Pyrrha's day,
as in Deucalion's, rebuke the raging girl.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Laurel, dear one, you too break a tree-voice;
would that fair Nicaea had lived before, and then Apollo
would have chased a more delicate maiden, and Daphne would not have become a tree."
So he spoke; and on his pipe, near the chaste girl,
witness of his pain, he made a bridal song.
And the maiden spoke, laughing at the herdsman:
"Sweet is your Pan, piping Paphia's song;
often he sang of love and was no bridegroom of Echo.
Ah, how much Daphnis the cowherd sang; and at his song
the maiden hid herself the more in untrodden crags,
fleeing the song of the shepherd's cry. Ah, how much of Phoebus
Daphne heard singing, and her heart was not charmed."
So speaking she showed the fierce spear to the foolish herdsman.
But he, struck by the raging sweet goad,
not knowing that the Amazon was so loveless,
let fly an ill-loving voice, herald of his own death:
"Yes, I beg you, send the dear spear, and with your snowy
hand kill me, and I rejoice; not your lance,
I do not fear, bed-shunner, your sword, because it would grant
a sharpest end, that I may at last escape the bitter,
fixed wound of Eros, the fire feeding under my heart.
Let me die, since the doom is lovely; but if with a shaft,
bow-bearer next after Cypris, you too will shoot me,
by Paphia, do not send it at my neck, but fix
your shaft in my heart, where the shaft of the Loves is.
Rather throw your spear at my neck, do not strike my heart;
I want no other wound. But if it pleases you,
I will endure another shaft, that earth may cover me
both holding the wound of fire and pierced by iron.
Kill me, the love-sick one, do not spare your string.
You unman the iron whenever you touch your arrows;
of my own accord I stand a mark, with delighted eye
watching the fingers glittering about the notches,
drawing out again your honey-sweet string,
brought near your rosy right breast.
I die, a willing corpse of Eros, by a sweet doom;
I care nothing for death and do not fear the cloud of shafts,
watching your bare snowy hand
touching the bow and the lovely arrow.
Against me let fly all the shafts of your quiver,
against me send the murderous shafts; for more bitter
are the other fire-pointed arrows that harry me.
But if you kill me with your heart-charming bow,
maiden, do not burn my body with the accustomed pyre;
I want no other burning; but you, girl,
only pour sweet dust over me when I am dead
with your own hand, a last small grace, that one may say:
'The maiden pitied as she killed the man she slew.' And of the dead
let no flute of mine, no harp lie about my tomb,
do not throw down the shepherd's crook, witness of my craft;
but fix your shaft of the slain one high over my tomb,
still bathed in the gore of my love-sickness.
And grant me one last other grace high over my tomb:
let the flowers of love-stricken Narcissus arise,
or lovely crocus or the bindweed flower of the Loves,
and plant the springtime short-lived anemone
proclaiming to all my short-lived youth.
And if no pitiless sea or hills bore you,
shed a little tear for me, only so much as with dews
to wet the rosy tips of your lovely cheek,
and with your hand carve this word in mournful red:
'Here lies the cowherd Hymnus, whom, denied his bed,
the maiden Nicaea killed and gave burial to when dead.'"
So he spoke, and Nicaea was angered; and raging
she bared the deadly lid of the venom-shooting quiver
and drew out a straight-coursing shaft, and stretching it out
she rounded the curved horn of the back-strained bow,
and the windy shaft against the herdsman's throat

title: Dionysiaca
text:
as he spoke she let fly, and the irresistible wandering shaft
while he still poured out his speech sealed it with a bond in his throat.
But the corpse was not tearless then; for blaming
man-slaying Nicaea the mountain Nymph grieved,
mourning the dead Hymnus; and in her well-watered hall
the Rhyndacid girl, water-borne, unsandalled, lamented;
and the Naiads wept; and above Sipylus the neighbouring
rock of Niobe lamented more with self-poured tears.
And a younger girl, still untried in bridal Loves,
not yet companion of Bucolion's couch,
Naiad Abarbaree, often was indignant at the nymph;
and about the peak of Dindymon, near the thicket together,
the Astacid Nymphs reproached the ways of the Cybelean nymph,
and they uttered the dirge; and not so much over the burning doom
did the Heliades weep for dead Phaethon.
And gazing at the untamed heart of the murderous girl
Eros threw down his bow, and swore an oath to the herdsman
to yoke the unwilling maiden to Dionysus.
And with tearless eyes, upon her lion-car,
Dindymian Rhea lamented the fallen youth,
mother of Zeus, queen; and at the death of slain Hymnus
the maiden Echo, hating marriage, wailed.
And the oaks spoke: "Why did the herdsman sin so against you?
May Cytherea never, may Artemis never be gracious to you."
And Adresteia saw, she saw the murderous girl,
Adresteia saw the corpse twitching by the iron,
and showed the freshly-slain corpse to the Cyprus-born,
and blamed Eros himself. And by the well-leaved thicket
the bull's tears flowed in pity for Hymnus,
and the calf wept, and the grieving cow lamented
for the gasping shepherd, and seemed to cry out this:
"The fair herdsman is dead, and a fair girl killed him.
The maiden killed the one who longed for her, and instead of love-charms
gave doom as his wage, and in the love-stricken herdsman's
blood she dipped the bronze and quenched the fire of the Loves—
the fair herdsman is dead, and a fair girl killed him—
and grieved the Nymphs; she did not hear the mountain rock,
she did not heed the elm, nor reverence the pine
as it begged: 'Do not send the shaft, do not kill the herdsman.'"
And the wolf lamented Hymnus, the shameless bears lamented,
and with grim eyelids the lion wailed for the herdsman:
"The fair herdsman is dead, and a fair girl killed him.
Seek another rock, oxen, search out, bulls,
a strange mountain; for my sweet herdsman is dead with longing,
cut down by a woman's hand. To what thicket
do I lead my step? Farewell, pastures, farewell, beds of earth.
The fair herdsman is dead, and a fair girl killed him.
Farewell to me, peaks and mountains, farewell, springs,
farewell, Naiads, and my oaks. And both
Pan of the pastures and Phoebus cried aloud; let the flute wander.
Where is Nemesis? Where Cypris? Eros, do not touch the quiver;
pipe, sing no more; the clear-voiced herdsman is dead."
And the blameless gore of the wretched herdsman, slain by the Loves,
Phoebus showed to his sister, and Artemis herself lamented
the dead love of Hymnus, even if she was untried in the Loves.
16. In the sixteenth book I sing of bridal Nicaea,
the sleeping consort of unsleeping Dionysus.
Nor was the murder of the plaintive herdsman unavenged,
but taking up his bow and drawing his lovely arrow
impetuous Eros, unseen, armed himself against Dionysus,
who sat beside the bank of the smooth-pebbled river.
And swift Nicaea, after the course of her usual hunting,
streaming with unstoppable sweat from her labours among the loved crags,
washed her naked body in baths poured down from the mountains.
Nor did the far-shooting Eros delay: against the string
he set the tip-showing notch of the winged arrow,
he bent his bow round, and into the heart of love-maddened Lyaeus
he drove the whole shaft. And in the streams,
seeing the bare-skinned girl swimming, Dionysus
was shaken in mind by the fiery, sweet-maddening dart.
He went here and there, wherever the hare-club-bearing girl was,
now gazing at the curling locks of her hair
stirred by the circling breezes as she sped into her course,
now watching, where her tresses were drawn aside, the gleaming
nakedness of her neck, that sent out a light like the Moon's;
and he neglected the Satyrs and no longer delighted in the Bacchants;
and looking toward Olympus he spoke with a love-begetting voice:
'I will go where the dewy running-ground is, where the quiver,
where the arrow and the lovely bow, where too the very
couches of the unwed maiden breathe with perfume;
I will touch the nets' stakes and spread the toils with my hands;
I too will hunt, and bring down the familiar fawn.
And if, like some heavy-tempered Amazon, she should reproach me,
belching a womanish weight of honey-sweet threat,
to the knees of the angry girl I will bring my hand,
touching her lovely flesh as a suppliant — not lifting
an olive branch, since that is the tree of Athena,
the unwed and unbeguiled maiden, but instead of a bitter,
glistening bough, to my honey-sweet bride
I will lift up, in supplication, a cluster bearing the wine-dark fruit
of the honey-dripping vintage. And if she should be angered,
the maiden of the curved bow, let her not fix her spear in my flesh,
nor again draw the murderous arrow, but in shame
let her strike my body with the very tip of her sweet bow:
I care nothing for a stroke that charms the heart. And if she wishes,
let her seize my hair with her lovely hands,
tugging the willing locks of my bound tresses.
I will never restrain the maiden, but as though in anger
I will press her clenching right hand with a relentless grip,
taking her reddening fingers in a hooked clasp,
a comfort for the toil of Cypris — for the maiden
has plundered all the beauty of Olympus. Be gracious, Cerne!
Astacis has sprung up as a new rose-fingered Dawn,
another light-bearer has grown up — for the younger
holds her form unchanging: Nicaea is a Moon.
I longed, in my desire, to change my many-fashioned form;
were it not that reverence for my father's modesty holds me back,
I too, through the Tyrian water, a bull crossing the wet,
would carry my Nicaea unwetted over the seas
and swim — like the bridegroom of Europa — and unwilling
I would shake my back, so that, as the girl was tossed,
her all-white right hand might seize my horn.
I longed, were I a winged husband, that I might dance
lifting unshaken the woman upon my back,
as Cronides bore Aegina, so that after the bed I might make
the eagle, that other bird, a star to adorn the loves' wedding.
Yet I will not, by striking my wife's father with a thunderbolt,
grant my bride the wicked dowry of her father's ruin,
lest I grieve sweet Nicaea by his destruction.
Would I were a bastard bird with goodly wings, since she too,
our own maiden, loves winged arrows.
Rather, longing for Danae's watery shape of love,
I longed, were I become the golden shower as her husband,
myself the gift of wedlock, myself the spouse, that I might dance
pouring down on her the rich, loving shower of dew;
for it would befit my Nicaea, my fair-faced girl,
who has a golden form, to have a golden husband.'
Such words, raving with love, he cried in a frenzied voice.
And once, walking within a fragrant meadow,
he gazed at all the blossoming flowers, kin in hue to the girl,
and spoke a word to the misty breezes:
'Only now, scarcely, Nicaea, have I seen your shape here.
Did you not change your beauty into flowers? For gazing
on the fair-formed rose-bed I recognized your cheeks;
and your rose blooms unfading — for you wear
the inborn, never-ceasing, blushing anemone.
Turning my eye to the lily, I saw your snowy palms,
and beholding the hyacinth I saw your dark-blue hair.
Receive me as your fellow-traveller in the hunt; and if you wish,
I myself will bear the sweet burden of the stakes, I will carry
the high boots and the bow and the lovely arrows,
I myself — I have no need of the Satyrs. Did not Apollo himself,
beside the thicket, lift the nets of Cyrene?
What grudge is it, if I too handle the net? I do not toil
when I carry my Nicaea upon my own shoulders.
Nor am I greater than my father — for in the surging waters
the sea-crossing bull bore Europa undrenched.
Rosy maiden, why has the woodland so pleased you?
Spare your lovely limbs, and let no rocky,
unspread couch wear away your back upon the stones.
I will be your chamber-servant, if you wish; and in the hall
I myself will spread your bedding, and over it lay
the richly-dappled skins of leopards, and with them throw
the bristling, thick-haired hides of a lion's covering,
baring my own limbs; and you shall sleep sweet sleep
covered by the dappled fawnskins of Dionysus;
and a fitting screen of Mygdonian deer I throw on high,
stripping the Satyrs. And if you have need of hounds,
I will give you at once all my Pan's dogs together,
and bring other hounds from Sparta, those that my Carneian Apollo
rears for the loves of young men,
and I will summon the hunting hounds of Aristaeus;
and I will bring nets with their stakes and fitting gifts,
the high boots of Nomius and Agreus, who long ago knew
both the rich-meadowed pasture and the course of the toilsome chase.
And if you fear the flame of the summer-born thirsty season,
I will plant vine-shoots over your bed,
and the fragrant breezes of wine will breathe around you
as you lie within the midst of a covering of many grape-clusters.
Wandering maiden, of the love-stricken face,
pity your cheeks, smitten by Phaethon's heat,
lest the Sun's brilliance wither the beam of your limbs,
lest the winds spoil your perfumed locks:
sleep amid the roses and on the petals of the hyacinth,
resting your head on Dionysus your neighbour,
that you may kindle one revel for the four immortals,
for Phoebus and Zephyr and Cypris and Dionysus.
I would grant you, as plunder, a dark-skinned brood of Indians,
chamber-servants of your bridal bower — but why have I named
the dark race as escorts of your bed?
When does white Dawn ever mingle with black-cloaked Night?
Astacis, you are a younger Artemis — but I myself
will bring you sixty handmaids, dancers,
that I may make a countless choir to attend you,
equal in number to the handmaids of the mountain Archeress,
like the daughters of Ocean, so that Artemis
may not vie with you in hunting, even if she is mistress of the chase.
To you I grant the Graces of holy Orchomenus
as handmaids, taking over my children of Aphrodite.
But charm your unbeguiled heart with desire, and let my bed
receive you after the toil of the hunt, that you may appear
Artemis among the crags and Aphrodite in the bridal chambers.
What grudge is it, that you should hunt with hunting Lyaeus?
And if you have got a frenzy for battle, then, like a famed-bow Amazon,
you shall come to the Indian war, that you may be
Persuasion apart from strife and, when there is combat, Athena.
Take too, if you wish, the deer-slaying thyrsi of Lyaeus,
and become a fawn-slayer; and by your own hands
and by your own labours adorn my chariot,
yoking a leopard or lions to the bridle.'
So speaking he pursued the mountain girl, his neighbour,
crying out this word: 'Wait, maiden, for Bacchus your husband.'
But she, growing angry, raised up a mighty voice,
the maiden, hurling a furious mouth against Lyaeus:
'Go and say these things to some loving bride.
If you can drag the grey-eyed one or Artemis into wedlock,
then you have mighty Nicaea too as an obedient bride;
for I am companion-in-arms to both. But if there flees you
the unforeseen wedding of unlabouring Athena,
then neither will you charm the mind of the disobedient Archeress.
Do not seek the bed of Nicaea; nor let me see you
laying hand to bow and fingering the quiver.
Lest, after the herdsman Hymnus who perished, I bring you down too.
I will wound the unwounded Dionysus — unless against iron
you bear a flesh unscarred and unyielding to the dart.
I will imitate the high-crested sons of Iphimedeia,
and bind you with iron, inextricable chains,
just like your brother, and within a hiding-place
of bronze jars I will keep you too, after Ares,
until, fulfilling twelve circuits of the Moon,
you cast off your frenzy to the airy winds.
With woman-mad hands do not touch my quiver:
I have a bow, you a thyrsus; on the Astacian cliff
I send my arrow here against boars or lions,
Artemis' fellow-contestant, but over the rock of Lebanon
do you too hunt fawns, hunting alongside Aphrodite.
I do not accept your bed, even if you carry the blood of Zeus;
for if I wished to have a god as husband, I would not have
a soft-haired, ironless, feeble spouse of womanish form,
I would not have Dionysus, but there would be guarded for my bridal
a bridegroom either the famed-bow lord or bronze Ares —
one holding a bow, the other a sword as the loves' dowry;
but since I will accept none of the blessed ones, the frenzy
does not hold me even to call your father Cronion my father-in-law.
Seek another, Bacchus, a young and obedient bride.
Why do you hurry? You run an unattainable course, as once
Leto's son pursued Daphne, and as Hephaestus pursued Athena;
why do you hurry? This course is vain; for among the crags
the hunting-boots are far better than buskins.'
So speaking she left Bacchus. And ever beneath the grazing thicket
he sought the mountain-wandering maiden; and as he sped,
a hound ran with him, a faithful companion with a prudent heart,
which once, to mountain-loving Dionysus as he hunted,
high-horned Pan, the rearer of whelps, had given to keep as a gift.
And watching it as though it had understanding and a voice,
his fellow-ranger, his road-companion, his partner in toils,
Bacchus, raving with love, embraced it with a friendly speech:
'Why, wandering hound, are you the running-mate of Lyaeus,
you who deserve forever the longing Pan? Why do you alone
track with Dionysus as he tracks the maiden?
Has your keeper made you pitying toward loves?
Seek still our maiden, and do not, among the rocks,
leave Bacchus to wander alone over the mountains.
You alone pity me, and like a mortal, into the ridge of the woodland
you go after the leafy haunts of the wandering girl.
Toil for your king; and in return for your toils I will give you
a recompense: after the star Sirius of Maera,
I will lead you within the heaven and make you a star
near the earlier Dog, so that you too may ripen
the grape-cluster, shooting your gleam upon the Eileithyia of the cluster.
What grudge is it that a third Dog should rise? You too will shine
running beside the starry, hastening Hare.
If it is right, while pitying me, find fault with the chaste girl.
Turning a sidelong eye toward the ridge of Cybele's woodland,
because the woman still flees me, a god, as I seek her;
find fault with both, with Adonis and with Cythereia,
and pursue restless Echo, the wanderer through the mountain,
lest she make my bride still more a fugitive from the bed;
and do not leave your love-sick Pan near the girl,
lest he seize her and yoke her in compelled wedlock.
If you see the maiden, come swiftly, announcing it to Dionysus
by a witnessing silence or by intelligent barkings;
be the messenger of my desire; let some other hound wander
chasing either boars or lions from the crag.
Dear Pan, I call you most blessed, since even
your own hounds are born searchers-out of the loves.'
'You who play, many-shaped Fortune, with the mortal race,
be gracious, all-subduer; for after the mortal breed
you rule the whelps too, since this ill-fated wanderer
serves, after Pan, the longing Lyaeus as well;
find fault with the maiden, dear oaks; say it, you rocks:
even the hounds pity, and yet the Amazon did not show mercy.
There are prudent ones even among the whelps, to whom Cronion
gave a human mind, though he granted no mortal voice.'
He spoke near a plant; and through the leafy cluster,
hearing the voice of woman-mad Dionysus,
