the ancient Melia raised a mocking cry:
'Others, Dionysus, are hunting here, urging on their hounds
for the Archeress, but you hunt for Aphrodite;
sweet is he who dreads the soft-skinned, unwedded girl;
bold Bacchus has become a suppliant, a servant of the loves;
with his Indian-slaying hands he begs a feeble girl.
Your father did not know how, with mind-charming speech of desire,
to lead an obedient girl into wedlock, into marriage;
he did not entreat Semele, until he won his love.
He did not persuade Danae, until he plundered her maidenhood;
you know Ixion's wife, joined to Zeus,
and the bridal neighing and the horse-wedding;
you learned the playful ordinance of the loves with Antiope,
and the laughing Satyr, the false, mimic husband.'
So she spoke, mocking the timid mind of Bacchus.
And she went within the oak, her coeval. And upon the hills,
grieving, Dionysus followed the frenzied girl
with love-maddened feet; and the swift-sandalled Amazon,
restless, went over the topmost heads of the trackless rock,
stealing away the footprint from the searching Lyaeus.
And as her skin was lashed by Phaethon's fiery brand,
the parched lips of the thirsty girl grew dry, unmoistened;
and not knowing the trick of woman-mad Dionysus,
she saw the yellow water of the wine-loving river,
and drank the sweet stream, whence the fiery Indians had drunk;
and her mind whirled, and the girl raved in drunkenness,
and she shook her head, shifting with a double throbbing,
and she thought she saw a twin, capacious lake
as she rolled her eyes; and as her head grew heavy
she beheld the doubled ridges of the beast-feeding hill;
and slipping on the dust with trembling feet
she was dragged, self-rolling, onto the wing of neighbouring Sleep;
and the heavy-kneed bride was charmed by the bridal swoon.
Seeing her asleep, Eros pointed her out to Bacchus,
pitying Hymnus; but Nemesis laughed to see it.
And crafty Dionysus, with noiseless boots,
crept soundless to the wedding with a cunning beat of his feet.
He came near the girl; and gently, drawing the topmost
fastening, the guardian of her inviolate girdle, he loosed it
with a sparing hand, that sleep might not let the maiden go.
And the earth, opening her fragrant childbed,
gave birth in travail to a plantation, in favour of Dionysus,
and lifting up a great vine-bearing canopy
the plaited stake was weighed down with clustering fruit;
and the bed was shaded with leaves — for of its own accord
the vine's tendril girdled the well-vined couch;
and many a wandering grape-cluster, high in the air with wine-dark fruit,
was shaken here and there by the breezes of Cypris,
and shrouded them both; and with celery-bearing cluster
the lovely shoot of the vine, its yoke-mate, made drunk
the woven ivy, climber upon the swelling vintage.
And the crafty wedding was like a dream-bed,
having sleep for its partner; and she was robbed of maidenhood,
the slumbering girl, and beheld, as escort of the loves,
sleep the under-servant of the wine-tottering wedding.
And the breeze, in the high-coursing leaping of the frenzied wood,
restless, self-shouting, wove a hymn of the loves,
and the wind-roaming song of the mountain-dwelling wedding
the maiden Echo answered with shamefaced lips,
the daughter of Pan, late-voiced; and dancing above the ground
the flute resounded, singing 'Hymen, O Hymenaeus';
this lovely wedding the mountain pine proclaimed.
And the wind-roaming soul of the herdsman, darting up,
stirred the sleeping maiden with nightly dreams:
'There are Furies even for one who loves, well-wed girl;
if you fled Hymnus your bridegroom, you have been wedded to Dionysus;
crookedly you give judgement, chamber-keeping maiden bride;
for you kill the one who loves, and pursue the one who does not woo.
Maiden, you gave brazen sleep to Hymnus who loved you;
maiden, sweet sleep has destroyed your maidenhood.
Pitifully, laughing, you saw the blood of the herdsman struck down;
more pitifully, lamenting, you have seen the blood of your maidenhood.'
So speaking, like to shadowy smoke,
the tearful soul of the love-stricken herdsman sped away,
and unreachable plunged into the all-receiving hall of Tartarus,
bearing envy of Bacchus and his wine-tottering wedding.
And striking out a bridal sound on his clear reeds,
hiding the envy beneath his heart, the hymn-singing Pan
spoke a reproachful song against another's wedding.
And one of the love-maddened Satyrs, beside the neighbouring thicket,
an insatiable gazer at the unseen wedding,
told the Bacchic tale, having seen the fair-maiden bed:
'Horned Pan, do you still alone run after Aphrodite?
And you too — when will you be the bridegroom of the pursued Echo?
And you too — when will you contrive such a helping trick,
an aid for your own unwedded wedlock?
Dear Pan, become you too a planter instead of a herdsman,
and renounce the shepherd's crook, and beside the rock
leave the cattle and the sheep — what will the herdsmen do for you?
Wake, and plant you too the wedding-arranging wine of the loves.'
The tale was not yet ended when the goat-feeding Pan cried out:
'Would my father had taught me the trick of marriage-fulfilling wine!
Would that, like Bacchus, I ruled the mind-deranging grape!
Then I too would have fulfilled the much-wandering frenzy of my loves,
seeing sleeping and drunk the ill-maiden Echo.
Be gracious, this pasture of mine, since beside the neighbouring spring
I water these sheep, but with the wine-loving stream
Dionysus drags unbeguiled maidens into wedlock.
He has found a drug for love, his own plant: away with the milk
of goats, away with the milk of our sheep — for it cannot
bring sleep upon desire or drag a maiden into wedlock.
I alone, Cythereia, am forced — alas for the loves!'
The pipe of Pan fled the unwedded wedlock
and hailed with joy the just-accomplished wedding of Dionysus
with self-sounding strains; and the more — to his accustomed song
the answering Echo replied as Syrinx sounded:
'Dionysus, mortal-charming shepherd of the bridal wine,
you alone have become blessed, since, when the bride refused,
you found wine, the wedding-arranging helper of the loves.'
Such a word the love-sick, grieving Pan recited,
holding envy and longing for marriage-fulfilling Lyaeus.
And having accomplished his love and his desire of the wayside bed,
Dionysus rose up on his unspeakable sandal.
And the bride, waking, blamed the river spring,
angry at sleep and Cypris and Dionysus,
drenched with a tearful rain; and grieving
she heard still the remnants of the Naiads' bridal song,
and the herald of the bed of love-stricken Lyaeus —
shaded by the leaves of the vine she saw the couch
covered with the bridal fawnskins of Dionysus,
self-announcing the secret bed; she saw too
her own maiden girdle filled with the bridal dew.
And she gashed her rosy cheeks, and beating
both her thighs she roared with a plaintive voice:
'Alas for my maidenhood, which the Euian water snatched away;
alas for my maidenhood, which the sleep of the loves snatched away;
alas for my maidenhood, which wandering Bacchus snatched away.
Away with the deceiving drink of the Water-nymphs, away with the bed!
Hamadryad nymphs, whom shall I blame? For my maidenhood
sleep, Eros, trickery, wine have plundered.
Even Artemis has renounced maidens — but she herself,
why did Echo, all her body, not tell me, "flee the bed"?
Why into my ear, only that I might not hear Bacchus,
did Pitys not whisper, and Daphne not speak,
"Maiden, beware of drinking the deceiving water"?'
She spoke, and gushed up a much-weeping rain of the eye.
And now she longed to press a sword against her neck,
now, self-rolling, she wished to fall from the mountain
headlong at the last, slipping in the dust;
and she longed to wipe out the drink of the bridal spring,
had not the earlier flood, changed from the moisture of Bacchus,
murmured white water and no longer the stream of Lyaeus.
And she entreated Cronides and Artemis, that he might dry up
the courts of the Naiads, made dusty in thirsty ground.
Often she strained her eye through the mountain, in case she might find
the unsteady footprint of the unseen Dionysus,
that a woman might strike the god with her bow, that she might subdue
the cluster-bearing deity; and she wished still more to destroy
with fiery fire that whole bridal vine.
Often, beholding through the mountain the tracks of Bacchus,
she shot, aiming her arrows at the airy gusts;
often she lifted her spear and stood facing her mark,
that she might strike the body of the unwounded Dionysus;
but in vain she let fly, and did not hit Lyaeus.
And she was angry at the river and swore that never from its spring
would she drink the deceiving water with thirsty lips;
she swore too to keep a sleepless eye through the nights,
she swore to sleep no other sweet sleep in the mountains.
And she was angry at the guardian hounds, because they too
had not then armed themselves against woman-mad Lyaeus.
And she sought a high remedy against death by hanging,
crushing her neck, entwined in a strangling bond,
shunning the mocking blame of her companion youth.
And unwilling she left the ancient beast-nurturing wood,
ashamed to appear before the Archeress after the bed.
And filled with the drop of holy Lyaeus' seed
she bore a burden in her womb; and when the labour was fulfilled
the life-warming Hours delivered a female birth,
and confirmed the nine-circuit course of the Moon;
and from the wedlock of Bromius the god-sped girl flowered,
whom he named Telete, ever rejoicing in festivals,
the night-dancing girl, follower of Dionysus,
delighting in castanets and in the double-beaten oxhide.
And beside the wine-loving lake the god built
a fair-stoned city, Nicaea, which he called
by the name of the nymph Astacis, after his Indian-slaying victory.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
17. In the seventeenth book I sing of the first-hunted War
and the stream of the honey-dripping river made drunk with wine.
Nor, when he had taken alive — unshaken, fettered by sleep
through the drunkenness of unmixed wine — the unwounded race of Indians,
did Dionysus entrust the battle to the winds of forgetfulness;
but again he lifted the Phrygian thyrsus, for to the war-cry
of high-crested Deriades, who summoned him, he hastened,
leaving unremembered the crafty, wine-heavy love
of the Amazon's child and the slumbering wedding.
And the god led the way, bearing, as herald of the race of Zeus,
a heavenly beam upon his gleaming face;
and around the Lydian car of Giant-slaying Dionysus
were ranks of thyrsus-bearers, and he was girdled with warriors
on either side, appearing in the midst, and he flashed back at Olympus;
in beauty he hid them all — and seeing him you might soon say
he was the fiery sun amid the widely-scattered stars.
And the lord armed his army's ironless War,
with no sword, no death-bringing ash-spear, but instead of bronze
holding for his weapon the unbreakable ivy; and wheeling it
through the cities of Asia, and fixing it in the soil of Asia,
he wildly drove the savage car of the Cybeleïd goddess,
shaded with coeval ivy on its vine-shoot harness,
lashing the speeding chariot with a flower-haired whip;
and he made the eastern land drunk with the Maronian vintage.
And the whole host of Bacchants flowed as Bromius' comrades in arms,
holding courage from the earlier battle's grace, when, with twin
embracing arm, sweet-maddened and ironless,
Silenus, heavy-kneed, a sluggish wayfarer,
lifting an armed Indian — a thinking, voiceless corpse —
withdrew; and when, reveling with the twofold rhythm of her feet,
the unveiled Bacchic Mimallon rattled her castanets
over an Indian still sleeping, and clasping his neck
hunted her plunder, a self-charged prey of battle . . .
And from city to city he went, and to the rich
plain of neighbouring Alybe he came, where, close at hand,
rolling a Zeus-fallen swell with its wealthy streams,
Geudis whitens with the channel of its treasure-holding waters,
scouring the hollow of its silver bed.
There, as he passed by the deep-rich rock,
Bacchus, fellow-traveller of the ox-horned Satyrs, a wayfarer on foot,
was received in a desolate hut by a man of the fields,
Brongus, a mountain-roaming dweller of unhewn glens,
inhabiting a houseless house under the unwrought foundation
of earth-born rocks; and as a giver of good cheer,
mixing the snowy dew of a milked she-goat,
the host shepherd soothed him with a milky drink,
with worthless foods and rustic cups,
and loosed one wool-fleeced sheep from his fold,
that he might carve a sacrifice for Dionysus;
but the god restrained him, and the old man obeyed the unbending
nods of Bacchus, and leaving the sheep untouched
he set some shepherd's meal before willing Lyaeus,
making a dinnerless dinner of an uncarved table,
such as is told of Cleonaean Molorchus,
those things which, as he hastened to the lion-slaying contest,
he made ready for Heracles; and in heaps he threw upon the table
the autumn flower of the olive that swims in brine,
Brongus, taking the model of a loving herdsman,
lifting in plaited baskets the fresh-set cheese,
moist, round-shaped; and the god laughed, beholding
the simple dinners of the country folk, and to the hospitable herdsman
turning a gracious eye he touched the scanty table,
devouring insatiably; and ever he remembered that
scant feast of the bloodless board,
beside the supper of his own mother, mountain-dwelling Cybele.
And he marvelled at the rugged gates of the round court,
how toil-working Nature had carved the dwelling, how without art
the cliffs had been rounded into answering courses.
But when lord Bacchus had taken his fill of the pastoral fare,
then, stirred by the divine breath of Bacchus,
the countryman piped the wonted song of Pan,
Brongus, pressing the double-sounding flute of Athena,
hymning Dionysus; and the god delighted his heart in the song,
and mixing in a bowl the newly-flowing moisture of the press:
'Receive, old man, this gift, a respite from all care;
nor do you need milk, holding the sweet-smelling dew,
the earthly likeness of heavenly nectar, such as Ganymede
draws and gladdens great Zeus with on Olympus.
Let go the longing for your old milk; for of new-born
she-goats, when the udders are pressed, the snowy moistures
do not delight men, nor do they loose their cares.'
So speaking he gave, as a guest-gift of the pastoral table,
the well-clustered vintage, mother of toil-loosing wine;
and the lord taught him the flower-loving work of the vineyard,
to bend the vine-twigs round in the well-nourishing trench of plants,
cutting the tops of the aged, flourishing cluster,
to raise the young shoots of the wine-bearing grape.
And leaving the herdsman and the ridge of the wild woodland
he hastened to another mountain war against the Indians;
and urging on the mountain-running track, his companions the Satyrs,
he came back again to consort with his handmaid frenzied Bacchants.
And thirsting for slaughter and for thyrsus-fair battle,
holding the deep-booming trumpet of the Tyrrhenian sea,
he sounded on the conch a song, escort of Enyalius,
gathering his folk; and he made the mighty warriors drunk,
drawing the men with hotter thoughts toward War,
destroyers of the un-Bacchic Indian breed.
These lord Dionysus marshalled for the battle of the Indians;
but Astraeis, going unreachably, brought word to Orontes
of the enslaved tribes of the Indians, and cried with a grieving voice:
'Son-in-law of spear-bold, battle-abiding Deriades,
hear me, and hearing be not angry; and I will teach you
the drug-wrought victory of unarmoured Dionysus.
There was battle between the Indians and the Satyrs: aslant
roared the line of Bassarids, and my folk was arrayed against Lyaeus,
flashing with shields; and watching the javelin-bearers
the Lydian, that man of many wiles, made my warriors shudder.
And there stood up the champion of the unwarlike Satyrs — not a spear of combat
bearing in his hand, nor holding a naked sword, nor on the string
drawing toward a straight-pathed mark the wind-borne shaft;
but he held a bull's horn, and in the hollow tip
he carried a liquid drug, and into the channels of the silver river
he poured down all his crafty dew,
reddening the sweet stream with the moisture; and out of the battle,
parched in the heat, all the fiery Indians who drank
held a conscious madness and struck up the dance;
and a deadly sleep fell upon them, and unbending,
maddened past all restraint, they bedded down upon their oxhides;
others lay down upon unspread pallets,
giving over their sluggish bodies to unsleeping sleep,
a prey to the feeble Bacchants and to Dionysus.
And these, without battle and without keen iron,
the women plundered into slavish yoke-bondage,
with their burdened limbs, and over the shoulders of the enemy
the warriors, like living corpses, were lightly carried,
some still spewing out the deceitful moisture of Bacchus,
enslaved by necessity to the unwarlike Satyrs,
maddened by the drugged stream. And out of the battle
I alone was left, still untaught of the murderous dew,
fleeing with unwetted lips the deceiving water.
But beware the drink, spear-wielder, lest after the cunning,
ironless, bloodless victory of Lyaeus
some other trick take alive in War the remnant of the Indians.'
At his words, heavy-wrathed Orontes grew the more enraged,
and swiftly came back to battle; for half-finished
was the contest, and the foundations of another fight were being laid.
While the mountain-running Ares armed the Indian host,
meanwhile the Bassarids, high on much-winding Taurus,
hastened to battle, and the Bacchants marched together,
arms-bearing, and the unarmed Beasts; some, breaking off the bases
of the glens, lifted them up, others a high-stretched
headland of the hill; and as the battle began
they fell upon the enemy; and many-cleft ravines
were hurled in spirals against the Indian heads.
And bounding upon the cliff with slender feet
the Pans armed themselves in madness, of whom one of them,
seizing with skilful hand the neck constrained by his grip,
tore open the foeman with his goat-hooves,
gashing the mid-flank along with the heavy corslet;
another, with the well-curved points of his long-shooting horns,
snatching an Indian wanderer upright and pierced through,
lifted him impaled at the middle, and into the airy ways
flung him high-flying upon his two horns,
headlong, self-rolling; and another, like Deo of the sheaves,
brandishing in his hand the reed-cutting sickle,
as if it were the corn-ear of battle, the sheaves of warfare,
reaped the broods of the foe with the hook-clawed bronze,
making a revel for Ares, a harvest-feast for Dionysus too,
cutting the heads of the enemy; and he held out to Bacchus his witness
the curved sword stained with the dew of men.
Pouring out a bloody libation to Dionysus,
he made the Fates drunk too, pouring the drink of Enyalius;
and as another stood his ground, the goat-fed Pan, gripping him,
twisting a bond of interwoven hands upon his neck,
flung the well-corsleted foe upon his horn,
his flank cloven with the two-edged point;
another, slaying with his crook a man who charged,
crushed the brow-frowning topmost forehead through the middle.
And bold Orontes heartened the Indian host,
pouring out a threatening speech with a high-manly voice:
'Come, friends, let us rouse War against the Satyrs;
do not tremble at the Ares of battle-fleeing Dionysus;
and let none of you drink the yellow water,
the deceiving, maddening drugs of the sweet spring,
mangled by the hand of Lyaeus, of the ill-fated Indians;
lest, after so many heads, sleep destroy us too.
Come, let us fight again with confidence; and when shall the unwarlike
Bacchus openly set my War against him?
If he can, let the fugitive champion abide me, that he may learn
what champions Deriades arrays for War.
Let him fight with leaves, I with fiery iron.
To me who hold a bronze spear, what will the Lydian do
hurling his oaken shaft of clusters? But this warrior,
this feeble fellow, I will drag away bound, heavily fettered,
this womanish Dionysus, attendant of Deriades;
this one with the woman's soft skin — leave all
the Indians, so many, and fight you alone against Orontes.
Sweet is he who twirls the loosened locks of his hair,
sweet the lovely champion of the Bassarids; but they too,
the women, shoot with beauty and not with arrows.
Your servants I will join to the woman-mad Indians,
dragged to the beds of spear-won wedlock.'
So speaking, hot Orontes ran upon the champions,
reaping the twofold harvest of Ares; nor did any dare
to abide the opposing onset of so great a champion,
not bold Eurymedon the fiery, nor his brother Alcon;
for Astraeis, the Satyrs' champion, fled, nor did any
of the Sileni stand his ground. And with stormy foot
the son-in-law of Deriades, terrible, raged,
lifting against the Centaurs a windy boulder,
and he struck Hylaeus; the shaggy-breasted herdsman's
topmost forehead he crushed, casting a millstone of rock,
and he battered his head-guard with a ravine-torn missile,
the fashioned likeness of false skill in customary gypsum,
the imitation of a true helmet, a fence for the eye;
and it fell on the ground in many splinters, like fiery
ash, and there came white dust; but he, sinking down,
embraced the ground with his arm beside his rocky spear.
And of another Centaur, through the well-horned head,
striking the shaggy forehead with his double-edged ox-cleaver,
he shore off the curved bull-horn;
and great he fell to earth, and bounding on his head
half-dead he rolled, and beat the dust with his ears;
and raising his body up on a last foot he raved,
holding a mirthless, rolling-footed dance of death;
and the monster crashed out a sound, like a bull sending forth
a harsh bellowing from a grinning throat,
struck in the head. And striking Helice, loveless Erembeus
drove the bronze into her breast, and the white circle of her bosom
the dark hand scored with reddening blood;
and her, fallen in the dust, the javelin-hurling winds
joined to another grief, lifting up her robe;
and from her flesh gushed the lovely gore; and in shame
with her right hand she gathered up her fleeing tunic,
guarding the bared mysteries of her snowy thigh.
And the god, beholding the shifting victory of the foe,
and the Satyrs cowering, crashed out into the battle-din,
like an army of nine thousand from loud-thundering throats
pouring an answering echo from gathered mouths.
And swift-kneed Orontes fought alone against Bromius,
mortal though he was, and challenged the god with a mortal voice.
Both came together to the battle, of whom the one
held a spear, the other a sharpened thyrsus. And on the top
of Bacchus' unwounded head, casting his blow, overweening Orontes
vainly struck Bromius' sharp horn;
for lord Dionysus, of the unharmed head,
held a bull-shaped likeness of the Moon-bright forehead,
not to be cut by the crushing iron of the ox-cleaver,
as horned Achelous is sung, whose horn once
Heracles cut off and took as a marriage-dower; but Lyaeus
held the heavenly likeness of the ox-eyed Moon,
having the unbreakable growth of a divine horn,
unshaken by the foe; and the bold Indian against Bacchus,
heavy-booming, like an airy gale,
hurled a second time, and the point was bent back for him,
touching the fawnskin, like lead. And against his target
casting the wine-dark thyrsus at the broad shoulder of Orontes,
Bacchus willingly missed; and mocking Lyaeus
with his ivied spear the god-fighter Orontes said:
'You who array a womanish host against my battalions,
if you can, make war with your womanish thyrsus,
if you can, do battle in the front; and if you charm the minds of mortals,
all-subduer, then charm one single, unbeguiled Orontes.
Stand and fight, and you shall know what a valiant
chieftain my old Indian Hydaspes rears.
I was not born of Phrygia, whence women are mannish,
having reaped the unsown corn-ear of unwedded youth;
I am no ironless servant of feeble Lyaeus.
Drugs will not save your champions; and your
frenzied handmaids I will plunder, and out of the battle
I will bring the Sileni as servants to my king,
and all your cowering Satyrs I will destroy with my spear.'
So spoke, shouting his war-cry, the army's champion; and hearing it
lord Bacchus was angered, and with a vine-cluster
he struck him on the chest, sparingly; and by the worthless
clustering flower struck, his corslet was split;
yet the Bacchic point did not touch his sheltered flesh,
nor graze the surface of his body; but as his iron tunic
broke, heavy-booming Orontes drew back, naked;
and toward the eastern verge he strained his eyes
to Phaethon facing him, and spoke his last word:
'Sun, who cleave the air through your fiery chariot,
casting your light over the neighbouring Caucasian furrow,
halt your car for me, and tell Deriades
of the enslaved tribes of the Indians and self-slain Orontes
and the little man-breaking thyrsi; tell too of the
drug-wrought victory of battle-untried Dionysus,
and the stream of the mind-deranging river made drunk with wine;
and tell how the unwearied host of iron-bearing Indians
the women cleave apart with their slender leaves.
And if you still remember the bed of your Clymene,
save Deriades, the offshoot of your race,
who bears the blood of Astris, the girl said to be your daughter.
I did not yield to womanish Bromius; I call as witnesses
the Sun and the boundless Earth and the god of the Indians,
the pure water. But you, farewell, and be gracious to the battle
of the warring Indians, and bury Orontes, who has perished.'
So speaking he drew his sword, and fixing it in the midst of his belly,
heavy-fated he leapt upon the self-slaying iron;
and he rolled into the river and gave his name to Orontes.
And beholding him still breathing and gasping,
lord Bacchus spoke, pouring out a mocking echo:
'Lie there, corpse, in foreign waters; and your
dying Deriades let his father Hydaspes hide.
You both, father-in-law and son-in-law, I will destroy,
instead of a murderous spear and a sharpened sword
shaking Euian thyrsi and a vine-clad point.
But slaying you with the blood-red iron,
you did not drink the delicate streams of the honey-dripping river;
and the river covered you, and you missed the sweet wine.
If you wish, drink the whole stream alone; but you will not
need the river's streams, having drunk the Acherusian water,
deadly; and with the man-slaying flow and the bitter stream
holding a belly swelling, pregnant with Fate,
taste of Cocytus, and if you wish, drink Lethe,
that you may forget War and the bloody iron.'
So he spoke, mocking the wet corpse. And swollen,
on the unsteady waves the dead Orontes was dragged along;
and as he swam through the stream with cold limbs
the river-banks belched up the breathless corpse.
The Nymphs entombed him and wailed the dirge over him,
the Hamadryad nymphs, beside the root of a golden laurel
around the river's flow, and they wrote high upon a tree:
'Here lies the army's champion who dishonoured Bacchus,
the Indian Orontes, slain by his own hand.'
Nor yet was there an end of the joyless battle; for half-finished
was the contest and the strife unaccomplished; and high-shining
the Indian Ares raised the war-cry; and in the renewed battle-din
the unfinished Bacchic frenzy, belching out the Lydian
weight of madness, the maenad Enyo
reveled into another battle,
hurling at the foe with man-slaying clusters,
maddened for Ares; and by the shoot-loving Lyaeus
the enemy were slain with the oaken iron,
holding a bloody wound; and as, by the unarmoured Bacchant
with her clustering spear, the iron was cloven,
the bronze-tunicked Indians marvelled that with sharp ivy
their breasts were laid bare, newly wounded; for more easily
the bearers, without shelter of a corslet, were shot.
And of others there was unspeakable, manifold slaughter, beneath whose gore
their tunics, cloven by the leaves, were reddened
as they fought, where Taurus stands; and the Bacchants encircled
unbending, like a crown, the ranks of the yoked Indians.
And the bold flute piped a song of slaughter; and in the battle
the Bacchants, servants of battle-untried Dionysus,
struck by axes and double-edged swords,
were all, like a tower, unharmed; but the soft-haired
foes were slain by slender leaves;
and one after another there were stuck fast in the long-shooting trees
the thick darts of the Indians, and the pine was pierced
by the far-flung spear, the fir was struck, the laurel was shot,
though it was the tree of Phoebus, and in its shamefaced leaves
it hid the cloud of long-winged arrows sent against it,
lest Apollo see it shot through with darts.
And with bare hand, without shields, without iron,
the Bacchant shook her rattles, and the shield-bearer fell;
the drums crashed out, and the warriors danced;
the cymbals clashed, and the Indian man bent his neck
to Lyaeus as a suppliant. And in the thin skin of fawns
the unbreakable points of the javelins were turned aside;
and the bronze-heavy, unbending helmet was cut by foliage.
And one champion of the war-maddened Satyrs, striking a man,
threw Euian leaves, and of the newly-wounded bearer
the bronze tunic was split by the clustering ivy.
And beholding the scales of battle with their shifting swing
foretelling the victory of Indian-slaying Lyaeus,
Astraeis, unreachable, withdrew, escaping his doom,
cowering before the long-leaved spear of Dionysus.
Meanwhile Aristaeus, scattering life-giving drugs,
healed every wound of the Bassarids with Phoebian skill.
On the blows of one he laid the Centaur-herb;
of another, weighed down, he cleansed the bloody dew
by pressing out the blood; and he healed the plaintive Bacchant,
grinding many kinds of plants for the girl's wounds,
whether of foot or hand or breast or flank.
And when another champion was struck by a murderous arrow,
he drew out the swift point, and pressing the wounds with his hand
he made the bloody dew spurt up little by little;
to another he brought his hand, and scoring the surface of the wound
he cut away the parts rotted by the drugged shaft with a knife,
laying his sparing fingers with the very tips of his hand;
and with the green flower of the life-sustaining earth he mixed
the cunning travail of the evil-averting bee,
sprinkling with his hand the pain-killing moisture of Bacchus;
and others, wounded, he healed with a Phoebian voice,
murmuring a dread, many-named hymn of song,
mindful of the life-sustaining mysteries of his father's craft.
So he healed the shifting wound. And as they fought,
already the barbarian-tongued womanish War ceased.
And the Bassarids took alive many warriors
from the battle; and many of the foe, leaving the Taurus heights,
returned to the region of the Indian land
with vain hopes, to the house of Deriades,
the broad-spanning drivers of measureless-lived elephants.
And drawing the Satyrs after the strife into a vintage dance,
pastoral Pan made music, pouring out a victory echo.
And Blemys of the woolly head, champion of the Erythraean Indians,
lifted up the bloodless branch of olive in supplication,
bending his slavish knee to Indian-slaying Dionysus.
And the god, beholding the man bowed to the ground,
took him by the hand and raised him up, and together with a many-tongued folk
of dark Indians he sent him off, holding him far away,
since he loathed the rule and the ways of Deriades,
to the verge of Arabia, where beside the neighbouring sea
he dwelt on a prosperous soil and gave his name to its citizens;
and Blemys came swiftly to the mouth of seven-channelled Nile,
to be the sceptred ruler of the like-skinned Ethiopians;
and the foundation of ever-summery Meroe received him,
the eponymous leader of the later-born Blemyes.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
18. In the eighteenth book Staphylus and Botrys come,
inviting the mountain-roaming son of Thyone to a feast.
And already winged, many-mouthed Rumour flew,
running beneath every line of the cities of Assyria,
proclaiming the name of cluster-bearing Dionysus,
and the bold Indian War and the splendid-clustered vintage.
And Staphylus, hearing of the ironless army of the Satyrs
and the vine-decked rites and the Euian sacraments of Lyaeus,
longed to behold Bacchus; and urging on his son Botrys,
the lord of the Assyrians, high on his wind-swift car,
met Dionysus of the clusters as he passed by.
And seeing him approaching, and the silver-wheeled wagon
and the harness of leopards and the bright reins of lions,
unshorn Botrys reined in his father's chariot;
and sceptred Staphylus leapt down from his car,
gazing at the halted track of the leopards of Dionysus;
and bending his knee, propping his footstep upon the ground,
stretching out an olive-branch with god-fearing hand . . .
And the lord soothed Dionysus with a friendly speech:
'By Zeus the protector of suppliants, your father, Dionysus,
by Semele the god's child, do not pass my son by.
I have heard how Lycaon received your father,
him together with the blessed ones, and slaying his son with his hand,
Nyctimus, set him before your unsuspecting father,
and touched a single table with all-ruling Zeus,
beside the verge of Arcadia; and over the heads of Sipylus
Tantalus, as they tell, gave hospitality to your father,
and carving up his own son, set him before the gods as food;
and the broad shoulder of Pelops, the part that Deo feasted on,
shaping it with ivory, with a false, cunning ornament,
Cronion brought back to life the carved-up son,
joining the limbs that had been divided among one another.
But why, Dionysus, have I named to you Lycaon the child-slayer,
host of the blessed ones, and Tantalus the air-walker,
the cunning thief of the nectar-cups,
proclaiming a man hostile to ambrosia and nectar?
Zeus and Apollo Macello entertained in one feast . . .
And when the Earth-shaker uprooted all the Phlegyae into the sea,
breaking the whole island apart with his trident,
he spared both women and did not overthrow them with his trident.
And you too, bearing the likeness of your hospitable father,
for a single dawn step within my halls;
grant grace to both, to Botrys and his father.'
So speaking he persuaded him; and Dionysus mounted his car,
blessing his house, and Dionysus followed after;
and bold Botrys lifted up the horse-whip,
and travelling along the bull's deserted verge in winding course
he drove his ancestral car, and led the way for Lyaeus
to the Assyrian land; and on the neck-harness
receiving the golden reins of the Mygdonian car,
Maron, the charioteer of Bromius, insatiable of the lash,
hurling the unsparing whirr of the beast-guiding whip,
drove the storm-swift wagon of leopards;
and the Satyrs, running before, struck up the dance,
leaping about the mountain-running car of Lyaeus;
and many a flower-loving Bacchant ran here and there,
holding the trackless path with a passable foot, and the fold of the rock,
narrow and ladder-like, she measured with swift step,
and clashed with her hand and her well-rhythmed sandals,
stealing away the toil of the deep-cliffed road,
frenzy-driven; and the Pans high on the customary rock
danced with well-greaved feet in the dust,
striding across the headland of the untrodden crag.
But when, as they journeyed, the royal court appeared,
far-shining, gleaming with the many-coloured ornament of its stones,
then fair-haired Botrys, leaving his father's car,
went swift-sandalled into the house, a wayfarer leading the way,
making ready all things at once, and with a loving spirit
he set out the varied dinners of a rich table.
While Botrys still arranged the feast for Lyaeus,
the lord of varied gifts showed Bacchus
the artful beauties of the stone-paved hall,
from which a marble, richly-wrought radiance streamed,
kin in hue to the sun and to the answering moon;
the walls grew white with silver metals,
and flashing the sparks of men upon the face
was the lychnis, named after the lamp; and the house held too
the wine-dark amethyst, adorned with reddening, fiery stone,
resting upon the hyacinth;
and the pale agate spat out a smoky gleam,
and the serpentine glittered with the spotted forms of its scales;
and the Assyrian emerald belched up a green radiance.
And spread about the halls in a column-line,
the golden surfaces of the wooden roof grew red
with rich rafters; and of many-cleft metals
the bright floor was variegated with well-pebbled art;
and the gateway, broad in compass, in some well-carved wood,
held the delicate likeness of newly-sawn ivory.
Such things the old sceptred king showed to Bacchus his witness;
and scarcely did he bend his step within the god-receiving court,
holding Dionysus by the hand; and with slow-yielding foot
the god strained his wandering eye in winding turns;
and the god marvelled at the starry, gleaming ornament,
beholding the gold-wrought court of the hospitable king.
And the lord roused his handmaids and urged on the slaves
to carve, for the Satyrs of bull-horned Dionysus,
the herd of well-fed bulls and the flocks of sheep.
And as Staphylus pressed on, swift-working was his command
to the answering slaves; and many bustled,
servants of the feast; and the bulls were carved
and the sleek lines of the grazing sheep. And there was dancing;
and fragrant breezes breathed through the lyre-filled house,
and made the streets of the sweet-smelling city steam;
and broad moistures of wine made the whole house drunk.
And the cymbals clashed, and beside the well-sounding table
the pipes of Pan hummed, the woven flutes roared,
and the circle of the loud-thundering oxhide
crashed through the hall with twofold beatings,
and there was the rattle of castanets to accompany the supper. And in the midst
heavy with wine, bearing the unsteady rush of a trembling foot,
Maron went here and there, shaken by frenzy,
turning his upright step back from the floor,
propping his hands upon the shoulders of two Satyrs,
appearing in the midst; and he was lifted by the throbbing
of another's foot, with a tawny skin, and in the midst, sending out
purple beams from his whole gleaming face,
the answering likeness of the Moon's horns,
in his left hand lifting a newly-flayed wineskin,
swollen with the customary wine, slung round his neck-belt,
and in his right a cup; and the Bacchants encircled
the old man bounding with the shifting throb of his feet,
as though about to fall, his head reeling,
yet never falling. And drunken-tottering themselves,
the handmaids and the slaves revelled in the dance,
having tasted for the first time the unfamiliar sweet wine.
And the wife of King Staphylus, mother of a noble son,
the clustering Bacchic dew made drunk, Methe;
and heavy-headed she asked the Bacchants to drink again,
bounding about the wine-receiving bowl of Lyaeus;
and she shook her head, shifting with a double throb,
leaning her hair upon her shoulder with a swinging sway,
restless, turning back here and there; and about the ground
the Bacchant, taking with her hands the frenzied Methe,
who was again and again about to fall on her slippery sandals,
raised her up.
And Staphylus too was drunk; and from the wine-loving cup
his cheeks grew red with the wine of the cluster;
and the freshly-bearded boy, together with Staphylus his father,
bound his unplaited tresses with unfamiliar ivy,
girdling them like a crown; and changing step upon step
with rivalling feet, Botrys danced in spirals,
turning his right foot in turn from the left;
and Staphylus leapt with the dancing throb of his feet,
leading his curved step circled in a running track,
propping his arm upon the neck of Botrys the dancer;
and he blessed the drink of choir-weaving Dionysus,
restless, shaking here and there the loosened locks
that streamed upon his shoulder; and Methe herself danced too,
leaning her arm both on her son and on her husband,
in the midst of Staphylus and Botrys; and she could feel
the threefold delight of the interwoven dance.
And Pithos, half-old, shaking his grey hair to the winds,
stuffed up to the teeth with the sweet-drinking stream,
heavy with wine danced, turning his drink-tottering step;
and with the sweet drops belched up from his throat
he whitened his tawny, foaming beard.
And they drank the whole day; and as the cups were drained,
all the western land was covered by the shadowy gloom
with its blackening edge, and with a faint light
the dapple stars lit up, and the two-coloured air grew dark,
as Phaethon set beneath the shadowy cone,
holding still a small remnant of Dawn behind him on his path;
and silent Night clothed the darkness with her own skin,
inscribing the sky with a starry tunic.
And after the bowl of drunkenness, after the dinners of the table,
Botrys together with his father and wine-pouring Dionysus,
sorted in order upon the well-spread couches,
took the gift of sleep and consorted with dreams.
But when, with rosy glimmerings, the messenger of Dawn,
faintly-shining, the dawn-light marked off the shadow-leaving mist,
then fair-haired Bacchus sprang from his morning bed,
shaken by hope of victory; for in the night
he had cut down the Indian race with his ivied thyrsus,
pursuing the deceiving image of a sleep-born battle.
And hearing the noise of the Satyrs and the thud of javelins
he shook off the tumult of the dreamlike warfare,
scattering his warlike sleep; and he held in his heart
the dread fear of a prophetic, threatening dream;
for he had seen the imitation likeness of the battle of Lycurgus,
a forerunner of things to come, that bold, within the thicket,
hard-fighting from the crag, a lion with raging throat
had startled Bacchus, still leaping and not touching iron,
into fear, and driven him to the sea,
hiding in the deeps, fleeing the beast's threat;
and he had seen another terror, that a bold lion was pursuing
the thyrsus-bearing women, his throat gaping,
bloodying them with his claws; and as the women were torn,
the sacraments rolled in the dust from the initiate's hand,
and the cymbals lay on the ground; and a Bacchant, turning round,
fastened bonds about the lion's jaws,
binding a vine-rope tight upon his head,
and wove about the lion's neck a strangling bond;
and the female throng ran upon the beast, one upon another,
and gashed his grim feet and hands with thorns;
and scarcely, when he had been girdled with the curling cluster,
did Artemis take him alive; and from the heavenly bosom
a fiery lightning, darting down upon his face,
made the beast spin back, a blind wayfarer.
Such a dream Dionysus beheld; and from his bed
rising upright he put on, stained with the slaughter of Indians,
his bronze, starry tunic upon his breast,
and girdled his hair with a crooked serpent-bond,
and fastened his feet with reddening boots,
and lifted the thyrsus in his hand, the flower-loving spear of Enyo;
and he called for a Satyr attendant. And the divine,
answering echo of the Bacchic mouths hearing,
lord Botrys awoke, and put on his tunic;
and Pithos, sleeping . . . But when Methe heard the voice,
she scarcely lifted her head, and as her head grew heavy
she slept again in sluggishness; and still at dawn the wife
remained, gathering sweeter sleep upon her eyes,
and late she left her bed with slow-yielding foot.
And cluster-loving Staphylus accompanied Lyaeus
as he hastened on his way, holding out guest-gifts,
a golden jar with silver cups,
from which of old he always drank the milk of milked goats;
and he gave embroidered robes, those which beside the water of the Tigris
Persian Arachne had fashioned with delicate thread.
And the lord of many gifts uttered a word to Bromius:
'Fight for me, Dionysus, and do deeds worthy of your father;
show that you bear the race of Cronides; for in fresh youth
your father, still a boy, hurled the earth-born Titans from Olympus;
hasten you too in battle
to destroy the overweening earth-born race of Indians.
I remember a tale, which to our father
Assyrian Belus once told, the guardian of my soil,
my father's father, and I will tell it to you myself:
when watery Cronos lifted the jaw of his marriage-robbing sickle,
when he rushed upon his mother's couch
and cut the male corn-ear of his father's unwedded ploughings,
the forerunner of the Titans, he fought with your father,
and broad-bearded Cronos kindled War,
hurling frosty spears against Cronion,
casting the cold, wet missile; and sharp-pointed
from the air were sent the hail-shaped arrows.
And more than the Sun, fire-bearing Zeus armed himself,
with a hotter spark loosing the petrified water.
But when you lash the raw-devouring lions into the Indian fray,
do not tremble at the elephants, since your Zeus who rules on high
crushed high-headed Campe with the thunderbolt,
whose whole crooked body was of many shapes; for of alien growth,
twisted, self-coiling, a thousand crawlers
from her viperous feet kindled aslant War,
belching long-shadowing venom; and about her neck
bloomed fifty varied heads of beasts;
and some roared with lion-heads
in the form of the unmarked Sphinx's grim face,
others spurted up foam from boar-tusks,
and with the gathered phalanx of many-whelped heads
there was an exact likeness of Scylla's face;
and at her middle body a double nymph appeared,
shaggy with venom-shooting serpent-clusters;
upon her breast, down to the topmost fold of her thighs,
with sea-monster scales her bastard shape grew rough,
high-stretched; and the nails of her widely-scattered palms
were set aslant in the form of a hook-clawed sickle;
and from her topmost neck, through her resistless back,
a self-coiling scorpion, hanging high by the tail of her neck,
crawled, whetted with a hail-sharp, keen sting.
Such was the spotted-shaped, coiling Campe that was lifted up,
and whirling earth and air and the depth of the brine
she flew with the discordant throb of her dark wings,
darting tempests and arming storms,
the Tartarean nymph, black-winged; and from her eyelids
a wandering flame belched up far-reaching sparks.
But your heavenly father Zeus slew so great a beast,
and conquered the Cronian, viperous War.
Become you too the very likeness of your father, that I may call you
the destroyer of the earth-born, second after Cronides,
when you have reaped the hostile corn-ear of the earth-born Indians.
This battle befits you, like to his; for of old
your father overthrew the Indian, the champion-of-the-fray
of Cronion, the son of the soil, adorned with towering limbs,
whence the Indians won their race;
your father fought against the Indian, and you fight against Deriades.
Become for me the very likeness of Ares too, since he also
overthrew so great a god-fighting son of Echidna,
spitting the dread venom of ill-shaped Echidna,
who got a double, yoked form, within the thicket
of his mother shaking the coiling circle of his spine;
him Cronos held, boundless, hurling the thunderbolt,
Ares hissing with serpent-feet,
when, lifting his hands over the circle of his breast,
he made war on your Zeus, and in the airy path
set the clouds in rows upon his high-crested head,
and the birds that strayed onto his crooked hair
he often seized together and feasted in his capacious throat;
this one, in his prowess, your brother Ares slew.
I do not call you lesser than Ares; for you might vie
with all the children of Zeus, since with your murderous thyrsus
you show as much prowess as Ares fights with the spear,
and you accomplish, like Phoebus, your contests; and a beast-slaying
son of Zeus, another, I entertained in my hall;
for yesterday well-winged Perseus came to my house,
leaving the bright Cydnus, neighbour of Corycus,
like you, friend, and he said that, named after his swift foot,
he had marked out a newly-built city among the Cilician men;
but he was lifting the topmost heads of the unbeheld
Gorgon Medusa, while you lift the wine-dark fruit,
the messenger of good cheer, the forgetter of mortal grief;
Perseus slew the sea-monster beside the Erythraean sea,
and you overthrew the race of the Erythraean Indians.
Slay Deriades, as you slew the Indian Orontes,
worse than the sea-monster; for grieving
Perseus saved Andromeda, but you, with greater victory,
save the starry maiden bitterly oppressed
under the bidding of unjust Indians,
that I may kindle one revel
for Gorgon-slaying Perseus and Indian-slaying Dionysus.'
So speaking he returned again to his hall,
the delicate lord, the host of Bromius; and hearing
the king speak, thyrsus-frenzied Dionysus delighted
in the goading speech, and raged for battle,
hearing of his father's war with charmed ears;
and he reproached Cronides, and wished for a greater victory
yet to come, a third, after the twofold war with the Indians,
holding rivalry with Cronides. And calling Pherespondus,
descendant of the heavenly herald, like to the breezes,
the wise son of Iphthime, he embraced him with a friendly speech:
'O child of Hermes, my beloved herald,
go and announce this to lordly Deriades:
"Lord, either, apart from battle, receive the gifts of Lyaeus,
or make war on Bromius, and you will be equal to Orontes."'
He spoke; and swift-sandalled, going from land to land,
the herald accomplished his path to the eastern verge,
holding his father's staff. And on his golden car
lifting the cluster, the heart-cheering fruit of the vintage,
walking from city to city on many-bending feet,
he filled all the Assyrian land with his vintage,
holding out to the countrymen the grape-decked flower of the vineyard.
While beside the wing of the eastern, fiery Eurus
he measured the Syrian soil with his wandering wine-dark car,
meanwhile doom fell upon Staphylus too; and in the hall
the slaves rent the tunic upon their breasts,
and the handmaids raised the wail; and the breasts grew red,
struck by their palms; and of the many-wailing women
the circles of their faces were gashed by mournful nails.
And late, returning again upon his cluster-rich car,
Dionysus came back and entered the court of Botrys,
holding memory of the loving table of Staphylus;
and as he beheld Pithos with downcast face,
he prophesied the doom of his Staphylus by wise silence,
of his own accord; and calling Methe he questioned her with a word:
'Tell me, woman, what has befallen you, that you have changed your form?
I see you squalid, having left you gleaming;
who has quenched your unspeakable beauty? No longer do you send
the inborn purple fire from your wine-dark cheeks.
And you, old man, do not hide it, from where do you pour these tears?
Who cut, broad-bearded one, your flowing beard?
Who shamed your grey hair? Who rent your tunic?
And you, offshoot of the wine-loving mother Methe who bore you,
child of my Staphylus, from where have you got a hairless head?
What envy has spoiled your curling hair?
Your tresses no longer streaming upon your white shoulders,
unplaited, send forth the breath of Tyrian perfume,
no longer, when frenzied, from your head
do your cheeks shoot a rosy gleam.
How do you wear these robes soiled with poured dust?
Where have the royal robes of the Tyrian sea gone for me?
No longer do I recognize you, your face withering.
Where has sceptred Staphylus gone up, that I may know?
Tell me, who has snatched your father away in a single hour?
I know your grief, even if you long to hide it;
I have no need of your voice; for of their own accord
your eyes announce your silent mourning;
I know your grief, even if you long to hide it;
your tears prophesy your pains, and your squalid
tunics cry aloud the doom of my Staphylus.
And envy has snatched away my hope; for I thought
that after the Indian war, together with King Staphylus,
I would lift up with my hands the bridal-chamber's evening fire,
the wedding of the close-fighting cluster being accomplished.'

title: Dionysiaca
text:
19. In the nineteenth, beside the tomb of Staphylus,
Bacchus rouses a delightful contest over a fragrant mixing-bowl.
So he spoke, and the youth, with a heavy goad in his fresh-grieving heart,
sealed his lips in a speechless silence,
overcome by tears that poured of themselves; and at last the mother,
Methe, who rejoiced in Lyaeus, recited her piteous words:
"The sleepless watcher of your dancing-round,
your own Staphylus, Dionysus, a sleep of bronze has lulled to rest;
your own Staphylus, Dionysus, the breezes of Charon have snatched away.
A double heavy grief has rushed upon me: the vine-clad
Bacchus has forsaken me, and my husband has fallen sick;
and I bore a common sorrow over them both,
over Staphylus dying and Lyaeus not at hand.
But of your richly-streaming fruit, dear Bacchus,
give me your cup brimful, that drinking
I may lull my heavy grief asleep with your sorrow-banishing wine.
You are my hope, Dionysus lover of the cry: only the fruit,
only let me see the mixing-bowl, and I shed no tears again."
So she spoke, and he pitied her, and mixing in a cup
the care-loosing liquor of evil-warding wine he offered it
to the young boy and the downcast mother; and both drank
the honey-flowing weight of the fruit in a heart-cheering draught;
and Methe's groaning was soothed, and Botrys' grief;
and the woman spoke some word to heart-charming Bacchus:
"You have come to me, dear Bacchus, dear light; no longer sorrow,
no longer grief holds me now that Dionysus has appeared;
you have come to me, dear Bacchus, dear light; for with your
drink of healing wine I have soothed my tears.
Not for my husband, not for my father's death do I mourn; nay, even from the cluster
itself, if you wish, I will part; for in both alike
I have Bacchus—as begetter and as son and as bedfellow.
I will follow, if you wish me, and come to your house;
let me be a fellow-traveller of the Bassarids; and if you wish,
I will carry your wands and your lovely fruit,
and to my lips I will press the wine-press flute.
Do not leave me a widow, lest I swell a double pain
for Staphylus dead and Dionysus gone away.
You have the cluster for your servant; let him be taught the dances
and the rites and the offerings and, if you wish, the war with the Indians;
and let me see him laughing beside the wine-loving press,
treading out underfoot the birth-pangs of your fruit.
And remember the aged Wine-jar; do not leave him
untaught of your rite or without his share of the sweet wine."
So she spoke, and with a smiling face the lord Bacchus
heartened Methe, and to the wine-loving nymph said this:
"Lady, giver of splendid gifts, second only to golden Aphrodite,
bestower of mirth . . . joy-giving mother of the Loves,
feast together with Lyaeus, who touches the banquet;
be a garland-bearer for Dionysus, like Aphrodite,
crowned with flowers and well-grown clusters;
the wreaths of your tresses shall make Victory jealous.
I will make you cup-bearer, second after gold-throned Hebe;
you shall rise together with the vine-clad Lyaeus,
a fellow-traveller and attendant of the Bacchic cups,
and they shall call you Methe, the mortal-delighting surfeit of wine;
the cluster I will call the care-banishing fruit of my harvest,
and the grape that bears the cluster I will name from Staphylus,
the birth-pang of the vines and the dew of the vineyard.
Nor apart from Methe shall I be able to feast,
nor apart from Methe do I ever raise the revel."
So speaking, beside the tomb of Staphylus the wine-fallen
Dionysus, banisher of grief, set up a willing contest;
and dragging forth a fine-bearded goat and a male bull
he set them as a double prize, and called the players of the lyre
to compete, the contestants of the Pierian song;
he set them as a double prize, and urging the competitors,
the men skilled in the sweet-sounding lyre, he coaxed them with a word:
"Here we raise an Attic revel; for to the prize-winning
man who conquers I will grant the pale-hided bull,
and to the man defeated I will hand over the shaggy goat."
So spoke Bromios, and a man who strikes the lyre leaped up,
Oeagrus, a citizen of the chill Bistonian soil,
holding the plectrum that hangs beside the lyre; and after him
rose Erechtheus, dweller in hymn-singing Attica.
Both came into the midst as competitors of the contest,
players of the lyre; and they wreathed their hair
with leaves of bay; and they girded up their robes.
Beginning, they made their fingers quiver with the accustomed beat,
pressing the answering string of the outstretched gut in turn,
clasping the ends, that it might be neither too high-pitched,
nor ever, slackened, soften the manly song.
And first, having won the lot, with skilful rhythm
Erechtheus, dweller of Cecrops' land, struck the lyre,
singing the ancestral hymn: how in holy Athens
Celeus also gave hospitality to Deo, all-mother of Life,
with her boy Triptolemus and old Metaneira,
and she gave them grain, when, sowing snow on the furrow of earth,
Triptolemus found seed upon his ear-bearing car;
and beside the new-built tomb of Celeus dead,
with tearless eyes Deo lamented the harvest-feast,
yet, consoling them again with a heart-charming word,
she quenched the heavy grief of Triptolemus and Metaneira;
so too the king of the Assyrians gave Dionysus
hospitality in his own hall; and the lord, in return for his table,
granted him the Euian gifts and the vine-clad fruit,
and when Staphylus the wine-loving king had died,
he stayed his son Botrys from lamenting care,
and lulled the sorrow of his mournful wife Methe.
Such things the skilful lyre-striker played; and at the rhythm
all alike were charmed; and together with thyrsus-bearing Lyaeus
they marvelled at the fitting, lovely-voiced Attic song.
Second, lord Oeagrus, weaving a shifting hymn,
as the father of Orpheus, sharing the hearth of his familiar Muse,
struck up a two-line harmony with a Phoebean strain,
brief of word, clear of speech, in some Amyclaean fashion:
"Fair-haired Hyacinthus Apollo brought back to life,
and Staphylus Dionysus will make to live forever."
Not yet had the revel ceased, but the people cried out
with auspicious words from throats of one tongue,
and the Satyrs roared all together; and from his seat
Bacchus leaped up restless, shaking up and down
his right hand, and Botrys ran forward, with the cry of "euoi"
honouring the well-rhythmed harmony of the singer;
and the lord crowned the head of Oeagrus with ivy,
and the father of Orpheus, striking the earth with his foot,
gladly received the unyoked bull as the wage of his song;
and around him in rows his comrades leaped for joy.
And the wide-bearded goat, swelling his grief and his envy,
with shamed hands the citizen of Athens led away.
Then fair-haired Iobacchus, bringing them with unsparing hand,
set worthy prizes for the dance-weaving victory:
an aged mixing-bowl pregnant with fragrant wine,
golden, that held measures past telling, gushing for the thirsty earth
the four-year-old liquor of Lyaeus,
the skilled Olympian work of Hephaestus, which once Cypris
gave to her vine-clad brother Dionysus;
and a smaller bowl he set in the midst of the contest,
of silver, gleaming, round, which once to Bacchus
the king of Alybe gave as a guest-gift, dwelling in his halls
beside the wealthy soil, where in the recess of the earthly mine
the black hollow whitened with elbows of silver;
about its rim, upon the bossed crown of its edge,
ran twining ivy, and round about it was wrought with golden ornament;
this he brought and set, with its deep-hollowed belly,
a wine-vat still breathing the younger weight of the fruit,
must, the drink of unwedded intoxication; for there is no blame
that the man defeated should drink the unsobering dew.
But when Bacchus had set the prizes in the midst of the contest,
he called those skilled in the dance with a summoning voice:
"Whoever shall compete, wheeling with skilful foot,
and conquer in the judgement of the running foot, let him take
both the golden mixing-bowl and the pour of sweet-drinking wine;
but he who falls, shaken by the slip of an unsteady foot,
and dances the worse, let him receive the lesser gifts as well;
for I am not the same to all; but to the prize-winning
man who has conquered in the graceful dance-treading contest
no gleaming tripod, no swift horse will I grant,
no spear and breastplate stained with the blood of Indians,
rousing the javelin-throwers to the straight-coursing discus;
no course of fleetness is stretched out here, no point of a spear
that carries far; but to Staphylus, the king who has perished,
a man who loved the leap, I honour the play-loving feet;
nor do I hold out gifts for the fly-strong wrestling,
nor is there a horse-race, nor are these the games of Elis,
nor the bridegroom-slaying course of Oenomaus; for our
turning-post is the dance, our starting-lines the leaping of feet,
the nimble hand and the twisting bound, and the nod of a face
ever-moving restlessly, and the speaking silence
that wheels the fingers and the dancer's glance."
At such a word from him horned Silenus rose up,
and thrice-old Maron, with heavy-sounding foot, leaped forward,
eyeing the great golden flashing mixing-bowl,
not because it was golden and the better, but because alone
it held the richly-streaming, most ancient weight of dew
up to the very edge of its rim; and love of the sweet wine
made him young, and the Bacchic scent overpowered his grey hairs;
and he twirled his feet, testing his own strength,
lest heavy old age had stopped his limbs that had forgotten the dance.
And the old man with his voice appeased the soul of Staphylus,
pouring a sober word from his shaggy chin:
"I am Maron, the fellow-contestant of grief-free Lyaeus;
I know not how to weep; what have tears to do with Dionysus?
The circles of my feet are my burial-gifts beside your tomb;
receive me smiling; Maron knows no cares,
Maron knows no wailing, no weight of mourning sorrow;
I am the lovely servant of grief-free Dionysus.
Be gracious to your Maron, even if you have drunk the waters of Lethe,
grant the grace that I may drink the pour of ancient wine,
and let Silenus drink the new weight of the new fruit.
And for Staphylus after death, as for one alive, I will dance,
since I prefer the dance to the savoury-loving table;
for you, Staphylus, living and not breathing, I dance,
striking up a revel over your tomb; I am Bacchus' man,
not the servant of Phoebus, and I have not learned to sing dirges,
such as among the Cretans lord Apollo trilled,
weeping for lovely Atymnius; and of the Heliades
I was a stranger, alien to Eridanus
I am, no kinsman of Phaethon the perished charioteer;
I am no dweller of Sparta, I lift no mournful flower,
shaking the delicate petals of the much-wept hyacinths.
Today, whether you sit beside Minos and judge alike,
or whether you hold the flowery court of Rhadamanthys,
walking softly in the groves of the Elysian meadow,
hear your Maron; and I, in place of cups,
with truceless lips belch out a thoughtful libation;
be gracious to your Maron, and grant me a wine-dark victory,
a victory that all admire; and I, above your tomb,
will pour the fair first-fruits of my golden cups,
beginning from my bowl, after the prize of my victory."
So speaking, Maron danced with twisting foot,
shifting his right foot to take the place of the left,
tracing an intricate silence with a voiceless hand;
and he rolled his wandering eyes, the image of words,
weaving an intelligent rhythm with a cunning gesture;
and he shook his head and wished to toss his locks,
had not the bare brow of his hairless head lacked them.
Nor, as an old man bearing Titan blood,
did he picture with eloquent gesture the Titan race,
not Cronus or Phanes the elder, nor the offspring
of the Sun-Titan, coeval with the equal-aged universe;
but leaving all this and the flood of ancient matter,
in skilful silence he figured the cup-bearer of Cronides,
stretching the goblet to Zeus and cheering the choir of the other
immortals ever with cups close-following one upon another,
or pouring the holy dew down into the mixing-bowl;
and his harmony was a sweet drink; nay, even
the maiden Hebe he danced, drawing the nectar;
and looking toward the Satyrs he pictured the form of Ganymede
with speechless hands, and whenever he looked toward the Bacchants,
in thoughtful silence he showed the gold-sandalled Hebe.
Such things Maron traced, plying his versatile fingers,
and he reined in the skilful onset of his well-rhythmed foot,
completing the many-bending measures of the restless dance.
And he stood trembling, watching with a sidelong eye
who would conquer whom, who would reach his own house
bearing the larger mixing-bowl, brimming with drink.
And Silenus danced; and of his much-turning art
his silent hand traced the cunning tokens.
And then such was the figure of his hands: as once a great
contention fell upon the son of Cyrene and Dionysus
over the drink, and the blessed ones came together; not then was there boxing,
not running, not then the discus for prizes: for the son of Phoebus
the cups lay as the instruments of care, and for Dionysus,
and two mixing-bowls, the one a pour of aged wine,
the other bearing the new gifts of the branch-loving bee;
and Cronides sat as judge, and for the prize-winners
a delicate contest was stretched out over the honey-dripping victory;
the cups lay as instruments; and, like gold-winged Hermes,
Love himself, the lovely, stood as steward in the midst,
holding in one hand both ivy and a shoot of olive,
to Bacchus the ivy-flower, to Aristaeus holding out
the shoot of olive like the wreaths of Pisa,
the holy emblem of Pallas. And in a honey-mixed cup
first Aristaeus, mixing the birth-pang of the bee,
offered the immortals a skilful draught, cheering
one after another, and dealt the goblet to each in turn;
to them at the beginning of the richly-dropping dew
the surfeit came most sharp, but as the cups were drawn
they refused the third, and touched not the fourth,
and blamed the swift surfeit of the honey; but of the sweet-drinking
Dionysus, in his soft tunic, drawing from the mixing-bowl,
lifted two cups and held them out with a twin motion,
the first to Cronides, the second he gave to Hera,
the third goblet to his father's brother, the Earth-shaker;
and in order he mixed for all the gods together and for Zeus his father,
who delighted; and to the one downcast alone,
smiling, he stretched the goblet to jealous Phoebus;
and they were charmed in mind by the many-scattered cups,
and grew ever the thirstier the more they drank,
and asked again for another, and there was no surfeit of cups.
And the immortals raised the cry, and entrusted to Bacchus
the right to bear the prize of victory for the sweet-drinking vine;
and drunken, unconquerable Love, the steward of the contest,
crowned the hair of Lyaeus with clustering ivy.
This with skilful hand horned Silenus wove,
and he stayed his right hand, and on a much-leaping sandal
he was lifted from the ground and sent his glances into the air,
now joining his feet yoked together one upon the other,
now, parting them, he sprang with a counter-shifting art;
at another time, much-twisting, dancing above the floor,
upright upon his heels he shook with a winding leap;
and on his right foot, unbending, he propped himself,
holding the fingertip of the other foot, or bending his knee
with joined hands, or the outstretched fold of his thighs—
Silenus heavy-kneed, holding the upright onset of his foot;
and he raised his left foot upon his flank and shoulder,
lifting it in a spiral, and by a backstrained art
he raised the curved foot aloft, winding it about his neck;
and in the swift whirl of the homeward-circling dance,
on his back, self-twisting, he bent with a circular art,
showing his outspread arched belly to the air,
crossing the same unending turning-post like a garland;
and his head was carried sidelong, as though ever
touching the floor and yet not grazing the dust;
and with shaggy foot Silenus tore the ground,
unstable here and there, in a Bacchic frenzy of leaping feet.
And then his knees grew weary, and as his head shook
he slipped, on his back, self-rolling, upon the field;
and he was shaped into a river: his body gushed water
in self-flowing streams; and as his forehead changed
his horns surged into an arching channel,
and the surge crested, churned high upon his head,
and his belly, full of fish, was hollowed into sand;
and as Silenus was poured forth his hair changed
into self-grown rushes; and over the river, close beside,
the sharp-pointed reed whistled, shaken by the breezes,
self-grown. And Maron bound up the sweet victory,
holding in his arms a mixing-bowl crammed with sweet wine;
and as Silenus was poured forth, as a prize, like a libation,
he took the silver mixing-bowl and flung it into the streams,
and made drunk the pourings of the dance-weaving river,
whence the place is named from the mixing-bowl, and of the sweet-drinking
Silenus murmuring the Euian water is heard.
And Maron spoke some word to the river-spring:
"Maron does no violence to you, Silenus; but into you I will cast
the reddening wine, and call you the wine-receiver.
Receive, you insatiable of drink, your own wine; receive Bacchus'
silver mixing-bowl, and you shall be silver-eddying.
Rolling-footed Silenus, even in your pourings you dance,
the whirl of your feet even in the surges you keep,
still you revel in your watery form; but be gracious
to the Bacchants and the Satyrs and the wine-giving fruits,
and guard the Silenoi, the offshoot of your stock;
and to deep-drinking Maron be kind, and let me not see you
stealing away the eagerness for victory even in the rivers.
With your waters rather swell the wine of the Maronian fruit;
be of one mind with Dionysus even among the rivers.
Foolish one, who taught you to contend with your betters?"
Another Silenus again, exchanging an overweening pipe,
lifted his proud neck and came into strife with Phoebus;
but he, stripping the hairy skin, binding him to a shoot,
made of him a breathing wineskin, and high upon a tree
hidden within he bellied out the mimic shape of the wind,
as though once more the unsilent herdsman were singing;
and pitying him, Delphic Apollo gave him form,
and made a river of the same name; still of that
shaggy Silenus the winding water is told,
and it belches a wind-roaming din, as though ever
the Phrygian pipe were piped on answering reeds.
And you too changed your body, having kindled strife with a better,
wholly like the former Silenus. But may you no more
seek the unsandalled, familiar Bacchant nymph,
the loose-haired mountain Bacchant; for the boundless brood
of the loose-locked Naiads delights you.
No more seek the serpent-bonds of Lyaeus,
plying eels, the crooked birth-pang of the streams,
and, fitted with spotted scales instead of serpents,
fishes creep upon your streams.
And if you have been parted from clustering Dionysus,
the more I count you blessed; for you too swell the cluster;
what more would you wish, bearing as the nourisher of your floods
Zeus after Bacchus, the begetter of the whole brood?
In place of your Satyrs, ranks of rivers; in place of the wine-press,
you dance upon the back of roaring Ocean.
A like form you have even among the waters; and there is no blame
that Silenus, his brow plumed with ox-horns,
should hold a bull-shaped, horned river-form."
So spoke Maron; and all marvelled to see the winding water
of Silenus the wide-poured tumbler,
the equal-natured likeness of the much-bending river.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
20. The twentieth pursues the ox-cleaver of murderous Lycurgus,
when Dionysus is driven into the fish-filled deep.
The contest was dissolved; and the Satyrs, with thyrsus-bearing Dionysus,
lodged in the wealthy halls of the cluster.
As they feasted, the wine-flushed Seasons came reveling among them;
and there was the after-supper beat of drums, and the shrill pipe
sounded broad and clear, and drawing from the cups
the cup-bearers toiled beside the unresting feast;
and the guests, fawning, kept calling for the attendants
to ladle out more wine; and the Bacchant leaped up,
whirling cymbals, and of the leap-loving girl
the unbound, unveiled locks were shaken by the breezes.
And the vine-god, summoning the wife of Staphylus,
wiped away her squalor and adorned her with a wine-dark robe;
and cleansing the broad-bearded Wine-jar, foul all over,
he wrapped him again in a white tunic,
casting away the mourning garments stained with strewn ash;
and no longer wetting his cheeks with self-poured tears
did Botrys groan, but, obedient to Dionysus,
he opened the fragrant chests; and as they were opened
a sparkle blazed from the many-eyed robes;
thence taking the bright royal garments of his father Staphylus
he put on the cloaks stained with purple murex,
and feasted with Lyaeus, who touched the festal cheer.
As they delighted, the star Hesperus rose up,
holding back the light of dance-delighting dawn.
And the ranks of the guests, by turns within the court,
took the gift of sleep upon their deep-strewn beds.
And the Wine-jar beside Maron went up into one bed,
gushing forth the fragrant draught of the nectarous vat,
and they made each other drunk, sending forth an equal breath
the whole night through. And Eupetale, the nurse of Lyaeus,
kindling a torch, for both Botrys and Dionysus
made ready a double sea-purple bed for the two;
and in a neighbouring chamber, apart from the Satyrs, away from Lyaeus,
the handmaids spread a golden couch for the queen.
And to Bacchus came a dream, Strife the nurse of war,
seated upon a mimic car of lions,
holding the form of Rhea, the rattle-loving goddess;
and Fear drove the yoke of the dream-chariot's car,
a counterfeit Attis shaped in answering limbs,
and, holding a shrill voice, soft-skinned in male form,
he counterfeited the charioteer of Cybele with a female voice.
And standing beside the head of slumbering Bacchus
roving Strife rebuked him, and spoke with a war-rousing voice:
"You sleep, god-born Dionysus; but to battle
Deriades summons you, and here you raise a revel;
and your stepmother, beholding your fugitive war,
Hera mocks you, while you drag your army into a dance.
I am ashamed to appear before Cronion, I shrink from Hera,
I shrink from the immortals, that you have wrought nothing worthy of Rhea;
the destroyer of the Titans, the champion of his father,
Ares with his proud neck throughout heaven I flee,
who lifts a shield drenched in the wonted gore;
and your sister more than you—the self-perfected child
of a noble father's fertile head, who had no mother,
Pallas of the gleaming helm I dread, since she too,
female Athena, blames male Bacchus as a sluggard;
the thyrsus yielded to the aegis, since once proud Pallas,
lifting the aegis, crowned the gates of Olympus,
scattering the stormy war of the Titans,
and honoured the wise birth-pang of her father's head;
and you shame the fertile fold of Zeus's thigh.
Behold, how Hermes and Apollo laugh,
the one still lifting the twin shaft stained with the gore
of the high-crested sons of Iphimedeia,
the other holding the destroying rod
over the slain, many-eyed herdsman; but I flee my own heaven,
shunning the reproach of war-shunning Dionysus.
And beholding the thyrsoi of Lyaeus at rest,
the maiden archer blames the leap-loving Dionysus,
the dancer who loves the crags, she the steerer of a car
of worthless deer, the slayer of swift hares;
the mountain-roaming one blames, near mountain Rhea,
the driver of leopards and the charioteer of lions.
The house of my son Zeus I disown; for on Olympus
I shrink before Leto, who still exults and boasts,
who stretched her bow against me, the defender of her own bed,
the slayer of earth-born Tityos, smitten with desire.
And by twin pains I am scourged, since I behold
grieving Semele and the star of noble Maia.
You are not like the children of Zeus: you did not slay with the shaft
threatening Otus and high-footed Ephialtes,
you did not slay Tityos with your winged arrow,
not bold Orion sick with love, not the champion of Hera,
Argus, the ox-watching son of grief-swelling earth,
the watcher of Zeus's ox-horned wedding;
but beside Staphylus and Botrys you weave a revel,
inglorious, ironless, singing a wine-feast hymn;
you shame the earthly race of the Satyrs, since they too,
touching the bloodless Bacchic dance,
have entrusted all their hope of war to cups.
There is feasting too after the fray, there is dancing
after the Indian war within the halls of Staphylus;
the harps will dry up again after the warlike victory;
without toils one cannot dwell in the inaccessible heaven;
no easy road belongs to the blessed; out of valour
the heaven-rushing path of Olympus draws one to the pole.
Endure you too your manifold toils; for the heavenly
court of Zeus Hera, in her wrath, prophesies for you."
So speaking she flew away. And the god leaped up from his bed,
still holding the dread crash of the threatening dream . . .
And bold Botrys sprang up, and put on his tunic
that hurled rays of the Sidonian sea,
and bound his fitted feet with a golden sandal;
and guarding the cleft collarbone upon his tireless shoulders
he clasped the bright cloak of the sea-mantled kings,
casting upon his loins his father's lordly girdle,
holding the sceptre. And the Satyrs yoked the blood-red wagon
of leopards for the hastening Dionysus;
and the Silenoi shouted; and the thyrsus-bearing Bacchants
bellowed; and the gathered armies, marshalled for the Indian war,
rushed in ranks; and the pipe of Enyo roared;
and the leaders ordered the chosen battalions.
And one, leaping upon a back with a rider's bound,
into the course of the rushing, raging bear lashed its mane
as it sped; another, pricking the shaggy-haired belly,
drove a wild wandering bull with his crook,
joining his slackened feet about both its flanks;
and another mounted the spine of the shaggy-breasted lions,
gripping the neck-locks for a bridle.
And leaving his father's hall together with his inheritance,
ruddy Botrys, stretching a four-yoked car,
drove in company with cluster-loving Dionysus,
holding his servants behind; and with her mother Methe the bride,
in a white tunic, mounted the silver-wheeled wagon,
and Phasyleia, the steerer of the yoke-straps,
upon the mules' necks shook the golden whip;
and the broad-headed Wine-jar, stretching the rearmost car,
followed in service to both Botrys and Dionysus.
Nor was he without his reward; taking him into the land of the Lydians
the lord Bacchus set him beside the vat pregnant with wine,
receiving the poured weight of the richly-dropping fruit
in its wine-holding vessels; whence, keeping this name,
with its purple hollow the jar beside the neighbouring vat
stands, still receiving the Euian gifts of Bacchus,
the token of the former Wine-jar; and had it gained a mortal voice,
such a word it would have belched, hearing the revel of the Satyrs:
"I am the Wine-jar, named after the former, and beside the vat
I receive the sweet stream of the vines; and of the Assyrian
Staphylus I was the servant, and of Botrys, and both
I nursed as infants, an old foster-father; and still both,
as though alive again, I lift up in my flanks."
And so the lord Bacchus was destined to accomplish these things
in after time, late. And passing through Tyre and journeying through Byblos,
and the well-wedded water of the fragrant river Adonis,
and the crag of Lebanon and the haunts of the Cyprus-born,
he came to Arabia, and beneath the fragrant trees
he marvelled at the long-leaved ridge of the Nysaean thicket
and the steep-built city, nurse of javelin-bearing men.
There a certain man, blood of Ares, a murderer dwelt,
holding in his shuddering ways the likeness of his father,
lawless, dragging blameless strangers to their death,
mad with frenzy—Lycurgus; and of those slain with the sword
he crowned his gate with human heads,
like Oenomaus and of his time, for whom once the wretched
maiden was kept in her father's unwedded halls,
a widow, growing old, still no ship for the marriage-Loves,
until the son of Tantalus, furrowing the horse-driving swell,
bearing the unwetted four-yoked car of the Earth-shaker,
held the bridal course, when in a wheeling circle
crafty-minded Myrtilus accomplished a deceitful victory,
having wrought a treacherous axle with mimic wax,
out of pity and love for wailing Hippodameia;
and the course was profitless; and beneath the Sun's car
the wax-set form was warmed by the flaming brand,
and the loosened, short-lived axle hurled away its wheel.
Such was Lycurgus, of like manner; and burden-bearing
