a bronze shield of cunning workmanship, in whose round
many marvels were studded, the labour of the Lemnian anvil.
And the host had armed itself, of many fashions, for the fray with the Indians
who pressed on in their droves; one, guiding his richly wrought car
swiftly into the conflict with flesh-cutting ivy,
mounted upon leopards; another, with bristling harness,
yoked the mountain-ranging chariot of Erythraean lions
and drove the grim pair; and another, dismayed by none,
hurling at the dark ranks of the Indians,
unshaken, took joy in lashing an unbridled bull,
and one, springing up onto the back of Cybele's bear,
charged at the foe, and whirling his wine-dark thyrsus
put to flight the drivers of the long-shanked elephants;
another, casting at the host with flesh-cutting ivy,
held neither sword nor round shield, nor the deadly
spear of battle, but, shaking the curling leaves of plants,
slew a bronze-clad man with a slender frond.
And a thunderous din crashed out, like a pipe's blast;
the Sileni shouted; the Bacchant women advanced to war,
flinging fawnskins like breastplates across their bosoms.
And one of the mountain-roaming Satyrs, as though driving a colt,
with legs astride sat upon the back of a lioness.
The Indians raised their answering war-cry, and, mustering its fighters,
the barbarian pipe of War, host-gathering, blared aloud;
garlands were on their helmets, breastplate clashed on aegis,
the thyrsus rioted against the spears, and against the buskins
stood matched the answering greaves; and of the yoke-fellow bearers
the lines of oxhide shields leaned one against another,
and footmen against footmen, and against the high-crested head
the Pelasgian helmet thrust the Mygdonian helmet.
And there was a turmoil of champions, each in his own kind: one, lifting himself,
whirled the airborne leap of the Bacchic dance,
one, fallen, groaned, another beat time with his sandal,
one, struck, gasped out his life, another bounded for Lyaeus;
another, hurling a martial sound from his lips,
sang the spear of Ares, while one sang the banquet of Dionysus;
and War crashed in concert with the rite of Bromius,
the euhan rattles rang out, and, leader of the tumult,
the trumpet, mustering the people, sounded with the lyre,
mixed gore with the libation, and stirred slaughter into the dance.
There by far the first, light on his own foot springing forth,
Phalineus hurled his javelin against Deriades,
and struck the unbreakable iron tunic;
yet the deadly point, for all its straining, did not touch the flesh,
but, glancing aside, fixed itself in the ground; and in his fury
valiant Corymbasus, marking the foe rushing close
upon Deriades, came upon him, and as he sped on
severed his throat full in the middle, striking with his blade,
and reaped off his head; and as the skull was cleft
Phalineus, blood-stained and headless, fell to the ground.
And about him a clamorous battle rose; the very tip
of Phlogius' brow Dexiochus shaved away with bronze,
striking the brow's edge as the helmet split in two;
but he, in terror, shifting his knee a little from his knee,
sheltered beneath the long oxhide of his brother,
as when Ajax received his brother, the archer Teucer
of Dardanian stock, into his sevenfold shield,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
hiding the kinsman who shared his toil behind a father's buckler.
At once Corymbasus, drawing his sword from the sheath,
flung Dexiochus headlong with a stroke across the neck;
and swiftly, leaping upon the gasping corpse, ran about it
frenzied Clytius, leader of the footmen; and high-plumed,
quick and dismayed, he hurled at Deriades;
but Hera turned the champion's spear aside,
angered both at Clytius and at India-slaying Dionysus;
yet the swift leader did not wholly miss; for, piercing
the monstrous throat of the irresistible beast,
he slew the straight-standing elephant of Deriades;
and, labouring in its anguish, the towering beast, ambidextrous,
shook the whole car with its dark neck;
and tossing the crooked jaw that juts before its face,
blood-stained, it strained back the bonds of the yoking harness;
but the swift-handed driver, bending the well-fastened yoke
with his sword, cut the team-binding traces
of the neck-straps; and from the broad stall
Celaeneus took another, high to view, and yoked it new.
And Clytius was bold, in the hope of unreproached victory;
he called out to the slayer of Dexiochus in a raving voice,
pouring a deadly word upon the insolent throat:
"Stand, dog, do not flee, Corymbasus, and I will teach you
what manner of javelin-men attend on Lyaeus.
You I will carry off as spoil to Phrygia, and the cities of the Indians
this spear of mine shall ravage, and after India-slaying victory
I will make Deriades the servant of Dionysus;
let some unwooed girl loose her maidenhood,
receiving the shaggy-breasted wedlock of a Satyr,
an Indian woman defiled beside the Mygdonian Hermus."
So he spoke, and Corymbasus was wroth, and while Clytius
uttered his late-battle words, he sheared through his throat;
and the head flew up aloft at the leap of Fate,
sprinkling the dust with bloody drops.
And, leaving the dancing corpse to whirl back again,
Corymbasus put the Sileni to flight, foremost of the Indians,
foremost in manhood after Morrheus and the king.
And striking the spearman Sebes above the rim of the breast
he drove the bronze spear into his flesh, and as the bloody
shaft was dragged out he laid him in the heaped dust.
Then he rushed at Oenomaus; he, fleeing like the winds,
withdrew to the host of Bromius with terrified foot;
and marking him, Corymbasus pursued behind, and in his back
full in the middle drove the spear; rushing in its onset,
the point sprang out by the navel through the belly's far side;
and he, pierced about with the bloody iron,
fell forward, freshly slain, and slid into the dust;
and over his eyelids the death-bringing darkness covered him.
Nor did the monstrous champion cease from battle; but four
well-helmeted fighters were slain by one slayer,
Tyndarius and Thoon and Autesion and Onites.
And many a freshly slaughtered corpse there was, not falling
forward to the ground, nor stretched supine on the floor;
but, dead, unshaken, it propped itself upon the earth,
altogether like a champion still fighting, as though brandishing a spear,
as though stretching the swift bow and drawing the shaft at its mark.
And a valiant corpse, longing for War even after its doom,
forced the threads of the Fates, like a light spear
poised to strike, pierced from the scattered bows
by their shafts from head to the very feet,
an upright image of Ares; and the fighters gazed
with marvelling eyes upon the spearman who was dead,
still gripping his spear and not casting away his shield,
a dead javelin-man and a breathless shield-bearer.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And one, struck by the Athenian's grim iron,
reaped off his right hand, smiting the arm's end;
and the hand, tumbling in a dancing leap of slaughter,
fell freshly severed, entwined with its fellow shoulder,
streaking the streaming back with tawny dust.
And now, drawing the long spear of the leaping hand,
with far-flung shaft he would have had his War recovered,
and the left hand, spear-wielding, fought in turn its match;
but the hostile man, coming from the opposite path, forestalled him,
and with answering blade struck the left hand off at the root;
and the palm fell to the ground, and, casting at the slayer,
the far-flung stream of bloody dew sprinkled it
in crimson drops, and over the floor the wretched hand,
self-rolling in its leaps, bounded in its frenzy,
reddened with blood, and its curved fingers upon the ground
it locked with deft middle and hooked-nail grip,
as though clasping again the strap of the oxhide shield.
And it spoke a word, shedding the tears of Ares:
"Yet another hand I long for, that I may accomplish
with three palms deeds worthy of Tritogeneia;
even without hands I will pursue the hostile man;
this is the remnant of my manhood still left, that one may tell
the dexterous boast of the Athenians, that they too,
excelling even with their feet, fight on when their hands are cut away."
So speaking, he ran upon the champions like the winds,
making ready, weaponless, a battle for the destroyer.
And they, beholding him, marvelled each at the other,
and the fighters ringed the half-finished champion about
in throngs; but he alone received with unsparing blade
the alternating stroke of iron answering iron;
and hardly did he fall to the ground; he was a likeness of Ares,
guarding for a late-born dweller the memory of a father.
Not then alone was the company of foot-travellers cut down,
but among the horsemen too was slaughter; one marched on
bringing doom to another; driver overtook driver,
either cleaving with his spear the back of one who fled before,
or striking on the breast one who came against him near,
and thrust him from his horse, freshly slain, into the dust.
And a horse, struck above the flank by an arrow,
flung headlong to the ground its hurled-off driver,
just as the swift-flying Pegasus, companion of the wandering breeze,
borne aloft, shook off Bellerophon;
another, in his terror, from the slippery back,
upright, falling through the horse's belly to the ground,
stuck head-foremost, hanging, and about the earth,
casting his head, rolled, leaving his feet upon the horse's back.
And the mighty Cyclopes ringed the fighters about,
helpers of Zeus; and against the misty host
Argilipus blazed, lifting a light-bringing brand.
And he was armed with the earth-born, fire-pointed thunderbolt,
fighting with torches; and the swarthy Indians trembled,
astounded at the fire that answered the heavenly bolt;
and a fiery champion he was; upon the heads of his foes
the sparks of the earth-born thunderbolt were shot;
and the Cyclops conquered ash-spears and countless swords,
shaking hot bolts and the smoking point,
holding the brand for a bow; and one Indian after another,
countless, he burned up, the man, with his archer's flame,
no single Salmoneus, but with a bastard thunderbolt he confounded them;
not one god-fighter alone did he slay; not for one alone
did Evadne lament, as her Capaneus withered away.
And Steropes had armed himself, whirling a mimic flash,
bringing against the lightnings of heaven an answering gleam,
holding a quenchable glitter, which the Western flame begot,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
seed of Sicilian fire and of the smouldering hearth;
and he had a covering like a cloud, and in its inmost depths
hid and again revealed his flash with a double quiver,
bearing the likeness of the heavenly light; for the lightning,
coming, holds its gleam fleeting yet recovered again.
And Brontes fought, striking out a ringing strain,
pouring an answering echo with thunderous crashes;
and with the strange drops of an earth-born snowfall,
shedding a made, short-lived, fair-weather water
in mimic streams, he became a bastard Zeus without clouds.
And, leaving the cunning crash of his counterfeit thunder,
he armed himself with Sicilian iron for the slaughter of the foe,
and, brandishing his hammer aloft above his shoulders,
he battered the heads of his enemies thick and fast with the iron;
he struck the dark ranks turn and turn about, as ever
he beats the forge-wrought anvil with Aetna's clangour.
And, breaking off the crag of a long-based watch-rock,
with a rocky spear he charged down upon Deriades;
and hurling a vast stone with unsparing hand
against the black-skinned king as he armed for battle,
he struck his shaggy breast with the ravine-point;
and he, drunk with so great a millstone of a rock,
was weighed down over all his breast; and Hydaspes warded off
the slaughter of his stricken son. But the bold one, faint from his wound,
shook from his tireless hands his rushing spear,
the bronze, twenty cubits long, and flung his shield to the ground
with shame-filled palms; and drawing a feeble breath,
struck on the rim of the breast by the marble point,
he fell head-foremost from his lofty car
like a vast, towering fir—and the fir, falling,
runs about the boundless bosom of the wide plough-land—.
And the Indians, pouring round him, lifted him into the chariot,
fearing the misshapen Cyclops, lest with some cast
he take up yet another high-stretched crag of the hill
and slay the king with the rugged bolt,
having a length equal to that of high-crested Polyphemus.
And in the middle of the grim champion's brow blazed
the round flash of his single-eyed face;
and, cowering before the grim Cyclops' glance,
the dark-skinned Indians were shaken with astonished fear,
thinking from heaven that the Olympian Moon,
rising against the face of the earth-born Cyclops,
flashed at the full, shielding Lyaeus.
And father Zeus, beholding the Cyclops' mimic battle-rage,
high in the clouds laughed, because, receiving from the earthly clouds
a strange rain through an untried bosom,
the earth was snowed upon then, yet the thirsty air,
bearing its naked back unwetted, held no streaming dew.
And Hypsachis armed himself; marching beside his brother,
shaking with a towering hand a shield as great as a cliff,
high in the clouds Elatreus held a vast fir-tree,
cutting the heads of foes with his tree of a spear.
Euryalus armed himself; and, cleaving in the tumult
the great host that fled the plain as far as the sea,
penning the ranks of the Indians into the fishy gulf,
he conquered the foe across the spear-bearing deep,
whirling his sword, twenty cubits long and upright, through the water;
and with his long ox-cleaver, cutting a sea-neighbouring rock,
he flung it at the foe; and many of the unburied
learned the nets of a twofold, sea-drenched Fate,
by the surging War and by the jagged bolt.
With them another kinsman, excelling, Halimedes,
a monstrous Cyclops, raged in Bacchic frenzy with his towering limbs,
and put the foe to flight; and guarding his face
he held before it the bossed back of his round oxhide shield.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And, marking him, Phlogius, avenger of the slain Indians,
bent his bow, and, drawing a winged shaft, was minded
to strike him full in the middle with the arrow;
but, learning of the onset aimed straight at him,
the high-headed Cyclops, swerving sidelong, avoided
the cast of the rushing arrow; and he, shaking a crag,
flung the rugged bolt at Phlogius; but he, fleeing,
stood beside the car of ox-horned Deriades,
and hardly avoided the air-roaming marble point,
staying there; and, wroth at Phlogius' escape,
Halimedes, splitting open his deadly throat,
slew twelve men with one bellow of his voice,
pouring forth the man-destroying roar of his raving cry.
And the Cyclopes' war-shout crashed upon Olympus
with terrible tongues. And the dancers of War,
the Dictaean Corybantes, advanced to the tumult.
Damneus made war, pursuing the hostile tribes . . .
and on the plain was the war-cry; and to the troubled Bacchants
Prymneus came, calm, like a stern-wind breeze
that saves a sailor riding the road with the storms;
and much-prayed-for he came to the host, as comes
to the storm-tossed ships the calm Polydeuces,
lulling the heavy wave of the storm-breeding sea.
And with lighter feet Ocythous startled the fighters;
many he slew with a swift doom,
one mastering with his spear in close fight, one with a bolt
from afar, another cutting down with his grim blade;
another still running before, fled like the winds,
the frenzied one overtook, plying his wind-swift knees,
in his running altogether like Iphiclus, who, hastening
the soles of his feet, grazed the surface of the untrodden calm,
and held his airborne course above the ears of corn,
treading the topmost unbending path of the asphodel with his feet.
Such a storm-foot was Ocythous. And in the tumult
Mimas set up the whirling-foot of rhythmic War,
and startled the host, whirling his dance-beating sword,
holding the mirthless armed leap with knowing foot,
as when, rousing a din in the ears of Cronus,
Pyrrhichus, beating his Idaean shield with the swords,
raised the battle-cheering strain of lying Echo,
stealing away the hidden, again-grown youth of Zeus;
with such a mimic armed leap of the dance
bronze-clad Mimas whirled his airy lance;
and, cutting the heads of foes, the iron harvests of battle,
with India-slaying axes and the double-striking blade,
he held up the first-fruits of the enemy, with Bacchus for witness,
and, in place of the ox-sacrifice and the wonted wine,
pouring a libation of blood upon Dionysus.
And, wheeling on his restless foot with knowing tread,
helmet-flashing Acmon went, the comrade of Ocythous;
he fought unshaken, like a forge-wrought anvil,
lifting his Corybantic shield, in the midst of which
often the infant Zeus slept his sleep upon the mountains;
and the house of Zeus was a little cave, where that
holy goat nursed him with her false, milky teat,
welling up the strange wise milk, while the oxhide,
with theft-hiding crashes, made the shield-wielding Echo roar,
struck in the midst of its back by the tumbling iron.
For which cause Rhea, fashioning a false stone,
set it as the antidote for the son of Cronus on Cronus' table.
And bright-eyed Idaeus entered the revel of War,
a dancer of battle, whirling his nimble step,
irresistible, driven by the goad of India-slaying strife.
And Melisseus startled the whole dark rank,
with unshaken courage; and, keeping faith with his name,
he mimicked the dread stings of an armed bee;
and aiming his marble at the javelin-man of the dappled Curete,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
at his match Melisseus, Morrheus missed,
he missed; for it is not fitting to destroy the Corybantes with a millstone.
And, coming together into one, the dancers of joyless Ares
held a common yoke of War; and about the car
they wreathed Deriades round with oxhide shields, garland-wise,
clashing their armour, and in the rhythmic tumult
they ringed a tower about him with shield-bearing dances.
And the air-roaming echo ran up to the halls of Zeus,
and the fair-footed Hours feared the din of both.
29. In the twenty-ninth Ares withdraws from the wars,
as though hastening to another wedding of Cytherea.
And when Hera marked the slaughtered ranks of the Indians,
she cast hard-fighting courage into proud Deriades.
And the dread lord took on a still greater goad of love for battle;
and pouring a raving voice upon his champions,
he ran along the whole dark line of his battle-array,
drawing back the whole fleeing host to the conflict once more,
winning one by gentleness, another by threat.
And bolder he grew; and gathered together of themselves
the Indians streamed to the fray at their king's summons.
And far-shooting Morrheus split the whole rank of the Satyrs,
now sending against the foe from his back-strung bow
an air-roaming cloud of thronging arrows,
now whirling his rushing spear in turning sweeps,
and startled the horned race of the Sileni.
And Hymenaeus of the fair locks fought, brandishing his sword,
seated upon the back of his swift Thessalian horse,
cutting down the dark Indians with his rosy hand;
he flashed with splendour; you might see him, in the midst of the Indians,
a gleaming Morning-Star, the running-mate of the ugly dark;
and he put the foe to flight, since for his beauty's sake
Dionysus breathed inspired valour into him as he fought.
And Iobacchus, seeing him excel in the tumult,
took joy, and did not want as the fellow-toiler of his battle
the lightning of the son of Cronus so much as the spear of Hymenaeus.
Whenever the youth drove his colt rushing into the fray with the Indians,
Dionysus lashed the necks of his cunning-wrought beasts,
and brought his car close beside the youthful horse, lingering near,
cherishing the boy, as Phoebus cherished Atymnius; he stood ever
near at hand, and longed to appear, lovely and valiant in one
and the same fashion, like the young man; and in the tumults
he touched the clouds, sharing the fight with Hymenaeus.
One thing alone troubled him, that from earthly stock
he was a son of Phlegyas, and not of Cronus' offspring.
And he stayed ever beside him, as a father guarding his child,
fearing lest some far-shooter, loosing an arrow,
should shoot the boy; and as the shafts came on
he stretched out his right hand, shielding Hymenaeus.
And to him as he excelled he spoke this word:
"Send your shaft, dear boy, and Ares rages no longer;
with your beauty you struck Bacchus, the archer of the Giants;
strike too with your arrows witless Deriades,
the god-fighting king of the foe, that one may say,
'Hymenaeus, with one shaft, hit both,
the flesh of Deriades and the heart of Dionysus.'"
So Bromius spoke, and far more did lovely Hymenaeus,
the far-shooter, lay hold of the battle, and rejoicing in him
frenzied Dionysus plunged the more into War,
and startled the whole dark race from its very roots;
and one, seeing Dionysus in the unsparing storm of battle,
the insatiable archer of Indian heads,
spoke such a word to greedy Melaneus:
"Archer, where are your bows and your windy arrows?
Soft-robed women are shooting us down.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Come, send a shaft at short-lived Dionysus;
let the Olympian fame of his name not lead you astray;
never tremble before Bacchus, who from an earthly father
drew swift-fated blood, and lied that he was Zeus's offspring.
Come now, send your shaft, and, if you hit your mark,
you will receive the boundless gifts of a deep-rich king,
if he sees Dionysus, the proud son of Thyone,
set upon the pyre, mastered by your bolt;
one shaft would end the whole war. And for both,
lift your hands in water and pray to mother Earth;
with truthful lips promise to perform
sacrifices to both after the victory; and at the altar
let bull-shaped Hydaspes have a horn-dragging bull,
and let the dark earth receive a black-skinned lamb."
So speaking, he won over the arrow-shooting Melaneus,
a man whose wits wandered, goaded by the frenzy for possessions;
and he, silent, bared the lid of his quiver,
took a shaft and held it ready, and drew the wonted string,
bending the bow with the backward-straining pull of his hand,
and, propping the very point of the iron against the bow,
he brought the bloody oxhide string close to his neighbour breast;
and the straight-coursing shaft was turned from Dionysus
by Zeus's restraint, and the blood-stained thigh of fair-garlanded
Hymenaeus was grazed by the winged arrow.
Nor did the wandering arrow, hung aloft, escape Dionysus,
flying with a whir, the running-mate of the unsparing breeze;
but he unmanned the cast of the rushing shaft as it sped on,
and blinded the deadly far-shot of Melaneus;
and the Paphian struck away the barbs of the bolt,
his sister, granting the favour to longing Dionysus,
and turned the shaft so far from the flesh, as when a mother
drives a wandering fly from her child still slumbering,
gently fluttering the edge of her robe before his face.
And the savage wound of his flesh, through the reddening thigh,
Hymenaeus, near at hand, showed to neighbour Bacchus,
shedding a lovely tear beneath his brows, that he might mark
the right hand of evil-averting Dionysus for a helper,
needing a life-preserving healer; and he, taking
Hymenaeus by his white hand, set him upon his own car,
and leading him away from the loud-roaring tumult,
set him down, heavy-headed and sluggish, on the shadowy ground
beside a neighbouring oak; and as Apollo
groaned for Hyacinthus, struck by the man-slaying sharp discus,
blaming the breath of the jealous Zephyr's gust,
so too Dionysus plucked at his hair again and again,
weeping with unweeping eyes for Hymenaeus.
And, seeing the barbs of the arrow standing outside the flesh,
he took welcome courage; and from the bloody thigh,
feeling the white-and-red double wound of the reddening flesh,
with sparing palms he drew out the tip of the arrow.
And, marking the tears of the lamenting youth,
he was wroth at both, both at Ares and at Melaneus;
and wiping away the sweet sweat of Hymenaeus,
with reproachful lips he poured forth a secret voice:
"A bull killed the vine; Ares will destroy Hymenaeus.
Would that he had slain all the fighters I armed,
and left this one alone unwounded; for in war
what grief stirs me when a Cabeirus is cut down?
When does the wound of a Satyr ever, ever trouble Bacchus?
Let the grape-tending Silenus fall; let the swarm
of Bassarids wander; only let me see my boy unharmed.
Let the famous archer be merciful; if Aristaeus falls,
what mourning is ever mine, who calls his bee's labour
dearer than the dewy fruit of the vine?
It was not, it seems, fated for me to escape a boy's grief,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
since soon perhaps I shall again lament this boy as dead.
What heavy envy assailed them both? If it is right to tell,
Hera, looking on Bacchus with jealous eye
and on the young reaper of the black-skinned race,
grudging the young and longing Lyaeus,
armed furious Ares to strike Hymenaeus with a shaft,
though he wore an Indian, bastard, unfamiliar face,
that she might grieve the heart of love-sick Lyaeus.
But, stretching my shaft or straining the bloody bow,
I arm myself against treacherous Melaneus, that I may exact
the debt of vengeance owed for lovely Hymenaeus.
If you die, Hymenaeus, leaving War unfinished,
I withdraw from the fight and lift the thyrsus no more.
I will let all the enemy live,
reaping one man only, your slayer Melaneus.
Deriades did not slay you, though he is wroth at Dionysus.
Be merciful, Cytherea: after the bold son of Myrrha,
ruthless Ares drove down another gentle Adonis,
drove him and touched the rosy flesh, and through the thigh
once more the gore of the Loves just now gushed upon the ground;
but, granting the favour to your longing Dionysus,
send me here Phoebus your brother, who knows the art
that loosens pain, and he shall heal the boy. Hold, my voice:
let Phoebus be untroubled on Olympus, lest I rouse him,
reminding him of the lovely wound of Hyacinthus.
Send me, if you will, Paeon; let him come:
he has no part in longings, he is a stranger to the Loves.
I see another kind of wound; for in wars
one man, struck in the flank, is reddened by the spear,
another has the toil of the hand by the sword, one by a bolt
in the side, another through the ear; but in the heart
I share the deadly wound with Hymenaeus who bears it."
He spoke, and was startled, with sidelong eye askance,
gazing upon the wound of graceful Hymenaeus.
And, twining the Bacchic-loving flower about the thigh this way and that,
feeling the white-and-red double wound of the reddening flesh,
he brought the boy back to life with his healing ivy,
sprinkling Hymenaeus with the defending wine.
And as when the swift-working rennet, hastening to curdle the milk,
stirring it, parts the liquid from the snowy dew,
that the goatherd may make it set,
shaping it in the basket's round mould with wheel-like sole;
so he healed the bloody wound with the art of Phoebus;
and the young man, made whole, had his War recovered again,
having found the pain-healing hand of Dionysus.
And drawing his far-shooting, air-roaming shaft to its mark,
he bent his bow again, and, aiming with his bolt,
gave a wound in answer to the arrow-shooting Melaneus.
And his bold prowess sped on; following Lyaeus,
he ever struck down men and was no longer left behind by Bacchus.
And as when some shadowy likeness of a man, breathless, creeping,
near at hand and unmarked, journeys keeping pace with the man,
and ever follows him as he hastens, and as he stands
it stands, and as he sits it sits beside him, and at the table
with mimic hands feasts as his fellow-traveller;
so the youth stayed keeping pace with wine-dark Bacchus.
Nor did Dionysus cease from battle; but, piercing
a man clean through, he lifted him impaled on his thyrsus,
upright and high in the air, and on the airy path
raising the Indian aloft, he showed him to jealous Hera.
And, fulfilling War under his three surnames,
divine Aristaeus, skilled as the Hunter of Ares,
fought as Nomius, brandishing his crook in his hands,
the far-shooting bridegroom of Autonoe; and in the tumults,
bearing a famous bow, he imitated his own father,
with overweening courage from his arrow-shooting mother,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Cyrene of old, daughter of Hypseus; and the raving,
hostile man, fearless Hunter, he took alive in bonds,
hunting him like a beast; and against the destroyer of his foes
with practised hand he poised a heavy stone, such as he had set
to press out the flowing labour of the rich olive;
and he routed the enemy with the proud man's wonted whirl,
shaking that bronze, which, brandishing in his hands,
he used to scare the maddened stings of the roving bee.
And of Thracian Samos the fire-strong townsmen,
two sons of the Lemnian Cabeiro, raved in Bacchic frenzy;
and since their father Hephaestus glowed with the breath of fire,
their eyes shot up kindred sparks.
For them there was a car of adamant; and around it the colts,
beating the battered dust with bronze hoof,
belched a harsh neighing from their throats,
which their father Hephaestus wrought with inimitable art,
breathing a threatening flame from their teeth,
just as for Aeetes too, the mighty lord of the Colchians,
he fashioned the twin-yoked pair of bronze-footed bulls,
making them brazen harness and a fiery plough-beam.
Eurymedon drove, and with fire-stricken bridle
he reined in the fiery jaw of his iron-footed horses;
and in his hand a Lemnian spear, which his father's anvil had wrought,
he lifted in his right, and on his well-made thighs
he hung a light-bearing sword; and if any man,
lifting some small stone with the tips of his nails,
struck the fire-running back of the whetted blade,
sparks of themselves were shot from the iron.
And Alcon fitted his hand to the smoking bolt,
whirling the festal torch of his father's Hecate.
And shaking the bosses of their high-crested helmets,
the Dictaean Corybantes advanced to the tumult,
goaded into the fray; and with rival bronze
their bare swords clashed upon the battered oxhide shields
in answering bounds; and the rhythm of the shield-bearing dance
they imitated with the winding beat of their feet,
raving for Ares. And of the mountain-dwelling herdsmen
the Indian offspring was cut down by the Curete's iron;
and one man slid headlong into the dust,
hearing the bellow of the deep-booming oxhide drum.
And one, lifting up the flower-loving spear of War,
a Bassarid, cast it; and of the unbacchic race
many male heads were cut down by a woman's thyrsus.
And, lifting a crested watch-crag with shaggy hand,
cutting off the topmost peaks of a mountain, Leneus armed himself,
sending the jagged point against the foe.
And the Bacchant raised her cry around; and vine-arrows
whirled in the hands of the ivy-bearing women.
There, weaving a song for both Ares and Dionysus,
Eupetale armed herself, and with grape-loving leaf
she sent the goading ivy, the thresher of iron,
destroying the Indian offspring with her oaken cluster.
And, routing a cloud of foes with her man-breaking thyrsus,
grape-loving Terpsichore leapt into the tumult,
whirling deep-booming cymbals with twin bronze;
not so much did Heracles drive off the Stymphalian birds with his din,
holding deep-sounding bronze, as Terpsichore drove off the host of the Indians,
clashing the war-Echo of the dance.
And heavy-kneed Trygie was left apart from the crowd,
last of all, and rooted her feet in fear; and none of the Sileni
stayed beside her; they left her there alone,
terrified, needing a helper; and to wine-loving
Maron she stretched out her hands, but Maron refused the old woman,
because she was breaking up the dances of the strong-wine-loving Corybantes
and of the Satyrs; and she ever prayed the gods that she might be slain,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
old and useless, beneath the spear of Deriades;
and Calyce fought, standing beside Dionysus,
frenzied. And in the quivering beat of her drunkenness
Oenone reeled, running before; weighed down in the tumult
her knees laboured, and of the wine-loving nymph
the swollen tresses of her head whirled about.
And there was a heavy-booming groan; and in the rival tumult
Astraeis pursued Staphyle, and Celaeneus pursued Calyce.
And spear-wielding Morrheus drove off the phalanx of the Sileni,
smiting it with his ox-cleaver; and at one shout of the driver
Astraeus was shaken, Maron fled, Leneus sank to his knees,
the three children of shaggy Silenus, who without a marriage-bed,
unsown, self-begotten, sprang up from his mother's plough-land.
And Doryclus startled lovely Lycaste . . .
To these the god brought aid, and on the freshly wounded women's
wounds he sprinkled remedies; and from the Enyalian iron
he rescued Gorge, worn at the tip of her unfilleted foot,
binding her foot fast with a fetter of the vine-tendril;
and he quenched the fresh-flowing ichor of Eupetale with wine,
and soothed the streaming blood of Staphyle with a song;
and Myrto's wounded palm he healed with myrtle,
and saved Calybe, drawing the bolt from her shoulder,
sprinkling the bloody wound with the draught of the wine-vat;
and he stopped the pain of Nysa's freshly wounded face,
anointing her cheek this way and that with white gypsum;
and with unweeping eyes he groaned over Lycaste.
But when thyrsus-mad Dionysus had soothed the pains
of the Bassarids by his art, he fought with a mightier battle.
And one, possessed by the leaping wit-stealing frenzy,
a Bassarid, a raving Maenad of War, went after the Indian Ares,
about you, Lydian god; and from the Bacchant's tress
a flameless fire of itself blazed down her neck.
And, rousing the ill-matched swarm of the mighty champions,
the pipe crashed out the host-gathering Echo of Ares,
and with both palms of the din-loving Corybantes
the rims of the double-striking oxhide were beaten,
the cymbals rattled, and, changing its strain,
the sweet-melodied Panic pipe piped out battles;
and the phalanxes of the foe roared in answer; and in throngs
the winged arrows whizzed up from the air.
The bow twanged, the stone hummed, the trumpet bellowed.
But when they reached the ford, where, borne along in its flood,
Hydaspes reddened the white water with his drunken stream,
then Bacchus shouted from his deep-booming throat
as loud as the nine-thousandfold swarm of War roared,
uttering the dread cry of their shouting mouths in one; and unsteady,
shunning the tawny flood, the Indians sank to their knees,
others on the plain; and the host of Bacchus was parted,
slaying the foe both on the floor of earth and in Hydaspes,
gasping with parching thirst, when over the earth
the dawn had reached its midmost, and the hot wayfarer trembled
at the noonday lash of the blazing Sun.
And the vine-god challenged the lord of the Indians,
pouring a threatening word from his raving throat:
"What fear is this? If the chief of the Indians boasts the river's race,
I have blood from heaven; and overweening Deriades
is meaner than Lyaeus, as much as Hydaspes is meaner than Zeus.
If I will, I stand near the clouds; if I should wish,
my straight-coursing shaft will reach even to the Moon.
But if you are proud, wearing your horn-dragging form,
then, if you can, fight in the van against ox-horned Dionysus."
So he spoke, and the fighters bellowed with a roar;
and one strove against another, sharing the fight with Dionysus.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And on his goat's feet gentle Pan fought,
and, sharply grazing the whole flank of the archer,
with his whetted hoof he ripped open the belly of Melaneus,
exacting vengeance for the wounded Hymenaeus,
that he might lighten the fire-sealed grief
of Dionysus mourning with unweeping eyes.
And frenzied Iobacchus rushed upon the battle,
and touched the clouds and laid his hands on Olympus,
now lengthening his tall body, neighbour to the heaven,
and now planting his sole on the earth, and striking the air with his head.
And as they fought, the Evening Star came on,
loosing the foundations of the India-slaying battle.
And to Ares as he slept there came, at Rhea's nod,
a guileful vision of a dream, weaving its varied phantoms,
crying out such a word in a bastard shadowy shape:
"Ares, Ares, you sleep, ill-fated in love, lying alone,
bronze-clad; but Hephaestus holds for the second time, high upon the bed,
your Paphian, your former Aphrodite,
and has driven from his halls the Grace, the jealous bride;
dragging back his ancient wife to her marriage again,
Love himself shoots the unwilling Aphrodite,
granting the favour to his father Hephaestus. But she too,
untaught in longings, Athena persuaded great Zeus,
the guileful maiden, that she might escape Hephaestus,
remembering the bastard bed of the earth-bred Hymenaei,
lest after the death of the former Erechtheus, from a male breast,
she should rear another younger son of the plough-land.
Wake, and going to the Thracian foot of the cliff,
behold your Cytherea within her wonted Lemnos;
behold how the propylaea of Paphos and the seats of Cyprus
a fellow-marshalling swarm of Loves has wreathed with flowers,
and hear the Byblian women singing of Aphrodite
and of the young love of the returning wedlock.
Ares, you are robbed of your Cyprian; for the man-slaying
swift Ares the slow one has outrun. Sing too yourself
of Aphrodite joined to fiery Hephaestus.
Set foot in Sicily, and the Cyclopes standing at the furnace
beseech for me; for they too, knowing the noblest toil
of Hephaestus, jealous of his cunning works,
are fashioning a snare for you, and like your ancient bond
they will make a younger one of the same kind, that you too,
pressing both in cunning fetters they cannot loose,
may bind the thief of your marriage with your avenging chain,
fastening rolling-footed Hephaestus to Aphrodite;
and all the gods of Olympus will praise you
for hunting in bonds the plunderer of your bed.
Wake, and become a weaver of guile yourself; wake, take thought
of your ravished bride. What are the troubles of Deriades to you?
Be silent for our sake, lest Phaethon hear the tale."
So she spoke and flew away. And at once, shaking off sleep,
gazing at the freshly traced early light of Dawn,
hot Ares leapt up, rousing Phobos and Deimos
to yoke his bloody, swift-running car; and they obeyed
their hastening father; and with curved-tooth bridle
dismayed Deimos, fastening the jaws of the horses,
bound the captive neck in servile harness,
and tied the yoke-strap around it; and Ares mounted the car;
and Phobos drove, guiding his father's chariot,
borne from Lebanon to Paphos, and from Cythera
he turned the restless car to the horned land of Cyprus;
again and again he looked toward Lemnos, and more than all
jealously eyed the fire-breathing hearth,
tracking the Cyprian with rolling, jealous foot,
to see whether he might catch sight of her by Hephaestus' furnaces,
standing there as before; and he feared lest the smoke
should dim his sight of darkened Aphrodite.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And he ran past Lemnos up to heaven, that with iron
he might raise a bridal War for the blessed ones,
against Zeus and Phaethon and Hephaestus and Athena.
30. In the thirtieth, to the nether house of necessity
Eurymedon sends Tectaphus, cut down, to Hades.
So Ares ran to the seven-zoned heaven,
jealous, heavy in his wrath. And dancing into the fray,
bold Dionysus fell upon the swarthy host,
now leaping among the foremost with earth-shaking bound,
now in the midst of the champions; and with his javelin-thyrsus
he reaped the harvest of the dark battle,
and raged, cutting down the tribes of the hostile phalanx;
and he gave heart to the Satyrs for the War of Deriades,
when Bacchus saw that Ares had left the fight of the Indians;
one strove against another. And entrusting to Dionysus
the right wing, the fierce front of the cluster-bearing tumult,
Aristaeus ran along the left horn of the battle.
And Morrheus, still gazing on the servants of Bromius
fighting with leaves and the flowering bolt,
broke into a wondering voice to witless Deriades:
"Deriades, what is this marvel? My fighters fall,
struck by thyrsus-wands and by worthless leaves,
and the shieldless slay the armed; and unbending
the Bassarids, though struck by axes and the double-edged blade,
remain unwounded. If it is right to tell,
you too, sceptred lord, leave your bronze-wrought spear
and lift the murderous wine-dark thyrsus, since with their ivy
the enemy excel far more than with iron.
Never have I seen such a fashion of battle; the worthless
thyrsus-javelins are mightier than spears.
Give me too a green shaft to wield in the fray; for our arrows
have been beaten by the unwarlike fennel-rod;
give me tawny buskins to wear, since even
unbroken greaves give way before the high boots.
What use is it, if I have a bronze shield, when women
excel the more unarmed, and in the tumults
whirl cymbals, and the fighters sink to their knees,
and the helmet yields to garlands, and the breastplate to a fawnskin?
Often, in the path opposite unwounded Dionysus,
I thought to slash open his unbreakable flank,
sending well-aimed spears, and, as it touched Lyaeus,
the sharp, unbending bronze of my javelins was bent."
So he spoke, and the bold lord smiled, and at his son-in-law
bent sidelong eyes, with silence the herald of his anger;
and he hissed out at him a threatening cry:
"Why do you tremble at unarmed Dionysus, childish Morrheus?
A pleasant thing, to fear the sportive War of the Satyrs."
So speaking, he gave his son-in-law courage with fearless threat.
And monstrous Morrheus armed himself against the champions of Bromius;
he wounded Eurymedon, grazing the midst of his groin
with the bloody spear; and rushing through the thigh
the raving point cut the rich, flesh-leaving flesh;
and with sinking knee he fell to the ground. And bronze-clad
Alcon did not neglect his fallen brother,
but came as a champion for the hard-pressed man, lifting his spear
and well-whirled shield; and he covered the whole fighter,
towering the man's body with his buckler, and at the foe
shaking his point this way and that in turning sweeps,
brother defended brother; and standing over the wounded man,
like a lion over its cubs, he roared from his throat,
pouring a Corybantic voice from raving lips.
And, marking him wheeling on knowing foot,
the champion of his fallen brother Cabeirus,
monstrous Morrheus raved like Typhon in his kind,
armed against the two brothers, that their mother
Cabeiro might weep for her twin children destroyed,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
cut down in a single dawn by one iron.
And now he would have given both to an equal doom,
but, drawing the breath forced through his lips,
Eurymedon called on his Lemnian father with his voice:
"Father, fire-breathing lord of the toilsome craft,
grant me the favour owed me of old, when alone
Deo, the harvest-goddess, snatched away three-headed Sicily,
the gift of looking on hidden Persephone's wedding,
and you checked your western bellows-bags at evening,
and the broad hearth and your snatching fire-tongs;
but I startled her, shielding my father,
the helper of your anvil; and from me
the black air is heated by your Sicilian spark.
Save your child for me, whom savage Morrheus has wounded."
He spoke, and fiery Hephaestus, springing from heaven,
whirled the kindred, much-splitting, leaping fire about,
turning the fiery bolt in his palm; and about the neck
of Morrheus the self-coiling, prudent flame wound itself,
wreathing his neck with the fire-warming noose of necessity,
twisting; and after the fiery garland of his throat
it leapt to the farthest sole with a treading bound
and twined a fire-woven cord about the champion's foot,
shaking on the ground a steady gleam with footstep leaps;
and his head was heated as the helmet caught fire.
And now he would have fallen, struck by the flaming bolt,
had not Deriades' father Hydaspes warded it off;
for he sat watching the battle high upon a rock,
bull-formed, with a bastard shape in mortal likeness;
he brought him back to life, pouring counter-flowing water,
cooling the hot breath of the fire-stricken face,
wiping the ashy filth from the helmet;
and snatching Morrheus, he cloaked him in dark mist,
hiding his limbs covered in a purple cloud,
lest the light-bearing god of both crafts should kill him,
brandishing the Lemnian death-bringing kindling fire,
lest, with the first one dead, old child-loving Hydaspes
should see yet another of Deriades' sons-in-law destroyed,
and weep for the doom of Morrheus together with Orontes.
But torch-bearing Hephaestus drove off all the fighters
who stood around his freshly wounded son, and high on his shoulder,
raising his son, he leaned him against a neighbouring oak,
apart from the din, and brought the fallen one back to life,
sprinkling life-giving remedies on the wounded groin.
Nor did Morrheus stay forgetful of his former battle;
but he armed himself again, having fled the fiery War
and the flashing champion and the smoking point;
and laughing at Phlogius, the much-turning son of Strophius,
he slew him, the dancer of leap-loving Dionysus,
who at the tearless banquets of Lyaeus
would whirl the supple fingers of his answering hands,
and, miming the death of Phaethon with prudent hand,
made the guests shed unwonted tears,
weeping over the doom of the feigned Phaethon;
and weaving a young man, smouldering and self-rolling,
he gave woeful grief to ungrieving Dionysus.
Seeing him leap, spear-wielding Morrheus said:
"This is another kind of dance you wove beside the table;
stretching out a laughing dance beside the mixing-bowl,
why now do you weave a groaning dance after the fight?
But if the goad of Dionysus' dancing holds you too,
celebrate the mysteries for Hades, and you will need no gypsum,
wearing the self-dyed, dust-grimed circles of your face;
and, if you will, dance beside lament-loving Lethe,
and let mirthless Persephone delight in your song."
He spoke, exulting, and rushed on like the storm,
and put the Sileni to flight. And with his irresistible blade
shield-wielding Tectaphus joined him, whom once Deriades

title: Dionysiaca
text:
bound and hid within a hollow pit.
Nor did he find escape from doom a second time; for under necessity
who can ever ward off a man's hateful death,
when pitiless, all-subduing Fate bids him die?
For no cunning could find a way to save dying Tectaphus,
who then in his frenzy drove off the host of Lyaeus,
cutting the sport-loving limbs of the fair-horned Satyrs;
and he reaped the throat of battle-rousing Pylaeus,
and struck the brow of Onthyrius with his unsparing blade,
and clove broad-chested Pithos with his iron.
And now he would have slain another throng of thronging Bacchants,
but swift Eurymedon spied him, and stood against him,
shaking his double-mouthed Corybantic blade in his hand;
he crushed the edge of his brow; and as the head split,
upright there spurted up a fountain of bloody dew;
and the champion fell to the ground, and, sprinkling the dust,
half-dead he rolled, and of the earth-dug pit
he groaned for the ancient evil and the threads of his late-coming Fate,
and, still remembering the cunning love-charm
of his evil-averting child, he roared in a wailing voice,
and as he wailed the tears ran down with his gore:
"My mother and my nurse, guileful, ill-wedded maiden,
why did you not come near me, when I came near to doom?
Why now have you not helped me again, fearless maiden?
Where has your life-giving charm gone? Do you keep faith,
faithful to your living father and not to your dying one?
If cunning can bring a man back from Hades,
seek me another, better cunning, seek a crafty
counsel against death, that beyond the earth's hollows
I may escape the gates of Hades even in the wars,
if there is any homeward path from the pit of no return."
Such a word he spoke with difficulty, and his voice obeyed no longer.
And seeing her freshly wounded father high upon the tower,
the piteous, many-tearing maiden welled up a mournful voice,
airy; and she fouled her crooked hair with dust,
baring her breast where her tunic was torn,
and beat her head; and to her incurable father,
as though he heard, she uttered such a voice:
"Son and father, heavy-fated child of your milk-giving girl,
today, with you dead upon your breathless lips,
what other life-giving milk have I, by which, wretched,
I may bring your soul back, recovered, to you?
What other helping breast shall I hold out again?
Would that I could deceive even Aidoneus.
For you, father, one other gift is kept; for I will not leave
you alone among the dead; but from your slain girl
receive too the blood of her neck after the milk of her former breast.
Come, guardians of Deriades, and in his stead
show me another recess within the earth, where, going,
I may make my dead father live again;
Hades is not like guardians, that I may accomplish
another pain-loosing cunning to aid my father.
I would wish for that murderous sword, that I might die,
heavy-hearted, slipping upon my father-slaying iron.
This man, who cut off the head of my father,
slay Aerie too after Tectaphus, that one may say:
'Both father and child he laid low with one blade.'"
She spoke, shedding tears; and her grief grew greater.
And against the twin hosts she fanned the flame of War . . .
And with his sword Morrheus killed the Taenarian Dasyllius,
who never threw away his shield before the foe,
the Amyclaean townsman, unshaken before his enemies,
driving his spear by the bone of his right jaw.
And he killed mountain-running Alcimacheia, who in one frame
had manhood and beauty surpassing her youthful prime,
the daughter of Harpalion, the cluster-loving father,

title: Dionysiaca
text:
who was so daring that she came even into the house of Hera
lifting the ivy, which the Argive goddess loathed
as much as she loved the reddening, wonted pomegranate;
and she lashed the well-made image with her wine-dark thyrsus,
striking the bronze body with her vine-cluster,
dishonouring the heavy-wrathed stepmother of Lyaeus.
Nor did god-fighting Lemnian Alcimacheia escape
the grim anger of Hera who laid hold on her; but in a foreign
land she was buried, and after the wars
she did not see her father Harpalion a second time, nor saw her homeland,
Lemnos, the bridal of Jason's Hypsipyle;
but among strangers she was hidden in the heaped dust,
meeting an avenging doom. Ah, greatly wretched,
she lost Harpalion and was robbed of Lyaeus.
Nor was furious Morrheus sated with cutting down
the god-mocking maenad Alcimache; but her too,
dwelling in Elis, on the Olympian floor of the plough-land
beside the stream of Alpheus, the garland-loving river,
he killed, Codone, still a maiden. Be merciful, Fates,
he had no pity on the tresses of her withering head,
nor on the rosy ray of her dust-fouled face;
nor, seeing on her breast a nipple like a rounded apple,
did he pity it, the unbending goad of her girdle,
nor did he reverence the gash of her deepening thigh,
but he killed so great a beauty before its time; and wounded,
she fell to the ground; and pursuing countless
fair-robed maenads, helmet-flashing Morrheus killed,
he reaped Eurypyle and Sterope and Soe with his blade,
and cut down Staphyle, and wounded ruddy Gigarto,
and, piercing above the rosy nipple,
he reddened the breast of Melictaena with his murderous iron.
And the envious Telchines advanced to the tumult,
one holding a vast fir-tree, one a cornel
bush whole and uprooted, another, breaking off
the peak of a crag, smashed it down, and went to the fray of the Indians,
shaking the javelin-stone with frenzied forearm.
And fickle Hera, bearing down upon Lyaeus,
gave might and courage to proud Deriades,
and as he excelled she granted him a light-bearing radiance
for terror to the foe; and as the warrior armed,
a deadly gleam flashed from his Indian shield,
and over the crest of his helmet a leaping flame blazed.
And bold Bacchus trembled, when he saw of Deriades
the boss of his fire-stricken shield flashing,
and the air-roaming gleam of his kindled helmet;
seeing him, Dionysus was astounded, and dared not
meet him, and, perceiving the cunning of Hera who armed him,
with unwilling feet he withdrew from the battle.
And then the Indians, taking courage, went to the fray,
now that Bromius had left the fight; and watching,
Deriades cut down the rank of thronging Bacchants,
whirling his spear this way and that in turning sweeps.
And grieving, Iobacchus climbed to the ridge of the wood,
and left to the winds his hope of driving the fight,
trembling at his stepmother's savage anger. But Athena came
from heaven; for high-ruling Zeus had sent the messenger before,
that his fleeing brother, terrified with fear of Hera,
she might draw back to the battle with changed purpose;
she stood behind, and gripped the tawny hair of Bacchus,
appearing to him alone, the grim goddess; and from her face
her eyes shot up a fiery flash;
and breathing wise sparks upon Lyaeus,
reproaching and angered, she spoke in a war-loving voice:
"Where do you flee, Dionysus? Why fear instead of fight?
Where are your valiant thyrsus-wands and your vine-arrows?
What tale shall I cry to my son of Cronus about you?
What lord of the Indians did I see destroyed in the fight?

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Deriades lives, and Morrheus still fights on.
What heaven-born inborn valour were you showing?
Did you set foot in Libya? Did you have the contest of Perseus?
Did you see the eye of stony Stheno, or the
hard-fighting, bellowing throat of Euryale herself?
Or did you mark the tresses of snake-haired Medusa,
and did the chasm of her scattered serpents wind about you?
Semele did not bear a warlike child; but Gorgon-slaying,
a worthy son, did Acrisione bear to my Zeus;
for winged Perseus did not shake off my sickle,
but honoured Hermes, the giver of his sandals.
I have a neighbouring witness, the rocky beast of the sea;
ask Cepheus of me, what the harpe of Perseus wrought;
ask the East and the West; for both alike,
the Nereids tremble at the husband of Andromeda,
the Hesperides sing of the reaper of Medusa.
Aeacus, undismayed, is not like Bacchus,
he did not flee Deriades, he did not tremble at the fight of the Indians.
Did the Arabian champion frighten you again yesterday? Ever since then
I shrink from seeing furious Ares, the father of Lycurgus,
crying out the weakness of war-fleeing Dionysus.
Your father and mine did not tremble at the battle,
when the Titan gods were arrayed against Olympus.
What Orsiboe did you carry off, mistress of the Indians?
Your Rhea did not see Cheirobie won by the spear.
Be merciful, glory of Zeus: I will not call you brother,
Deriades who flees, nor the race of unwarlike Indians.
But take up your thyrsus-wands and remember the fight again,
and lead the host; and to the armed Bacchant women
you shall see well-armoured Athena sharing the fight,
lifting the aegis, the unwounded weapon of Olympus."
So speaking, she breathed might into Bromius; and he, bold in heart,
fought a second time, and of the victory to come
he entrusted all his hope to Tritogeneia.
Then whom first, whom last did Bacchus slay,
when insatiable Athena gave him courage for battle?
He slew a hundred of the foe with his pitiless thyrsus,
and gave a wound to many, striking with his spear in many ways,
either with the tendrils of plants or with the well-budded cluster,
or casting a stone, a rugged bolt; and the stricken
were driven, with a din, into Bacchic frenzy by the divine lash.
And he wounded the left shoulder of Phringus with his sharp thyrsus;
but he, leaping, withdrew untouched; and as he fled
Melisseus laid him low with his whetted ox-cleaver.
And thyrsus-mad, far-shooting Dionysus rushed at Egretius,
whirling his Bacchic-loving spear; and flying
the Bacchic point of the spear whizzed through the air,
eager to strike the man, and, when Egretius had fled,
it fell upon the Bolinges, and the battle-rousing Arachotae
it startled into fear; and with his strong-wine-loving leaf
the dread tribes of the spear-bold Salangae were cut down;
and the host of the shield-bearing Arieni was startled;
and pursuing the champions of Phringus and Egretius,
Euius startled the whole host of the Uatocoetae;
and valiant Iobacchus thrust Lygus from the bloody
tumult; and Meilanion, who lay in wait by a tree,
the guileful one, he wounded with his wine-dark thyrsus,
as he shot at the Bassarids with hidden bolts;
but hard-fighting Hera took him alive unharmed,
because he had armed himself with guile and often assailed the Bacchants
with secret wars; and ever a rock hid him,
or a high-headed plant, as he lurked stolen among the leaves,
shooting at men with unmarked bolts.
And the Indians sped after the man-slaying tumult,
trembling at the valour of unconquered Dionysus.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
31. In the thirty-first, Hera coaxes
Sleep against the son of Cronus, and Persephone against Bacchus.
So Bacchus, stung by the goad of the Indian war,
ranged round the bosom of the Erythraean field,
shaking his golden curls beside his snow-white cheeks.
But Hera, swelling with envious cares,
scored the upper air with a menacing foot,
gazing there at the host of the far-scattered Indians
threshed down by the man-slaying thyrsus of Lyaeus.
And another anger she roused beside the Erythraean sea,
seeing the tangled remnants of Andromeda's bonds
and the stone upon the sand, that grim portent of the Earthshaker.
Grieving, she turned her eye aside, lest beside the sea
she should behold the bronze-forged sickle of Perseus, Gorgon-slayer.
For already, whirling his swift-kneed foot through the air,
across the thirsty Libyan ridge Perseus was ferried,
swimming on his wings; and stealing the wandering eye
of the one-eyed sleepless old daughter of Phorcys,
he entered the hard-to-tread cave, and like a reaper beside the rock
mowing whispering corn, the slanting harvest of her hair,
he cut through the labouring throat of the Gorgon,
and reddened his sickle; and as Medusa was hewn down
he washed his blood-stained hand in the snaky dew,
severing the head; and with his golden blade, midwife of a child,
that twin-bearing neck gave birth to the breed of the horse.
And the envious anger of Hera seethed in her heart
as she belched out her jealousy at Perseus and Dionysus.
She longed to charm both the eyes and the mind of the son of Cronus
into a deceiving marriage, and onto the wing of sweet Sleep
drawn down upon the bed, so that by some cunning craft,
while Zeus still slumbered, she might bear down on Lyaeus.
So she went to the dark, all-receiving hall of Hades,
and found Persephone, and cried out with crafty words:
"Most blessed I call you, since you dwell far from the gods;
you have not seen Semele dwelling within Olympus.
I fear that I shall behold Dionysus, whom a mortal womb bore,
wielding the lightning after Zagreus,
or lifting the thunderbolt in earthly hands.
You have been robbed, fruit-bringer; beside the corn-rich Nile,
in place of your mother Demeter, the sheaf-bearer who bore you,
they hold revel for another, and a bastard, some bountiful Deo,
bull-shaped and horned, is proclaimed—Inachian Io.
And Ares, whom indeed I bore, whom a heavenly womb brought forth,
my own son, fettered in an earthly inglorious bond,
Ephialtes hid within a jar, binding him fast about;
nor did my heavenly husband Zeus avail him,
but the child of Semele he rescued from the fiery brands,
and the infant Bacchus, still a babe, he saved alive from the bolt,
that half-finished bastard son; while Zagreus was being hewn
with knives, he did not fight for the heavenly Dionysus.
This stirs me the more, that the son of Cronus gave the starry pole
as bride-gift to Semele, and Tartarus to Persephone:
heaven is kept for Apollo, in heaven Hermes
dwells; but you have this house full of darkness.
What good was it, that wearing the lying shape of a serpent
he plundered the unplundered bond of your maidenhood,
if after the bed he was to destroy your labour-pains?
Zeus the lord on Olympus has a house full of stars,
to his brother who rules the waters he gave the salt water as a prize,
and the murky gloom he gave as a home to your husband.
But arm your Furies against wine-dark Bacchus,
that I may not see a mortal bastard wielding the sceptre of Olympus.
Have reverence for Zeus's consort who entreats you, have reverence for Deo,
have reverence for pure Themis who entreats you, so that the Indians
may breathe a little while Dionysus is shaken back;
be to me in my grief an avenger, since the son of Cronus
gave nectar to Bacchus and the gore of Enyo to Ares.
Let not Athens hymn a new Dionysus,
nor let him win a prize equal to the Eleusinian Dionysus,
let him not exchange the rites of the elder Iacchus,
let him not dishonour the basket of Demeter with his fruit."

title: Dionysiaca
text:
So speaking she confounded the whole mind of Persephone,
as her face was wetted with feigned tears,
prattling her wiles. And goddess nodded assent to goddess,
and gave her Megaera for companion, that she might accomplish it,
bearing the baleful eye, the will of jealous Hera.
And she, darting on a stormy sandal,
thrice was lifted up, and on the fourth reached the Ganges;
and she showed the Indian dead to grim Megaera, that throng,
and the sweat of the army and the manhood of Dionysus;
and Megaera, beholding the Indian-slaying labours of Lyaeus,
in her jealousy grudged them more than heavenly Hera.
But Hera rejoiced in mind, and to the serpent-haired goddess,
laughing a sardonic laugh, broke into downcast speech:
"So the young kings of Olympus play the champion,
so the bastards of Zeus hurl the spear! From Semele
Zeus bore a single child, to destroy them all,
the gentle and blameless Indians; but let him learn,
unjust Zeus and Bacchus, how great is the strength of Megaera.
Ah me, what a lawless mind has high-ruling Zeus!
With the unjust Tyrrhenians he does not fight, who, having learned
stolen, violent customs aboard their evil-guesting ships,
plunder the goods of others and sail the Sicilian sea;
he did not slay the impious race of the Dryopes, whose life is spears
and slaughter; but the Indians, who cared for piety, he slew,
whom all-cherished Themis perhaps suckled at her breast.
Ah me, what a lawless mind he has! For an immortal
a mortal man has burned—so great and such a one—Hydaspes,
a mortal man has burned, whom heavenly Zeus begot."
So speaking she flew through the upper air; and in silence,
beneath the neighbouring hollow base of the Caucasian crag,
having exchanged the shuddering snaky form of her limbs,
like an owl in shape she stayed there, until she should behold
great Zeus slumbering; for so queen Hera had told her.
But Hera herself went to the western water of Chremetes,
plotting, where the heavy old Libyan Atlas labours,
bent beneath the heavenly whirl,
and she sought Iris, bride of love-sick Zephyrus,
the messenger of Zeus when he is in haste, that she might accomplish
from the air a wind-footed envoy to shadowy Sleep.
Summoning her, she soothed her with friendly words:
"Iris, golden-winged bride of plant-nurturing Zephyrus,
mother of Love who brings good birth, with stormy sandal
hasten to go to the western house of gloomy Sleep;
seek him too about sea-beaten Lemnos; and if you find him,
tell him to charm the eyes of unbending Zeus
for a single dawn, that I may help the Indians.
But change your body, and taking the ugly form
of the black-girdled goddess Night, mother of Sleep,
become dark, false-named—for I too,
with answering limbs, when there is need of necessity,
change my form into Themis, into Cytherea, into Artemis.
And promise the marriage of Pasithea, for whose beauty
he longs, that he may accomplish my need; I need not teach you
that a man mad for women will do all things upon a hope."
So she spoke, and the goddess golden-winged Iris flew,
scanning the air, and toward Paphos, toward the land of Cyprus,
she strained her unswerving eye, and higher than Byblos
she watched the wedded water of Assyrian Adonis,
searching for the roving track of wandering Sleep.
She found him beside the nuptial slopes of Orchomenus;
for there again he tarried, winding his mind-wandering step,
haunting the lovely gateways of Pasithea.
And changing her body, turned about, unseen Iris
put on the unknown face of dark Night;
and the wily one drew near to Sleep; and like a mother
with mind-stealing words she uttered a beguiling voice:
"My child, how long shall the son of Cronus scorn me?
Is it not enough that Phaethon does me violence, since the dawn
itself shoots its darts at me, and morning pursues me?
Zeus begot a bastard son, to put my Sleep to shame.
One mortal shames me and my son; for all night long
kindling a light-bearing torch with his mystic spark,
Bacchus blots me out, and waking he afflicts you.
Sleep, why are you called all-subduer? No longer do you charm
waking men, since the bastard gleam of earthly Lyaeus
has conquered my revel; for with brighter torches
he hides the flames of my stars.
One mortal, light-bringer, shames me, since he covers,
great though it is, the ray of my Moon.
I am abashed before the dawn that laughs over Mist,
since I keep a bastard nightly gleam; for by another's
false-made Phaethon I, daytime Night, shine.
But you, dear boy, be wroth with the twofold ordinance,
with the mystic Satyrs and with sleepless Dionysus;
do a favour to your grieving mother, do a favour to Hera,
and charm the unbending eye of high-ruling Zeus
for a single dawn, that I may help the Indians,
whom the Satyrs harry and Bacchus still rouses.
Sleep, why are you called all-subduer? If you will,
turn your eye for me, and by seven-gated Thebes
you shall see the son of Cronus again waking all night;
loose the wantonness of unjust Zeus; for Amphitryon,
far from his own chamber, an iron-clad exile,
wars on; but Zeus sits beside Alcmene within doors,
holding insatiate the three-mooned bridal mist.
Let me not see Zeus waking through a fourth night also.
But, child, arm yourself against the son of Cronus, lest again,
lest again he fill up the ninefold mist.
Remember the earlier Mnemosyne; lying with her
nine nights he stayed, keeping a sleepless eye,
holding the much-childed sting of unwearied unions.
Another all-subduing god, twin-winged, like to Sleep,
little Love, conquered the son of Cronus with a small dart.
Pity too the dark-skinned offspring of the earthborn Indians;
do a favour; for they are of the same colour as your mother;
rescue the dark ones, dark-winged one; and do not afflict
the earth, coeval with my father, from which alone
all sprang, as many as dwell in Olympus.
Do not tremble at the son of Cronus, when his consort Hera is gracious;
do not tremble at Semele, whom her own husband burned.
Not the fiery lightning shall be able to match you,
not the heavy-roaring thunder of the clashing clouds;
only ply your wings for me, and upon his unswerving couch
Zeus stays unshaken, as long, Sleep, as you bid.
I have heard that you long for one of the Graces; but in your heart
holding the sting of the bridal chamber, guard yourself, and do not afflict
the mother of Pasithea, Hera, wardress of the bridal yoke.
And if you dwell beside Tethys by the Leucadian rock,
help Deriades, whom Indian Hydaspes begot;
keep faith with your neighbour, since your loud-sounding neighbour
Ocean was the forefather of Deriades."

title: Dionysiaca
text:
So speaking she persuaded him. And as though hearing his mother,
Sleep was startled, and swore to charm the eyes
of unsleeping Zeus, even to the course of the third Dawn;
but Iris asked him only to fetter the son of Cronus
in slumber for one single course of the dawn.
There Sleep stayed, awaiting the hour of fair wedding.
And swiftly the goddess Iris flew back homeward;
hastening, she brought the blameless word to her queen.
And Hera flew on stormy foot through the air,
and wove another guile, how she might come near to Zeus
bearing the girdle aloft, the mind-charming band of desire.
And she sought the Paphian; above Lebanon, alone,
the Assyrian, she found Aphrodite in the wilds,
seated; for the Graces had gone to the dappled flowers
of the gardens, those vernal dancers of Orchomenus,
one plucking Cilician saffron, another longing to bring
balsam and the plantation of the Indian reed,
another the fragrant herb of roses.
Astonished, unexpected, she sprang up from her seat,
the daughter of Zeus, Aphrodite, when she saw the wife of Zeus;
and seeing her grieving, she uttered a versatile voice:
"Hera, wife of Zeus, why are your cheeks gone pale?
Why, my queen, are your eyes downcast?
Has rain again become a thievish, showering Zeus?
Has he again become a bull, a watery wayfarer among the waters?
Does some Europa again do you violence? Or some other
Antiope wedded in a shaggy bed by a false Satyr,
while Nycteus, her father, refuses his consent?
Does some new horse, wise-minded, press toward another marriage,
sending forth a bastard neighing from mimicking lips?
Has he wooed another Semele with the bridal brand,
and shaken the lightning that steers the Loves?
Does he dance toward the bed of a fair-horned heifer,
pouring forth a loving bellow? If you will,
you might rouse another bull-watcher, a spy on Zeus,
a herdsman marked with sleepless eyes—Argus.
Tell me, since I ask, and what strength I have, I will help."
So speaking, the goddess embraced her with a guileful word:
"Cyprian goddess, let us leave the floor of Olympus to mortals;
Zeus has brought Semele up to Olympus, the mother of Bacchus,
and he will bring Dionysus too into the upper air. What house
shall receive Hera? Or to what place shall I go? I am ashamed,
lest I behold Semele, the bastard queen of Olympus.
I fear that I shall see the house of gloomy Iapetus,
lest he seize me and drive me, after Cronus, out of Olympus.
I fear, lest after the midwife, putting nectar to shame in heaven,
he plant the vine—as they call it—even among the blessed.
May that never come to pass, Justice and Earth and Water!
Let him not bring the vine-shoots into the upper air, nor for the sake of praise
let me call heaven vine-clad after star-clad,
nor drink another drink after the sweet nectar of Olympus.
I fear that I shall see steadfast Athena drunken,
that she may lift her spear against Ares and Cytherea,
that with the staggering drop of mind-staggering Dionysus
the wine-stricken stars, raging against one another,
may raise up daring Enyo in heaven,
that, made bacchic, all the dwellers of Olympus
may mimic the rites of the shield-bearing Corybantes.
Is that god-hated shame not enough, that I behold
the Trojan youth, Zeus's servant of the cups,
shaming heaven and Hebe, the cupbearer of Zeus,
when with earthly hands he draws the sweet nectar?
In shame I will go down to earth; to them both
I will leave the upper air, to Ganymede and Dionysus;
I will leave the upper air, the house of Semele. Let one house,
heaven, be theirs both, both Perseus's and Dionysus's.
I will come to my own Argos, to the splendid city of Mycenae,
to dwell on earth; and with my grieving mother
Ares himself shall follow, your bridegroom; but you too
set foot in your own Sparta, and let it receive, well-armoured,
together with bronze-clad Ares, the angry Aphrodite.
I know whence I draw these sufferings: my father's Fury
demands of me requital for my outraged parent,
because, bearing down in the battle of grandsire Cronus,
the Titaness Hera assailed him as he fought beside Zeus;
fair were it for me to see Dionysus in the midst of Olympus
seated near Love, sharing a hearth with the foam-born,
lifting the aegis after the son of Cronus and Athena.
But, goddess, help me, and as a remedy for my distress
give me the embroidered girdle, your all-charming band,
for one single dawn, that I may charm the eyes of Zeus,
and, while Zeus sleeps, may help my Indians.
Twice I have become your mother-in-law; for of my own
son Hephaestus and of Ares you became the bride.
Grant the long-delayed favour, since the dark-skinned Indians
became the hosts of Erythraean Aphrodite,
on whom in his anger Dionysus has fallen, against whom too
woman-mad, loveless, child-begetting Zeus has raged,
and brandished the lightning, fighting in arms beside Dionysus;
give me the helping girdle, in which alone
you charm all things in one; and I am worthy to wear it,
since I was born of the yoke and am a fellow-worker of the Loves."

title: Dionysiaca
text:
32. In the thirty-second are battles, and the bed of slumbering Zeus, and the madness of Lyaeus.
So speaking she persuaded her; and crafty Aphrodite
yielded to her gainful words, and drawing from her bosom
gave to willing Hera the girdle of the Loves.
And she spoke a word concerning the charming band:
"Receive this girdle, a remedy for your distress;
you will charm all things in one with the desire-guiding girdle,
the Sun and Zeus and the upper air and the choir of stars,
and the unstable stream of boundless Ocean."
She spoke, and sank into the Assyrian Lebanese rock.
And Hera entered the star-roaming circle of Olympus,
and swiftly adorned her all-white form;
often, smoothing the wandering tress let down
to her forehead, she set straight the straying cluster of her hair;
and she moistened her braided locks with fragrant oil,
whose far-shadowing scent, when it stirred, through air and sea
made the whole earth drunk with the breath of perfume.
And on her head she had an all-glittering wreath, in which were many
brilliant gems, companions of Love, from which the Cyprian fire
sends bright sparkles as they are shaken;
and she had that stone which draws men into desire,
bearing the bright name of love-stricken Selene,
and the stone that yearns for love-begetting iron,
and the Indian love-stone, since it too
sprang from the waters, kin to the foam-born,
and the dark hyacinth, still dear to Phoebus;
and about her tresses she bound a love-bringing herb,
which Cytherea loves, as the rose, as the anemone,
and wears it when she is about to lie with the son of Myrrha;
and she bound her flanks crown-wise with the unwonted girdle;
and she had a dappled robe, most ancient, on which had flowed
in the secret love of a bride's union with brothers
the bridegroom's blood, still a remnant of her old maidenhood,
that she might remind her husband of their wedded love;
and washing her brow she covered it with a flashing veil,
and clasped the brooch, the key of her tunic;
and having dressed her body and gazed in the mirror,
like a feather or a thought Hera ran through the air.
And she came near to Zeus; and seeing her, high-ruling Zeus
was lashed by the goading girdle into hot Loves;
and as Zeus looked on, his eyes were enslaved;
and the son of Cronus, watching her, questioned her with a word:
"Hera, why have you come to the eastern clime of earth?
What need brought you? Why do you walk here today?
Do you again, in anger, arm yourself against wine-dark Bacchus,
and long to help the overweening Indians?
Speak." And with laughing mind much-contriving Hera,
mad with jealousy, spoke, beguiling her bedfellow:
"Father Zeus, another dear errand keeps me; for I do not come
pursuing alien cares of Indian Ares
and Indian-slaying Dionysus, but to the burning halls
of neighbouring Helios at the sunrise I go
in haste; for winged Love, beside the water of Tethys,
stung by the goad for Rhodope, daughter of Ocean,
has renounced the marriage-yoke; and the world has become a wanderer,
and life is useless when the unions are gone;
him I go to summon, returning here;
for you know that I am called the Yoke-goddess, since my own
hands command the birth that brings offspring to fulfilment."
To her, crying out such a word, her hot husband replied:
"Dear bride, leave off your strife; let my proud Dionysus,
mowing down root and branch the unbacchic race of Indians,
take his joy; and let the bridal bed receive us both;
for it is not desire of an earthly wife, nor of a goddess,
that has so set my heart raging with the charming girdle . . .
not when I loved Taygete the Atlantid, from whose bed
the eldest-born city-guardian Lacedaemon grew up;
not so much did I love Niobe beside neighbouring Lerna,
daughter of first-born Phoroneus; nor so much Io,
the roaming Inachian, the cow-eyed, who beside the Nile
bore the offspring of Epaphus and first-born Keroessa;
not so much did I come to desire of the Paphian, for whose bed
I begot the Centaurs, casting seed in the furrow of earth;
as now I follow your sweet desire—do you too,
as one born of the yoke and mistress of the race,
shoot your bedfellow with Cyprian darts?"
So speaking, he rolled the golden clouds into a tower
and enclosed himself in a curving, rounded canopy;
and there was a fashioned likeness of a bridal chamber, which then in a circle
the many-coloured form of the heavenly rainbow
crowned with purple, and for Zeus and his bright-armed bride
it was an unbidden shelter of the dewy union,
and a self-made image of the chamber of necessary love.
And they joined in the sweet ordinance of gracious marriage;
and the earth, unfolding her fragrant childbed,
crowned the bridal bed with lovely flowers;
and the Cilician saffron sprang up, and the smilax grew,
and to the female herb beside it twined the male leaves,
as though the delicate husband breathed desire even among the flowers,
and a double shoot adorned the bed of both,
covering Zeus with saffron and his consort Hera with smilax;
and to wise silence the sharp love of Zeus was shown
by the lovely narcissus leaping upon the anemone.
Nor did any of the immortals look on the shadowed bed, not then the Nymphs
their neighbours, nor all-seeing Phaethon, nor even the eye
of cow-eyed Selene beheld the imperishable union;
for with thick clouds the shelter of the bed was girdled,
and Sleep, companion of the Loves, charmed the eyes of Zeus.
While Zeus lay sleeping delicately among the flowers, charmed,
holding his consort in his arms upon the unseen bed,
meanwhile the many-shaped Fury that roams the mountains
was armed against Dionysus by the nods of Hera;
and she crashed a din upon the eyes of Lyaeus,
shaking, heavy-thundering, her viperous scourge;
and she tossed her head, and from her serpent locks,
shuddering, shaken, a deadly echo hissed,
and jets of venom sprinkled the lonely peak . . .
Now showing the likeness of a beast's face,
fearfully mad she bristled, a lion with thick-haired throat,
rushing at Dionysus with bloody jaws.
Him, held fast in the leap of mind-stealing frenzy,
Artemis watched, and wished to drive off the madness,
but heavy-thundering Hera from on high frightened her,
hurling a torch; and the mistress of the hunt gave way,
in anger at her stepmother; yet some guardian there was of Bacchus
in his madness, and she checked his beasts with a threat,
and fastened his hunting hounds with a bond,
binding tight the tangled trace of the neck-straps,
lest they should harm the flesh of mind-distraught Dionysus.
And Megaera, blackening in her nether tunic,
came again into the gloom, darting at Lyaeus
phantoms of many shapes; and against Bromius many
venom-shooting drops were shot from her head,
and grim sparks; and ever within his hearing
the Tartarean hiss of the mind-stealing scourge whistled.
And Dionysus, suffering, within the lonely thicket
ranged the hard-to-tread mountains with wandering foot,
shaken by a demonic gasping; and about the rocks,
like a gadfly-maddened bull, he butted with his horns,
pouring a harsh bellow from his frenzied throat;
and Echo of evil sound, leaving Pan and her after-voice,
bellowed with a maddened cry,
answering the bold answering sound of Dionysus.
And dappled deer and shaggy lionesses he pursued,
storm-swift Bacchus, following the mountain-roaming chase;
no bold lion came near him; the frightened
bear, startled, hid in a hollow rock,
cowering before the madness of threatening Lyaeus,
receiving in her grim ears the god-driven sound;
and the long serpents leaning on a rock,
licking gently, he sheared off with his pitiless thyrsus;
and he shook the peaks with his long-pointed horn,
slaying the suppliant tribes of unbending lions;
and he uprooted the oaks of the fruitful field,
and pursued the Hadryads; and shooting the hills
he drove the Naiad Nymphs from their river, wanderers.
The Bassarids strayed and did not touch Lyaeus,
and the Satyrs, shuddering, hid themselves in the sea,
