nor did they come near him, awed at the weight of his threat,
lest he should rush at them, pouring a discordant sound,
hurling snow-white foam, the witness of his madness.
But Deriades, with overweening boldness, fell upon the Bacchants,
by the nods of Hera, while Dionysus was shaken.
As when, roaring in the swell of wintry breakers,
the unsailable sea rages with opposing storm-blasts,
snowing the drenched air with towering waves;
and the stern-cables, by the unsparing onset of the wave,
the squalls have snapped, and rolling the sail with a gust
the furious blast stripped the bowed mast bare,
girt round with sails, and the yard was wrenched askew,
and the sailors in distress gave up their hope to the sea;
so then the Indian War-god roused the whole host against Bacchus.
There was strife in no order, nor was the clash of men
equal, nor the contest fair; for tireless,
returning, rousing the war-cry, bronze Ares thundered on,
bearing the likeness of the champion Modaeus, who more than others
insatiate of battle delighted in the joyless gore,
to whom slaughter was sweeter than a feast; and on his shield,
like the snaky coils of the Gorgon's locks,
bearing the painted image of fair-tressed Medusa,
he was like to Deriades, of the same colour; and then, of that
horror-bringing form having the laughterless likeness of face,
and bearing the twisting tress and the device of the shield,
fearfully mad, host-rousing Ares was borne into the fray,
and cheered the champions. With one-tongued war-cry,
though Bacchus was not present, the fearless Indians roared,
and deadly Ares thundered back a nine-thousandfold din,
having roaming Strife as his fellow-worker; and in the tumult
he set Phobos and Deimos, the attendant of Deriades.
And the army of lonely-roaming Dionysus was stung to madness
by Deriades and by Ares, running beside the slumber of Zeus.
The mingled phalanxes of the like-zealed battle
girdled with iron the whole rank of the Bassarids,
and many fleeing were slain by the slayer,
struck down by swords. Homeric Muses, tell me,
who died, who fell beneath the spear of Deriades:
Aibialus and Thyamis and Ormenius and Opheltes,
Criasus son of Argasus, Telebes and Lyctian Antheus
and Thronius and Aretus and the fair-speared Moleneus
and brave Comarchus; and one upon another was stretched out
by the spear of Deriades, a dead host; and as they perished,
one lay sprawled on the ground, another on the streams
floated, bearing the wavy fray, another in the sea
nearby was subdued, and as he was driven by iron
the Arab Nereus entombed in the waves the newly-wounded man;
another ran on stormy foot through the mountain,
fleeing death; another, leaving the spear fixed
midway through his back, made for the inner shade of the thicket,
needing the absent averter of evil, Dionysus.
Boastful Echelaus fell by an untombed doom,
struck by the man-breaking stone of towering Morrheus,
a Cyprian, still bearing the newly-traced circle of his beard,
wholly like a high-leaved palm; and in the tumult
the delicate unshorn youth rolled, shaking his torch,
struck at the tip of the hip, where with binding-bond to the flesh
Nature fitted the axle of the thigh, joined to its socket;
and he died, still grasping the kindled mystic pine,
and gasping, he turned his head to ash with his own torch,
burning his twining locks with the smoking brand.
And boasting over him, scoffing Morrheus cried out:
"Boy, stranger to your reputed nurse,
youth Echelaus, you have belied your descent from Cyprus;
you do not have your race from Pygmalion, to whom Cypris gave
the long course of a long-lived life;
your bridegroom Ares did not save you for your Paphian;
nor did your Cytherea give you the boundless rounds
of returning years, nor an unlimping chariot,
that you might escape your doom on a death-averting car,
ever driving the heavy-kneed course of mules.
I erred—you have your race from Cyprus; for swift-dooming
Ares has subdued you too, like the son of Myrrha."
So speaking, spear-shaking Morrheus charged among the foot;
and seizing rolling-footed Bilithus and slaying Denthis,
and cutting the neck of the dancer Erigbolus,
with his far-flung spear he frightened the Phrygian warriors;
and Sebes he laid low headlong with a jagged dart;
and pursuing the phalanx of the Thebans and Actaeon,
he slew Eubotes, a townsman of the Cadmean land,
the comrade of Actaeon. With one-voiced war-cry
many, fleeing the boundless might of Deriades,
all together slipped headlong into the nets of yoke-mate Fate,
dying by the self-slaying, threshing iron,
by the casts of a single man; and falling on one another
they were strewn in rows in the bloody dust—
Crimisus, Imaleon, Phrasius, Thargelus, Iaon,
among whom, as they were hewn down, Coilon fell in their number,
and a corpse, Cyes, rolled in a bloody doom;
and slaughter unspeakable there was; and as they were cut by the hostile iron,
the thirsty ground bathed itself willingly in the gore,
receiving the strange shower of the Warlike snowfall.
And there was rout of the Bacchic phalanx; for unsteady
the footmen were shaken, and toward flight the well-stoned bits
of the war-shy drivers were drawn back in fear;
of whom one, mountain-roaming, sank into a hollow rock,
another, going beneath the long-leaved slope of a thicket, sat down
hidden in the leaves, another into a lions' cave,
another sought the lair of an irresistible bear;
and one, escaping over a high-crested headland,
with mountain-roaming feet ranged the topmost hill.
A Bacchant passed by the lairs of a newly-delivered beast,
treading the headland with frightened sandal;
for she no longer cared to hold the lions' rock,
but reached the strengthless nest of deer
with her enfeebled ways, since the Bacchant had turned her former mind
into the heart of a deer instead of a lioness.
And one of the storm-footed Satyrs ran on frightened foot,
sandalless, like the unsteady breezes,
fleeing the god-defying weight of the threat of Deriades.
And old wandering Silenus pursued the crags;
often he fell to the ground with face in the dust,
crouching, heavy-kneed, on slippery sandals,
again raising up his shaggy body; and among the hills
he hid instead of fighting, and the Euian spear by necessity,
the thyrsus that cared for the storms, he left, that was no fighter,
and barely escaped the spear of well-helmeted Morrheus.
And sluggish Erechtheus retreated on hesitant feet,
straining backward his fair-rounded eye,
ashamed before his city-guardian Athena who loves the fray.
And unwilling Aristaeus refused the Bacchic Maenad combat,
struck on his left shoulder by an arrow.
And he avoided the army of spear-bold Corybantes,
wounded along his shaggy breast—Melisseus,
grazed at the nipple's tip by an Erythraean point.
And the grim Cyclopes, shameless, on nimble foot
hastened in awe to flight, with whom, fleeing,
unshaken Faunus left behind the Indian War.
And drawing the whole army of the fair-horned phalanx into flight,
the eldest-born, fugitive, Parrhasian Pan retreated,
and on silent feet sank into the shady wood,
lest unstable Echo see him fleeing through the mountain,
and laugh at him and call him weakling.
And then all the champions fled; but in the tumult
Aeacus alone was left there, and fighting
he lacked the unconquered Dionysus, who was not present;
yet even so he stayed there. And from the crag the Nymphs,
the Naiads, hid in the deep halls of the water;
some, companions of the Hydaspes, others, fleeing,
made their dwelling in the streams of the Indus near the path,
others were companions of the Sydrian waters, and others in the Ganges
wiped off the newly-shed gore; and these, then, many,
coming in droves to the watery channels,
the silver-footed Naiad with hospitable gateway
received into the courts of her billowy maiden-bower.
Others hid in the shady clusters of the Hamadryad,
sinking into the opening oaken hollows.
And many beside the water-bearing springs by the rock,
the Bassarids wailed in streams; and with newly-poured
tearful shower from the lament-loving face
the deep-bosomed fountain, filled, grew all empurpled,
mourning the heavy grief of unmourned Dionysus.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
33. In the thirty-third, impetuous Love subdues Morrheus,
inflaming him for the beauty of Chalcomede.
But he, borne on the roaming leap of his feet,
swift-kneed, rushed like a fair-horned bull,
pouring a deadly gasping in the swell of mind-changing madness.
And a Grace, swift-sandalled, beside the Erythraean garden,
plucking the fragrant plantation of the reeds,
that within the fire-breathing Paphian cauldrons
mingling the molten travail of Assyrian oil
with Indian flowers she might make perfume for her queen,
when she had plucked all manner of dewy herb,
gazed at the whole place; and beside the neighbouring thicket,
watching the madness of her father Lyaeus,
she grieved and wept, and with affectionate yearning
with mournful nails she scored her cheeks;
and she watched the Satyrs cowering before the War-goddess,
and saw Codone and short-lived Gigarto
lying upon the untombed dust;
and she pitied Chalcomede on stormy sandal,
fleeing the spear-point of maddened Morrheus,
and she was shaken, envious, for the rose-faced girl,
lest she should ever surpass Aphrodite in beauty.
Grieving, she went up to Olympus, in mournful silence
hiding the pain for her father Lyaeus;
and changing the bloom of her fair-rounded cheek to pallor,
she dimmed the glittering radiance of her face.
And as she went downcast, Adonian Cypris addressed her,
crying out such a consoling word, and from her face,
from Pasithea's, she perceived the grief in heralding silence:
"Dear bride, what has befallen you, that you have changed your form?
Maiden, how have you altered your blushing shape?
Who quenched the springtime ray of your face?
No longer does the silvery gleam flash from your limbs;
no longer, as before, do your eyes laugh.
But tell me your cares. Is it that my son
afflicts you, and you love beside a love-stricken rock,
like Selene some herdsman? Or did Love
goad you too with his girdle, after the Dawn?
I know whence your cheeks have grown pale: that he weds you,
a maiden, the misty bridegroom, wandering Sleep;
yet I will not force you, unwilling, nor will I join
to white Pasithea a dark-skinned husband, Sleep."
So she spoke, and the Grace wept and answered with a word:
"Plant-sower of the everlasting world, mother of the Loves,
no herdsman troubles me, nor the bold desire of Sleep.
I am not the love-sick Dawn nor Selene,
but the roving labour of Lyaeus distresses me,
my father shuddering at the Furies; and for your
brother Dionysus, if you can, be a champion."
She spoke, and told the queen all her father's labour
and the boundless phalanxes of the Bassarids whom Morrheus slew,
and the whole fugitive army of the Satyrs; she told too
the demonic scourge of Dionysus being shaken,
and Gigarto wailing, gasping upon the ground,
and she told of Codone cut off untimely; and in shame
she declared the grief together and the beauty of Chalcomede.
And changing the rosy spark of her face,
laughter-loving Aphrodite cast her wonted laugh.
And she bade Splendour go as messenger, to summon
her impetuous son Love, the air-roaming one on high,
the begetting steersman of the human race.
And the Grace turned her step, and with much-turning face
gazed at sea and earth and heaven, where she might find
the unsteady track of Love, since he plies his wings everywhere,
circling the four-cut rim of the world.
She found him about the high peak of golden Olympus,
shooting nectar-drops from cups;
and beside him stood a boy, his playmate, sporting delicately,
fair-haired Hymenaeus; and the work of his high-minded mother,
the heavenly one, skilled in the course of the stars,
he made the prize of victory—a rounded ball
to play with, the rival image of the cunning form of Argus;
and winged Love, lifting his mother's fair-rounded
golden necklace, set it down, of sea-born Aphrodite,
the bright all-glittering ornament of victory; and a silver
cauldron lay in the contest, and the image of wine-pouring Hebe
stood as a mid-shown mark; and lovely Ganymede,
cupbearer of the son of Cronus, was umpire of the contest,
bearing a garland in his hands. And of the wine-loving casts
there was a lot, marking off the differing fingers of the hands;
and some they raised upright and held out, and others on the wrist
of the hand were fastened, joined in a yoke-mate bond;
and for both there was lovely strife. Delicate-haired
Hymenaeus, drawing first, took the cup, and sending
the flying nectar-drop on high into the air
he cast it over the cauldron; and not then did he show
to his mother the Muse a vow fulfilled; for the drop, shot high in the air,
darting from the cup, struck the middle air,
but turning the cast aside with a dancing throb,
drawn back again about the face of the image
silently struck the top of the soundless head.
Second, subtle-minded Love, by a skilful rule,
took the lovely cup, and prayed to the Cyprus-born
secretly in his heart, and stretching an unswerving eye
toward the mark, he shot, sending the far-flung moisture;
and the drop of the nectar drink, whirling back,
straight, unbending, above the temple of the image
from the air, heavy-sounding, crashed upon its brow;
and the delicate image cried out, and for the son of the Cyprus-born
the golden cauldron rang out a triumphant echo;
and laughing Ganymede gave Love the delicate crown;
and swiftly taking the glittering necklace and lifting the ball
he held the double prize of the well-dropped contest,
and leaping with his feet, tumbling with his head,
exulting, bold Love danced; and from his adversary,
often grieving, he drew down the hand from his face.
And Splendour stood near him; and the prizes of the mind-delighting
lord she received in her hands; and she nodded to the boy
to come apart, and into Love's ears, with witnessing silence,
spoke the crafty word of her lying queen:
"All-subduer, unsubdued, life-bringer, coeval with the world,
make haste, since Cytherea is being forced, and none of her
handmaids stays beside her; the Grace has fled, Persuasion is gone,
and unsteady Desire has retreated; and to you alone
she sent me, needing your unconquered quiver."
So she spoke, and Love questioned her, that he might learn all;
for all young people, when they hear the beginning
of an endless tale, are eager to hear the end;
and he poured out the unbridled cry of his lips:
"Who has grieved my Paphian? That I may arm my hand
to fight against all. If my mother is being forced,
I will stretch the all-subduing bowstring against the son of Cronus,
and make him again, gadfly-stung, the marriage-thieving bird of the Loves,
an eagle, or some bull, a swimmer of the sea;
and if Pallas has stirred her and the lame god has grieved her,
kindling the light-bearing brand of the Cecropian lamp,
I will fight against both, against Hephaestus and Athena;
and if the arrow-pouring huntress with her hare-staff draws her to anger,
drawing the fiery Olympian sword of Orion
I will madden Artemis, and drive her out of heaven . . .
lifting on my wings my companion, the son of Maia,
who calls in vain the worthless helper, Persuasion;
and leaving my darts and the fiery knot of my quiver,
with laurel leaves I will lash willing Phoebus,
binding him fast about with the speaking hyacinth;
nor do I tremble at the might of the War-god, nor will I weary
of scourging Ares, fettered with the sweet girdle;
and I will drag the twin luminaries down as servants
to Paphos from heaven, and bring as attendants to my mother
Phaethon with Clymene, Selene with Endymion,
that all may know that I subdue all things."
He spoke, and whirling his straight-coursing foot in the air
he outran Splendour with the twin whirring of his wings,
until he came to the house of hastening Aphrodite.
And taking him about the middle with serene face,
with open joyous arm she embraced the boy,
lightening on her knees the dear burden; and as he sat,
she kissed the boy's mouth and eyes; and touching
his mind-charming bow and handling his quiver,
as though breathing anger, she broke into a crafty voice:
"My child, you have forgotten Phaethon and Cytherea;
no longer does Pasiphae pursue the bellowing bed;
the Sun mocks me, and the blood of Astris arms
the warlike Deriades, the son of her own son,
the destroyer of the Bassarids of woman-mad Dionysus,
and the driver of the love-stricken Satyrs of Bromius.
This stirred me the more, that in mortal shape
war-rousing Ares, having the War-goddess as his fellow-worker,
heedless of his old love for Aphrodite,
by the nods of Hera was armed against Dionysus,
fellow-traveller of the Indian king. But in the fray
let Ares champion Deriades, and you champion Lyaeus;
he has a spear, but you a mightier bow, before which bends his knee
highest Zeus and impetuous Ares and lawful Hermes;
even Apollo, famed for the bow, fears your bow.
And if, dear boy, you would gratify your foam-born mother,
champion the Bassarids and our Dionysus.
But going, unapproachable, to the eastern clime of earth,
to the Indian land, where a handmaid of Lyaeus
there is among the Bacchants, surpassing the bloom of her age,
named Chalcomede, lover of maidenhood—and if both
Chalcomede and Cypris within Lebanon you should behold,
you cannot, dear boy, tell which is Aphrodite—
going there, help lonely-roaming Dionysus,
shooting Morrheus for the beauty of Chalcomede;
and a reward worthy of your archery I will put in your hands,
a well-wrought Lemnian crown, like the gleams
of the fiery sun; and you, sending the sweet shaft,
do a favour to both, to Cypris and to Dionysus;
glorify your bird and mine, the marriage-arraying bird of the Loves,
the herald of gladness, of the life-yoking unions."
So spoke the goddess; and greedy Love sprang up from the bosom
of his mother, and lifted his bow, and on his little
shoulder hung the all-subduing quiver;
and winged, he flew through the upper air; and about Cerne
wheeling his light wings before the casts of the Dawn,
he flew smiling, that so great a charioteer
of the heavenly chariots he had inflamed with a few darts,
and the gleam of the Loves had conquered the gleam of the Sun.
And swiftly, coming into the midst of the Indian throng,
he steadied his bow upon the neck of Chalcomede;
and aiming the shaft about the circles of her rosy cheek
he sent it into the mind of Morrheus, and oaring his course
with the swimming of his wings, running on a yoke-mate track,
he climbed up to his father's starry bolts,
leaving the Indian pierced by the fiery arrow.
And ever here and there, shaken by the shaft of desire,
where the maiden went, the love-sick Morrheus went,
holding a gentle sword, lifting a sparing spear,
and his bold mind was lashed by the girdle of Desire;
and stretching about her his love-mad encircling eye,
by Cyprian promptings he drew his unyielding gaze.
But she, with crafty mind, beguiled the lord of the Indians,
as though longing, and the girl took the impress
of a false image of desire; and Morrheus reached for heaven,
borne on idle hope; for in his heart
he thought the maiden held a shaft equal to the Loves',
foolish man, since he sought to charm a chaste girl
with his dark limbs, and remembered not his own form.
And laughing at him, with playful guile the girl,
appearing near, provoked the love-sick one, and to her adversary
she told of the wind-footed knees of the unwedded bride,
how once she fled Phoebus, running with the North wind,
how beside the watery flood of the streaming river
she set her maiden foot beside the broad-flowing Orontes,
when the earth, gaping beside the mouth of the well-watered lake,
received the pursued girl in its pitying bosom.
At her speaking such a word, Morrheus leapt up in joy,
and one thing alone stirred him, that Daphne in pursuit
even a god did not overtake, and Apollo did not defile;
and he called Phoebus slow; and ever he blamed the earth,
that it hid the maiden untried in marriage;
for he feared, trembling with the sweet fire, lest she too
should be Chalcomede, lover of maidenhood, like Daphne,
lest, seeing her flee, he should run a vain course,
toiling toward unfulfilled desire, like Apollo.
But when night arose, the lulling-to-sleep of battle,
Chalcomede came to the ridge of the lonely wood,
seeking the tracks of mind-distraught Dionysus;
not then bearing the rattles and Euian cymbals of Rhea
did she celebrate the rites of unsleeping Lyaeus,
but downcast, not touching the dance,
she held an unwonted silence on lips never silent,
knowing the sickness of the protecting Dionysus.
And on hesitant feet slow Morrheus came barely along,
watching the bride with backward-turning eye,
blaming swift-coursing Phaethon; and his mind, following,
he kept companion to Chalcomede; and distressed,
with Cyprian whispers he belched up a womanish cry,
darting the nightly shaft of the Loves beneath his heart:
"Be gone, shaft and warlike bow; for a lovely
mightier other shaft compels me; be gone, quiver;
the girdle has conquered the strap of my shield.
No longer do I arm my warlike hand against the Bassarids;
but my father's god, leaving water and earth,
I will set up an altar to both Cypris and Dionysus,
casting away the bronze spear of Ares and Athena.
No longer, torch in hand, will I arm myself; for
the torch of the Loves has quenched the brand of feeble Ares;
I am struck by another, hotter fire. Would that I too,
would that I were a Satyr, woman-mad, that I might dance
in the midst of the Bassarids, and resting my arm upon my hand
might fasten the bond of love about the neck of Chalcomede.
Let Dionysus drag the attendant of Deriades into Phrygia
beneath the yoke of slavery, and in place of my fatherland
let prosperous Maeonia receive me as her dweller;
I wish to hold Tmolus after Caucasus; and casting off my
first name of Indian, let me be called a Lydian,
bowing the slavish neck of Love to Dionysus;
let Pactolus bear me along; what is my father's Hydaspes to me?
Let the sweet house of Chalcomede hold me; for in the wars
Cypris together and Bacchus, with both their darts,
have fallen upon the kinsmen of Deriades, that one may say:
the girdle slew Morrheus, and the thyrsus killed Orontes."
Such things he cried; and with loud-roaring care
he wasted away, remembering Chalcomede; for in company
the sparks of the Loves grow ever hotter.
For already, leaping with self-born throb,
silently the soundless cone of cloudless darkness grew black,
and trembling joined all things in one silence;
nor did any Indian wayfarer hurry his step through the city,
nor did the working woman ply her wonted craft,
nor in her hands beside the spindle-loving lamp
did the wandering spindle, going round its self-turned circle,
unsteady, stretch out for the dancer in the drawing of the thread,
but heavy-headed beside the wakeful lamp
the toiling woman slept; and a serpent, quietly creeping,
lay fallen, and with its head drawing back its returning tail,
of its sleepy belly it reined in the coil of its spine;
and a high-stepping elephant beside the neighbouring wall
slept an upright sleep, resting its back against an oak.
And then alone, sleepless, rushing out, soundlessly creeping
with backward-returning, coiling feet, Morrheus was worn away,
leaving Cheirobie alone sleeping in her chamber;
and having heard a tale from some ancient sage
among the Cilician men, holding battle near the Taurus,
learned in the inspired sting of the starry Loves,
gazing at the bright court spread out in the air,
he watched the bridegroom of Europa, the Bull of Olympus;
and stretching his much-wandering eye along the axle-sinew
he watched Callisto and the unsteady coil of the Wain,
knowing that a female heard the female tale,
the bastard body of the mimic huntress
in unknown limbs; and rising above the Bull
he watched Myrtilus, the fire-breathing Charioteer,
because he helped in marriage, and for the race of Hippodameia
made a counterfeit shape in the wheel-running wax,
until Pelops won his bride; and near Cassiopeia
he saw the long-winged eagle, the husband of Aegina,
and he wished for such a thievish guile, that he too
might loose the maidenhood of unwedded Chalcomede,
and he spoke a word, keeping a sleepless eye:
"I have heard how, all like a Satyr, high-ruling Zeus
wedded the maiden Antiope in a guileful shape,
in a mimic love of frolic-loving unions;
such a body I too wish to have, that I might dance
into the army of the fair-horned Satyrs, coming unknown,
that I might accomplish the bed of wine-loving Chalcomede.
I know, Cytherea, whence you are angry with the sons of the Indians;
your arrows trouble the neighbours of the Sun;
not yet have you lost the memory of your reproved bonds.
Phaethon did not beget me; why do you trouble me, Aphrodite?
Cow-watching Pasiphae did not bear me, nor am I
the brother of Ariadne. Speak, stones, your rocky voice.
I long for Chalcomede, and she refuses. Be gone, quiver,
be gone, bloody bow and windy arrows;
Ares did not save me when Aphrodite armed herself;
little Love subdued me, whom proud Bacchus did not slay."
Such things in vain by night the love-sick Morrheus spoke.
Nor did the wing of mind-distracting sweet Sleep lull
bed-fleeing Chalcomede, since she had a longing for death,
fearing maddened Morrheus, lest, dragging her,
the hot man should yoke her in forced unions
while Bacchus was not present; and by the Erythraean sea
she turned her nightly step and cried to the deaf wave:
"Melis, I count you blessed; for you once, untaught in the Loves,
casting your body into the sea by a self-willed whirl,
escaped the bed of woman-mad Damnameneus;
I count your maiden-loving doom blessed; for the gadfly-mad
bridegroom against you the daughter of the sea, Aphrodite, armed,
and the sea guarded you, even though Paphian was your mother,
and you died in the surge still a maiden. But may even
Chalcomede, willing, the water of the sea hide,
while Morrheus longs for her, untried in marriage,
that I, a new Britomartis, may be called bed-fleeing,
whom once the sea received and gave back to the earth,
when she scorned the Cyprian loves of Minos.
The Earthshaker, love-mad, did not affright me,
as he did maiden-loving Asteria, whom in the sea,
wandering, he pursued back and forth, until
her, unsteady, riding companion to the shifting breeze,
Apollo rooted unshaken in the waves.
Receive me, receive me, sea, in your hospitable bosom;
take Chalcomede after Melis; take too
the younger Britomartis who refuses marriage,
that I may flee Morrheus and your Aphrodite;
pity Chalcomede, helper of maidens."
So speaking, she was shaken in mind beside the neighbouring sea;
and now, self-rolled, she would have sunk into the wave of the sea,
but Thetis helped, doing a favour to Dionysus,
and changing her form she stood beside Chalcomede,
and having the shape of a Bacchant uttered a consoling voice:
"Endure, Chalcomede, do not fear the bed of Morrheus;
you have me as an auspicious bird of your unbroken maidenhood,
a witness keeping watch over your unwedded bed.
I am Thetis, bed-fleeing, like you, I too,
like Chalcomede, a lover of maidenhood; and from heaven
Zeus my father pursued me and wished to drag me to marriage,
had not old Prometheus checked him in his longing,
prophesying that he would beget a son mightier than the son of Cronus,
lest one day the child of Thetis bear down on her father
and drive out the son of Cronus, as high-ruling Zeus drove out Cronus.
Be for me crafty and life-bringing; for self-slain,
if you die untaught in the unwedded unions,
the hostile Indian will destroy the whole rank of the Bassarids;
but beguile him, and you will save from death
your fugitive army, while Dionysus is being scourged,
feigning the empty desire of the Paphian; and if Morrheus
should drag you to bed, refusing marriage,
you do not need Cypris as helper; for of our
girdle you have a boundless guardian serpent for defence;
and our Dragon, taking it after the war of the Indians,
Dionysus will set in the star-shining circle,
an unceasing herald of your unbroken maidenhood,
near his own light-bearing Crown, when he accomplishes
the great starry sign of Cydonian Ariadne;
and rivalling the Arctic Dragon, your dragon
will flash for mortals, flashing together with the Serpent-holder.
Hereafter you will praise sea-born Thetis, when you behold
your fiery star flashing together with Selene.
Be of good courage for the marriage's sake; for your husband
will not loose the fast knot of your maidenhood,
no, by yourself and by Dionysus who touched my table,
no, by yourself and by your thyrsi, and by Aphrodite of the sea."
So she spoke, beguiling; and with a cloud she hid the girl,
lest the guards should behold her, or a watchman,
keeping a thievish track with crafty foot, a wayfarer of the night,
or a bold woman-mad goatherd, and the evening
maiden drag to the wayside unions.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
34. While the Bacchant women are slain on either side, in the thirty-fourth book
Deriades arms himself against them within his towers.
The mountain-roaming girl, with swift and whirling foot,
keeping her tread soundless, passed into the ridge of the forest;
nor did Thetis linger upon the shore, but she too
entered her father Nereus' weed-grown halls of the deep.
Now, straining his eye through the cloudless air,
Morrheus gazed his fill upon the starry circles of heaven,
and spoke a word, lashing his heart with cares:
“My mind drifts, shifting this way and that; not one counsel,
not one purpose holds me; manifold longings
have wheeled their ring about me, and I cannot finish a single one.
Shall I kill the lovely Chalcomede? But what shall I do
if, by desire after her death, she should kill me in turn?
Or shall I leave her living, unwounded, and openly
draw the maiden to a wedding? But in my heart
I dread Deriades, and I pity Cheirobie.
No, I will never kill the maiden; yet if I overcome her,
how can I live, when I shall look upon the maiden no more?
I waste away when I am parted from Chalcomede a single hour.”
Such things Morrheus spoke in vain, and went, that man of many devices,
seething with the pains of love-stricken care.
As he wandered, doubling back high above the bank,
having left the bed of the solitary, unforgotten nymph,
bold Hyssacus, lying awake, marked him; and crafty as he was,
he discerned the hidden goad of unfathomed loves,
that most faithful servant; and with a wily speech he questioned him,
pouring out this beguiling word from his throat:
“Why, leaving your bed and your sleeping bride,
do you wander here and there through the dark, undaunted Morrheus?
Has Deriades perhaps frightened you with a threat?
Is Cheirobie angry with you in a jealous heart,
thinking you love some spear-won Bacchant woman?
For when they see their husbands raving with love,
women are forever envious over a secret passion.
Or has bold Desire, the all-subduer, perhaps levelled against you
the bridal sparks of his sleepless quiver?
Do you long for one of the Bassarids? As I hear it,
three are the Graces, dancers of Orchomenus,
handmaids of Phoebus; but of dance-weaving Lyaeus
there are ranks of three hundred Graces, of whom one alone
shines forth surpassing all, even as the Moon herself
with brighter beams hides the gleam of the stars,
shooting her well-rounded radiance abroad.
And she is armed with twin shafts under one law,
striking with beauty and casting her blade of iron;
this is Pasithea of the glancing helm, whom the Bacchants
call Chalcomede; but I myself will name her
silver-footed Artemis, or Athena of the golden shield.”
So speaking, he fell silent; and drawing down the edge of his brow,
with shamefaced lips, Morrheus, unhappy in love, spoke:
“Truly Dionysus plunged beneath the sea's wave
in fear of Lycurgus, and from the depths of the gulf below
he armed the Nereids, and came from the brine bringing
to the war his sea-dwelling sister Aphrodite;
and instead of a bridal and sweet-scented robe
he gave her an iron corslet to wear, and instead of the girdle
he bestowed a bronze spear; and changing her former name
he called her Chalcomede, Aphrodite under arms.
She is a companion of the Bassarids; and against them both,
unknowing, I fight—against Cypris and against Dionysus.
Why do I lift my furious spear in vain? Yield, my spear-point.
If the Paphian overcame the hurler of the thunderbolt,
if she tames the sceptred lord of wars with her own spark,
if she set the fiery Phaethon ablaze with a greater fire
and drives the burning one—what could I do with iron?
Tell me some counsel to aid me against the Cyprus-born.
Shall I wound Eros? Whence shall I overtake the winged one?
Shall I raise a spear? He fights with fire. Shall I draw a sword?
He has a bow; and that bow is fire fastening on my heart.
Often have I been wounded in battle; but, worn down,
the healer saved me by his life-preserving craft,
twining over the wound the pain-killing flower of herbs.
Hyssacus, do not hide it: what varied drugs must I sprinkle
to heal within my heart the wound of the Loves?
Against my foes I am ever bold; but when I behold
Chalcomede present, my spear-point turns to a woman's.
I do not tremble before Dionysus; yet I cower before a woman,
because, sending a flash from her love-darting face,
she shoots me with her form, and I draw my bow no longer.
So then I have looked upon one of the Nereids; if it is right to say it,
either Thetis or Galatea fights at the side of Dionysus.”
He spoke, and treading slowly on the very tips of his feet,
lest he should wake his bride asleep in the night,
he came back to the chamber; and from the dark-bosomed nymph
he turned his eye far away, and longed that, appearing,
Chalcomede might shine and rise like the dawn.
Vexed beneath downcast Love, he fell upon his couch;
and the sleepless servant, with a longing for sweet sleep,
Hyssacus, slept again upon his ox-hide.
As Morrheus slumbered, a vision of a dream beguiled him,
darting up through the ivory gates that cheat the mind,
and spoke a word of lovely deceit:
“Receive Chalcomede, willing now, bridegroom Morrheus;
receive your bride to your bed after the wars.
By day you gladdened my sight when you looked on me;
by night lie beside the love-loving Chalcomede.
There is a grace even in a sleeping marriage; there is even
the lovely, sweet sting of dream-wrought weddings.
I longed to hold you in my arms—and near at hand is Dawn.”
So speaking, she flew away; and Morrheus leapt up from sleep,
and marked the light of Dawn beginning, who steals away wedlock;
and he fancied he held Chalcomede his desire; and at once in silence
he spoke, feeding the deceitful hope the Cyprian had given:
“Threefold, O Dawn, is the light you bring, for you carry
Chalcomede, and lead the radiance, and drive away the night.
Comforter of sleepless Morrheus, may you too appear,
Chalcomede, rosier than rose-crowned Dawn;
never do the meadow Hours bring such a rose.
Graceful maiden, your cheeks possess
a springtime meadow that time knows not how to wither;
your flowers bloom even when the Hours bring autumn;
your lilies shine even in winter; and there surrounds
your body the blushing anemone that never fades,
which the Graces tend and the winds do not destroy.
You have adorned your name, foremost in iron;
your name befits your manhood; and Chalcomede—
not without cause they call you so: for bronze-clad Ares begot you
upon the bed of Cypris, mother of the Loves, in his dancing.
All call you Chalcomede; but I alone will name you
Chrysomede, since you have the beauty of golden Aphrodite.
I am persuaded that from Sparta you draw your descent; for, as I think,
iron-mailed Aphrodite gave birth to Chalcomede.”
Such a word he uttered upon his wakeful bed.
But when, sending a gleam from her reddening face,
the far-shooting Dawn, herald of battle, sprang up,
Ares, rouser of armies, was arming the Indian race;
and then, harnessed, from their well-rolling beds
the Indians streamed together to the chariot of Deriades.
But the Bacchants, with unconquered Dionysus not present,
poured into the plain downcast; and in their hearts
no longer confident, they marched out to the din of battle,
but were shaken with fear; and no longer with man-breaking frenzy
did the bronze-clad women rave as before,
nor from the deep-voiced, bellowing throat
did they fling up foam, but in soundless silence
the ringing backs of the untanned ox-hide stayed still;
no torches blazed with the flame of the warlike pine,
belching deadly smoke; but beneath the goad
of the divine whip the warriors grew soft as women.
No Satyrs shouted; the wonted noise of the pipe
that rouses the fray did not boom; in unbacchic battle
the Sileni fought soberly, nor, smearing their faces
with vermilion of one hue with the dark gore,
did they redden a tawny mark in a false shape
for terror; nor were their foreheads daubed with white gypsum
and sprinkled as before; nor, having drunk with their lips
the warm, fresh-flowing blood of a desert-roaming lioness,
did the storm-swift Pans rave in the battle,
but for fear they became gentle; and timorous,
with sparing, noiseless hooves they struck the ground,
checking the dread, mountain-running leap of the dance.
But overweening Deriades rushed on to manly battle,
shaking the point of his horn like a helmet-crest;
and Morrheus, leaping upon the women's phalanx, raved;
for Chalcomede no longer stood as companion to the Bacchants,
so that he might revere her, and when the women charged,
reddening with blood, might check his point;
but then there joined the fray among the foremost fighters
a lovely young maiden, a far-famed bowing Amazon,
wearing light raiment and a flashing tunic
upon the plain; for wise Thetis had told her so, to save
the whole toiling host while Dionysus was shaken from his place.
There, cleaving through the image of a face like the Graces',
Morrheus took alive eleven helpless Bassarids,
whom after Chalcomede he had chosen; and of the Maenads
he bound the backstrained hands with a bond not to be loosed,
and dragging the loose-haired rank under the yoke of slavery
he gave them as captive handmaids to his father-in-law Deriades,
a second bride-gift for his wife, for whose bed's sake
he had waged the bride-winning war beside high-crested Taurus,
when he bound with the marriage-bond the young royal maiden
of Deriades, Cheirobie of his own age;
for the chief of the Indians had taken no wedding gift
for his daughter, no lovely gold, no marble stone of the sea
with its sheen, but herds of cattle and flocks of sheep
Deriades refused, and to his battle-rousing warriors
he joined his daughters in marriages that took no gifts,
having Morrheus for son-in-law and nine-cubit Orontes;
and to two foremost fighters he wedded his own offspring,
Cheirobie to Morrheus and Protonoe to Orontes;
for Morrheus was not like men of earth,
but with the high-necked shape of Giant limbs
he imitated the ancestral might of the earthborn Indians,
having the native stock of towering Typhon,
when beside the neighbouring rock of the fire-bred Arimoi
he displayed his kindred valour to the witness Cydnus,
bringing the bride-gifts of the marriage, the sweat of the Cilician contests,
a possessionless bridegroom, who won his bride by valour.
So once, to the iron that wooed for Morrheus' marriage,
Assyria bent the knee, and into the yoke of Deriades
Cilician Taurus bowed his rocky neck,
and bold Cydnus sank down; whence in the land of the Cilicians
Morrheus is still called Sandes, the Heracles.
And these things were of old; but in the later battle
Morrheus took the raving women captive with his unsparing spear;
and exulting, he poured out an unbridled cry:
“To you, sceptred lord, the treasures of your daughter,
the Bacchants, I bring first, and afterwards I will deliver Bacchus.”
As Morrheus spoke so, the lord of the Indians answered:
“Having Cheirobie without bride-gift, helmet-glancing Morrheus,
you gave me worthy gifts of a shield-bearing wedding,
enslaving the cities of the Cilicians with high-manhood victory.
Now once more you grant me new gifts; and if you will,
plunder still other Bassarids, and fill the whole house
of Cheirobie with handmaids; but for Bacchus
I have no need of Morrheus: with chains unbreakable I will bind him,
and drag Dionysus into the bondage of the slave's yoke.
Only guard yourself, for me, from desire of a spear-won bed,
lest I see you like the woman-mad Indians;
do not gaze at the eyes and silver neck of a Bacchant,
lest in your longing you wrong my jealous daughter.
But when I have destroyed the whole army of Bromius,
I will go to the Maeonian land, whence I will draw off
the boundless wealth of the Lydians, all that Pactolus swells;
I will come to vine-rich Phrygia, where Rhea
is the nurse of Bromius, and I will lay waste the neighbouring
rich plain of silver Alybe, that I may carry off
the gleaming, snow-white backs of the wealth-gushing mines;
and I will sack the land they call seven-gated Thebes,
and burn the fiery house of Semele, where the bridal chambers
still bear the warm remnants of a wedding withered away.”
So spoke the lawless king; and from his son-in-law of Enyo
Deriades received the whole rank of handmaids,
the gifts of battle, and to Phlogius and Agraeus he gave the Bacchants
dragged by the hair; and in a bond all of one weaving
unbreakable thongs were bound about their hands.
These Phlogius led, the heralds of the king's victory,
and paraded them bound through the city. And high uplifted,
some, beside the gateway of the well-carved hall,
were strangled, their entwined necks crushed in a deadly bond;
to others he gave a warm doom of fiery destruction;
and some were entombed in earth-dug streams
in the hollows of a well, where from the depths of the gulf
with hand passing to hand the forced water is drawn up;
and one, within the wet, deepening cavity,
half-seen, unmoved, spoke with an answering voice:
“I have heard that to the Indians earth and water are a god;
nor is this ever said in vain: for both
have armed against me of one mind, and I am set midway
between death by earth and destruction by water,
and I hold a twin-yoked doom close: for a muddy,
strange bond holds me, and I lift my foot no longer,
but, having rooted my fixed knees in the wet clay,
I stand unshaken, ready for the Fates;
a river too pursued me, yet I did not tremble at the streaming water.
Would that this too were a sounding flood, that here also
I might oar my hands and cleave the dark water.”
She spoke; and at her opening throat the down-flowing streams
receiving little by little, she died an unburied death.
But Morrheus, fettered by the sweet goad of Chalcomede,
drove the whole ironless host of the Maenads
into the beetling city, pricking them from behind with his spear.
As when a shepherd, into the recesses of a spacious fold,
driving into one the scattered ranks of mingled sheep,
guides the wool-fleeced flocks with his crook
all together, and many herdsmen marched along with him,
hemming the sheep in with a shared sweep of the arm,
headlong, in close order, fitted close, lest ever from the flock
as it is penned a stray swarm should wander off the path;
so he, penning the female throng within the gateway,
into the steep-built city storm-footed Morrheus drove
the whole Bacchic rank, torn away from the war.
And toiling, he kept up a vain stratagem, so that from the battle
leaving the fair-women plunder, the migrant prey,
he might drag Chalcomede under the yoke of servitude,
a fellow with the other women, that for him forever
she might be a handmaid by day and a bedmate by night,
and might perform in turn the works of two goddesses,
the secret works of Cypris and the open loom of Athena. . . .
But Morrheus, the spearman, was not negligent; for to Deriades,
fighting at close quarters, he entrusted the fugitive women's war,
and against the Bacchic phalanx he rushed in manly battle,
that he might hem in the men as well; and in the fray
they were driven to flight. But the stormy maiden
stood, arrayed before the city, near the tower,
a maiden unveiled; and of the love-maddened women
with feigned gestures the maiden imitated the manner,
rolling her eyes; and outside her wonted girdle
the white tunic reddened against her blushing breast;
and Morrheus, beholding, was delighted, and through the thin robe
discerned the swelling curve of her breast.
And a well-wrought stone, like the rounded discus,
the maiden snatched up, a monstrous load for a wagon,
and hurled it at well-helmed Morrheus with knowing skill;
and the stone, borne from the air with a sharp whirr,
struck the rim of his shield, where the gold-wrought image
bore the counterfeit form of Cheirobie in a lying shape,
and shore off the fashioned head, and as it was struck,
with its marble edge scoring the carved face
it ground away the rounded image of the imitated form;
and Morrheus, blessing his shield, leapt up again and again,
and laughing in his heart he uttered a secret voice:
“Fearless Chalcomede, young rosy-fingered Persuasion,
delicate ornament of Cypris and of well-corsleted Athena,
Bacchic dawn and never-setting Moon,
you have scraped off the painted form of my wife; would that of the real
Cheirobie herself you had reaped the neck, the true bride.”
So speaking, he pursued before the city the unwedded maiden,
keeping a threatening tongue, not arming his hand,
hurling a word, not piercing the maiden with his spear,
lifting in a gentle hand a spear that spared her;
and a deceitful Echo rang of his grim shout,
as of a chief truly wrathful yet kindly; for both at once
he kept a laughing mind, and showed anger on his face.
Gently whirling it, he sent the wavering point
at the useless target, on purpose; and she, fleeing,
swift-kneed, ran along, a companion to the airy breezes;
and as she stretched out with the windy rush of her knee,
the breezes fanned up her clustering locks,
baring a neck that vied with the Moon;
and with sparing feet, on purpose, Morrheus ran,
now at the bare tread of her foot, free of well-stitched sandals,
gazing at her rosy ankles, now marking
the back-streaming, coiling tresses of the wandering hair,
he pursued Chalcomede; and he cried with a sweet word,
pouring a gentle, calm speech from his throat:
“Wait for me, Chalcomede, the warrior who longs for you.
Your splendour saves you, not your running; not so much do spears
know how to strike a man, as the sparks of the Loves.
I have not become your foe, do not fear; for as I fought,
your beauty conquered my brazen spear-point.
You need no spear, no shield; for the ray of your face
is like a sword to you, like a furious spear,
and far more than the ash-spear your cheeks prevail in battle.
The dread strength of my hand is loosed; for it is no shame,
if I hold my furious spear conquered, since even
savage Ares himself grows soft as a woman when Cypris stands by.
Receive me as a fellow with your Satyrs; for in wars
the Indians will be the bravest, so long as I still arm my hand.
But if you will, like a servant I will toil for Dionysus;
if you will, slay me, at the neck or at the flank;
I care not for death, pierced by your spear;
only mourn for me when I have fallen; and as you weep,
the tears of Chalcomede will bring me back even from Hades.
Maiden, why do you tremble, because I lift a gentle spear?
Looking on your coiling locks above your shoulders
uncovered, I have laid aside the helmet from my hair;
gazing at the fawnskin, I loathe to wear the corslet.”
As he spoke, the woman passed him by and mingled with the Bacchants,
and, turned aside from the path of murderous Morrheus,
fought boldly and contended in manly battle.
And then, leaving the eddy of the ill-sounding din,
the Bacchic throng took breath, while Morrheus drew back.
And the phalanx of the Bassarids before the city, striking with his sword,
Deriades pursued, until he drove them near the towers,
penning the whole rank within the opened gate
of the high-crested wall; and driven by the iron,
torn from their wonted woodland, they came within the city;
and the unsteady ranks, along the unaccustomed circuits of the road,
marched here and there, scattered apart, to the wing of Eurus,
to the ridge of Zephyrus by the western quarter of the earth,
some wandering by the border of Notus, some of Boreas
the Bassarids were driven; and the man-hearted constraint
the Maenads exchanged, and again became women,
and renounced battle, and of the distaff-loving craft
and of the wool-baskets they remembered, and longed once more
to tend the spinning-thread of Athena and no longer the thyrsus of Lyaeus.
And destroying the snow-white rank, the dark-skinned man
kept up the inmost rout of the city-guarding battle.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
35. In the thirty-fifth book look for the Love that is Morrheus' foe, and the slaughter of the Bassarids, and the warfare of women.
Deriades, immense, fought in the raving battle,
and the lord of the Indians rushed upon the servants of Bromius,
now hurling with his long spear, now hewing
with his hilted sword, and with rough-edged darts
he was carried on shooting, and with sharper arrows.
So the women were driven in rout through the city, within the towers,
by the spear of Deriades; and in the many-tongued din
the clash of both was heard; and with reddening gore
the well-paved streets of the city were stained crimson
as the women were slain with a clamour throughout the town.
Unbending, the old men upon the high-crested towers
watched the battle; and over the rooftops the women too
gazed upon the whole thyrsus-bearing rank;
and one, leaning over the hall against her nurse,
a maiden of trailing robe, beheld the women's war,
and, heavy with tears, wept over a slain girl of her own age.
Nor did any man seize and force a lovely bride,
because the king had commanded his woman-mad peoples
to shun the hostile beds of spear-won weddings,
lest, heeding the Paphian, they should be careless of war.
And one, leaping over the ground in the dust,
a maiden, was stripped bare; and as her tunic was dragged off
she was armed with splendour, and the warrior who longed for her
she wounded, wounded herself—her form became her dart,
and dying she conquered; and against her foe her bare
thighs were armed, archers of the Loves.
And now, having a breathless corpse for his desire, like Achilles,
marking another Penthesilea upon the ground,
he would have kissed the cold lips of the dust-covered bride,
had he not dreaded the weight of Deriades' threat.
And he gazed at the flesh of the bare, refusing girl,
and marked her white ankles and the folds of her uncovered thighs,
and touched her limbs, and again and again laid hold of her breast,
swelling and rosy, still like an apple;
he longed too to mingle in love; and, worn out at last,
he belched up such a lovely, senseless cry:
“Rose-armed maiden, your luckless-loving slayer
you have wounded, though wounded; dead, you subdue the living,
and you too shoot your destroyer with your eyes.
My spear was conquered by your beauty; the flashings
of your face rout me as much as the points of javelins;
you have a breast like a bow, since more than arrows
your breasts prevail, archers of the Loves.
Strange and unbelievable is the desire I hold, that I pursue
the dead love of a girl, a wedding that has perished;
a breathless sting holds me, the breathing one; if it is right to say it,
let these lips become voiced and breathing again,
that I may hear, maiden, a word from your sweet mouth. . . .”
Crying such a word, the maiden as she rolled upon the ground,
whom you slew, whom you despoiled, reckless one, he left behind;
“Whom your bronze cut down, do not touch my tunic;
why do you grip the flank you wounded? Cease, wretch,
from fingering my wound, which you gave me. Let the spear go to ruin,
let the boldness of my hand go to ruin, for, leaving
the Sileni bristling beneath their grey hair
and the whole misshapen race of the Satyrs, instead of old men,
instead of shaggy-breasted creatures, it subdued a tender woman.”
“But, fingering the wound of your love-stricken flesh,
what plant, passing along the ridge of a flowering forest,
shall I call to your aid, a helper for your wound,
aged life-giving Cheiron? Or whence shall I find
drugs, the mysteries of the toil-loosing art of Paeon?
I would I had what they call the Centaur's herb,
that, twining a pain-killing flower over your limbs,
I might save you living from Hades whence none return.
What magic hymn have I, or starry song,
that I may pour out a strain in a god-summoning, pleasing voice
and lull the blood of your wounded flank?
I would I had near here the life-bringing spring,
that, casting the pain-killing water upon your limbs,
I might soothe your lovely wound, that even
your very soul I might bring back to you, recovered.
Glaucus, who roll the whirling round of countless years,
if it is permitted, leaving the recess of the barren sea,
show me the life-preserving plant, show me that one
of which once you tasted with your lips, and you draw
an immortal life, wheeling in the course of ever-flowing time.”
So speaking, he passed by, hiding the dead love in his heart.
And the bride leapt up, avenger of her slain husband,
Protonoe, mourning still her dead Orontes;
and she crossed the women's phalanx; one might have thought her
another man-opposing Atalanta of the Red Sea.
And Cheirobie, taking up the shield and spear of Morrheus,
rushed upon the Bassarids, and was like Gorge,
who once, when well-towered Calydon was shaken,
brandishing the ox-hide shield of her brother Toxeus,
fought, woman though she was, against angry Meleager.
And Orsiboe, appearing with her battle-rousing husband,
imitated the courage of warlike Deianira,
when by the inhospitable rock of Parnassus
she armed against the Dryopes and became a woman Amazon.
Many were hemmed in within the wide-spaced halls,
and boundless was the groaning of the battle beneath the roofs;
and another plunged into the fighting along the streets,
a maiden rousing the fray; and over the rooftops still others,
the women, armed themselves with missiles of stone;
and the inmost phalanxes thundered the war.
While Ares roared throughout the battle-rousing city,
hewing down the Lydian, mountain-running tribes of the Bassarids,
meanwhile Chalcomede stood alone before the wall,
having turned back her homeward course from the battle,
awaiting frenzy-maddened Morrheus, if from anywhere he should come;
and then, straining his much-coiling, love-maddened eye,
when he marked the maiden, wind-footed Morrheus came,
flinging his swift knees into a lovely race.
And of her, as she fled, the wind lifted her robe;
and he was charmed still more by the unclad beauty of her form,
gazing at the white, unfilleted maiden running before him.
But she beguiled him, and spoke with a bashful voice,
cowering before Morrheus' swifter course:
“If you truly seek my bed, bridegroom Morrheus,
lay aside your iron corslet, even as Ares dances
to a wedding in soft raiment when he mingles with Cypris,
clad in snow-white garb, like Apollo,
so that Desire and Cypris may yoke under one bond
us both, mounting the marriage bed,
Morrheus to furious Love, and Chalcomede to Aphrodite.
I will not receive a brazen husband upon my bed,
crimson with blood and grimed with dust;
but cleanse your body in the stream, that you may appear
like Phaethon bathed in the outpourings of Ocean;
cast away your warlike shield, cast away your point,
lest your death-bringing spear should ever strike me;
lay aside for me the dread helmet of your hair,
for the crest unnerves me when your helmet is shaken;
let me not see the false shape of your iron face;
what desire gladdens me when your form is hidden?
No longer will I set foot in Maeonia; nor in the bridal chamber
will I receive, if you wish it, Bacchus as bedmate after Morrheus;
I too will be an Indian woman, my friend; and instead of the Lydian,
I will honour with offerings the Aphrodite of the Red Sea,
the secret bedmate of Morrheus; and in the battles
let an Indian man have me, fighting at the side of Aphrodite;
for sending equal shafts, and double ones, even into me,
Desire has joined one anguish upon us both,
into the heart for Morrheus and into the mind for Chalcomede.
I have toiled, hiding my desire for you; for a husband
a modest maiden does not challenge to Aphrodite.”
So speaking, the woman won over the luckless-loving warrior
with her falsehood; and laughing, unhappy-in-love Morrheus said:
“It is no shame that Morrheus, the well-helmed warrior,
should hold a brazen spear in the bridal chamber of Chalcomede,
that I may embrace you, rightly named, lifting my bronze;
yet I refuse the bloody spear, nor do I
touch the shield; but as you wish, washed, I dance to you
with bloodless hands, and I will be another kind of bedmate,
a naked Ares after the fray, holding naked Aphrodite.
I refuse the daughter of Deriades; I myself will drive
my jealous bride unwilling from the halls;
no longer will I arm against the Bassarids, if you bid me,
but I will fight against my own dear townsmen; I will destroy the Indian,
holding the wine-dark thyrsus, not lifting the brazen spear;
I will cast away all my arms and shake the delicate flowers,
fighting at the side of your king Dionysus.”
So speaking, Morrheus shook the ash-spear from his hand,
and unfastened the helmet from his sweating head,
and let drop the baldric of his dripping ox-hide,
bathed with the toil-drops of his wonted shoulder;
he loosed the brazen tunic too from his breast,
the bloody corslet. And the arms, lying on the ground,
of longing Morrheus, Cypris showed to Ares,
conquered by the unarmoured form of Chalcomede;
and she spoke a word, and goaded her own bedmate:
“Ares, you are despoiled; Morrheus has renounced wars,
wearing no corslet and no sword; but a lovely woman,
longing for her, he has shaken the arms from his hands.
You too, refuse your furious spear, and you too in the sea
wash yourself, stripped of your shields; for unwarlike
Cypris excels Ares more, and has no need
of a shield, nor ever lacks a spear; for both at once
my beauty was my spear, and my form became my sword,
and the rays of my eyes are arrows to me;
a breast shoots farther than a spear; for lovely Morrheus
became a bridegroom of the bower instead of bold with the spear.
Do not set foot in Sparta, where the warlike citizens
have a brazen image of Aphrodite under arms,
lest she, wielding a spear, should strike you with her iron.
You do not wield the spear so much as the brows do; not so much do spears
wound men, as glances strike;
look upon your servants, the underlings of the Loves,
and bow your bold neck to unconquered Cytherea.
Ares, you are conquered, since, letting go the brazen spear,
Morrheus has slipped on the bridal fawnskin of Chalcomede.”
So spoke laughter-loving Aphrodite, mocking the battles,
taunting Ares, marshal of weddings; and beside the sea,
leaving his tunic untended upon the shore,
warmed by sweet cares, Morrheus bathed,
being naked; and he cleansed his body in the cold sea,
holding the warm little dart of the Paphian; and in the streams
he prayed to the Aphrodite of the Red Sea, the Indian one,
hearing that Cypris is offspring of the sea;
and having washed, he came up dark again; he kept the form
that nature had brought forth, and the brine did not change
the man's body, nor altered his colour, ruddy though it was.
And on an empty hope he washed his flesh; for snow-white,
lovely, he yearned to appear to the unwedded girl;
and he adorned his body with a linen, snow-white robe,
such as warriors ever wear beneath the corslet.
And, standing speechless upon the shore, she kept silence,
crafty Chalcomede; and turning aside the girl
drew her chaste glances from the cloakless Morrheus,
ashamed at the man's uncovered body; for to look upon him
the maiden, being a woman, shrank, the bathed man.
But when she saw a lonely place, fit for a bed,
stretching a bold hand to the bashful bride,
of the chaste girl's untouched garment he laid hold;
and now, grasping the girdled maiden in a strong embrace,
with the bridal spark he would have forced the raving girl;
but a serpent leapt up from her undefiled bosom,
a helper of the unwedded, unmarried maiden, and about her girdle
the ample creature coiled, with a guarding sweep around her waist;
and as it hissed sharply from its never-silent throats
the rocks bellowed; and Morrheus quivered with fear,
hearing the neck-borne bellow of the false trumpet,
gazing at the champion of the unwedded maidenhood;
and the all-coiling guardian terrified the warrior,
winding its crook-circling tail about the man's neck,
its spear a greedy mouth; and many were shot at him,
the viperous arrows hurling their venom;
some, darting from her unfilleted hair,
some from her serpent-tressed waist, some from her bosom,
hissing war, the warriors raved.
While Morrheus stood before the high-crested city,
dragging crafty Chalcomede to a fruitless marriage,
meanwhile the well-armed warfare of the Bassarid host
escaped the spear of unwearied Deriades.
For, leaping down from Olympus, swift-winged Hermes,
bearing the counterfeit likeness of Bromius' face,
summoned the whole Bacchic rank with a mystic voice;
and when the women heard the divine, Euian cry,
they came to one place; and gathering from the crossroads,
the whole nation of the Maenads, into the winding circles of the road
the swift-sandalled god led them, until he drew near the towers;
and over the guards in their ranks, with their sleepless eyes,
he poured sweet sleep with his all-charming wand,
furtive Hermes, the captain of the night; and suddenly
for the Indians there was darkness, but for the unseen Bacchants
there was an unlooked-for light; and of the noiseless women
wingless Hermes led the secret way through the city;
and with a divine hand the heavy bolt of the towering
gates he opened, and there was a sun for the Bacchants.
And when light-bringing Hermes drove the night by day,
overweening Deriades, with his threat unfulfilled,
sought the city-leaving, road-faring swarm of the Bassarids.
As when one in the night, amid deep-wealthy dreams,
delights in fruitless hopes, lifting
with rich hands the heaped wealth of a fleeting moment,
feeding the deceitful hope of sleep-born treasures;
but when, at the appearing of rosy dawn,
the vision of the dream of riches, dissolved, slips away,
with empty hands he wakes, lifting nothing,
having flung away the shadowy delight of mind-stealing dreams;
so then Deriades, while darkness held the streets,
delighted, thinking he held a self-yielded prey
of the Bassarids penned within the closed gates,
holding a false, profitless, shadowy victory;
but when the light shone, and he beheld the Bacchants no longer,
like a dream all ran away, and he cried with a mournful voice.
As if at Zeus and Phaethon he raged, and at Dionysus,
seeking the fugitive Maenads. And about the towers
the Bassarids cried out, unfilleted, with their Euian voice.
Deriades pursued a second time, and Zeus awoke
on the peaks of Caucasus, casting off the wing of Sleep;
and learning the beguiling guile of malign Hera,
he marked the Sileni in flight, he saw the Bacchants
hastening in herds from the crossroads, from the towers,
and Deriades shearing the Satyrs and reaping the women,
he marked behind them, the chief of the Indians,
and his son lying upon the ground; and about him the nymphs
were near in a circle; and he in the whirl of dust
lay heavy-headed, drawing a feeble gasp,
flinging up snow-white foam, witness of his frenzy.
And he convicted the ill-wrought guile of envious Hera,
and reproached his crafty consort with a goading word;
and now into the misty pit he would have locked
the sleep of dark Iapetus, his housemate,
had not Night entreated, the subduer of gods and men.
And scarcely lulling his deadly wrath, he cried to Hera:
“You have not yet had your fill of my Semele, hard-fighting Hera,
but are you still, perhaps, angry even with the dead? Did not
the bridal flame itself soothe your endless wrath,
the flame that scattered the bed of Zeus-stricken Thyone?
How long will you press upon Indian-slaying Dionysus?
Beware your former anvils again; those still,
those helpers are still at hand for me, with which I bound
and fettered your feet; and you, unstable above the earth,
held aloft in air and clouds an inescapable constraint;
and bold Ares saw you in the clouds, entangled high above earth,
bound, and he did not help his mother;
fiery Hephaestus did not avail; for he cannot
endure a single spark of the smouldering thunderbolt.
I will bind your hands again with the wonted golden chain;
and Ares I will fetter with unbreakable bonds
upon a self-rolling wheel, running its round, such as the wanderer
Tantalus, the air-roaming, or Ixion the exile;
and I will scourge him all over with wounds that never heal,
until my son shall conquer the sons of the Indians.
But you will do a favour to your Cronion, if you drive away
the panic-stricken frenzy of the scourged Dionysus,
and do not leave your husband angry, but, coming
to the well-pastured woodland of the unapproachable Indian crag,
give Bacchus the breast, after my mother Rhea,
that with his now more perfect lips he may draw
your holy drop, the forerunner of Olympus,
and make heaven passable for earth-treading Dionysus;
and anointing the body of Lyaeus with your milk,
quench the foul defilements of the mind-robbing disease.
And I will fit out for you a worthy gift; for in your
honour I will set in Olympus a circle like the dew,
named after Hera's milk, that I may glorify
the dear-to-all moisture of your evil-averting breast;
only guard yourself against the child-loving threat of Zeus,
and do not fit out yet another guile against Dionysus.”
So speaking, he sent the relenting consort Hera
by necessity to ward off the affliction of the Bacchant,
gracious, well-met, to terrified Dionysus,
that with milk-dews she might anoint
the body of Bromius with her hand from her god-nourishing breasts.
And Hera did not neglect it; with the pain-healing teat,
with its divine drop, anointing the body of Lyaeus,
she shook off the savage defilements of the demonic frenzy;
and she kept a twofold envy, with a face that hid it,
beholding the manhood and the splendour of Dionysus,
and with envious hands she touched the maddened Bacchus;
and drawing up her tunic at her lips
she bared her breast full of ambrosia,
squeezing it, gushing a flood from her jealous teat;
and she revived him; and of long-tressed Lyaeus
with her long eyes she measured all that bloom,
whether ever an earthly womb had borne so great a form,
whether so great was spear-wielding Ares, or so great Hermes,
whether Phaethon was such, or sweet-voiced Apollo;
and she yearned to have him in heaven as the bridegroom of Hebe,
had not high-ruling Zeus, after a time, granted her
fated Heracles, who wrought twelve labours, as bedmate.
She, having warded off the maddening affliction of Bacchus,
high-shining, mounted a second time to the choir of the stars,
lest she should look upon the ironless army of Dionysus
fighting with fennel-rod and clustering vine,
and the champions slain by the little, man-breaking thyrsus.
Nor did the son of Zeus neglect the fight, but, having armed
his warriors, turned back and cried an army-rousing voice,
twirling in his Giant-slaying hand the flesh-cutting ivy:
“Fight boldly a second time; for in the wars
Zeus again stands forth as our champion, gracious to his son
Bacchus, and from heaven, as the shield of Dionysus,
the choir of the immortals has come, and Hera rages no more.
Who will fight against the lightning of the son of Cronus? Or when do cowardly
foes await the arming of the thunderbolt?
I will appear the equal of my father; for in the wars
my Cronion conquered the earthborn Titans,
and I too will conquer the earth-born race of the Indians.
Today you will behold, after the cluster-bearing victory,
Deriades a suppliant, slow to be persuaded, and the choir of the Indians
bowing the neck to a serene Dionysus,
and the river bearing the drunken-staggering Euian water;
and you will see our foes beside the mixing-bowl of Lyaeus
drinking yellow water from the wine-flowing river,
and the bold Indian king, held fast by the wine-dark ivy,
entangled in leaves and clustering vine,
bearing bonds like those which, after the surges of frenzy,
the god-fearing Nysian Nymphs still proclaim,
witnesses of our valour, when with the noose of ivy
my bold-working harvest, binding the god-fighting man
with a throttling bond, put Arabia to flight,
Lycurgus forced down with a knot of clusters.
But after so great a wheeling round of battle has rolled by,
despoil the plunder of the foe and the treasures of the sea,
the gleaming pebbles, and to my mother Rhea
remove the women dragged by the hair;
and avenge the fallen champions, over whose doom
I am worn with sharp cares; and in my heart
I both rage and grieve at once, because I behold
Deriades living and Opheltes unburied,
reproaching, after his doom, the idle hand of Lyaeus;
no longer does Codone arm herself, no longer does poor
Alcimacheia, the spearwoman, fight; but even
Aebialus himself was slain, and still I hold back the thyrsus.
I am ashamed before Arestor after the fray, lest he should hear
that, dying, the dead Opheltes found no helper;
I cannot pass through the city of Corybantic Crete,
lest his father Agelaus should bewail his perished child,
hearing the unavenged slaughter of Antheus who was slain;
I am ashamed to appear before Minos; for in his tent
Asterius lies stricken, whom more than the others
I will rescue; for he draws his race from Europa; but, saving him
sound and homeward, I will bring back to his father
my kinsman after the fray, that Cadmus may not hear
that Asterius lacked Dionysus, who left the battle.
But fight again, and in this one thing I will help you all,
by slaying that one single destroyer of so many.”

title: Dionysiaca
text:
36. In the thirty-sixth, after the defilements of frenzy, Bacchus arms against Deriades, changing his shape.
So speaking, he heartened his rejoicing leaders;
and Deriades on the other side armed his warriors.
And to either phalanx the gods who dwell on Olympus,
divided, came as pilots of the war,
some the helpers of Deriades, some of Lyaeus.
Zeus, lord of the blessed, high-throned above Cerne,
held the scales of war apart; and from heaven
the watery dark-haired one challenged the fiery sun,
Ares challenged the grey-eyed goddess, Hephaestus Hydaspes;
and against Hera stood Artemis of the mountains;
and to the war came well-rodded Hermes against Leto's son.
And the twin-clashing echo of the holy battle roared
for both bands of the blessed; and as they rushed into the fray
Ares, seven roods broad, fought with Tritogeneia,
and flung his furious spear; and at the unwounded goddess
he struck the middle of her aegis, and from her unscathed head
he drove the serpent harvest of her Gorgon hair,
wounding the shaggy shield of Pallas; and the sharp
point of the unbending spear, sent with a whirr,
scored the fashioned tress of the counterfeit Medusa.
And the war-rousing maiden, charging in her turn,
motherless Pallas, lifted against Ares her kindred spear,
that one which, wearing it at her birth with bronze of her own age,
she leapt forth from her father's child-completing head.
And the towering Ares, struck, bent his knee to the ground;
but Athena, setting him up again, whirled him round
and gave him unwounded after the fray to her dear mother Hera.
Against Hera contended, as the fellow-fighter of mountain-roaming
Dionysus, mountain Artemis, and her straight-stretched
bow she bent; and in the rivalrous din
Hera, taking a cloud of Zeus packed about her shoulders,
held it like an unbreakable shield; and Artemis, shaft after shaft,
sending through the airy circle the wandering arrow
at the useless target, emptied her quiver,
and packed the whole unbreaking cloud with arrows;
and it was like the air-roaming form of cranes
flying in a ring, in a wheeling round one after another;
and the arrows were fixed in the shadowy cloud;
and the uncut veil kept the wounds bloodless.
And Hera lifted a hard, wind-borne missile,
and whirling in her hand the packed mass of hail
she battered Artemis with the ravine-rough bolt;
and the marble point shattered the curved circles of the bow;
nor did the wife of Zeus break off the fight; but Artemis'
breast she struck full in the midmost; and she, struck
with the icy spear, poured her quiver to the ground.
And mocking her, the bride of Zeus spoke:
“Artemis, strike beasts; why do you match yourself with your betters?
Climb the crags; what is battle to you? Wearing your worthless
hunting-boots, leave the greaves to Athena;
and shake your guileful nets; for beast-slaying
dogs hunt for you, not winged arrows;
you do not wield the lion-slaying shaft; for of your feeble
toils the sweat is but cowardly hares;
care for your deer and your fair-horned car,
care for your deer; why should you honour the son of Zeus,
the driver of leopards and charioteer of lions?
But if you wish, keep the bow, since Eros bends the bow;
maiden who flee the bed, helper of birth-pangs, the ferryman of the Loves,
the girdle you ought to have, the helper of childbed,
with the Paphian, with Eros; for you rule over birth.
But, pilot of the race that completes generation,
go to the bridal chamber of child-bearing women,
and shooting women with the arrows of childbed
be like a lion beside the bride in labour,
a helper of birth-pangs instead of a lover of war. But of your own
chastity cease to boast for the sake of a chaste girdle,
since, taking the likeness of your limbs, high-ruling Zeus
weds unwedded maidens; still that
image of yours the Arcadian woods proclaim as a bed-thief,
the wedding-maker of unwedded Callisto, and your
witness, the sentient bear, the hills still bewail,
blaming the false, love-mad shape of the Archeress,
when a female bedmate entered a woman's bed.
But, casting away your useless quiver,
leave the fight to your better, Hera; and if you wish,
as a birth-goddess make war on marriage-completing Cytherea.”
She spoke, and Hera passed by the worn-out Artemis.
Her, drunk with fear, carrying her from the tumult,
Phoebus embraced with both his downcast arms,
and leading her, set her within a desert thicket;
and returning, unapproached, he joined the divine battle.
And the fiery champion stood against the champion of the deep,
Phoebus, in conflict with the lord of Poseidon; and on his string
he set an arrow, and lifted a brand of Delphic pine
in either hand, ambidextrous, that he might arm
radiance against the wavy sweep and arrows against the trident.
And the smouldering point and the watery arrows
fell upon one another; and as Phoebus armed,
the ancestral Ether of Ares thundered its strain,
a thundering peal; and the stormy trumpet,
the echo of the sea, rang upon the ears of Phoebus;
and broad-bearded Triton boomed on his wonted conch,
half-man, unfinished, from the loins a green-grey fish;
and the Nereids shouted; and rising above the sea,
as the trident was shaken, Arab Nereus bellowed.
And hearing the louder din of the heavenly phalanx,
the nether Zeus cried out, lest the Earth-shaker, smiting
the earth, lashed by the floods with an earth-shaking quake,
should heave the harmony of the cosmos out of place with his trident,
lest ever, moving the foundation of the nether pits,
he should make visible the seat of the unseen earth,
lest he should rend every vein of the channels of the deep,
pouring migrant water into the Tartarean recess,
flooding the nether, mouldering gateway.
So great a din, then, arose as the gods met in strife,
and the nether trumpets thundered; and both
gentle Hermes, lightly wielding his wand, reined back;
and to the three immortals he joined one voice:
“Brother and son of Zeus, you, far-famed archer, leave to the storms
your brand and bow, and you the point of your trident,
lest the Titans laugh at the battle of the blessed,
lest, after the Cronian war that threatened Olympus,
Ares be a second time a kinsman-foe to the immortals,
lest I see another fight after the rout of Iapetus,
and lest, after Zagreus and over latter-born Bacchus,
Zeus in his anger burn the whole earth with his fire
and flood the rim of the everlasting cosmos a second time,
raining waters on the molten ether; nor let me see
the chariot of the Moon drenched in airy seas;
let not Phaethon hold again a cold fiery gleam.
But yield to the elder pilot of the sea,
granting a grace to your father's brother, since the Earth-shaker,
lord of the sea, honours your sea-girt Delos;
let not the love of the palm and the memory of the olive leave you.
Who again, Earth-shaker, is a Cecrops here to judge,
who again, another Inachus, has cried up his city to Hera,
that you arm against Apollo too, as against Athena,
and hold another fight after your former quarrel with Hera?
And you too, horned father of great Deriades,
beware the flame of Hephaestus, after the torch of Bacchus,
lest he burn you up with his fire-pointed thunderbolt.”
So speaking, he checked the kindred war of the gods.
And then the frenzied Deriades, heavy in wrath, took up again
the renewed battle, when he saw the Bacchants unharmed;
and watching the war of restored Dionysus,
he goaded his fugitive leaders to the fray;
and a threat common to foot and horse,
barbarous, he thundered from his deep-voiced throat:
“Today either I will drag Dionysus by the hair,
or the Bacchic war will blot out the race of the Indians.
Set against the Satyrs a constraint
to ward them off; and let Deriades arm against Dionysus.
Burn the leaves of the vine and the manifold instruments of Bacchus,
and set the tents ablaze; and the Maenads
bring as slave-women to lordly Deriades;
and with fire wither the hostile thyrsi; and of the ox-horned
Sileni and the manifold heads of the Satyrs,
reaping the harvest with the threshing iron,
wreathe all the halls with the bull-horned heads.
Let not Phaethon yoke his fire-bright horses for the setting
before I bring the Satyrs and Bacchus in chains,
bound, and dappled, mangled by my spear,
wearing a torn tunic over his breast,
having flung away the thyrsus; and of the long-tressed women
reduce the vine-decked hair to ashes with my brand.
Be bold, and after the Indian battle
sing the man-ennobling victory of Deriades,
that even an army of later-born men may shudder
to contend with the unconquered earthborn Indians.”
He spoke, and going from one champion to another,
he goaded the drivers of the measureless-living elephants,
and set the leaders of the foot among the throng
fighting tower-fashion. And in the rivalrous din
thyrsus-mad Dionysus drove the rank of desert-roaming beasts
into the fray; and the mountain-bred warriors
raved roaring beneath the divine whip,
and many a maddened beast was armed from the mouths;
and the serpents, spitting from their raw-eating fangs,
sent forth far-shooting jets of venom into the air
with the hissing chasm of the bellowing throat,
leaping sideways; and darting upon the foe,
the viperous arrows had their target of themselves;
and with crooked coils the bodies of the Indians were girdled
as they were wound, and a rope bound their mortal feet
as they rushed into the run. And the war-mad women
imitated the battle of serpent-shooting Phidaleia,
who once, holding the goad of women's battle,
conquered her foes with viperous clusters. . . .
And one, hurling from her mouth a far-shadowing spear,
spat the venom-darting shaft at Deriades,
and with the murderous spray the steel corslet was wetted.
And the corpse lay on the ground, struck by a living missile,
breathless, holding a breathing dart. And on the straight-footed,
humped ridge of the elephants, leaping up,
a leopard hung aloft with a bound of its paws;
and again and again it fastened on the beast's head,
and held aloft the course of the long-legged elephants.
And a great swarm fell, hearing from deep-thundering throats
the dread roar of the desert-roaming lions;
and one was conquered, trembling at the bellowing of a bull,
and beholding the grim point of the ox's horn
