did the wheeling Bears dance upon each other's loins,
but they mingled with the South, and beside the Western pool
they washed their unwetted feet in the strange Ocean.
But Zeus the father struck Phaethon down with the thunderbolt
from on high, rolling of himself over the stream of Eridanus;
and binding the harmony recovered again with its ancient bond
he gave the horses back to the Sun, and the heavenly
car he gave to the dawn-rising, and beside the ancient turning-post
the fair-footed Seasons, attendants of Phaethon, ran their course.
And the whole earth laughed a second time; and from the air
the rain of life-begetting Zeus cleansed all the fields,
and with its moist drop quenched the wandering torch,
all that over the whole earth from their fiery throats
the blazing horses, neighing, spat from heaven.
And the Sun rose, guiding his car that ran its course again;
and the seed grew, and the threshing-floors laughed again,
receiving the former life-giving gleam of the air.
And Zeus the father set Phaethon among the stars of Olympus,
like the Charioteer, and named after him; and the heavenly
gleaming Car, stretched out with his shining forearm,
he holds in the likeness of the Charioteer darting to the race,
as though again, even among the stars, longing for his father's car.
And the fire-burned river rose up into the pole of stars
with Zeus's approval, and in the starry circle
the curved water of fiery Eridanus wheels round.
And the sisters of the swift-fated, fallen charioteer
changed their form into a plant, and from their mourning trees
they let a rich dew drip from their leaves.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
39. In the thirty-ninth, after the waves, you behold
Deriades fleeing the fire-blazing fleet of the Indians.
So speaking, Hermes, beyond overtaking, went to heaven,
leaving joy and wonder to his brother Dionysus.
While Bacchus was still marveling at the disordered pouring of the stars
and at fallen Phaethon, how among the Celts
he slipped, fire-burned, into the Western stream,
meanwhile the foreign ships drew near, which on the sea,
guiding them in lines to the sea-fighting War of the Indians,
the Rhadamanes sailed over the unwashed brine,
striking the sea with alternating strokes,
drivers of the watery battle; and for eager Lyaios
the escorting wind hissed against the answering hulls.
And Lycus led the way, driving his car upon the waters,
grazing the unscored stream with his horse's hooves.
But measureless Deriades, towering high above the racing towers,
gazed cloud-wise upon the sails of the ships
with an angry eye, and, hearing in his arrogance
that an Arab craftsman had built the war-rousing ships,
he swore to bring War against the woodcutting Arabs,
and threatened to lay waste the city of Lycurgus,
mowing down the Rhadamanes with the destroying iron.
And the fearless Indians, gazing at the fleet, trembled,
watching the sea-beaten War, until even
the knees of bold Deriades himself were loosened;
but with a feigned laugh on his calm face
the Indian king commanded from three hundred islands
of his elephant-grazing land, along the hard-trodden ankles of its shore,
to lead a host; and the swift herald went upon the path,
walking on his many-winding feet from land to land;
and the keen fleet came from the scattered islands
at the king's call; and he, stretching his bold neck,
drawing the fair-helmeted ships to the war of the sea,
heartened the whole host, and spoke with a high-minded voice:
"Men, whom my steadfast Hydaspes reared,
now fight again with confidence; and bring
blazing fire to the war, and kindle boundless pine,
that I may burn the newcome ships with the blazing brand,
and hide the water-coursing host in the sea
with their spears, with their breastplates, with their hulls, with Dionysus.
If Bacchus is a god, with my fire I will destroy Bacchus;
is it not enough that, sprinkling his many-faceted drugs in the streams
with Thessalian flowers, he reddened my Hydaspes,
and seeing it I kept silence, and quietly still
endured to look upon the yellow streams of the polluted river?
For if this stream had been from a stranger river,
and my father had not been warlike Indian Hydaspes,
then I would have filled this flood with poured dust,
abolishing the grape-laden smell of Dionysus,
and journeying through the drunken stream of my father
with dusty feet I would have run across the unwetted water,
as is told among the Argives, how the Earth-shaker
made the water dry, and the horse's hoof scored
the Inachian dust of the parched river.
He is no god, no god, this man; he has lied about his lineage.
For what Olympian aegis of Cronion does he brandish?
What spark has he of the Zeus-hurled thunderbolt?
What heavenly lightning of his father does he lift?
The son of Cronos does not arm for war with wine-dark ivy;
I do not liken the clatter of tambourines to the thunder's tune,
nor will I call the wands like the bolts of Zeus,
nor will I name his earthly breastplate equal to the cloud of Zeus;
when do I liken his dappled fawnskin to a spangled star?
But you will say that he received the grape and the pouring of wine
as gifts from Cronion his plant-nurturing father;
to one who bears Trojan blood and is some country herdsman,
Zeus gave to wine-pouring Ganymede the nectar of Olympus,
and wine was not like nectar; give way, you wands.
Bacchus feasts with the Satyrs upon the earth;
Ganymede feasts with the heavenly immortals.
And if this man were mortal, sprung from a heavenly father,
with Zeus and the blessed ones he would have touched one table.
I have heard how once his own throne and the scepter of Olympus
Zeus gave as a gift to Zagreus, an elder Dionysus,
the lightning to Zagreus and the vine to wine-dark Bacchus."
He spoke, and rose to battle; and the peoples thronged together
with spear, with shields, and the late hope of victory
in the land-war they removed to the sea.
And to his champions Dionysus called with a frenzied voice:
"Brave children of Ares and of well-armored Athena,
whose life is the works of war and whose hopes are contests,
hasten to abolish the race of the Indians upon the sea too,
having achieved a sea-victory to follow your victory on land.
But, the carriers of the sea-fight's slaughter,
doubling your spears, twin-plaited in a paired bond,
the sea-fighting joined together, clad about the mouth with bronze,
mingle with the enemy a sea-startling Enyo,
forestalling them, lest, lifting the fire-gleaming brand in his hand,
Deriades burn the warlike timbers of the ships.
Fight without fear, Mimallones; for the watery-warring
hopes of the enemy are empty boasts; and if, after toil,
the lord of the Indians did not finish the fight on land,
seated on the crests of his towering elephants,
cloud-high, beyond reach, unwounded, neighbor to the air,
yet I never lack champions, nor will I call
another helper besides Cronion my father,
the driver of sea and air; but if I wish,
I arm Poseidon my father's brother
to abolish with his trident the whole Indian line;
and a broad-bearded champion, offspring of the Earth-shaker,
Glaucus I have as my fellow in arms, neighbor of my Thebes,
the sea-citizen of the Aonian field of Anthedon;
Glaucus I have, and Phorcys; and as it is lashed by the sea,
Melicertes will sink the hull of Deriades,
honoring kindred Dionysus, whose mother once
nursed the infant Bacchus, since sea-dwelling Ino gave
one milk to both, to Palaemon and to Dionysus;
and of the prophetic old man, who once foretold our victory
that should come upon the sea with his deep-sea voice,
I am the friend, of Proteus; and my Thetis
arms for the fight the daughters of Nereus, and in the battle-din
my Ino, fellow in arms of the Bassarids, puts on her armor;
and I will arm for war Aeolus too, that I may see
Eurus hurling his javelin and Boreas wielding his spear,
the son-in-law of my champion, the ravisher of the Marathonian bride,
and the Ethiopian South wind, the shield-bearer of Lyaios;
and Zephyrus much more, in the storm-driven din,
will harm the hulls of the enemy; for he has
as bedfellow my Iris, the messenger of Zeus. But in silence,
far from the good-wand war of the Indian battle-din,
let rough Aeolus stay quiet, having bound with the accustomed bond
the windy bag he tightened, nor upon the sea
let the winds prevail with Indian-slaying blasts;
but I will finish the fight, brandishing my ship-destroying wands."
So speaking he armed his confident leaders.
And already the herald trumpet of war stood ready,
and the pipes of Ares sounded forth a battle-rousing tune,
gathering the host, and the smitten ox-hide shield
rang out the bronze-clashing echo of the sea-fight,
and the army-rousing pipe shrieked a din that thudded with it;
and instead of the rock-voice, the war-remnants of sound,
the sea Echo answered the late-speaking Panian voices.
For them as they fought there was tumult, and a cry arose
of men calling out; and the host fought with accustomed skill,
ringing round the whole army garland-wise, and in the midst
the Indian fleet was hemmed by the even-rowing ships
into the likeness of fish caught in a net; and to the Aeacids
Aeacus, foretelling the watery War of Salamis,
as the battle began, uttered a god-fearing voice:
"If once before, hearing my suppliant cry,
you drove the seedless drought from the broad-acred field,
bringing life-giving water to the thirsty land,
grant again the same late-fulfilled favor, Zeus of the rain,
honoring me with water here too; and let someone say,
beholding our victory: as upon the earth
Zeus honored his own son, so on the seas he honors him.
Let another, an Achaean man, say: in one ordinance
Aeacus is Indian-slaying and life-giving; for he does both,
cutting off the heads of enemies and giving fruit to the furrow,
he brought joy to Demeter and gladness to Dionysus.
And rescue the voyage of our ship; and as into the parched
and earthly hollow I led the life-bringing water,
so I proclaim a death-bearing surge from the deep flanks
fighting against the armies and hulls of Deriades.
But, father, lord of life, lord of the battle-din,
send me the eagle bird, the herald of my race,
on the right for my champions and for your Dionysus;
and let another bird come on the left for the enemy;
and let these be the diverse tokens for both:
the one I shall behold, carried on a seizing talon,
scored with the sharp sting of its sharpened claws,
lifting up a huge dead horned serpent,
announcing the end of the horned enemy;
and to the host of the enemy let another, black-skinned, come
with dark wings, foretelling the slaughter of the Indians,
the black sign of self-wrought death; and if you are willing,
with thunderous crashings prophesy my victory,
and sending the lightning of Bromios as childbed-fires
honor your son again with fire, and let the thunderbolts
shoot at the fair-helmeted hulls of the enemy.
Yes, father, remember Aegina, lest you shame your bride's
bridegroom, the wing-shaped bird of the Loves."
So speaking he made war, and casting his eye
to the airy paths, full against the returning Bear,
Erechtheus entreated his son-in-law and cried out a word:
"Boreas my son-in-law, arm yourself, and for your bride's
fighting father straining your helping breath
grant a sea-victory as the bride-gift of your chamber;
to the hulls of Bromios bringing a ship-saving breeze
give a favor to both, to Erechtheus and to Dionysus;
but lashing the maddened sea against the ships of Deriades
arm your storms with a billowy blast—
for you are experienced in battle, since you yourself
dwell in Thrace, experienced, just like Ares—
and bringing a storm-breath against the enemy's phalanx
arm yourself against Deriades with a frosty spear;
and setting a storm-driven Enyo against the enemy
shoot the foe with a hail-shaft,
bearing faith to Zeus and to Pallas and to Dionysus.
Remember Cecropia of fair maidens, where the women
embroider with the shuttle the marriage-hymn of your Loves;
and honor Ilissus the wedding-decker, where the bride,
the Attic girl, your long-since consort, the seizing breezes carried off
as she sat unshaken on your unmoving shoulder.
I know that another wind will come as fellow in arms,
the Eastern, neighbor to the enemy; but in the battle
I do not fear bold Eurus, since the winged winds
all, as many as breathe, are attendants of Boreas;
and let the champion of the Ethiopians, upon the Southern edge of the field,
Corymbasus, return no more, but be subdued,
having as hot fellow-fighter his own Ethiopian South wind,
having drunk the cold death-bearing water over the sea;
I care nothing for Zephyrus, when Boreas arms.
Show your accord with your father-in-law; and from heaven
with you for my Bacchic armies will fight
with his trident Poseidon, and Athena,
she for her own dwellers, he for the offspring of his brother;
and fiery Hephaestus, honoring the blood of Erechtheus,
will come kindly to the watery War,
whirling his battling flame upon the hulls of Deriades.
And grant me to conquer in the waters too, and after the victory
let Erechtheus bring his host unharmed to Cecropia,
and let Athens sing of Boreas and Oreithyia."
Crying out such a word, the sea-whirling man laid hold of the fight
with his skillful spear, and like a dweller of Marathon
he had a longing for the sea-fight; and in the oar-loving battle-din
Ares was then a fair-armed sailor, and in his palm
Fear held the rudder, and the steersman of the battle-din,
Terror, loosed the cables of the javelin-bearing ships.
And the phalanxes of the Cyclopes sailed the sea,
shooting at the hulls with the crags near the shore;
and Euryalus cried his war-cry, and in the sea-roaring din
cloud-high Halimedes was stung to battle.
And against the twin armies sea-Ares thundered
after the land-fight, and with a sea-roaring shout
upon the Bacchic hulls the hulls of the Indians flowed on;
and there was slaughter on both sides, and the waves boiled with gore,
and a great host of both fell; and with new-shed
blood the back of the dark sea grew red.
And many here and there, falling in the pouring of death,
the swollen sailors floated upon the sea;
and with the eddies, having the ferrying winds for whirling,
the dead crowd was dragged along, running with the unsparing breeze;
and many beneath the self-rolling whirl of the battle-din
slipped into the stream, and drinking by necessity
the bitter water perceived the threads of underwater Fate,
weighed down by the breastplate; and the black water of the swollen sea
covered the like-colored bodies of the dark dead
in the seaweed depth, and with the water-coursing wearer
the bronze tunic was buried in the muddy clay;
and the sea became a tomb. And many were entombed
in the jaws of sea-monsters, and in its fishy throat
a seal, tossing the breathless corpse, entombed it,
belching forth the yellow stream of blood. And of the slain
the sea drank up the armor, and of the newly-slaughtered wearer
of itself the crested helmet floated through the water
as the bond was loosened, and on the storm-driven
flood of the wandering sea the rounds of many an ox-hide shield swam
with their wet baldric. And much beneath the wave-tips
the reddening foam bubbled up from the gray brine,
flecking the all-white pouring with a bloody trail.
And Melicertes was reddened with bloody drops;
and Leucothea raised her cry, the nurse of Lyaios,
holding her neck high, and for the Indian-slaying victory
the Nymph crowned her hair with the flower of the seaweed;
and Thetis without her veil, leaning up out of the sea,
propping her hands on Doris and Panopeia,
stretched a glad eye toward good-wand Dionysus.
And from the deep Galatea, through the sea's gulf
half-seen was borne, grazing the calm,
and at the sea-startling Enyo of the murderous Cyclops
gazing she was shaken, and changed her cheeks with fear;
for she hoped to see Polyphemus in the Indian battle
fighting in arms with Lyaios against Deriades;
and trembling she entreated sea Aphrodite
to save the son of Poseidon doing valiant deeds,
and besought the dark-haired, child-loving sire
to shield Polyphemus as he fought, for his son's sake.
And the daughters of Nereus circled round the bearer
of the deep trident; and propped upon his trident
the sea Earth-shaker gazed at the neighboring battle,
and watching the host of well-armored Dionysus,
jealous as he saw the Enyo of the other Cyclops,
to watery-warring Bromios he broke out with a much-reproachful voice:
"To the battle-cry, dear Bacchus, gathering so many Cyclopes,
and leaving one alone far from the fight,
for seven years' time you have a many-circled contest,
feeding the shifting hope of an endless war,
since the champions of your great contest
all need one unconquered Polyphemus;
but if my son the Cyclops had come to your fight,
and had brandished the prong of my father's trident,
then, fighting in arms with Dionysus over the plain,
he would have crushed the breast of bull-horned Deriades,
and cleaving the great dread throng with my trident
he would have killed the whole race of Indians in one dawn.
My other son of old, holding a hundred hands,
helped your father, the destroyer of the Titans,
many-armed Aegaeon, when, drawing Cronos to flight,
he stretched out the wide-scattered tribe of his towering palms,
having a high-necked mane that shadowed the sun,
and the grim Titans were banished from Olympus,
cowering before the Enyo of skillful Briareus."
Such a word he spoke in envy with an indignant voice.
And Thoosa in shame held her cheeks downcast,
since love-mad Polyphemus was not present at the war.
And as the toil of the loud-roaring battle-din came to its end,
Nereus beheld his accustomed sea streaming with blood;
and the Earth-shaker marveled at the yellow back of the sea,
seeing the man-eating fish and, with the multitude of corpses,
the unwetted back of the neighboring sea bridged over . . .
And the Bacchic phalanxes flowed on against the blazing host.
And the boundless army of the enemy lay dead, of those who in the fight
were struck with swords and sharp-piercing arrows.
On one a shaft fell above the flank, and another, struck
with the bronze spear above the rim of the middle temple,
had his wound dug deep as his head was scored.
And many here and there of the wide-scattered rowers,
cleaving the sea with alternating oars,
whitened the dark, close-following pouring with foam,
and there was useless toil for the eager rowers,
and the bound cables, with the helping iron,
the steersman cut, and split the rope with his sword.
And of both phalanxes, sending a whir through the air,
flowed the long-shadowed rain of unwandering arrows;
of which one struck the very middle of the mast, and another, passing through,
made the well-twisting sail boom, running with the breezes,
another was fixed in the forestays, and another in the mast-step
lay fallen, and another, a shaft wandering through the air,
hit the topmost of the high-crested yard-arm,
and another was stretched out on the benches; and close at hand
others, straying from the steersman's path,
unsteadily grazed the tips of the rudder's peak;
and Phlogios famed for the bow, drawing a wind-swift shaft,
struck the ship's deck and did not hit Lyaios.
And one might see upon the sea a fine-winged wandering shaft
twined about the curving folds of a crooked octopus;
and one missed another; and with the Erythraean iron
another, hurling at Dionysus, struck a pompilus fish;
and Corymbasus shot with his spear, that he might hit
a Satyr's oar-blade, and the lance, darting past,
scored the double tail of the water-coursing fish
with its sharpened point; and aiming his iron
at the useless mark of unwounded Dionysus
Deriades sent his spear, and straying from Bacchus
the deadly point busied itself with the back of a dolphin,
where the curving neck of the fish joins its crest,
and the dolphin, self-twisting at the accustomed circling goal,
half-dead leaped with the spring of dancing Fate;
and many here and there, tumblers of destruction,
the fish danced as their backs were scored.
And Steropes fought in front; and high-footed Halimedes,
taking in his hand a crag of the sea-born hill,
hurled it at the enemy; and the wandering ship sank,
struck by the rough stone in its wheeling round.
And one lance, thrown across one hull, neighbor to a hull,
yoked both, the sea-running point of the spear,
binding the two ships in a common bond
as they were crowded cloud-wise; and there was a discordant echo.
And the fleet of both held a four-yoked Enyo,
of which one was about the back of the opposite blazing Eurus,
another by the wing of dewy Libs, another by Boreas,
and by the Southern edge. And with alternating gusts
swift-kneed Morrheus, stepping from hull to hull,
frightened the sea-startling Enyo of the Bassarids,
doing valiant deeds in the waters too; but with his wand
Euios wounded him and drew him back from the watery fight,
and toiling in pain Morrheus went to the city.
While the divine wound that had fallen to his lot the demonic hand
of the pain-loosing Brahman healed with Phoebean art,
murmuring a chattering hymn beneath a divine song,
meanwhile against the enemy Lydian Ares pressed on.
For them there was a battle-rousing voyage, and Enyo held
the lead of the sailing, and of the sea-clashing battle-din
there was a tumult of both kinds; for of the enemy
all who were shot with hard arrows
or with murderous leaf-points or spears or swords,
oaring their unaccustomed hands into the black water
with unsteady strokes were entombed in the sea;
but if any warrior of Bromios fell into the brine struck,
tossing his palms he swam, cleaving the waves
with sea-fighting hands, and in the sea-roaring din
fighting in the surge he split the water along with the men.
And Cronion inclined the scales of the sea-battle,
making ready a watery victory for Dionysus;
and with the deep trident the dark-haired god armed himself,
fighting against the foe, and driving the unwetted
car of Poseidon, Melicertes raved in bacchic frenzy.
And riding on four storms across the sea,
towering up the waves, the winds armed themselves,
wishing to abolish the line of the enemy's ships,
some helpers of Deriades, some of Lyaios;
and Zephyrus was armed, and the South wind hissed against Eurus,
and Boreas, bringing the opposing Thracian blast,
lashed the wild back of the maddened sea.
And guiding the battling fleet of Deriades
Strife led the way of the fight; but of the ships of Dionysus
with Indian-slaying hand Victory swelled the sails.
And setting his battling conch to his wet lips
Nereus bellowed a tune with the sea-trumpet;
and Thetis rang out the tune of the war-Echo,
shielding Lyaios with her father's waves.
And Eurymedon the Cabeirus, lifting his accustomed brand,
found a stratagem to help the fight; for his own
long ship he set ablaze, kindling a willing fire;
and at the Bacchic nods, leaping about the sea,
and with slanting curves stepping from hull to hull,
the wandering torch swam into a self-twisting circle,
burning here and there the line of the wide-scattered ships.
And seeing the glare of the fire-stricken sea
a Nereid without her veil sank into the depths of the deep,
fleeing the watery fire through the blazing water.
And the Indian throng withdrew to the land, leaving the sea;
and Phaethon laughed, that after his former bonds
out of the fire of Hephaestus the sea-fighting Ares fled again.
And Deriades, beyond reach, seeing the flame running with the breezes,
flew to the plain, tossing his knees more swiftly,
fleeing the watery War of sea-battling Dionysus.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
40. The fortieth holds the slaughtered captain of the Indians,
and how Dionysus entered Tyre, the homeland of Cadmus.
Nor did Deriades escape all-seeing Justice, nor even
the unbending threads of Fate's unbreakable spindle;
for Pallas Athena, beholding him in flight—
she was seated above the sea upon a jutting crag,
watching the sea-battle and the strife of the armed Indians—
sprang up from her lookout and put on a man's shape.
With cunning words she beguiled the captain of the Indians,
wearing the likeness of Morrheus, and to favour Lyaeus
she checked Deriades; and as if anxious for the fray
she shouted a dreadful word with much-reproaching voice:
"You flee, Deriades? To whom have you left the war of the ships?
How can you show yourself to your countrymen? Or how face
the war-steadfast Orsiboë, if she should hear
that Deriades is in flight and will not stand his ground before women?
Have shame before Cheirobie, breaker of men, lest she perceive
you cowering from Lyaeus' ironless battle—
she who, holding a furious spear and heaving up a shield of oxhide,
fought against the Bassarids at her husband's side.
Give way to me, leave the fray to Morrheus; and if you wish,
I myself will play the champion and destroy unwarlike Bacchus.
I will not call you father-in-law while you flee; rather let your daughter
Cheirobie have another husband—for in shame
I will leave your city behind, and go to the land of the Medes,
go to Scythia, that I may not be called your son-in-law.
But you will say: my wife, well-armed, knows the war-cry.
There are Amazons about the Caucasus, where many
women play the champion far better than Cheirobie;
there, captured by the spear, a strong bride without dowry
I will lead to marriage, if I choose, one of them—for into my chambers
I do not receive the child of a war-shunning father."
So speaking she persuaded haughty Deriades,
and gave him courage a second time, that he might be slain,
struck down by the man-killing thyrsus as Bromios fought.
And the bold one, not knowing that cunning Athena stood beside him,
hearing the chiding speech of the false Morrheus,
cried out a comforting word with abashed lips:
"Spare your words. Why do you blame me, fearless Morrheus?
He is no warrior, no warrior, this one, ever changing his body.
For indeed I am at a loss whom I fight or whom I strike.
Eager to hit Dionysus with a winged arrow,
or to smite the middle of his neck with the sword, or to cast my spear
and pierce him through the belly as I long to do, instead of Lyaeus
I overtake a dapple-backed leopard rushing upon me . . .
As the lion fights I hasten to cut its neck,
and instead of the lion I spy a bold and horrible serpent;
striving against the serpent I watch the back of a bear;
into its hump-arched mane I hurl my furious spear,
but in vain I draw the long shaft; for instead of the bear
appears an air-roaming, woundless, flying flame.
I see a boar coming on, and I hear the lowing of an ox;
instead of the swine I behold some bull above its slanting brow
hurling against our elephants, with its blue-grey
horns, a javelin; and I whirl my own sword
against the manifold beasts, and yet I subdue not one beast.
I spy a plant and draw my shaft, but as it flees
I see toward the airy mark only the arching water.
So, trembling at the many-drugged marvels of his craft,
I shrink from the ever-shifting battle of Dionysus;
but again I will arm against Bromios, until I expose
the artful sorceries of guile-stitching Dionysus."
So he spoke, and armed himself a second time in his wonted frenzy,
and again upon the plain the battle roared, and as he fought
Dionysus was armed once more after the strife at sea;
and he had forgotten the earlier victory of Bromios,
when, his neck enfolded by a tree-like bond,
he raised up a much-prayed-for plea with Bacchus as witness.
But again he was the god-fighting champion; and he held a purpose
of two minds: either to take Bacchus or to make him a slave.
Three times he cast his spear, and missed, striking the air;
but when for the fourth time he ran upon wine-dark Bacchus,
hurling his uplifted spear at a useless target,
overweening Deriades called upon his comrade in the contest,
his son-in-law—but Morrheus was no longer to be seen;
rather Athena, turning aside her wile-weaving shape,
stood beside the vine-clustered god; and as he gazed
a god-sent terror loosed the knees of Deriades.
He knew that the deceiving image of human form
bore a copy of the answering face of Morrheus,
and he understood the beguiling guile of wise Athena.
Dionysus, seeing her, rejoiced, and in his heart
he knew that lying Athena fought at his side.
And then the vine-clustered god, in his wrath, raged in his frenzy,
high-towering, vast, equal to the rock of Parnassus;
he pursued swift-running Deriades; but the other in flight,
light, stretched himself out as a runner with the hurrying winds.
But when he reached the place where the war-breeding water,
with raging wave, old Hydaspes murmured,
there he stood, vast, beside the river's banks,
as if he had his father, a comrade in the contest, a roaring fighter,
a watery spearman against the armed assault of Dionysus.
But the vine-god, hurling his flesh-cutting thyrsus,
only grazed the topmost skin of Deriades.
And he, struck by the ivy spray that destroys men,
slid headlong into his father's stream,
bridging the whole water with his long limbs
of his own accord. And the gods, after the long war of the Indians,
with all-ruling Zeus returned again to Olympus.
The Bacchants raised the cry together for unvanquished Dionysus,
hymning the fray, and many gathered round
piercing the whole body of Deriades with their spears.
Orsiboë wailed upon the much-lamenting towers,
mourning her husband, lying newly slain;
with mourning nails she scored the circle of her face,
and tore the unkempt cluster of her twisted hair,
and poured smoking dust upon her head.
Cheirobie shrieked aloud over her dead father,
and struck her dark arms, and bared the whole
breast of her silvery robe, rent in two;
and Protonoë, barefoot, scratching her cheeks,
disfiguring the circle of her dust-stained face,
wept for both her husband and her father,
holding a double grief, and cried in mourning voice:
"Husband, young you have perished out of life; you have left me
a widow in the halls, untried in childbirth;
I bore no infant son for comfort; not after victory
did I behold my returning husband a second time—rather by the sword
he was slain by his own, and gave his name to a river,
and died among strangers, so that I must call my husband
seedless, self-slain, returnless, watery Orontes.
I mourn them both, Deriades and Orontes,
perished alike by a watery doom; for man-slaying
Deriades the wave hid, and the stream covered Orontes.
I have not become wholly like my mother; for Orsiboë
sang of her daughters' weddings, untimely cut down;
she saw the marriage of Protonoë, received Orontes as son-in-law,
and yoked Cheirobie to an unconquered husband,
whom even great Bacchus fears; Cheirobie tends
her dear husband alive, and neither thyrsus
nor stream laid him low; but I suffer doubly,
my husband gone and my father destroyed.
Cease, nurse, vainly consoling your child;
grant me to keep my husband, and I will not bewail my father;
show me some child, a comfort for my husband's pain.
Who will take and carry me to broad-flowing Hydaspes,
that I may kiss the dear billow of the honey-dripping river?
Who will take and carry me to the holy glens of Daphne,
that I may embrace Orontes even in his streams?
Would I too were a lovely stream; would that I myself,
rained over with tears, might appear there as a fountain,
where my well-watered husband, dead, rolls his billow,
a watery bride; and I shall be like Comaetho,
who once, having loved a lovely river,
takes joy even now in holding her husband Cydnus in her arms—
a tale I hear cherished among the Cilician men;
but I, longing, will not pass by sweet Orontes,
like fugitive Periboea, nor ever, reining back
the winding water, will I guard myself against my watery husband.
But if it is not fated for me to die beside neighbouring Daphne,
let father's-father Hydaspes hide me in his waves,
that I may not sleep in the arms of a horned Satyr,
that I may not see the Phrygian revel, nor shake cymbals in my hands,
that I may not perform the playful rite, nor behold
Maeonia, nor see Tmolus, nor the house of Lyaeus,
nor the heavy-burdening yoke of slavery, nor let anyone say:
the daughter of Deriades, the spear-bold king,
serves Dionysus as a captive after the war."
As she spoke, the women wailed in pity with her,
whose child, whose brother had died, whose fathers,
or whose newly-bearded husband untimely. And from her head
Cheirobie, tearing her hair, gashed her cheeks;
she was scourged by a twofold pain, and for her father
she mourned not so much as she was wroth against her husband;
for she had heard of Morrheus' love-maddened compulsion
and the deceiving guile of chaste Chalcomedeia.
And she spoke a word, rending her tunic:
"Sparing his ash-wood spear, Morrheus slew my father;
nor was he avenger of the dead; but desiring hated
Chalcomede, he drove not on the women's war,
but still favours the Bassarids. Tell me, you Fates:
what envy sacked the Indian city? What envy suddenly
fell upon both the daughters of Deriades?
Dying in the war, Orontes made his own bride
Protonoë an unkempt mourning widow,
and Cheirobie her husband renounced while she yet lived.
Worse than my sister's are the sufferings I endure;
Protonoë had a husband who defended her nurse,
Cheirobie had a husband, destroyer of her fatherland,
a useless warrior, a follower of the Cyprian goddess,
valiant, ever-shifting, of one mind with Lyaeus.
Against me my marriage too was armed; for through our
Morrheus' desire the city of the Indians was plundered;
I was robbed of my father for a man's sake; I who once was haughty
and a king's daughter, I who once was mistress of the Indians.
I too shall be one of the handmaids; and soon, wretched,
I shall call my handmaid Chalcomedeia my mistress.
Today you hold the Indian seat, deceitful Morrheus;
tomorrow, self-summoned, you will go to the land of the Lydians,
serving Dionysus for the beauty of Chalcomede.
Openly hold the bed of Chalcomede, bridegroom Morrheus;
for no longer do you fear the grim mouth of Deriades.
Give way: the serpent calls you again, who pursues you,
sending its hiss as guardian of an unplundered marriage."
Such things the grieving, heavy-weeping bride spoke;
and Protonoë shrieked a second time. Upon both
the mother, leaning her downcast hands, cried aloud:
"The hopes of our fatherland have fallen; no longer do I behold
my husband Deriades, and no longer Orontes my son-in-law.
Deriades is dead; the city of the Indians is plundered;
the unbreakable wall of my land has toppled. Would that me too
Bacchus would take and destroy along with my perishing husband,
and, taking me, would cast me into swift-flowing Hydaspes,
since the earth refuses me; let the father-in-law water hold me,
and let me behold Deriades even in the waters; let me not see
Protonoë led unwilling after Dionysus,
nor ever hear again the piteous lament of Cheirobie
dragged to the love of spear-won wedlock;
let me not look upon another husband after Deriades.
Would I might share a hearth with the Naiads, since even
Leucothoë, living, the dark-haired god received,
and she is called one of the Nereids; and instead of white
another, with dark feet, I shall appear, a water-Ino."
Such things the trailing-robed women mourned,
standing in rows upon the loud-roaring towers.
But the Bacchants clashed their hands, casting aside the war-cry,
shouting such a word from their like-voiced throats:
"We have won great glory; we have slain the captain of the Indians."
And laughing Dionysus leapt for joy of victory,
and, taking breath from his toil and the bloody contest,
first he buried the row of unburied corpses,
raising a single boundless tomb in a wide hollow,
a confused funeral pyre a hundred feet about; and around the dead
the Mygdonian pipe, of varied music, sounded its dirge,
and the Phrygian flute-players wove a manly strain
with mournful mouths, and the Bacchants danced
to the tender singing of Ganyctor in Euian voice;
and the Berecyntian double pipes of Cleochus beneath the mouth
bellowed a fearful Libyan lament, which once both
Stheno and Euryale, with one many-throated voice,
wailed shrilly over newly-cut Medusa
as the two hundred serpents spoke upon her heads,
from whom, as they mourned, the twisting hiss of their hair
proclaimed a many-headed dirge for Medusa.
And, ceasing from his toil, and cleansing his limbs with water,
he gave the Indians, now freed from strife, a god-fearing lord,
choosing Modaeus; and over a shared cup
the Bacchants feasted, and touched a single table,
drinking yellow water from the wine-flowing river.
And the dance was beyond telling; many a Bassarid
leapt up, striking the ground with frenzied sandal,
and the Satyr, beating the deep-thudding earth with his foot,
revelled with sidelong tumbling leaps of his feet,
leaning his arm on the neck of a maddened Bacchant;
and the foot-soldiers of Bromios danced together with their shields,
and, whirling the armed circles of the rolling dance,
imitated the rhythm of the shield-bearing Corybantes,
and the host of horsemen stood in the helmet-flashing dance,
hymning the all-subduing victory of Dionysus.
None was without sound; with like-tongued shouting
the Euian echo ran up to the seven-zoned vault.
But when the revel of the toil-loosing feast had passed,
taking all the spoil of victory after the war of the Indians,
Dionysus remembered his ancient homeland,
dissolving the seven-year foundations of the war.
And the warriors plundered all the wealth of the foe:
one held Indian jasper, another the veins of painted
Phoebean hyacinth, and the green-tinted backs of emerald;
another, beneath the lookouts of fair-founded Imaeus,
drove on the upright pace of spear-won elephants,
and one, by Emodus' deep-cavernned hill,
proudly drove the migrant chariot of Indian lions,
and another, fastening a knot upon its neck,
hastened to drag a leopard to the Mygdonian shore;
and a Satyr was carried along, and with a wine-loving spray,
lashing on a spotted tiger that ran before him, he revelled;
another came home leading to his Cybeleian bride
a fragrant nursery of sea-fed reeds,
and a flashing stone, the gift of the Erythraean brine;
and many a captive bride of dark complexion,
fresh-wedded, was dragged from the chamber with her new husband,
yoking her bound, enslaved neck beneath the collar.
And lifting in her hand a flowing heap of wealth,
the god-driven Bacchant went to the lookouts of Tmolus,
hymning the revel for the homecoming Dionysus.
And Dionysus shared out the spoil of battle to his host,
sending all the people, his comrades in arms, back homeward
after the Indian war; and the people hastened away
lifting marbles, the Eastern gifts of the sea,
and birds of varied form; and on the homeward journey,
hymning the revel for unconquered Dionysus,
all reveled, leaving behind the memory
of the whole laborious war, scattered to run with
the Northern breeze; and each, holding the offerings of victory,
came late and returning to his home. But instead of his homeland
Asterius alone, near the unwashed-footed Bears,
about the stream of Phasis settled in a cold land
beside the Massagetan gulf, dwelling
beneath the snowy ankles of starry Taurus, his father's father,
fleeing the Cnossian city and his male-childed lineage,
hating Pasiphaë and his own father Minos,
and he preferred Scythia to his own land. But Bacchus, with only
his own Satyrs and his Indian-slaying Bacchants,
after the Caucasian war of the Amazonian river,
entered Arabia a second time, where, dwelling often,
he taught the people of the unbacchic Arabs to lift
the mystic fennel-wands; and from the growth-rich thicket
he crowned the Nysian mountains with the clustering spray.
And, leaving the deep-shaded grove of Arabia's ridge,
he measured the Assyrian path, a wayfarer on foot,
and longed to see the land of the Tyrians, the homeland of Cadmus;
for there he bent his step, and gazing at the boundless robes
he marvelled at the varicoloured works of Assyrian craft,
beholding the silver-white work of Babylonian Arachne;
and he gazed at the garments dipped in Tyrian dye,
that shoot forth purple sparks of the sea,
where a sea-working dog, feeding along the shores,
its inmost teeth seizing the wondrous fish with its grey jaws,
purpled its snowy cheeks with the blood of the shellfish,
crimsoning its lips with watery fire, with which alone
the bright robe of the sea-cloaked kings once grew red.
And beholding the city, he rejoiced—the city which the Earth-shaker
girdled not with a whole wet belt of sea,
but it received an Olympian shape, such as the moon weaves
near to its full, leaving a gap with one of its horns.
And to him as he gazed, the land set midway, yoked to the brine,
a double wonder befell, since Tyre lies in the sea,
divided into a land mass, and joined to the sea
with three flanks she fastened one girdle;
unmoved she was like a swimming maiden,
and gave her head, breast, and neck to the sea,
spreading her hands midway in the twin sea,
whitening her body with the neighbouring sea-foam,
and propped both her feet upon mother earth.
And the Earth-shaker, holding the city with an unshaken bond,
the watery bridegroom swims about her, as if joining
his foaming arm to the encircled neck of his bride.
And Bacchus still marvelled at Tyre, in which alone
the herdsman, neighbour by the road, mingled with the sailor near him,
piping along the strand, and the goatherd with the fisherman
hauling his net, and with answering oars
the clod was furrowed by the plough as the waters were cloven;
and the companions chatted near the sea-side thicket,
the shepherds . . . with woodcutters, and in one place roared together
the surge of the sea, the lowing of oxen, the whisper of leaves,
cable, plant, voyage, grove, water, ships, freighter, plough-handle,
sheep, reed, sickle, skiffs, nets, sails, breastplate.
And gazing on these things he broke into a much-marvelling voice:
"Whence have I beheld an island on the mainland? If it is right to say it,
never have I beheld such beauty; for high-stretching
trees whisper beside the waves, and as the Nereid
speaks across the sea, the Hamadryad nearby hears,
and over the Tyrian seas and the sea-bordering fields
the gentle southern breeze, breathing from Lebanon,
with fruit-bearing breath pours forth a ship-saving gust,
cooling the field-dweller and drawing the sailor to his voyage;
and bringing the earthly sickle near the sea-deep trident,
Deo the harvest-bringer here speaks to the lord of the waters,
who drives his dry chariot over the silent calm,
to guide an equal course upon the like-zealous cars,
plying her whip on the airborne backs of her dragons.
O mistress, cared for by all, image of earth, likeness of heaven,
you hold the three-sided baldric of the conjoined sea."
So speaking, he passed on through the city, straining his eye;
and to him as he gazed the stone-paved streets
showed forth the gleam of the alternating ore;
and he saw the house of his ancestor Agenor, beheld the courts
and the chamber of Cadmus, and the unguarded maiden-bower
of Europa, once carried off, he entered,
holding in mind his own horned Zeus; and the primeval
springs he marvelled at the more, where through earth's hollow,
the water pouring forth and gathered back into a single hour,
with self-born streams loosed the nourishing water;
he saw the fertile flow of Abarbarea, beheld the spring
named lovely Callirhoë, and saw too
the tender bridal water of Drosera as she gushed forth.
But when he had marked all with his pleasure-loving heart,
he revelled into the house of Astrochiton, and the lord of the stars
he summoned, shouting such a word with mystic voice:
"Astrochiton Heracles, lord of fire, captain of the cosmos,
Helios, long-shadow-casting shepherd of mortal life,
riding in spirals over the whole vault with fiery justice,
whirling the son of time, the twelve-month year,
you bring circle after circle; and from your car
the age flows on, shaped now in old age, now in youth;
midwife of the wise birthless travail, the image of Mene,
you bring to birth the triple-curving moon, when dewy Selene
draws from your birth-giving ray her answering fire,
gathering the curved horn of the bull;
all-shining eye of heaven, you bear on your four-yoked car
winter after autumn, you bring summer, changing the spring.
Night, driven by your hurling torch,
gives way, unstayed, when, drawing the silver yoke,
the top-shining, upright horse's neck is lashed,
and as you shine the meadow, no longer shining brighter,
is dappled with the bright-gleaming stars;
washed in the streams of the eastern Ocean,
shaking off the fruitful moisture of your cold hair,
you bring the fruit-bearing rain, and on well-travailing Earth
you belch forth the morning watering of airy dew,
and you nourish the travails of the corn with your disc,
sprinkling the bounteous harvest through the life-bearing furrow.
You are Belus on the Euphrates, Ammon called by the Libyans,
Apis you are by the Nile, Cronus to the Arabs, Assyrian Zeus;
and bearing fragrant wood upon its hooked talon
the wise thousand-year bird, upon your sweet-scented altar,
the phoenix, bringing the end of life as its own self-sown beginning,
is born, the recurring image of equal time,
and, loosing its old age in the fire, exchanges youth for the fire;
whether you are Sarapis, the cloudless Egyptian Zeus,
or Cronus, or many-named Phaethon, or whether you are Mithras,
the sun of Babylon, the Delphic Apollo in Hellas,
or Marriage, which Eros sowed in shadowy dreams,
fulfilling the deceiving desire of a counterfeit bed,
when, from sleeping Zeus, as with the point of a knife
he scraped the watery seed upon the self-wedded furrow,
the crags were brought to birth by heavenly drops,
whether you are pain-slaying Paeon, or whether you are dappled
Aether, and you are called Astrochiton—for at night
the starry tunics light up the heavens—:
with kindly ears receive my voice."
Such a word Dionysus uttered. And suddenly,
holding an inspired form within the god-receiving temple,
Astrochiton flashed forth; and from his fire-eyed face
his eyes shot out a rosy gleam;
and the radiant god stretched out his hand to Lyaeus,
wearing a varied garment, the image of heaven, the likeness of the cosmos,
gleaming with golden cheeks and a starry beard;
and he gladdened him and soothed him with a friendly table.
But he delighted his heart at the unportioned feast,
touching ambrosia and nectar; and there is no blame,
if he drank sweet nectar after the immortal milk of Hera;
and he questioned Astrochiton, pouring forth an inquiring voice:
"Astrochiton, teach me, by the form of the earth, by the image of the island,
what god founded the city? What heavenly hand drew it?
Who raised the crags and rooted them in the sea?
Who wrought these marvels? Whence did the springs receive their name?
Who mingled the island with the land, yoked to its mother the sea?"
He spoke; and Heracles soothed him with a friendly tale:
"Bacchus, hear the tale; and I will teach you all.
Here once dwelt men whom alone, sprung from the same seed,
Aion beheld as coevals of the everlasting cosmos,
a holy race of an unwedded earth, whose shape then
the unploughed, unsown slime brought to birth of itself;
who, with native craft, fortified a city of even floors,
unshaken upon rocky foundations.
And once, by the well-watered springs, on beds of earth,
as the ground was scourged by the vapour of the fiery sun,
plucking the Lethean wing of mind-delighting Sleep,
they slept together; and, swelling in my heart a city-loving sting,
I lifted the standing footprint of the earthborn upon their heads,
and, holding the shadowy semblance of a mortal face,
I uttered an oracle from my speaking throat:
'Shaking off idle sleep, children of the soil,
make me a strange chariot of the passable sea; with sharp-cutting
axes cut me the spine of the pine-wood forest;
make me a clever work; and beneath thick ribs
nailing planks in close-set order,
bind together, unshaken, with a fitted bond,
a chariot of the sea, a first-sailing raft, which through the deep
may carry you; and let a curved end from end to end,
a first-fixed long beam, receive the whole support;
fasten the planks, fitted to the ribs, in a circle,
the dense pattern of a wooden wall; and high-stretching,
bound with fastenings, let the middle beam stand upright;
and fasten a broad linen cloth to the middle beam,
and intertwined ropes in turn, from whose bonds
spread out, belly out the cloth to the airy wind,
pregnant from the wind, ship-saving; and the newly-built,
gaping planks fence with slender pegs,
strewing them thickly upon the yoked walls
with wicker mats, lest the thieving wave be poured
into the hollow hidden draught of the gaping plank.
And the helm of the raft, the steersman of its watery course,
the much-turning charioteer of the liquid path,
whirling everywhere, wherever your mind draws you,
score the back of the sea with the wooden hollow,
until you come to the destined place, where two
unstable rocks float, wanderers in the sea,
which Nature named the Ambrosial, in which there flourishes
a self-rooted olive shoot, yoked together, of equal age,
at the midmost navel of the water-faring rock; and on its topmost
boughs you shall behold an eagle sitting beside it,
and a well-wrought bowl; and from the flaming tree
self-kindled fire belches forth wondrous sparks,
and the flame, unburning, feeds about the olive shoot;
and a coiling serpent dances about the high-leaved plant,
swelling a wonder both to the eyes and the ears;
for the serpent, creeping soundless, does not gird the high-flying eagle
with a threatening, slanting coil,
nor, spitting the death-bearing venom of its teeth,
devours the bird with its jaws, nor does the eagle itself,
seizing the many-coiled creeper with its talons among the thorns,
mount aloft and cleave the air,
nor scratch it with its sharp-toothed beak;
nor, borne upon the branches of the tall-trunked plant,
does the fire feed about the unharmed olive shoot,
nor does it wither the coil of the serpent's scales,
its fellow-dweller, neighbour by the road; and of the bird's own
interwoven wings the leaping fire takes no hold,
but sends its dear gleam, a vapour, into the midst of the plant;
nor does the unshaken cup, hanging on high, fall down
as the boughs are shaken, slipping with the winds.
And, having caught the wise coeval bird of the olive,
the high-flying eagle, sacrifice it to the dark-haired god,
pouring its gore upon the sea-wandering crags
and to Zeus and the blessed ones; and the unstable rock
no longer wanders, sea-borne, but with unmoving foundations,
girded of itself, joins to its unyoked fellow-rock.
And fix a city set upon both crags,
on either side, upon the base of either sea.'
Such an oracular word I uttered; and waking,
the Earthborn were stirred, and in the ears of each
the wondrous tale of the unwandering dreams ever buzzed.
And to them I revealed another portent after the winged dreams,
to them in their grief, swelling a city-founding spirit,
to be their future city-protector; and peering above the sea,
bearing an answering copy in equal shape,
the nautilus fish swam into self-taught sailing;
beholding it then like a ship of the sea,
and learning a well-made voyage without toil,
and fastening a raft like the fish of the deep,
they imitated an equal pattern of sea-sailing.
And the voyage was made; with the equal-weighted load of four stones
they steadied their measured sailing upon the sea,
and imitated the unshaken passage of the cranes,
which, within their mouths, a helper of the road,
lift a heavy stone, lest, as they fly,
the wind drive their light wings off course,
until they beheld that place, where with the gales
the crags sailed into a self-guided voyage.
And they set the raft beside the sea-garlanded island,
and stepped upon the rocks, where was the plant of Athena.
And to them, as they sought it, the hearth-bird of the olive,
the air-roaming eagle, stood of its own will toward its death;
and the Earthborn, taking the well-winged inspired prey,
reining back its back-strained head,
spreading out its bare, free throat,
sacrificed the self-offering eagle with the knife
to Zeus and the lord of the waters; and as the conscious bird
was slain by the iron, from its newly-slaughtered throat
the wondrous blood flowed, and with divine drops
it rooted the sea-faring crags in the sea
near Tyre beside the deep; and on the unbreakable rocks
the Earthborn built a deep-bosomed nurse.
To you, lord Dionysus, I have told of the earth-nourished blood
of the Giants, self-born, Olympian, that you may learn
the Tyrian, earthborn stock of your forefathers;
and about the springs I shall tell; for primeval
maidens were they once, prudent, against whose girdle
hot Eros was wroth, and drawing his desire-bearing shaft
he framed such a word to the marriage-shunning Nymphs:
'Naiad Abarbarea, maiden-lover, receive you too
this shaft, which all Nature has felt; here I will fix
the bridal chamber of Callirhoë, and sing the wedding-song of Drosera.
But you will say: I belong to the watery race, and from the streams
I came to be self-fulfilled, and a spring was my nurse.
Clymene was a Naiad and an offshoot of Ocean;
but she yielded to marriage, and she too was wedded,
when she saw the servant of Eros, the mightier dark-haired god,
stirred by the Cyprian sting; and primeval
Ocean, ruling the rivers and all the waters,
knows the love of Tethys and watery weddings.
Endure, you too, to bear what Tethys bears. And though she carries
the blood of so great a sea and of no small spring,
Galatea longs for singing Polyphemus,
and, of the deep, has a landsman for her husband, and from the sea,
charmed by the lyre, a wanderer she comes to the land.
And the springs know my shaft; I will not teach you
a watery desire; from the desire-smitten spring
you have heard the watery love of Syracusan Arethusa;
you have learned of Alpheus, who, by the moist bridal bed,
with watery hands embraces his wonted Nymph.
Bearing the blood of a spring, why do you delight in the Archer-goddess?
Artemis did not spring from water, as Aphrodite did.
Tell it to Callirhoë; do not hide it from Drosera too.
To the Cyprian you should rather give thanks, since she too
bent her neck to Eros, even if she is the nurse of the Loves.
Receive the goads of longing, and I will call you a water-dweller
in your race, in love a sister of Aphrodite.'
Such a word he spoke; and from his back-strained bow
he sent triple shafts, and at the well-watered bridal bed
he joined the sons of the soil in the love of the Naiads,
and sowed the god-born blood of the Tyrian race."
Such things Heracles, captain of heaven, spoke to Bacchus
with mind-delighting words; and he delighted his heart at the tale,
and gave to Heracles, which heavenly craft had wrought,
a golden-gleaming, light-bearing mixing-bowl; and Heracles
clothed Dionysus in a starry tunic,
and, leaving the starry-robed god as protector of Tyre,
Bacchus set foot upon the soil of another Assyria.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
41. The first of the forties holds whence, for the son of Myrrha,
Aphrodite bore another Cypris, Amymone.
Just now, above the brows of beetling Lebanon,
having fixed the bright-fruited cluster of autumn upon the earth,
he made drunk all the wine-bearing hollows of the field;
and he saw the bridal house of the Paphian; and roofing over
a deep-shaded grove with newly-planted shoots of the vine,
he gave a vine-clad gift to Adonis and Cythereia.
And there was a chorus of Graces; and from the growth-rich thicket,
leaping with a mounting throb upon the girdle of the vines,
the high-flying ivy was wreathed about the cypress.
But beside the neighbouring shore of law-administering Beroe—
tell, you Lebanon Muses, the hymn of Amymone,
and of the deep-dwelling son of Cronos and of well-hymned Lyaeus
the watery war and the vine-clad battle.
There is a city, Beroe, the keel of life, the harbour of the Loves,
sea-built, fair-islanded, well-verdured, where the spine of the isthmus
is narrow though long, where, midway between the twin brine,
its upright neck is lashed by the waves on either side.
But its parts beneath the deep-treed ridge of the burning East-wind
lie spread out toward Assyrian Lebanon, where for the citizens
the life-giving breeze comes whistling upright,
as the cypresses are shaken by the fragrant winds . . .
the old shepherd, fellow of the fisherman, made his music.
And there is a house of the country-folk, where often near the thicket
sickle-bearing Deo met Pan as he piped,
and some farmer, bending his neck over the plough-tree,
sprinkling the freshly-furrowed earth with the back-cast seed,
beside the foot of the pasture wood, near the neighbouring shepherd,
yoking his pair of bulls, the bent ploughman held converse.
But the city has other parts beside the seas, where she stretches
her breast to Poseidon, and the watery husband enfolds
the embryonic neck of the maiden with his dripping arm,
sending watery kisses upon the lips of his bride;
and from his deep hand the bedfellow receives in her wonted lap
the sea-fed flocks of the mere, the wedding-gifts of Poseidon,
the fishy, many-coloured banquets of the table,
leaping upon the sea-table of Nereus,
beside the northern foot, where, by the deep-waved shore,
the northern channel is drawn through a long hollow.
And about the southern neck of the mind-delighting land,
toward the Southern shore, are sandy paths
into the Sidonian land, where the varied trees of gardens
and the grape-clusters luxuriate, and with long-branched leaves
the shady road is stretched for unerring wayfarers.
And, slanting its stream upon the shore, the sea beats
about the dark-faced west, where with shrill-sounding wing,
as Zephyr rides over the western channels,
with a dewy whistle the Libyan elbow is fanned,
where is a flowery place, where, beside the neighbouring sea,
the plantations flourish, and from the fair-leaved trees
the living wood makes music with humming breath.
Here once dwelt men, coevals of the dawn,
whom self-begotten Nature, by some unwedded ordinance,
sowed apart from marriage—fatherless, unborn, motherless—
when, with the four-yoked bond of the mingling atoms,
the unsown slime, shaping a wise birth
mingled of water and fire and the vapour of air,
gave living soul to the offspring in its pregnant mud,
to whom Nature granted a fulfilling form; for they had not
the shape of primeval Cecrops, who with the venom-darting drag of his foot,
scraping the earth, trailed along with his serpent sole,
a dragon below, and above, from the loins to the head,
appeared a misshapen, unfinished, two-coloured man;
they had not the wild shape of Erechtheus, whom Hephaestus begot
upon the furrow of Earth, wedding her with bridal dew;
but, an image of the gods' offspring, from a native root,
the golden corn-ear of men was first brought to birth.
And they settled Beroe, the city, the first-sown seat,
which Cronos himself built, when, at the nod of wise Rhea,
he set a chill banquet for his all-gulping throat.
And taking the stone, Eileithyia, in his heavy load,
the missile of his pressed, many-childed offspring,
gulping the whole river's stream like a cloud,
he stood the birth-aiding water in his foaming breast,
loosing the swelling of his belly; and, driving forth in succession
his twice-born sons, his pregnant throat belched them up,
holding the birth-channel, the throat the place of delivery.
Zeus then was a boy, still perhaps an infant; never yet
splitting the warm cloud with a dancing throb
did the lightning flash, nor in the Titan war
were the helping thunderbolts of Zeus shot forth;
nor, as the clouds came together with bellowing whirl,
did the heavy-thundering rainy echo of thunder roar.
But the city Beroe was earlier, which together with the earth
first-appearing Aion, her coeval and fellow-grown, beheld;
not then was Tarsus, the delight of mortals, not then Thebes,
not then was Sardis, where, by the bank of Pactolus
that belches gold, the rich mud glitters,
Sardis, coeval with the Sun; not then the race of men,
not then was there any Achaean city, nor even
pre-lunar Arcadia; she alone sprang up,
older than Phaethon, whence the Moon got her light.
And, anticipating all the earth, in her all-mothering bosom
drawing the new-shining gleam of the sun's radiance
and the late-perfected light of unsleeping Selene,
first she shook off the cone of dark mist,
and thrust away the gloomy veil of chaos;
and, anticipating Cyprus and the Isthmian city of Corinth,
first she received Cypris at her hospitable gate
newly born from the sea, when the heavenly water,
pregnant, brought forth Aphrodite from the deep furrow,
where, ploughing the stream apart from marriage with a male gore,
the self-fulfilled offspring took shape in the daughter-bearing foam,
and Nature was the midwife; and, rising together with the goddess,
the dappled band, winding a circle round her waist like a crown,
girdled the body of the queen with a self-made cincture.
And the goddess, tracking through the water the soundless shore,
ran not to Paphos, nor to Byblos, nor set foot on the dry land
of the Coliad strand, but with a swifter
eddy she ran past even the city of Cythera itself;
and rubbing her skin with the seaweed cluster
she became the more empurpled; and of the waveless sea,
oaring her hands, she clove the goddess-bearing water
as she swam, and, spreading her breast upon the sea,
she beat back the silent brine furrowed by her sole,
and lifted up her body, and, as the calm was cleft,
with alternating feet she thrust the water behind;
and she set foot on Beroe; and the dweller of Cyprus
lied about the goddess's footsteps as she came from the sea.
First it received Cypris; and high above the neighbouring harbour
the self-grown meadows, belching up the moss of the grass,
bloomed here and there, and in the sandy bay
the shores grew red with rosy clusters,
and the foaming rock, pregnant with fragrant wine,
bore a purple birth at its torrent breast,
a shadowy shower of dew with the wine-press streams . . .
the silvery gush rippled in a milky channel;
and, whirling aloft the vapour of self-poured perfume,
the fragrant breeze made drunk the airy passages.
And then bold Eros, the first-sown beginning of offspring,
the life-bringing charioteer of the cosmos's harmony,
newly-appearing she bore upon the brows of the neighbouring harbour;
and the swift-footed child, shaking off the manly weariness of his feet,
anticipated the birth-aiding hour of the unmidwived womb,
striking the closed bosom of his unwedded mother,
warm still before the birth; and with a tumbling throb,
whirling his light wings, he opened the gates of delivery.
And quickly, leaping upon his mother's radiant forearm,
restless Eros bounded upon her unbending breasts,
stretched out on the child-nursing chest; and he had a longing
for food, self-taught; and of the unmilked teat,
biting the tip, pressed by the swelling of its fertile streams,
insatiate he drained all the milk of the swollen breasts.
Root of life, Beroe, nurse of cities, boast of kings,
first-appearing, coeval of Aion, contemporary of the cosmos,
seat of Hermes, plain of Justice, city of laws,
home of Euphrosyne, house of the Paphian, dwelling of the Loves,
the pleasant seat of Bacchus, the haunt of the Archer-goddess,
the offering of the Nereids, the house of Zeus, the court of Ares,
the Orchomenus of the Graces, the star of the Lebanon land,
coeval of Tethys, fellow-runner of Ocean,
who begot Beroe at his many-fountained bridal bed
mingling in the moist weddings of Tethys,
whom they named Amymone, when her mother
bore her in the deep bed of watery love.
But there is a younger tale, that she herself,
Cythereia, the steerer of the human race,
all-white, bore as mother to Assyrian Adonis;
and, fulfilling the ninefold course of the Moon,
she eased her load; and anticipating her with swift foot,
lifting up the herald of things to come, a Latin tablet,
to Beroe's travail came birth-aiding Hermes,
and Themis Eileithyia, and through the swollen bosom,
unfolding the veil of the straitened travail,
she eased the sharp shaft of the ripening birth,
holding the ordinances of Solon; and, pressed by the delivery,
leaning her heavy back upon the birth-loosing goddess,
Cypris was in travail, and high upon an Attic book
she bore the wise child, as Laconian women
travail with their sons upon a well-rounded oxhide;
and the newly-born offspring she spat from her female bosom,
having a male midwife, the judge, the son of Maia;
and she brought the babe to the light. And they bathed the girl,
the four winds galloping through all the cities,
that from Beroe they might fill the whole earth with ordinances;
and to her in travail, still the first messenger of laws,
Ocean gave the birth-stream to the waist of the cosmos,
pouring the girdling water with an everflowing baldric;
and with aged hands, upon the skin of the newly-born girl,
Aion her foster-father lifted up the swaddling robes of Justice,
prophet of things to come, that, changing the burden of old age,
like a serpent shaking off the coil of his feeble scales,
he might grow young again, bathed in the streams of the laws;
and over Aphrodite's god-sent daughter in travail
the four-yoked Hours struck up a concordant strain.
And learning of the Paphian's birth-completing travail,
the beasts revelled; and some lion, sporting tenderly,
with gentle lips embraced the spine of a bull,
sending a friendly lowing from his lips' edge,
and the horse, striking the deep-thudding ground with its rolling hoof,
clattered, beating out a natal sound,
and, leaping with a mounting throb of its high-stepping foot,
the dapple-backed leopard bounded against a hare,
and, pouring the howl's wail from its playful throat,
with unscratching jaws the wolf embraced the flock,
and some hound in the thickets, leaving the deer-rousing hunt,
holding another sweet sting, in a contesting dance
vied as a dancer with a capering boar,
and, raising its feet and entwined about its neck,
the bear embraced a heifer with a harmless bond,
and, often curving the kiss-loving rim of its temples,
the calf leapt up, licking the body of a lioness,
sending a half-formed lowing from its young jaws,
and the serpent touched the friendly tusks of the elephant;
and the oaks spoke; and with a serene face
smile-loving Aphrodite sent her wonted laughter,
beholding the birth-festal games of the delighting beasts.
On all she rolled the joyful circle of her gaze,
on all alike; only she would not look upon the delight
of the swine, like a prophetess, since in the shape of a swine
sharp-toothed Ares, hurling his death-bearing venom,
jealous-mad, was destined to weave doom for Adonis.
And taking Beroe, still a laughing babe, in the clasp of her hands
from her mother, the nurse of the whole cosmos,
the maiden Astraea, nurturer of the golden race,
nursed her at her prudent breast as she lawfully babbled;
and with maiden milk, gushing the streams of ordinances,
she moistened the child's lips, and let flow into the girl's mouth,
pressing out the elaborate travail of the much-pierced delivery
of the sweet-bearing Attic bee,
speaking honeycombs mingled in a wise cup;
and whenever, thirsty, she asked for drink, she held out to the girl
the Pythian water reserved, garrulous, for Apollo,
or the stream of Ilissus, which, breathing with the Attic Muse,
the Pierian Phoebean breezes ruffle upon its shore;
and curving a starry corn-ear into a cluster,
golden, like a necklace, she set it on the girl's neck.
And the bathing maidens, dancers of Orchomenus,
the handmaids of the Paphian, dear to the nine Muses,
drew from the spring the wise horse-water.
And Beroe grew up, fellow-runner of the Archer-goddess,
lifting the hunting-nets of her father the huntsman;
and she had the whole kindred form of the Paphian her mother,
and her radiant feet; and, peering above the sea,
Thetis, leaping with snowy capering sole,
saw another silver-footed Thetis; and in shame
she hid, dreading again the boast of Cassiepeia.
And, having marked another Assyrian unwedded maiden,
Zeus again was excited, and wished to change his shape;
and now, bearing the burden of Eros in bull-faced form,
dipping his hooves, he would have been carried, plying his step through the water,
lifting the undrenched woman upon his back,
had not the memory of the bull-horned wedding restrained him,
the Sidonian one; and a starry strain with jealous throat
the bridegroom of Europa lowed, the Bull of Olympus,
lest, making through the air the image of a like-shaped ox,
he should set up a younger sea-faring star of the Loves;
and Beroe, owed to the watery weddings,
he left as bride for his brother, guarding for the earthly bride
the marriage-strife of the Earth-shaker.
Such was Beroe, the bloom of the Graces; if ever the maiden
uttered a voice sweeter and more honey-flowing than the hive,
sweet-spoken, insatiate Persuasion sat upon her lips
and stung the prudent minds of unbewitchable men;
and the gathering of the Assyrian youth of her age was outshone
by her laughing eyes, the dart-throwers of the Loves,
with brighter graces, as much as the Moon hides the stars,
shooting her cloudless rays
when full; and white about the lowest ankles of the maiden
the tunics grew red upon her purple limbs.
There was no blame in this, even if, more than the youth of her age,
she got so great a beauty, since indeed about her face
the bright beauties of her two parents glittered.
Cypris then, seeing her, pregnant with a prudent thought,
whirled a swifter purpose, turning it about,
and, galloping her mind round the whole wandering earth,
measured the bright seats of the old-born cities,
that, as bright-eyed Mycenae held the name
of Mycene, girded with a wall-crown,
by the rules of the Cyclopes, and as, beside the southern Nile,
Thebe was named after primeval Thebe;
so she longed to mark out a city named after Beroe,
following the city-loving sting of the answering Loves.
And, taking thought of the line of Solon's evil-averting laws,
she stretched a sidelong eye toward broad-streeted Athens,
holding zeal for her sister the judge; and in haste
she whistled through the airy arch with her sandal
to the house of all-mothering Harmonia, where the nymph
dwelt in a house like the four-yoked pattern of the cosmos,
self-built; and four doors of the strong hall,
unbreakable, were girt about by the four winds;
and the handmaids guarded the round house, the image of the cosmos,
here and there; and as the portals were divided,
the handmaid Dawn ran round the gate of the East-wind,
and Sunset, nurse of the Moon, the portal of Zephyr,
and the South held the fiery bar of the Southwind,
and the North, the handmaid, dense with clouds, sprinkled with hail,
spread open the gate of Boreas.
There Charis, leaping forth, companion of the foam-born,
knocked at the Eastern portal of the East-wind; and within,
as the saffron gate of the East was struck,
Astynomeia the messenger ran up, and, beholding
Cypris standing beside the forecourt of the hall,
with returning feet came as forerunner to her mistress.
She, busy at the much-wrought loom of Athena,
was weaving a robe with the shuttle; and as the tunic was woven,
first she set the navel-earth in the midst, and round the earth
she made the heaven a sphere, marked with the pattern of the stars,
and fitted the conjoined sea to the yoked earth;
and she wrought the rivers in varied colours, and upon a human brow
a bull-shaped, horned, green-tinted image took form;
and along the lowest hem of the well-spun tunic
she circled Ocean, running round with the rim of the cosmos.
And her handmaid came, and near the female loom
announced Aphrodite standing at the forecourt.
And the goddess, when she heard, throwing down the threads of the tunic,
shook from her loom-toiling hands the wondrous shuttle;
and swiftly, covering her body with a snowy robe,
brighter than gold she rose above her wonted seat,
receiving Cythereia, and, springing up from her throne,
she honoured Aphrodite approaching from afar.
And long-robed Eurynome set the Paphian on a throne near her mistress;
and with troubled face,
watching Cypris with a downcast, witnessing look,
all-nourishing Harmonia soothed her with a friendly word:
"Root of life, Cythereia, plant-sower, midwife of birth,
hope of the whole cosmos, at the nod of your counsel
the unerring Fates spin the many-turning threads . . .
. . . prophesy to me who ask, and, as nurse of life,
as nurturer of the immortals, as contemporary of the coeval cosmos,
tell me: to which of cities are the organs of royal speech,
the unshaken reins of the toil-loosing laws, reserved?
For, since, stirred by the sting of his long-time desire,
holding the goad of Hera's, of his sister's, weddings,
longing through the time of three hundred years,
I yoked Zeus in marriage; and a thanks worthy of my works,
the wage of his marriage-chamber, he nodded with prudent head,
that to one of the cities which I obtained he would entrust
the ordinances of Justice; and I long to know whether to the land of Cyprus
or to Paphos these gifts are reserved, or to Corinth,
or to Sparta, whence Lycurgus came, or even
to the manly fatherland of my own daughter Beroe.
But have regard for justice, and grant harmony to the cosmos,
you who were born Harmonia, life-giving; for to you
the nurse of law-administering men sent me in haste,
the starry maiden; and the more, lawful Hermes
relinquished this privilege, that I alone might save by the ordinances of marriage
the violated men whom I sowed."
So she spoke, and the goddess emboldened her and answered with a word:
"Be bold, do not fear, mother of the Loves;
for in seven tablets I hold the oracles of the cosmos,
and the tablets are named after the seven planets.
The first is named after the well-rolling Moon;
the second is called the golden tablet of Hermes,
gleaming, on which all the rites of the laws are wrought;
the third, rosy, bears your name; for it carries
the type of your star, the Morning star; and of the seven-wayed
planets, the fourth is the central one of the Sun;
the fifth, reddening, fiery, is called Ares;
and Phaethon, the wanderer of Cronos's son, is named the sixth;
the seventh shows the name of high-going Cronos.
On these all the varied decrees of the cosmos, fated,
old Ophion engraved with Phoenician letters.
But, since you ask me concerning the laws of right-minded men,
to the eldest of cities I reserve these privileges:
whether, then, Arcadia was earlier, or the city of Hera,
whether Sardis was older, or whether even
much-sung Tarsus was the first city, or some other,
I did not learn; but the Cronian tablet teaches all these things,
which was earlier born, which was contemporary with Dawn."
She spoke; and led the way to the bright decrees of the wall,
until she saw the place where, concerning Beroe's fatherland,
a late-fulfilled prophecy the Ophionian craft had written
on the Cronian tablet, engraved in wine-dark vermilion:
"First-appearing Beroe was contemporary with the coeval cosmos,
named after a later-born nymph, whom the migrant
sons of the Ausonians, the consular lights of Rome,
will call Berytus, since she fell as neighbour to Lebanon . . ."
Such a prophetic word she learned. But when the goddess
had measured the wondrous beginning of the seventh tablet,
she gazed at the second, where, beside the neighbouring wall,
varied marvels of every kind of craft were engraved
with prophetic words: that first of all there should come to know
country-loving Pan the pipe, Heliconian Hermes the lyre,
tender Hyagnis the two-voiced strain of the well-pierced flute,
Orpheus the god-speaking streams of mystic song,
and Linus the Phoebean eloquence, the Arcadian wanderer
the twelve-month measures and the course of the Sun,
the mother of the begotten years on her four-yoked car,
and wise Endymion, bending his shifting fingers,
should know the restless cycles of the returning Moon,
threefold; and, mingling element with element, the unyoked with the yoked,
Cadmus should teach the rites of well-tongued speech,
Solon the spotless ordinances, and upon Attic torch
Cecrops the twin pair of unbreakable conjunction.
And the Paphian, after all the many-turning marvels of the Muse,
measured the dense works of the far-spread cities;
and over the middle rim of the painted tablet of the cosmos
she found there a wise, many-versed word in the Hellene Muse:
"When Augustus shall hold the sceptre of the whole earth,
to holy Rome the Ausonian Zeus will grant
dominion, but to Beroe he grants the reins of the laws,
when, armed upon shield-bearing ships,
she lulls to rest the war of water-fighting Cleopatra;
for before that, city-sacking wickedness will never cease
to disturb the city-saving peace, until
Berytus, the nurse of serene life, judges
both land and sea, with the unbending wall of laws
fortifying the cities, one city, the cities of the cosmos."
And the goddess, when she had learned all the Ophionian oracle,
went back to her own house, returning; and as her son sat
she set her golden-wrought seat near him,
and, taking him about the middle in her arms, with serene face,
embraced the boy in her outstretched, joyful arm,
lifting the dear burden on her knees; and both
his mouth she kissed and his eyes; and, touching
the mind-charming bow and handling the quiver,
as if vexed, she broke into a guileful word:
"Hope of all life, comfort of the foam-born,
the pitiless son of Cronos has alone done violence to my children;
for, having filled the nine birth-aiding cycles of the Moon,
wielding the sharp shaft of grievous birth,
I bore Harmonia, and she suffers varied pains,
grieving; but a girl in travail Leto received,
Artemis Eileithyia, the helper of women.
Child of Amymone, of one womb, I will not teach you
how I got blood from the sea and from the sky; but I wished
to accomplish a worthy work, that beside my mother the sea,
born from heaven, I might fix heaven also upon the earth;
but stretching upon the beauty of your sister . . .
charm the gods, and the more send an equal shaft, in one ordinance,
to Poseidon and to vine-clad Lyaeus,
to both the blessed ones; and I will grant you, worthy of your toils,
a fitting wage befitting your far-shooting:
I will give you a golden bridal lyre, which at the bridal bed
Phoebus gave to Harmonia, and I will entrust to you
a memorial of the city that is to be, that you may be,
even after the archer, a lyre-player, like Apollo.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
42. I have woven the fortieth a second time, where I sing
the pleasant love of Bacchus and the desire of the Earth-shaker.
So speaking she persuaded him; and with high-soaring sandal
hot Eros, unattainable, plying his wind-borne foot,
high in the clouds scored the air with his winged sole,
bearing his flaming bow. And slung from his shoulder
his quiver too, full of gentle fire, was loosened.
And as, through the cloudless sky, a swift wayfarer,
the upright star stretches itself with a long-drawn spark,
bearing a portent either to an army at war or to some sailor,
and writes upon the back of heaven with a trailing track of fire;
so then bold Eros, borne with a sharp whirring,
hurling the windy hum of his quivering wings,
whizzed down from the air; and beside the Assyrian rock
he joined two fiery shafts upon one string,
drawing into a like longing, by love of the maiden,
two suitors of like-zealous weddings,
the vine-clustered god and the charioteer of the sea.
Then the one, leaving the deep wave of the sea-neighbouring harbour,
the other, past the foot of Tyre, within the heights of Lebanon,
met at one place. From his grim car
Maron loosed the sweating leopard from its harness,
and shook off the dust and washed with spring water,
cooling the hot, chafed neck of the beasts.
There, coming unattained, Eros, upon the neighbouring maiden,
struck both gods with his twin arrow,
making Dionysus frenzied to bring treasures to the bride,
the gladness of life and the wine-dark cluster of autumn,
and stinging into love the steersman of the trident
to bring a double love-gift to the sea-neighbouring maiden,
the watery war of ships and the varied banquets of the table.
And he inflamed Bacchus the more, since wine rouses the mind
