to desire, and much more than the young, with maddening goad,
he held the bewitched, unbridled, obedient youth;
Eros shot Bacchus, fixing the whole shaft in his heart;
and he inflamed him as much as he bewitched, dripping the honey of persuasion.
And he stung them both; and through the airy path,
wheeling his course, fellow-runner with the dappled winds,
the bastard bird hovered on his swimming sandal,
shouting such a mocking word: if Dionysus stirs men with wine,
I rouse Bacchus with fire.
And the vine-god, stretching his eye opposite,
measured the tender body of the fair-tressed bride,
holding a wonder that channelled into desire; and, as it began,
his eye became the forerunning passage of the Loves.
Dionysus wandered within the heart-delighting wood,
secretly stretching a guarded eye toward Beroe,
and step by step he went behind into the maiden's path;
nor was there satiety in his gazing; for as long as he beheld
the maiden standing, so much the more he wished to look.
And, recalling the love of Clymene, he besought
the captain of the stars, the Sun, on his back-strained car,
to draw tight with airy rein his halted horse
and lengthen the sweet light, so that day might come slowly to its setting,
nursing again the recurring day with a sparing whip.
And, measuring his step on Beroe's footprints, foot by foot,
as if not knowing her, he ran about; and from Lebanon
stealthily hiding the trace of his hesitating foot, the Earth-shaker
gave way with a turning, slow-yielding sole,
and held an unsteady mind like the sea,
foaming with the waves of loud-roaring care.
And, insatiate of the sweet Lebanon wood,
Dionysus was alone beside the lonely bride,
Dionysus was alone. Tell, you mountain Nymphs.
What else more dear did he wish than, alone,
to see the maiden's skin, free of the ill-loving Earth-shaker?
And he kissed with countless kisses, creeping secretly,
the place where she set her foot, and the dust she trod
as the maiden, illuminating it with rosy sandal;
and Bacchus gazed at her sweet neck, and the ankles of the maiden
as she walked, and the beauty which Nature granted the bride,
the beauty which Nature found; and not in golden adornment,
anointed, did Beroe redden the rosy circles of her face,
empurpling her false cheeks with a bastard spark,
nor in the clear witness of answering bronze
did her beauty laugh, judging itself
in the lifeless image of mimicking sight, nor, with an artful rule,
often equalling the tips of her hair beside her brows,
did she set in place the migrant cluster of her wandering tresses.
But the woman-maddening man is far more, with a sharp goad,
stirred by the splendours of an unkempt face,
and the dirty locks of an unadorned head
are the more tender, when, unplaited and wandering,
they range in rows beside the snowy face.
And once, thirsting, she went to a neighbouring spring,
scourged by the vapour of the heavenly fiery Dog,
with parched lips; and bending her head down
she stooped, arching herself, and often into her mouth the maiden
with deep-cupped hands drew her native water,
until, sated, she left the streams; and as she withdrew,
Dionysus, bending his knee at the lovely spring,
hollowing his palms, imitated the lovely maiden,
drinking water sweeter than self-poured nectar.
And, beholding him stirred by the goad of desire,
the deep-bosomed, unsandalled spring-Nymph cried out:
"Cold water, Dionysus, you drank in vain; for the whole stream
of Ocean cannot quench the thirst of love.
Ask your father, that, crossing so great a wave,
the bridegroom of Europa did not quench his lovely fire,
but laboured still more in the waters; and of the water-faring
servant of Eros you have a witness, wandering Alpheus,
who, dragging waters through water with so many surges,
did not flee hot love, even though he was a watery wayfarer."
So speaking she sank into the kindred spring-water,
the unveiled Naiad, laughing at Lyaeus.
And the god, grudging against Poseidon, lord of the waters,
held fear and jealousy, since the maiden drank water
instead of wine, and broke into a deaf air with his voice,
as if he had the obedient maiden listening:
"Maiden, receive the nectar; leave the maiden-loving water;
flee the spring-drink, lest the watery dark-haired god
steal your maidenhood in the waters,
for he is woman-mad and crafty; you know the love
of Thessalian Tyro and the water-faring weddings;
and you too guard against the crafty stream, lest the false one
loose your girdle, as the marriage-thief Enipeus did.
Would that I too had become a stream, like the Earth-shaker,
and, murmuring, embraced beside the desire-smitten spring
my thirsty, unguarded Lebanon Tyro."
The god spoke; and changing the altered form of his limbs,
where the maiden was, Euios entered the shady wood
all like a huntsman; and to the soft-tressed,
unyoked maiden, misshapen and unknown, he drew near,
like a young man, and steadfast about his face
he fashioned a false mimicry of prudent modesty;
and now he gazed at the top of a lonely crag,
now into the deep-shaded ridge of the long-branched wood,
turning his longing eye toward a pine, at other times a fir
or an elm he watched; but, guarding his face,
with stealthy eyes he beheld the neighbouring maiden,
lest, transformed, she should escape him; for to a young man
gazing on beauty, the eyes of a maiden of his age
are a small comfort of the Cyprian Loves.
And he came near Beroe and wished to speak a word,
but was fettered by fear: O reveller, where are your thyrsi,
the man-slayers? Where the dreadful horns? Where, in your hair,
the grey, serpentine bonds of earth-bred dragons?
Where the deep-thundering bellow of your mouths? Ah, great wonder,
Bacchus trembled before a maiden, whom the tribes of Giants trembled;
fear of the Loves conquered the destroyer of the Earthborn;
and he who mowed down the race of so many war-mad Indians
feared one lovely, defenceless maiden,
feared a soft-skinned woman; and in the hills
with his beast-taming fennel-wand he soothed the lions'
dreadful bellow, and trembled before a woman's threat;
and to him a wandering word, beneath his startled mouth,
stretched toward his lips' tip, a neighbour to his tongue,
darting from his mind and creeping back to his mind;
but holding a bittersweet fear, in modest silence
he drew back into the light the recurring voice as it hastened.
And scarcely, beating beneath his mouth the late-spoken bond,
he loosed the delay-working silence of his modesty,
and questioned Beroe, pouring a deceiving voice:
"Artemis, where are your bow? Who seized your quiver?
Where have you left the tunic you wear down to your knee?
Where are those sandals of yours, swifter than the wheeling breeze?
Where the chorus of handmaids? Where the nets? Where the white hounds?
You make ready no deer-rousing course; for you do not wish
to hunt, where Cypris sleeps near Adonis."
He spoke, holding a deceiving wonder; and in her heart
the maiden smiled; and with an inexperienced purpose
she lifted her proud neck, exulting in the grace of youth,
since, though she was a woman, in form she was like a goddess;
nor did she know the guile of mind-wandering Dionysus.
And Bacchus grieved the more, since the maiden did not learn desire,
having a childlike disposition, and he wished that she might learn
his grievous sting, since, when a maiden knows it,
a late hope of the Loves is left for the young man
of love that is to be, but at a fruitless purpose
men long, when women are ignorant.
And the god, day upon day, within the pine-wood,
at evening, at midday, at morning, at the Evening-star, creeping,
remained beside the maiden, and wished still to remain;
for of all things there is satiety among men, of sweet sleep
and of well-sounding song, and when a man bends
into the dancer's course; but for the woman-maddened man alone
there is no satiety of desires; the book of Homer lied.
And, toiling, Dionysus bellowed beneath in silence,
struck by a divine scourge, digesting within
the hidden, heart-deep wound of the unsleeping Loves,
as when an unattained ox, going within a flat rock,
measured the wonted swarm of mountain-roaming bulls,
stung from the herd, whom, beside a fair-leaved thicket,
the ox-striking gadfly scratched with a sharp goad,
unforeseen, and, with his body struck by a small sting,
huge as he was, he was driven wild, and upright high on his back
he drew back his recurring tail,
arching, rubbing the spine of the rocks, and, in answer,
he slanted his sharp horn, striking the woundless air;
so Dionysus too, whom victory often crowned,
little Eros stung, striking with his all-bewitching goad.
And late, seeking a sweet remedy in Aphrodite,
he revealed to the Cyprian his sleepless compulsion,
and asked her counsel, the helper of the Loves.
And hearing the fire-breathing toils of Bacchus,
horned Pan laughed, but was broken in his purpose,
pitying the ill-loved, himself ill in love; and he spoke
the Cyprian counsel; and he had a small comfort of the Loves,
seeing another inflamed by the spark of one quiver:
"Suffering in common, dear Bacchus, I have pitied your cares;
how did bold Eros conquer you too? If it is right to say it,
upon me and Dionysus Eros emptied his quiver.
But I will tell you the many-turning ways of crafty desire.
Every woman desires more than a man, but in shame
she hides the goad of Eros, herself love-maddened too,
and she toils much more, since the sparks of the Loves
grow hotter, when women hide
the dart of the Loves pierced deep within their hearts.
For when they tell one another the compulsion of desires,
with toil-loosing converse they steal away their Cyprian cares.
But you, Bacchus, the channeller of your Loves,
bearing the blush of a mimicking, deceiving modesty,
as if holding a prudent, unsmiling look,
as if unwilling, stand near Beroe; and, brandishing your nets,
with a guileful wonder gaze at the rosy maiden,
praising her beauty, that Hera got not so great a one,
and call the Graces inferior, and to the form of both,
Artemis and Athena, attach blame,
and declare Beroe brighter than Aphrodite;
and the maiden, hearing your deceiving reproach,
stands the more, delighting in the praise; for she does not wish
to hear of all golden wealth as much as about her rosy form,
that her beauty surpassed the youth of her age.
And charm the maiden to love with a prudent silence,
sending opposite nods of your moving eyelids;
and, striking your open brow with unsparing hand,
show a false wonder in prudent silence.
But fear holds you near the prudent maiden;
tell me, what will one maiden do to you? She brandishes no spear,
she stretches no shaft in rosy hand; the maiden's spears
are her eyes, the dart-throwers of the Loves,
and the maiden's shafts are her rosy cheeks.
And as the wedding-gifts of your desire, the treasures for your bride,
do not shake out Indian stone or pearls with your hand,
as is the custom for the woman-mad; for to the Paphian
you tend your own form, sufficient; and of soft-touched
beauty, not of gold, do women long.
I need no other witness; for of soft-tressed Endymion
what gifts did Selene receive?
What love-gift did Adonis show to Cypris?
Orion gave no silver to the Dawn;
Cephalus gave no lovely wealth; but indeed alone
Hephaestus, lame as he was, for the sake of an unbewitching form
gave varied gifts, and did not persuade Athena;
his bridal axe did not avail; but, longing for the goddess,
he failed. But I will teach you, better than the yoking of weddings,
if you wish, another charm:
sound the lyre with your hand, the offering of your Rhea,
the tender, wine-pleasing image of Cypris; and with both
plectrum and mouth pour a varied echo.
First sing of Daphne and the course of unsteady Echo
and the after-voicing clatter of the unsilenced goddess,
that they hated the gods who desired them; but also
sing of Pitys herself, the bed-shunning, fellow-runner of the mountain breezes,
fleeing the unwedded weddings of Pan;
sing of her death, native, when she perished; reproach the earth.
And perhaps she will weep at the pains of the mournful nymph
and pity her death; and you, delight your heart in silence,
beholding the honey-sweet tears of the mourning maiden;
nor is there such laughter, since the more, in wine-dark form,
they are lovely, when women lament.
Sing of Selene love-mad for Endymion,
sing of the marriage of graceful Adonis, tell too of
Aphrodite herself, squalid, unsandalled, wandering,
tracking her mountain-roaming bridegroom; nor will it escape you,
hearing the honey-minded ordinance of your father's Loves.
To you I declare all these things, ill-loved Bacchus;
but you too teach me the charm for my Echo."
So speaking he sent away the joyful son of Thyone.
And Dionysus, holding a guileful, unsmiling look,
questioned the maiden about Adonis her father,
as a friend, as a mountain-roaming fellow-hunter; and as she stood
he brought his ill-loving hand near her breast, and the edge of her girdle,
as if unwilling, he pressed; and touching her breasts
the right hand of woman-mad Dionysus grew numb.
And once, in childlike manners, the maiden asked
the son of Zeus, who was present, who he was and whose son;
and scarcely he found a pretext beside the forecourt of Aphrodite,
gazing at the vine-clad orchard and the bounteous cornfields of the earth
and the dewy meadow and the varied trees,
with crafty manners; and, like a tiller of the soil,
about marriage he spoke some word in obscure voice:
"I am a tiller of your Lebanon; if you wish,
I will water your land, I will swell your fruit.
I know the course of the four seasons; and watching
the appointed turning-post, the autumnal one, I will cry this:
'The life-giving Scorpion rises, and it is the herald
of the fruitful furrow; let us yoke the oxen to the plough.'
The Pleiades set; when shall we sow the fields?
The furrows are in travail, when the dew falls upon the earth
dried by Phaethon. And near the Arcadian Wain,
when winter has rained, beholding Arcturus, I will say:
'The thirsty earth is sometimes wedded by the rain of Zeus.'
When spring rises, at morning I will cry to you:
'Your flowers have bloomed; when shall I pluck the lilies and roses?
Behold, how the hyacinth runs over the neighbouring myrtle,
how the narcissus laughs, leaping upon the anemone.'
And, seeing the grape-cluster as summer comes, I will say:
'The youthful vine ripens, untouched by the sickle;
maiden, the harvest has come; when shall we gather the autumn fruit?'
Your corn-ear has grown and craves the reaping;
I will reap the corn-bearing crop, and instead of Deo
to your mother, the Cyprus-born, I will offer harvest-fruits.
And receive me as the tiller, the labourer of your threshing-floor;
take me as the gardener of your foam-born mother,
that I may fix a life-bearing plant, and of the vines
I may know the new-budding unripe grape, handling it with my hands.
I know whence the apples sometimes ripen; I know how to plant
the long-leaved elm propped against the cypress;
I mingle the male palm, rejoicing, with the female,
and the crocus, if you wish, I rear fair beside the yew.
Bring me no gold for the sake of my tendance; there is no need of wealth;
I have my wage: two apples, one cluster of a single autumn's fruit."
Such things he spoke in vain, and the maiden did not answer,
not understanding the line of words of woman-mad Bacchus.
But the Insewn-god devised another guile against guile;
and from Beroe's hand he received the hunting-nets
as if marvelling at their craft, and, shaking them densely,
he whirled them about for a while, and often asked the maiden:
"What god made these tools, what heavenly craft wrought them?
Who made them? For I have a disbelieving mind, that jealous-mad
Hephaestus would make hunting-gear for Adonis."
He spoke, leading astray the mind of the unbewitchable maiden.
And once, high above the spread leaves of the anemone,
he slept sweet sleep; and the maiden came to him in a dream,
clad in bridal raiment. For the answering image
of a work that one does by day, one beholds by night;
the herdsman, sleeping, drives his horned oxen to pasture;
to the huntsman a vision of dreams shows nets;
and the tillers, sleeping, plough the fields,
and sow the corn-bearing furrow; and a man,
midday-resting, gripped by burning thirst in the parched heat,
deceiving sleep drives toward a stream, toward a channel.
So Dionysus too, holding the images of his toils,
sent his winged mind in a mimicking dream,
and held converse in shadowy weddings. And waking,
he did not find the maiden, and wished to sleep again;
and he brought back an empty grace of a fleeting bed,
sleeping in the petals of the swift-perishing anemone.
And he reproached the spread of the voiceless petals; and grieving,
he begged sleep together with Eros and the evening Aphrodite
to see again the same vision of his dream,
longing for the deceiving portion of marriage. And near the myrtle
Bacchus often slept, and did not get the bridal sleep.
But he had a sweet toil, and, desire-smitten himself,
limb-loosing Dionysus was loosed in his limbs by care.
And to Beroe's father, the son of Myrrha, a companion,
he revealed the art of hunting; and with the dart-throwing thyrsus
he put on the dappled skins of newly-slaughtered fawns,
secretly watching for Beroe; and as he stood,
the maiden, guarding against the restless eye of Dionysus,
hid her cheek, gleaming, with her robe.
And she inflamed Bacchus the more, since the servants of the Loves
gaze the more at women who are still modest,
and long the more for the hidden face.
And once, beholding the unyoked maiden of Adonis alone,
he drew near, and from his human form
he changed his shape, and stood before the maiden as a god;
and he told her his race and his name, and the slaughter of the Indians,
and the vine-clad dance, and the outpouring of sweet-drunk wine,
that he found for men; and with affectionate purpose,
mingling boldness, alien to modesty, with shamelessness,
fawning he spoke such a varied-worded voice:
"Maiden, for your love I dwell in heaven no longer;
your fathers' caves are better than Olympus.
I love your fatherland more than the sky; I long not
for the sceptre of Zeus my father so much as for Beroe's wedding;
your beauty is higher than ambrosia; of airy
fragrant nectar your tunics breathe.
Maiden, I hold a wonder, hearing of your mother Cypris,
that the love-charm left you unbewitched; and how did you alone
have Eros for your brother and not learn the sting of the Loves?
But you will say: a grey-eyed maiden, untried in weddings;
apart from marriage Athena sprang, and knows no marriage;
no grey-eyed one bore you, nor Artemis. But you, maiden,
bearing the blood of Cypris, why do you flee the rites of Cypris?
Do not shame your mother's race; and of Assyrian,
graceful Adonis, if you truly carry the blood,
learn the soft, marriage-fulfilling ordinances of your father,
and obey the love-charm coeval with the girdle of the Paphian,
and beware the hard-to-meet wrath of the nuptial Loves;
pitiless are the Loves, when, as a debt, when as a penalty
they demand from women the price of fruitless love;
for you know how, dishonouring fiery Cythera,
the maiden-loving pipe gave the wage of pride,
since, become a plant in a bastard reedy form,
she escaped Pan's love, but still sings the desires of Pan;
and the daughter of Ladon, the much-sung river,
hating the works of marriage, made her body a tree, the Nymph,
breathing, whistling, and with an oracular cluster,
fleeing the bed of Phoebus, she crowned the hair of Phoebus.
And you too beware dreadful wrath, lest hot Eros,
heavy in wrath, grow angry with you; and not sparing your girdle,
tend Bacchus a twofold one, both follower and bedfellow;
and lifting the nets of your father Adonis myself
I would spread the bed of my sister Aphrodite.
What worthy gifts will the Earth-shaker bring you?
Will salt water be reckoned to you as wedding-gifts,
and will he spread, breathing the foul sea-smell,
the skins of seals, the Poseidonian robes of the sea?
Do not receive the skins of seals; but for your bridal bed
I will grant you Bacchant handmaids, Satyr servants;
receive from me wedding-gifts and the vine-clad autumn fruit;
and if you wish the furious spear of Adonis, like a maiden,
you have my thyrsus for a spear; leave the trident's point.
Flee, dear one, the evil noise of the unsilenced sea,
flee the Poseidonian sting of the hard-to-meet Loves.
The dark-haired god lay beside another Amymone,
but the woman, after the bed, became a spring of the same name;
and he slept beside Scylla and made her a sea-rock;
and he pursued Asterie, and she became a desert island;
and the maiden Euboea he rooted in the sea.
This one woos Amymone, that he may make her too
stone after the bed; this one will grant
as the gift of his chambers a little stream or sea-moss
or some deep-sea shell. But I, for the sake of your form,
stand vexed, what gifts, what gifts to bring you;
the child of golden Aphrodite craves no gold.
But I will bring you many treasures from Alybe;
the silver-armed one rejects silver. To you I will bring
gifts gleaming from light-bearing Eridanus;
all the wealth of the Heliades your form puts to shame,
reddening white, and, weighing equal to the rays of Dawn,
like amber Beroe's neck glitters . . .
and the flashing stone; the form of your skin confutes
the precious marbles; lest I bring you, like a blazing lamp,
a fire-stone, your eyes send forth a gleam;
lest I bring you roses as gifts, springing from the rosy
calyx of the cluster, your cheeks are rosy."
Such a word he spoke; and within her ear the maiden,
pressing her two hands, fenced off her hearing,
lest she hear again another word dear to Eros,
hating the works of marriage; and to desire-smitten Lyaeus
she mingled toil with toil. What is more cruel than the Loves,
than when, with the raging goad of soul-devouring desire,
women flee the men who long for them
and the prudent ones lead the sting the more? And hidden within,
twofold is love, when a maiden flees a man.
So he was scourged by the love-stinging love-charm;
but he stayed away from the maiden; and to the ungirdled-tunic maiden
he sent his wandering mind, running with her as it hunted,
holding a bittersweet goad. And, rushing up from the sea,
plying his wet footsteps through the thirsty mountain,
Poseidon the migrant sought the maiden,
sprinkling the dry land with watery sole;
and as he still hastened, beside the well-pastured slope of the wood
the topmost crests of the mountain quivered with the throb of his feet . . .
he gazed at Beroe, and from foot to head
he measured the inspired youth of the standing maiden;
and sharply, through her thin raiment, as in a mirror,
with unerring eyes he marked out the shape of the maiden,
as if watching the topmost parts laid bare aslant,
the gleaming breasts, and, with the many-woven bonds
of the hidden breasts, he reproached the envious girdle,
whirling round and round the love-mad eye of his face,
gazing insatiate at her whole body; and love-maddened,
the Earth-shaker, lord of the sea, for the sea-Cythereia
toiling, made supplication, and beside the rustic flock
he soothed the standing maiden with a friendly word:
"All Hellas of fair women one woman confutes;
Paphos is sung no more, Lesbos no more, no more is the name
of fair-childed Cyprus spoken; no more shall I sing
of Naxos, sung as fair in maidens; but even Lacedaemon
herself was conquered in childbirth, in travail;
not Paphos, not Lesbos any more; but the nurse of Amymone,
the East, has plundered all the glory of Orchomenus,
tending one single Grace; for the youngest
of the three Graces, Beroe, sprang up as the fourth.
Maiden, leave the land, as is right; your mother
did not spring from the land, Aphrodite, daughter of the sea;
you have my sea, boundless, as a wedding-gift, greater than the land;
hasten to contend with the wife of Zeus, that one may say
that the bride of Cronos's son and the bedfellow of the Earth-shaker
rule everywhere, since of snowy Olympus
Hera holds the sceptre, Beroe gained the power of the sea.
I will not grant you the mad-eyed Bassarids,
I will not give a capering Satyr or a Silenus;
but as chamber-servant of your marriage-fulfilling bed
I will make Proteus your attendant, and Glaucus your underling;
receive Nereus too, and, if you wish, Melicertes;
and broad Ocean, roaring, girdled with the rim of the everflowing cosmos,
I will call your servant;
to you I will grant all the rivers as attendants for a wedding-gift.
And if you delight in handmaids too, I will bring you
the daughters of Nereus; and let her become, though she refuse,
the nurse of Dionysus, your chamber-servant Ino."
He spoke; and leaving the angry, hard-persuaded maiden,
he spoke a word to the air, pouring a windy voice:
"Blessed son of Myrrha, who got a fair-childed lineage,
you alone hold a twofold honour; you alone are called
both the father of Beroe and the bridegroom of the foam-born."
Such things the Earth-shaker was scourged by the goading love-charm;
and many gifts he stretched out to Adonis and Cythereia,
the wedding-gift of his love for the maiden. And with a like-burning shaft
Dionysus, bringing wealth, as much as beside neighbouring Ganges
the gold-gleaming travails of the mines brought to birth,
many a time in vain besought sea-faring Aphrodite.
And the Paphian was stirred, and for her much-wooed maiden
feared both suitors; and beholding, of both,
the like desire and jealousy of the Loves,
she proclaimed a contest for Beroe in a bridal war
and a warrior's marriage and a lovely battle.
And, covering her wholly in some womanly adornment,
Cypris set her upon the citadel of her fatherland,
the contested maiden, a tender prize of the Loves;
and to both gods she addressed one voice:
"I would, if I had got two children, that I might join
the one owed to the Earth-shaker, the other to Lyaeus;
but since I was not born to twin offspring, nor do
the spotless ordinances of marriage bid one bride
to be yoked to two alternate bedfellows,
let the bride-winning strife be over one wife;
for not without toil is Beroe's bed; and over the bride
let you both contend in a marriage-leading contest;
and whoever shall win, let him lead Beroe without bride-price . . .
let the oath be dear to both; since I fear greatly
about the neighbouring city of the maiden, where I am called its guardian,
lest I destroy the fatherland of Beroe for Beroe's beauty;
make your covenants before the wedding, lest after the battle
the sea Earth-shaker, robbed of victory,
should annihilate the land with the point of his trident,
lest, in wrath, Dionysus, over the bed of Amymone,
should ruin the vine-clad threshing-floor of the city.
And be kindly after the strife; and let both,
holding a love's zeal in the ordinance of concord,
adorn the bride's fatherland with brighter beauty."
So she spoke, and the suitors approved; and to both
a firm oath was the son of Cronos and Earth and Aether
and the Stygian drops; and the Fates confirmed
the covenants; and Strife waxed, the escort of the Loves,
and Tumult; and Persuasion, the bride-arrayer, armed them both.
And coming down from heaven, the watchers of the contest,
all who are dwellers of Olympus, waited with Zeus,
witnesses of the Lebanon battle high upon the rock.
There a great sign appeared to desire-smitten Dionysus:
a storm-swift hawk, loosing its wing pregnant with the breeze,
pursued a feeding dove; but a sea-eagle, suddenly
snatching it from the earth, flew into the deep,
lifting the bird aloft with sparing talons.
And Dionysus, seeing it, spat out his hope of victory;
yet still he came to the battle. And over the strife of both,
with smiling eye the father, the son of Cronos, rejoiced,
beholding on high the contest of his brother and his son.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
43. Seek now the forty-third book, where I sing
of the surging War-god and the vine-clad battle.
So Ares, the rouser of strife, the channel-cutter of the Loves,
sounded the bridal war-cry, the herald of the marriage fray,
and Enyo laid the foundations of a war for a wedding;
and brandishing the tumult against Earthshaker and Dionysus
Hymenaeus was furious, and dancing into the combat
he lifted the bronze spear of Amyclaean Aphrodite,
bellowing the harmony of Ares on the Phrygian pipe.
For the king of the Satyrs and the charioteer of the sea
the maiden was the prize; refusing in silence
to take the wandering bed of a sea-dwelling suitor,
she dreaded the watery wedding-chamber of the Loves below,
and longed rather for Bacchus. She was like Deianeira,
who once, when the bridal contest roared about her,
desired Heracles, and stood trembling at the inconstant river,
in dread of the bull-horned wooing of the stream.
And the cloudless upper air, holding a self-prompted course
in its whirling spin, trumpeted out a martial strain;
and pouring a grim bellow from his raging throat
the dark-haired one armed himself with the Assyrian trident,
shaking the sea-spear. And threatening the sea
Dionysus revelled toward the war-cry with his wine-dark thyrsus,
seated on the chariot of his mountain-roaming mother Rhea;
and a self-grown vine, springing up beside the rail
of the Mygdonian car, covered the whole body of Bacchus,
binding his shady locks with twin-yoked ivy;
and one of his lions, tossing its tangled neck beneath the yoke,
scored the surface of the ground with its sharp claw,
sending a rough roar from its snarling lips;
and the slow elephant, creeping beside a neighbouring spring,
gouged an upright prop with its unbending foot,
drew up rain-water with its parched lips,
and dried the streams; and when the waters were turned to dust
it led away naked and waterless the thirsty fountain Nymph.
And the god who rules the waters armed himself; among the Nereids
there was tumult; and dripping from their sea-backs
the deities went to war; with their long-branched garlands
the house of Poseidon was lashed, the water of the deep;
and as the leafy hollow of the earthly ground was battered,
the cultivated vines of Libanus were heaved up by the trident.
And a black-skinned heifer grazing near the sea
the frenzied women in furious leaping drove
into the Poseidonian herd; and as for the wide-eyed bull,
one of them, gripping its back, split the spine, another shattered
unshaken the two tips of its forked horn upon the brow;
and one cleaved its belly with her threshing thyrsus;
another cut clean through the bull's flank; half-dead,
flat on its back, of itself the bull rolled and sank to the ground;
and as the freshly-gored bull rolled in the dust,
one of them seized its hind feet and dragged, another grasped
and hauled the forefeet, and with many a whirling fling
they spun the cloven double hoof upright into the air.
And Dionysus marshalled the leaders of his host,
setting five battalions for the watery War.
Of the first rank the leader was Cilician Oeneus, rich in vines,
son of Ereuthalion, whom he begot near Taurus
when he wedded Phyllis in a rustic country marriage;
of the second the leader was black-haired Helicaon,
golden-skinned, with rose-red cheeks, and about his neck
a curl of his well-twisted hair was trailing down;
Oenopion led the third, Staphylus championed the fourth,
the two sons of Oenomaus, the wine-loving father;
and over the fifth ruled Melanthius, chieftain of the Indians,
whom Oenone the daughter of Cissus bore; and about the boy
his mother wove the topmost of fragrant garden leaves
and wound clustered swaddling-bands all round him,
having bathed her son in a vat pregnant with drink.
Such, shooting with their ivy-bearing shafts,
was the battalion that armed itself, comrade of the vine-clad Bacchus.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And he armed his host, pouring out a host-stirring shout:
Bassarids, fight! As Lyaeus arms himself
let my horned pipe, striking out a martial note,
sound an answering strain to the bellowing conch,
and let the drums thunder the brazen-throated din of battle
with their twin clappings; and dancing for the War-god
let Maron shoot Glaucus with his man-breaking thyrsus;
and bind the locks of Proteus with unwonted ivy,
and let him leave the Egyptian water of the Pharian sea
and, wearing a dappled fawnskin after his sealskins,
bend his bold neck for me; and if he can,
let Melicertes arm himself against drunken Silenus;
and the dweller on Tmolus among its mossy haunts,
old Phorcys, teach him to lift the thyrsus,
and let the old farmer of the land become a vine-grower;
and let a steadfast Satyr, shaking his fennel-wand,
draw thirsty Nereus out of the sea
with his country hands; and from new-planted gardens
wreathe the locks of Palaemon with a wine-dark band,
and bring him, serving in the deep of the Isthmian brine,
the charioteer of the sea, to mother Rhea,
the helmsman of lions with a sea-whip;
for I will no longer leave my cousin alone upon the deep.
I shall behold the battalion of the sea, won by my spear,
adorned with the fawnskin; and to the untried Nymphs,
to the Nereids, give cymbals; mingle with the Bacchants
the Water-nymphs; but of Thetis, even if she is a child of the sea,
guard her house alone, the hospitable goddess;
and bind the unsandalled feet of Leucothea to buskins;
and appearing on land as a fellow-traveller of Bacchant Euadne
let Doris lift my revel-rout's pine-torch;
and let deep Panopea, shaking off the seaweed of the brine,
wreathe her locks with a viper-cluster;
and let Eidothea, unwilling, take the clattering rattles;
and since she has love equal to her own love-maddened wooer,
what blame is it that Galatea should serve Dionysus,
that as a bride-gift she may complete for Amymone's sake
a robe with loom-toiling hand for the Libanian queen?
But let the race of Nereus be; for I do not wish
sea-faring handmaids, lest I rouse jealousy in Beroe.
And tossing the long-branched fringe of his hairy brow,
let my mountain-roaming Pan, gripping with weaponless hand,
strike Poseidon with his sharpened horn,
catching him in the midst of the breast with curving points,
or upon a crested cliff, and let him tear with his hooves
the twofold yoked circle of Triton's prickly backbone.
Let Glaucus, the sea-drenched servant of the Earthshaker,
serve Bacchus, lifting in his hands the clattering
drums of Rhea hung from a neck-strap.
Not for Beroe alone do I contend, but also
for the very fatherland of our nymph; let not the ruler of the sea, the Earthshaker,
shatter it as it stands unshaken, and reduce it to ruin with his trident,
sea-girt though it be;
since I will arm myself against him as he arms; for both reasons—
if it has won the neighbouring sea, it holds the countless plants of Bacchus,
the sign of my victory; for of the seaside . . .
But, after the more ancient Pallas, with Bacchus as witness
let another Cecrops come as judge, that the vine too
may be sung as a city-saver, just like the olive.
And when I have made the city take another shape, I will not leave it
near the sea, but cutting the rugged hills with my fennel-wand
I will bridge the deep brine that neighbours Berytus,
turning to dry land with crags the rock-bound water of the sea;
and the rough road shall be levelled by the sharp thyrsus.
But fight again, Mimallones, bold
in your accustomed victory; and the fresh-flowing blood of the slain Giants
my fawnskin still bears, growing dark with it; even now
the East itself trembles before me, and to the ground bends his neck
the Indian War, and shedding suppliant tears for Bromius,
shedding watery tears, old Hydaspes shuddered.
And after the watery struggle, holding the Libanian nymph,
one privilege I grant to the Earthshaker, since he longs for it:
if he wishes, let him sing the wedding-song of my Loves,
only let him not turn an envious eye upon my Beroe.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
Such was the word he spoke; and with threatening speech
the dark-haired one answered, mocking Dionysus:
Ashamed, Dionysus, I arm myself, that you matched yourself
against the spearman of the trident, you who fled the axe of Lycurgus;
come here, Thetis, look on: your Dionysus, having escaped,
gave fair ransom-gifts to the hospitable sea;
I never admire this, you torch-bearer; for from a mother-slaying
fire you sprang, and so you do deeds worthy of fire.
But, dear Tritons, help me, bind the Bacchants,
making them sea-faring; and of the mountain-housed bearer
let the drums of Silenus be swamped by the sea,
dragged off by the wave, and on the swelling stream
let the Bacchus-loving pipe of the swimming Satyr drift
into a self-coiling voyage; and in my watery hall
let the Bassarids spread my bed instead of Lyaeus'.
I have no need of Satyrs, I drag no Maenads to the deep;
the Nereids are better; but let the thirsty Mimallones
be hidden in the sea, and instead of wine-poured
drunkenness let them drink the salt water of my brine;
and let some Bassaris, driven by the watery point of Proteus,
roll of herself and slip into the sea,
turning a death-dance of somersaults for Lyaeus.
Drag off the battalions of the Aethiopians and the ranks of the Indians,
as booty for the Nereids, and of the foul-tongued nymph
bring to Doris the slave-children of Cassiepeia,
a late-fulfilled penalty; and on his unconquerable stream
let Oceanus shift the fiery star of Maera, bathed in his flood,
the forerunner of the unsleeping winepress-dance,
the vine-clad Sirius, away from Olympus.
But you, Lydian Bacchus, leave your feebler thyrsus,
seek some other weapon for yourself, and lay aside
the dappled fawnskins, the slight covering of your limbs; and if
the heavenly bridal flame of Zeus brought you to birth,
now make war with fire, fire-nurtured one, now with the thunderbolt
of your father do battle against the helmsman of the trident,
and lighten the lightning-flash and brandish your father's aegis;
for it is no Deriades who awaits you as champion, nor is this
the contest of Lycurgus, the small skirmish of the Arabs, but of a sea
so vast; and trembling even now at my sea-spear
heaven has learned of our deep-sea War;
and the high-pathed champion of my trident's point
Phaethon once tested, when invincible about Corinth
the sea-Ares armed himself for a starry battle;
and the sea was lifted up to the sky, and in Oceanus
the thirsty Wain was bathed, and in the waters of the neighbouring brine
the Dog dipped its hot jaws and was cooled, the Dog of Maera,
and the hollows of the deep haunts were heaved on high,
towering up the waves, and as the sea was lashed
the sea-dolphin met the heavenly Dolphin.
So speaking, with his trident he shook the recesses of the sea,
and with sounding surge and swelling flood
the water-streams roared, scourging the air.
And the host of the brine armed itself with dripping shields;
and beside the sea-drenched manger of Cronion of the deep
Melicertes brandished his under-sea spear,
yoking the Isthmian chariot, and beside the sea-running king's
car of the sea-greaves he hung his spear,
scoring the sea's surface with its three-fold point,
yoking the Isthmian chariot; and with the horse's neighing
the roar of the Indian lions clattered together.
And he drove a watery course; and as the car was stretched out
the dry unwetted hoof grazed the surface of the water.
And the broad-bearded Triton clamoured at the frenzied fray,
he who in his twofold limbs has a man-shaped form,
of alien kind, sea-green, from the loins to the head
but half-complete; and trailing from the curve of his watery loins
a forked tail is bent round in fishy fashion.
And with a watery lash, beside the sea-manger,
having yoked his chariot borne by a swift-rushing storm,
Glaucus scourged the mane of his unwashed-footed horses
and pursued the Satyrs. And in the sea-roaring tumult
horned Pan, a light wayfarer over the trackless waters,
unwetted, beating the brine with his goatish hooves,
leapt restlessly, striking the sea with his crook,
piping a war-strain on his syrinx; and amid the surges,
hearing the mimic windborne image of his own voice,
he ran across the sea-water with his mountain-roaming feet,
seeking the other sound; and windborne, that very
sea-echo, born of the pipe, was pursued.
Another, whirling a well-based island-crag,
hurled it upon the Water-nymphs, and the flung stone
shook the nursery-court of the Nereid Palaemon.
And Proteus, leaving the Isthmian swell of the Pallenian brine,
armed himself with a sea-corslet, a sealskin;
and round him in a garland streamed the swarthy Indians
at Bacchus' bidding, and ranks of curly-haired men
embraced the many-shaped herdsman of the seals.
But as the old man was hemmed in, his form was ever-changing:
for Proteus, weaving a counterfeit shape in his limbs,
marked himself as a dappled-backed leopard;
and self-formed he stood upright upon the ground as a plant,
making his limbs into a tree, and as the leaves shook
he hissed a false whisper to the North wind's breeze;
and scoring his back, adorned with painted scales,
he crept as a serpent, and as his middle hollow was pressed
he raised his coil aloft, and with a dancer's quiver
the tip of his stretched circling tail was set spinning,
and he reared his head, and spitting from his jaws
a darting venom he hissed through his gaping throat;
and shifting his body into a shadowy form
he bristled as a lion, rushed as a boar, flowed as water; and the band of Indians
fastened the watery stream with a threatening bond,
holding the deceiving water in their slippery hands;
and the crafty old man, changing his cunning shape,
took on the many-turning wiles of Periclymenus' form,
whom Heracles killed, when joining his two fingers
he crushed the false likeness of a counterfeit bee.
And the land-passage of the old man was ringed about
by the herds of sea-monsters, and the water of the sand-loving seal
splashed up loud-roaring from his opening throat.
And dragging into the Bacchus-loving fray the battalion of his daughters,
old Nereus armed himself with a watery spear,
leaping down with his sea-faring trident upon the elephants,
terrible to behold; and many neighbouring banks along the shore
were bent aslant by the sea-point of Nereus.
And the offspring of the Nereids joined with their father
in the war-cry of battle; and into the fray, high upon the sea,
half-seen, unsandalled, the dance of the brine raved in bacchic frenzy.
And rushing weaponless into the tumult of the Satyrs
restless Ino ran up to her old madness,
belching white foam from her frenzied mouth.
And grim Panopea, darting across the calm,
scourged the grey back of the sea-lioness;
and lifting the club of love-sick Polyphemus
sea-girt Galatea armed herself against the raving Bacchant;
and lifting unshaken on the backs of sea-bred creatures
the pilot-fish carried Eido dry through the water.
And as a charioteer driving with circling art,
slanting his whole horse to the left near the turning-post,
bends the right one, and slackening the rein
urges it on with the goad, pouring out a horse-driving threat,
crouching and bent forward, with his knees fixed on the rail,
his loins curved, and driving the willing horse
he lashes it a little with sparing, skilful hand,
casting his eye behind, and with his face turned back
watches against the car of the chariot following behind;
so then the Nereids about the watery turning-post of the contest
drove their fish, like swift-running horses.
And another held a sea-running course in the opposite direction,
a charioteer of a dolphin, peering up over the sea,
and riding upon the fishy back across the calm
held her water-maddened course; and some mad watery wayfarer,
a dolphin half-seen, split apart the yoked dolphins.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And the rivers clamoured into the battle of Dionysus,
encouraging their lord, and from their ever-flowing throats
the watery bellow of gaping Oceanus,
the Poseidonian trumpet, messenger of battle, roared;
and the seas were arched up, joining the trident in the fray;
the Myrtoan ran upon the Icarian, and close at hand
the Sardinian on the western, the Iberian was dragged against the Celtic,
swelling in its waters, and with the accustomed twin sea
the unstable Bosporus mingled its curving water,
and the streams of the Aegean, tossing together in a gust,
the hollows of the Ionian sea were lashed
in pairs, and by the ankles of the Sicilian frenzied brine,
towering up with its waves, the Adriatic brine clashed together,
cloud-high; and taking a conch beneath the water of the Syrtis
Libyan Nereus bellowed with his sea-trumpet;
and some land-faring wayfarer, leaping up from the surges,
planted his left foot on a peak, and with his right
cutting off the highest crests of a mountain with his earth-shaking heel,
hurled them down upon the head of an untouched Maenad;
and warring with the under-sea trident of Dionysus
Melicertes raved in bacchic frenzy with his mother's leaps.
And the battalions of the Bassarids advanced against the tumult,
of whom one, shaking the wandering cluster of her hair,
armed herself for the watery fray with murderous madness,
restless, driven to frenzy by the leaping dance of her feet;
and another, having settled near Samos at the Thracian
cave of the Cabeiri, leapt along the crag of Libanus,
tossing out a barbarous strain of the Corybantic din;
and another, high upon the child-bearing lioness from Tmolus,
binding her masculine hair with a snaky band,
a Maeonian Mimallon, unveiled, bellowed beneath,
and planted the print of her foot high upon the bank,
foaming over the sea with mimic jaws.
And the Sileni, gushing forth Cilician dew,
the drivers of the Mygdonian lions, armed themselves,
and leaping with a clatter upon the deep-sea throng
they raised in their hands the vine-shoot of Enyo,
and stretched out their hands to the lion's neck,
gripping its mane, and the unconquerable bearers
they boldly reined in with shaggy bridles.
And seizing the sinew of a ravine-cleaving haunt
Silenus warred with Palaemon, and the wandering Ino
he drove through the water with his ivy spear.
One strove with another; and a Bacchant was not ashamed
to rush against the trident with her shooting thyrsus,
a Bacchant though she was a woman; and shielding the sea
against scaur-loving Pan the wandering Nereus contended
with splashing arm; and with blood-red ivy
a mountain Bacchant drove the Pallenian deity,
yet did not overthrow him; and as he came on against Lyaeus
Maron shook off Glaucus with his shooting thyrsus.
And the cloud-high elephant, with an earth-shaking quiver of its limbs,
wheeling its planted foot with the unbending mass of its knee,
warred with its long lips against the ground-couched seal;
and the Satyrs rushed in tumbling tumult,
bull-formed, trusting in their horns, and as they rushed
their alien upright tail hung loose along their loins.
And the battalions of the Sileni streamed on, of whom one
mounted with parted feet upon the loins of a bull
pressed out the twin-sounding strain of his interwoven pipes.
And tossing her locks together with the dappled storm-blasts
a Mygdonian Bacchant clashed her yoked cymbals,
and lashed the arched mane of a raging she-bear,
facing the under-sea beast; and a wild
leopard, mountain-roaming, was driven by the goading thyrsus.
And one, possessed by a leap of mind-robbing madness,
leapt with unwetted feet upon the sea,
as if dancing upon the head of Poseidon;
she struck the waves with her foot, and threatened the silent
sea, and lashed the deaf water with her thyrsus,
a water-borne Bassaris; and from the nymph's locks
a self-kindled fire flashed down her neck,
without burning, a marvel to behold. And mournful by the shore
near the sea, beholding the strife
of sea-warring Dionysus, sorely suffering
Psamathe broke into a voice full of terror:
If you remember the favour of Thetis and of skilful Briareus,
if you learned how Aegaeon defended your ordinances,
King Zeus, restrain the raving Bacchus; let me not behold
the enslavement of Nereus over the death of Glaucus;
let not tear-streaked Thetis serve Lyaeus,
let me not see her a handmaid beside Bromius, doomed to look
on the land of the Lydians after the sea—Achilles, Peleus, Pyrrhus,
grandson, husband, son, mourned in a single grief;
and pity weeping Leucothea, whose husband
took her son and slew him, the son whom the child-slaying
points of the heartless father's knife carved up.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
So she spoke, and Zeus, who rules on high through the air, heard,
and entrusted the wedding of Beroe to the Earthshaker,
and soothed the bridal-making fray; for from heaven,
checking the unfulfilled bridal War,
the threatening thunderbolts ringed Bacchus about.
And the vine-god, shaken by the bridal arrow,
longed for the maiden; but his father Zeus who rules on high
checked his strain, striking the note of his thunder-trumpet,
and the ancestral voice reined back his longing for battle.
With reluctant feet the sluggish wayfarer drew back,
sullen, eyeing the maiden with a backward-cast glance;
and with shamed ears, as the marriage was sung over the sea,
he listened in jealousy to the wedding-song of Amymone.
And the sea-roaring syrinx hymned the half-finished marriage,
and rousing in the waters the unquenchable bridal fire
Nereus, chamber-attendant, hymned the bridal-bed of Amymone,
and Phorcys wove the strain; and with kindred course
Glaucus leapt up, Melicertes raved in bacchic frenzy;
and Galatea, beating out the yoked dance,
restless, wheeled with the leaping quiver of her feet,
and sang the marriage-strain, since she had learned to sing fair things
when she was taught on the shepherd's pipe of Polyphemus.
And having joined the watery wedding of Beroe
the bridegroom Earthshaker loved the fatherland of his bride;
and to the dwellers of Beroe, as a treasure of his own bed,
he granted the sea-victory of the sea-Ares.
And the marriage was blessed, since beside the deep bridal-chamber
Arabian Nereus brought a worthy love-gift,
the skilful work of Hephaestus, Olympian craft, for the bride,
bringing a necklace and bearing cups and stretching out spirals,
all that for the Nereids with inimitable art
the Lemnian workman wrought beside the waves, and in the midst of the brine
plied his fiery anvil and his under-sea tongs,
drawing the circling breath of his blowing crucible
with artificial winds, and as the furnace was kindled
the inmost fire roared unquenched amid the surges.
Nereus then gave these gifts of many kinds, and to the maiden
Persian Euphrates gave the elaborate form of a spider's web;
the Iberian Rhine gave gold; and like gifts of wealth-holding mines
old Pactolus came bearing
in carefully-guarded hands, because he trembled before the champion of the Lydians,
Bacchus his king, and trembled before his neighbour Rhea,
the city-guardian of his own Mygdonian land; and Eridanus
brought as shining gifts the amber of the Heliades
from the wealth-pouring trees; and from the silver rock
all the metals that Strymon and all that Geudis bears,
the dark-haired one gave as a bridal-gift to Amymone.
So beside his under-sea bridal-chamber the new-married
Earthshaker rejoiced; and to unsmiling Lyaeus,
in his envy, his brother Eros cried out a consoling word:
Why, Dionysus, do you still blame the bride-tending girdle?
The marriage of Beroe did not befit Bromius, but this
was a fitting marriage for the sea, since taking the child
of the deep-sea Aphrodite I yoked her to a sea-faring husband;
but a more delicate Ariadne I have kept for your chambers,
kin from the line of Minos; the worthless Amymone,
who bears the blood of the sea, I left for the sea.
But leaving the hill of Libanus and the water of Adonis
you shall come to Phrygia rich in maidens, where there awaits you
the unwetted bed of the Sun's child, Titanian Aura;
and having fashioned a crown of battle and the bridal chamber of a maiden,
bride-tending Thrace shall receive you, where also
spear-wielding Pallene calls you, beside whose bridal-bed
I will crown you, victor, with bridal clusters,
when you have accomplished the lovely wrestling-match of Aphrodite.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
So to his woman-maddened brother Bacchus spoke
furious Eros; and sending the fiery whir of his wings
the bastard bird was lifted up on his airy course,
and came to the house of Zeus. And from the Assyrian gulf
soft-robed Dionysus went up to the land of the Lydians
beside the bank of Pactolus, where in the gold-gleaming mud
the dark water of the rich earth is reddened;
and he set foot on Maeonia, and stood before his mother Rhea,
offering the royal gifts of the Indian sea.
And leaving the streams of the deep-wealthy river
and the Phrygian hollow and the race of soft-living men,
beside the northern land he planted his own vintage,
faring through the cities of Europe after the towns of Asia.
44. I have woven the forty-fourth book, where you may behold
women raving, and the swollen menace of Pentheus.
And now, leaving behind the Daulantian tribe of the Illyrian land
and the plain of Haemonia and the height of Pelion,
he came near to Hellas, and beside the Aonian shore
he set up his dances. And hearing the strain of the bellowing pipe
the shepherd set up revels for Tanagraean Pan;
and a spring made music, where, striking the surface of the ground,
the watery hoof of a horse carved out the eponymous water;
and Asopus danced, dragging his fire-breathing streams
and whirling his floods; and with her father Ismenus
Dirce danced, tossing her circling waters.
And once a Hamadryad, springing up from a leafy cluster,
half-seen, sang shrilly high upon her tree,
glorifying the name of cluster-bearing Dionysus;
and a fountain Nymph, sandalless, cried out in the same voice.
And the mountain-roaming clatter of the untanned oxhide
crashed upon the hostile ears of Pentheus;
and the lawless king grew enraged at the wine-bearing Bacchus,
and armed a warlike host, and bade the townsmen
fence about the gates of the seven-gated city;
and they barred them one after another, but suddenly
of themselves the bolts of the gates were thrown open,
and in vain the servants flung the long bars upon the gate,
striving against the airy winds.
No gatekeeper then, beholding a Bacchant, reined her back;
and the shield-bearing spearmen trembled
at the old weaponless Sileni; and with one-tongued shouting,
when the king cried out, heedless of his threat,
they often danced, and with their well-made oxhides
they performed the shield-shaking leap of a circling dance,
a counterfeit mimicry of the noise-loving Corybantes.
And in the mountains the raging she-bears cried out fearfully;
and tossing her jaw and her high-flying rush
the leopard was lifted; and some lion, gently sporting,
sent a soft growl to a she-lion of its own age.
And now of itself the court of Pentheus was shaken,
springing up like a ball from its unbending foundations;
and the gate shuddered, leaping with an earth-shaking quiver,
a forewarning of the coming woe; and of itself
the stone altar of Oncaean Athena trembled,
which Cadmus once built, when with slow-yielding spring
the city-bearing hoof of the tower-building heifer sank to rest;
and about the divine image of the city-guardian goddess
god-sent sweat gushed in self-flowing drops,
bringing dread to the dwellers; and from foot to head
the statue of Ares, messenger of things to come, ran with gore.
And the dwellers were shaken; and in fear there trembled the mother
of haughty Pentheus, and she raved in her mind,
remembering an earlier blood-red dream
that foretold bitter things, since formerly above her bed,
from the time when Pentheus seized his father's sovereignty,
all night, as she slept amid drowsy whispers, the phantoms
of a counterfeit dream terrified Agave,
leaping through the unerring well-horned gate;
for she dreamed that Pentheus, a dancing dainty wayfarer,
having dressed his male body in a woman's robe,
cast the purple-backed mantle of kings upon the ground,
lightly bearing a thyrsus and no longer the bearer of a sceptre;
and Cadmean Agave thought she saw him again
seated aloft, high upon a shady tree;
and the high-topped plant, where bold Pentheus sat,
the wild beasts ringed about, and with savage rush
they heaved up the tree, levering it with threatening tusk,
with rough jaws; and as the tree was shaken
headlong, rolling of himself, Pentheus was whirled round in a spiral,
and the raging she-bears mangled him as he crashed down;
and a wild she-lion, rushing at his face,
tore off his hand from the root, and the beast, raving unrestrained,
setting her foot on the throat of the half-cut Pentheus,
with her sharp claws sheared through his neck,
and lifted the bloody head with her ravening paw
as he was piteously torn, and showed it to Cadmus as witness,
brandishing it, and broke into a sinful human voice:
I am your beast-slaying daughter; I am the mother
of most blessed Pentheus, your child-loving Agave.
So great a beast I have slain; and of my lion-killing victory
receive this head, the first prey of my prowess;
so great a beast my sister Ino never slew,
nor did Autonoe slay; but you, the tokens of Agave's child,
fix up before your hall, your daughter's best-wrought work.
Such a grim-faced dream, pale-green, Agave saw.
Then, sore frightened, pushing away the wing of Sleep,
at dawn she called the god-speaking son of Chariclo,
and told the prophet of things to come her murderous dreams;
and Teiresias the seer bade her sacrifice a male
bull, a helper against the blood-red dream,
at the god-invoking altar of Zeus the averter of ill,
beside the tree of a tall pine, where Cithaeron
spreads high-headed; and to the Hamadryad Nymphs
he bade her offer a female sheep beside the thicket.
And he knew the cunning beast and the hunting Agave
to be the travail of her own womb and the child-destroying struggle
and the head of Pentheus; but in voiceless silence
he hid the deceitful image of the dream's victory,
lest he anger Pentheus his heavy-wrathed king.
Obeying the wise old man, child-loving Agave
went to the high-headed mountain, travelling with Cadmus,
Pentheus following; and beside the well-horned altar
a female sheep, companion of a horned male bull,
where there was a grove of Zeus, full of mountain woodland,
to Zeus and the Hamadryads as one offering joined
Cadmus son of Agenor, kindling a god-pleasing altar,
sacrificing to both; and as the fire was kindled
the savour, wandering in spirals, swam up with the smoke
in a fragrant eddy, and as the bull was slaughtered
the upright self-rushing jet of bloody dew
crimsoned the reddening hands of Agave with murder . . .
And winding round the neck-sinew in a garland
a serpent slanted its swollen, arching neck,
gentle, coiled about with a curving loop,
and with its trailing wreath ringed the head of Cadmus,
a mild snake, and its tongue licked round his cheek,
spitting friendly venom from its gentle jaws
as they opened; and a female snake garlanded the temples
of Harmonia, entwined among her golden clusters.
And Cronion turned the limbs of the twin snakes to stone,
because beside the mouth of the Illyrian serpent-feeding sea
Harmonia and Cadmus, with changing face,
were destined to take on a stony serpent shape.
And holding another fear after the earlier fear of sleep
she came home with her son and her father.
Such a phantom she once saw, and remembering the ominous dream
child-loving Agave was shaken with fear.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
And now through the seven-gated city Rumour flew,
proclaiming the rites of dance-weaving Dionysus;
and there was none without a dance throughout the city; the country streets
were garlanded with spring leaves;
and shading the chamber of Semele with green cluster
the still-smoking thunderbolt of the bridal spark
a self-grown tendril made drunk with fragrant fruit.
But gazing in horror at the manifold marvels of Bacchus,
holding overweening jealousy, king Pentheus surged with rage;
and pouring out the proud boast of an empty threat
reckless Pentheus cried such a word to his servants:
Bring me my Lydian servant, the womanish vagrant,
the attendant of Pentheus' table as he feasts,
who pours some other drink into the wine-receiving cup,
either milk or sweet stream; and the sister of his mother,
Autonoe, I will scourge with answering blows,
and let us cut the locks of unshorn Dionysus;
and casting the sounding cymbals to the winds
and the Berecyntian clatter and the Euian drums of Rhea
drag off the raving Bassarids, drag off the Bacchants,
the wandering handmaids of Bromius, whom in Thebes,
hurling them into the watery haunts of Ismenus,
mingle, the Naiads with the Aonian river-nymphs,
their agemates, and let old Cithaeron receive the Hamadryads,
yoked with other Hamadryads, instead of Lyaeus.
Bring fire, servants, since by avenging ordinance,
if Bacchus came from fire, I will deliver Bacchus to fire;
Zeus subdued Semele, I will destroy Dionysus.
And if he should make trial of my thunderbolt also,
he will learn what an earthly flame I have; for my answering fire
has won hotter sparks than the heavenly one;
today I will make the vine-god a thing of smoke.
And if he should raise a warlike fray, lifting his thyrsus,
he will learn what an earthly spear I have; and I will destroy him,
bearing his wound neither in the foot, nor the flanks, nor the breast, nor the side;
and I will not cleave with a poleaxe
the two curving horns of his bull-horned brow,
nor will I cut through the middle of his neck; but I will strike him
with a bronze spear, pierced into the fold of his thigh,
because he falsely claimed birth from the thigh of great Zeus
and heaven as his home; and I, instead of a hall,
instead of the gate of Zeus, will send him down below to Hades,
or, as he rolls and flees, I will hide him
in the waves of Ismenus, and there is no need of the sea.
I do not accept a mortal man as a bastard god; if it is right to say,
I will lie, like Dionysus, about my birth: not from earth-born Cadmus
do I draw my blood, but my father, the chieftain of the stars,
the Sun begot me, and Echion did not sow me;
the Moon-goddess bore me, and Agave did not bring me forth;
I am of the race of Cronion, and I am a citizen of heaven;
the star-roaming sky is my city; be gracious, Thebes;
Pallas is my consort, my wife is immortal Hebe;
queenly Hera offered her breast to Pentheus after Ares,
and holy Leto bore Pentheus after Phoebus;
I will wed Artemis at her desire; she does not flee me,
as once she fled Phoebus, the suitor of her maidenhood,
shunning the reproach of marriage with a brother.
And if the heavenly flame had not burned your Semele,
because of her son's reproach Cadmus would have burned his own house,
and called fire that kindled on earth a lightning-flash,
and named the gleam of his torches the spark of a thunderbolt.
So spoke the king, and the warriors advanced,
the arms-bearers, striving against the empty winds;
and the host was unspeakably great within the pine-clad wood,
seeking the tracks of the unseen Lyaeus.
While king Pentheus was giving orders to the dwellers,
meanwhile Dionysus too, watching the lightless night,
cried out such a word toward Olympus to the circling Moon:
O child of the Sun, much-turning, all-nurturing Moon,
Selene, helmsman of the silver chariot,
if you are many-named Hecate, and by night
with fire-bearing hand you brandish the revel-rout's pine-torch,
come, night-walker, dog-nourisher, since it delights you
that the dog-rousing nocturnal echo wails with mournful whimpering;
if you are Artemis the deer-shooter, and on the hills
hastening in fawn-slaying chase you hunt with Dionysus,
be a helper to your brother; for having won the blood
of primal Cadmus I am driven outside Thebes,
from the fatherland of my mother Semele; for a swift-doomed
mortal man, a fighter against the gods, harasses me; so by night,
nocturnal one, defend Dionysus the night-reveller as he is driven.
And if you are Persephone, the corpse-rouser, and your
souls serve the seats of Tartarus,
let me see Pentheus a corpse, and of grieving Dionysus
let your soul-conducting Hermes lull the tears to rest;
and with the lash of your Tisiphone, raving, or of Megaera,
with the Tartarean whip put an end to the mind-clouding threat
of earth-born Pentheus, since hard-contriving Hera
has armed the late-born Titan against young Lyaeus.
But subdue the lawless man, that you may honour
the title of primal Zagreus, Dionysus.
King Zeus, do you too watch the threat of the raving man;
hear me, father and mother; and as Lyaeus is put on trial
let your bridal lightning be the avenger of Semele.

title: Dionysiaca
text:
So he spoke, and the bull-faced Moon cried out from on high:
Night-shining Dionysus, plant-tender, comrade of the Moon,
care for your vine-cluster; the rites of Bacchus are dear to me,
since the earth ripens the travail of your plants,
receiving the dewy gleam of the sleepless
Moon; but you, Bacchus the dance-beater, stretching out your thyrsus,
care for your kindred, and do not tremble at the race of feeble
men, whose mind is ever light, whose threats even by constraint
the lashes of the Eumenides hold back.
With you I arm myself against the foe; and equally with Bacchus
I rule over senseless madness; for I am the Moon
of Bacchus, not only because I roll the months through the air,
but because I rule over madness too and rouse frenzy.
I will not let your earthly outrage go unpunished;
for already Lycurgus, having threatened Dionysus,
he who was once swift-kneed, who sharply pursued the Maenads,
wanders blind and lacks a guide.
And now about the reeds of the Erythraean banks
there lies, on this side and on that, a self-proclaiming witness of your prowess,
the dead throng of the Indians, and in his loathing stream
father Hydaspes hid the senseless Deriades,
struck by your ivy spear; but he, fleeing,
fell into his father's heavy-thundering, downcast flood;
the Tyrrhenians know your strength, when the upright
mast of the ships was changed and a vine-shoot grew,
self-formed, and the sail beneath shady leaves
of the cultivated vines, a fair-clustered canopy, was grown over,
and the forestays hissed with a viper-cluster
shooting venom, and casting away their human form
and reasoning aim, the foes, with changing face,
mindless dolphins, swim in the sea;
still they revel for Dionysus even amid the surges,
like tumblers leaping over the calm.
And the corpse, struck by your sharp thyrsus,
Indian Orontes, is hidden in the Assyrian streams,
still fearing even in the waters the name of Bacchus.
Such a word the golden-reined goddess cried to Bromius.
While Bacchus still conversed with the circling Moon,
meanwhile, granting a favour to Zagreus Dionysus,
Persephone armed the Erinyes, and grieving
helped her late-born brother Dionysus.
And they, at the grievous nod of the head of earthly Zeus,
the Eumenides, advanced against the hall of Pentheus,
of whom one, leaping forth from the gloomy pit,
brandished the Tartarean viper-lash,
and drew the stream of Cocytus and the water of Styx,
and sprinkled the house of Agave with an earthly drop . . .
as if foretelling the wailing and the tears of Thebes;
and the goddess brought the Actaean knife from Attica,
the ancient blood-stained knife of Itylus, with which once the mother
Procne, lion-hearted, with man-slaying Philomela,
cutting up her well-beloved offspring with the iron,
served it as dear food to child-devouring Tereus;
carrying that in her hand, the channel-cutter of slaughters, the Erinys,
with her evil-working claws scooping out the dust,
hid the Attic sword beside the mountain-grown root
of a tall pine, where the Maenads, where Pentheus
was destined to die headless; and gathering in a conch
the fresh-flowing blood of the newly-slain Gorgon Medusa
she anointed the tree with purple Libyan dews.
And these things the maddened Erinys contrived among the crags.
And with dusky feet into the house of Cadmus stepped
night-shining Dionysus, holding a bull-faced form,
brandishing the Cronian raving lash of Pan;
and driving to bacchic frenzy the unbridled wife of Aristaeus,
he called Autonoe, and cried with frenzied voice:
Blessed, Autonoe, more than Semele; for over the marriage
of your newly-wed son you vie even with Olympus;
you have seized the glory of heaven, since Artemis won a dainty husband,
Actaeon, and the Moon won Endymion.
Actaeon did not die, did not take on the look of a beast,
nor the long-pointed horn of a dappled deer,
he did not receive a bastard form, and did not falsify his shape,
he did not see his own hunting dogs as his slayers;
but with the empty-minded tale of evil-tongued mouths
the herdsmen lied about the fate of your son,
hating the bridegroom of the unwedded goddess.
I know whence this trick came; over another's marriage,
over a wedding, over the Paphian, women are jealous.
But darting on storm-swift sandal
hasten to come unhindered to the mountains; coming there
you will see Actaeon hunting with Lyaeus,
holding Artemis near, and bearing the gleaming nets of the hunt,
wearing the hunting-boots, and handling the quiver.
Blessed, Autonoe, more than Semele, because as the goddess
went to her marriage you became the mother-in-law of the archer-goddess;
more fortunate than fair-childed Ino, because of a goddess
your son won the bed, which haughty Otus did not win.
Bold Orion was not the bridegroom of the archer-goddess.
And rejoicing, grown young again for the sake of his son's bride,
your Cadmus revels beside your mountain-housed bridal-chamber,
shaking his snow-white hair in the airy winds.
Awake, and be you too a bride-tender, mother of fair childbirth;
this Love is fitting, since holy Artemis took as bridegroom
her brother's son and not a stranger as husband.
But when the bed-shunning goddess at last bears a child,
lifting the son of the chaste archer-goddess
show him to jealous Agave with your child-tending arm.
What blame is it ever, if the dog-rouser beside her bridal-chamber
wished to bear a hunting, hare-killing son,
like Actaeon and scaur-loving Cyrene,
riding in the swift car of his mother's deer?

title: Dionysiaca
text:
45. You will look upon the forty-fifth book, where Pentheus
binds a horn-dragging bull instead of Lyaeus.
So when Bromius had spoken, the bride ran out of the house,
held by a raving joy, that she might behold
the bridegroom Actaeon seated beside the archer-goddess;
and with her, hastening on stumbling foot, racing with the breezes,
to the mountain went the unveiled raving Agave,
and her mind, scourged by the goad of the Cronian lash,
shrieked out a senseless cry from her frenzied lips:
Against worthless Pentheus I arm myself, that he may learn
that Cadmus bore in Agave a bold Amazon.
Full of manhood am I too; if I wish,
even with bare hands I will overpower all of Pentheus,
and with weaponless hand I will rend a well-armed host.
I have a thyrsus; I lack no ash-spear, I brandish no lance;
but with my vine-spear I strike down a spear-wielding man;
I wear no corslet, and I will overpower the well-corsleted.
And tossing my cymbals and the double-beaten oxhide
I glorify the son of Zeus, and I do not honour Pentheus.
Give me the Lydian rattles; why do you delay, raving Hours?
I will go to the crags, where the Maenads, where the women,
my agemates, hunt together with hunting Lyaeus.
I am jealous, Dionysus, of lion-slaying Cyrene;
spare Bromius for my sake, you fighter against gods; spare him, Pentheus;
unhindered I will go to the crags, that I too
may sing the Euian song and wheel a dance-beating step;
no longer do I refuse the rites of clustering Bacchus,
no longer do I loathe the dance of the Bassarids; but I myself
fear Dionysus, whom an imperishable bed begot,
whom the thunderbolts of Zeus who rules on high baptized.
I will be swift-sandalled, lifting the nets
of the archer-goddess my companion, and not the threads of Athena.
So speaking she flew, a young Mimallon leaping,
performing the Bacchus-loving leap of the winepress dance,
crying Euoe to Bacchus and singing of Thyone;
and she called Semele the wife of highest Zeus,
and shrilled of the gleam of the bright-shining bridal thunderbolts.
And the dance among the crags was great; round about the rocks
cried out; and the plain of seven-gated Thebes was overrun
by an echo of many forms; and at the one-tongued shout
of the singers heavy-thundering Cithaeron crashed in answer;
and the dewy clash of the sea made music; and one might behold
the trees revelling and the cliff giving voice.
And one dance-beating maiden leapt out from her chamber,
when the horned pipe shrilled through its bored channels;
and the loud-echoing clatter of the untanned oxhide
drove the maidens to bacchic frenzy, and from their well-built halls
to the high-headed mountain it drove the women to be solitary Bacchants.
And one, goaded on storm-swift sandal,
a girl with loosened hair, rushed from the maiden's chamber,
leaving behind her shuttle and loom-finishing Athena;
and casting off the unkempt veil from her locks
she mingled with the Bassarids and became an Aonian Bacchant.
And Teiresias sacrificed to Dionysus the averter of ill,
setting up an altar, that he might restrain the outrage of Pentheus
and scatter the unappeasable wrath of Lyaeus;
but in vain he supplicated, since the thread of Fate had come.
And the wise seer summoned the father of Semele,
that they might share in the dancing of Dionysus.
With heavy feet old Cadmus danced,
crowning his snow-white locks with Aonian ivy;
and Teiresias, faring with him, wheeling his sluggish foot,
striking up a Phrygian revel for Mygdonian Dionysus,
went as a companion to Cadmus as he rushed into the dance,
leaning his aged arm upon the god-fearing fennel-wand.
And beholding the old men, his companions, with a sidelong eye,
Teiresias and Cadmus, reckless Pentheus cried out:
Cadmus, why do you rave? For what god do you rouse a revel?
Cadmus, lay aside the ivy from your defiled hair,
lay aside also the fennel-wand of mind-wandering Dionysus;
and lift the wise bronze of Oncaean Athena.
Foolish Teiresias, garland-bearer, cast to the winds
these leaves of your locks, a bastard crown; and instead of the thyrsus
lift rather your Ismenian laurel of Phoebus.
I respect your old age, and even of your own
beyond-measure years I honour the grey lock as a witness;
for if this old age and your hair did not restrain me,
I would have wound your hands in galling fetters
and sealed you a prisoner in a gloomy hall.
Your mind does not escape me; for grudging it to Pentheus
with crafty prophecies you make a man a bastard god,
having taken gifts from the Lydian deceiver,
gifts of the river said to be rich in gold.
But you will say that Bacchus discovered the wine-yielding fruit;
wine always draws the drunken to Aphrodite,
wine rouses the mind of an unsteady man to murder.
But he has the form and robes of Zeus his father, has he?
Wearing golden robes, not fawnskins, Zeus who rules on high
flashes lightning among the blessed; and Ares wars with men
holding a bronze spear, not lifting a wine-dark thyrsus;
Apollo is not horned with the horns of an ox.
Did a river not wed Semele, and the bride bear
a bastard horned son to a bull-horned husband?
But you will say: bright-eyed Pallas Athena comes to the manly fray
holding her father's spear and shield . . .
do you too, then, stretch out the aegis of your father Cronion.
So spoke Pentheus, and the wise seer answered:
Why do you harass Dionysus, whom Zeus who rules on high begot,
whom father Cronion bore in his pregnant thigh,
and whom god-bearing Rhea nourished with child-tending milk,
whom formerly, half-finished, still breathing from his mother,
the unburning sparks of the thunderbolt baptized?
He alone vies with sheaf-bearing Demeter,
having a fair-clustered fruit to answer her ears of corn.
But guard against the wrath of Bromius; and of impiety,
my child, if you wish, I will tell you a Sicilian tale.
Once the sons of the Tyrrhenians sailed the sea,
stranger-slayers, wandering mariners, plunderers of wealth,
seizing on every side the coastal flocks of sheep;
and many a one, here and there, from their spear-won ships,
an old sailor was rolled to a watery death,
half-dead, and another, shielding his flock,
a sturdy shepherd was reddened with murder among his grey hairs.
If a merchant then sailed the sea, if ever a Phoenician
held for sale the sea-purple robes of Sidonian deep,
the Tyrrhenian vagrant, seizing him out on the sea,
bore him off unforeseen upon his wealth-laden ships;
and some man, having lost his boundless cargo without recompense,
a Phoenician man, was ferried to Sicilian Arethusa
in bonds, exiled from his city, bereft of his plundered wealth.
But by guile Dionysus, changing into a cunning form,
deceived the Tyrrhenians; he put on a bastard shape,
like a lovely boy with an unmarked chin,
wearing a golden ornament on his neck; and about his temple
was the self-flowing radiance of a flashing garland,
of an unquenched ruby, and the green-glowing surfaces of emerald,
and an Indian stone, a sparkle of the bright sea;
and he put on his skin robes brighter than the circling Dawn
just now being inscribed, dyed with the Tyrian murex.
And he stood by the brows of the shore, as if he too
longed to set foot on the merchant ship. And they, leaping out,
plundered the radiant guile-weaving son of Thyone
and stripped him of his possessions; and a rope, running round,
was bound about Dionysus' hands behind his back.
And suddenly the youth grew great in divine form,
manlike, horned, rising up to Olympus,
striking the screen of the airy clouds; and with melodious cry,
like a host of nine thousand, he bellowed from his throat.
And the long cables became serpentine coils,
shaped into living things, into the curving backs of snakes;
and the forestays hissed; and the windborne horned god
ran up with his trailing spirals to the horn of the mast;
and shaded with green leaves, neighbour to the air,
the mast was a topmost cypress; and at the mast-step
the soaring ivy rose up, neighbour to the sky,
twining a self-coiling rope about the cypress;
and over the rudders, peering up out of the sea,
the Bacchic pole was weighed down with vine-fruit;
and as the stern of sweet-drinking Dionysus was weighed down
a fountain, spouting wine, raved with drunkenness.
And about all the benches, climbing up from the prow,
wild beasts grew; and bulls bellowed,
and a lion roared a grim cry from its throat.
And the Tyrrhenians cried out, and raved in madness,
goaded into terror. And from the plant-nurturing sea
the surging water-streams spat out flowers;
and a rose sprang up, and from on high, as in a garden,
the foam-bearing hollows of the sea were crimsoned,
and a lily shimmered amid the surges. And as they gazed
upon the false meadows their eyes raved in frenzy,
and a deep-wooded mountain appeared to them, and a woodland pasture,
and a dance of country-folk and the flocks of shepherds,
and they thought they heard the sound of a clear-voiced herdsman
piping a tune on his shepherd's pipe,
and hearing the strain of the clear, well-bored pipes
sailing in the midst of the boundless deep sea
they thought they saw land; and under mind-robbing frenzy
rushing into the deep they danced over the calm,
sea-faring dolphins; and with changing face
the race of men was shaped into a fishy nature.
And you too, my child, guard against the crafty wrath of Lyaeus.
But you will say: I have a valiant body, and I claim
the dread self-sown blood of the tooth-grown Giants.
Flee the divine hand of Giant-slaying Dionysus,
who once beside the foundation of Tyrrhenian Pelorus
crushed Alpos, the god-fighting son of Earth,
warring with crags and hurling hilltops as spears;
and cowering before the row of throats of the raging Giant
no wayfarer then trod that headland of rock;
and if some heedless one was borne along the untrodden path
lashing a bold horse, looking down from the crag
the son of Earth, with his many-sprung hands twined about,
entombed both charioteer and colt in his throat.
And often, dragging through the well-wooded mountain to his pasture
the flocks at midday, the old shepherd was carved up.
Then no Pan, the music-tending one, seated beside the goat-folds or the pens,
made melody on his joined reeds,
nor did Echo answer the sound of the lyre with later-uttered voice;
